One-Stops Report Reorder Business Good, Fill Poor THE ADVENTURES OF SHAM 69 — Polydor recording artists Sham 69 recently made their U.S. debut at Hurrah in New York and at the Whisky in Los Angeles to promote their “Adventures of Hersham Boys” LP, which will be released by the label later this month. Shown backstage in the top row at the Whisky (l-r) are: Dave Treganna of the band; Gregg Miller and Pete Herring, salesmen for Polygram Distribution; and Dave Greenwald, western regional promotion manager for Polydor. Pictured seated (l-r) are: Jeff Laufer, promotion manager for Polydor; Ricky Goldstein, Dave Parsons, and Jimmy Pursey of the band; Marty Goldrod, vice president and west coast general manager of Polydor; and Dave Flaherty, salesman for Polygram. Buddah Announces First Qtr. Releases (continued from page 8) tourists. Nevertheless, Held's assessment of Tone's reorder patterns was realistic. "Customers are buying more cautiously now." he said, emphasizing his accounts’ increasing sophistication in looking for "workable" product. “I’m telling my customers: ‘Don’t warehouse my product, I'm only a day away in service, buy what you need, try this or try that— but don't go crazy with it.’ They can return within their percen- tages, I can return within my percentages, and everybody hopefully will get healthier as the year goes along.” Sluggish Outlook Not all of the one-stops surveyed were sanguine about sales prospects. Wholesalers in major northeastern cities and Detroit blamed the marked economic downturn in their areas for slumping sales and a sluggish outlook. In Boston, Peter McDermott, president of Peter’s One-Stop, reported that sales were down from a year ago and termed reorder- ing by his accounts “conservative.” McDer- mott said that expensive multi-price product sets had cut sales on the retail level. He predicted a “very, very poor” first quarter, and expressed disappointment over cutbacks in new product from major manufacturers. In New York, David Abady, managing director of Tape King one-stop, blamed the “whole economy” for negative sales. One bright spot, however, was a sales spurt for “rap records”, inspired by the success of The Sugar Hill Gang’s "The Rapper’s Delight.” While he felt that “everyone is scaring each other into a bad recession," Abady was confident about the future of one-stops in major population centers. “One-stop business will always be around,” he said. "New York-type stores need them.” At Simpson’s Wholesale in Detroit, buyer Liz Adanandus was gloomy over slow sales since Christmas day. Pointing to severe un- employment in the Detroit area, she predic- ted that January — usually a good month for Simpson’s — would be “a total drag.” In Philadelphia, Norman D. Cooper, president of his self-named one-stop, was decidedly negative about the new year’s prospects.” “I think video is my answer,” Cooper said. “I think I'm going to get out of the record business and get into video." Cooper manager Phil Russano echoed the pessimism, pointing to sales and reorders markedly down from the post-holiday period of last year. Poor Fill If the one-stops differed in their assess- ment of the new year’s business prospects, VOICE BOX PROMOTES DURON WAX — Denny Duron’s latest LP, “The Winner," is being promoted with a football theme. Duron, who is presently head coach at Evangel College in Springfield, Mo., once played with the World Football League and the Washington Redskins. Presenting KSUD DJ (West Memphis, Ark.) Bob Faulkner with a copy of the waxing is secretary Claudia Price. they were nearly unanimous in voicing strong displeasure with the manufacturers’ response to their crucial fill requests. Wholesalers from coast to coast expressed the feeling that the manufacturers were un- sympathetic to their problems. At California Music Co. in Los Angeles, vice president Ron Ricklin complained about “very bad” fill, especially in recent months. Pointing to a deterioration in ser- vice from labels which have switched to branch distribution, Ricklin was bitter about his inability to get hit product like Michael Jackson’s “Off The Wall.” ! don’t have an outlook," Ricklin said, “I don’t know what to expect.” Simpson’s Adanandus reported that she was “unhappy” with her fill, citing major problems in stocking product like Natalie Cole/Peabo Bryson’s “We're The Best Of Friends.” Adanandus was sharply critical of “terrible” shipping response. Tape King’s Abody said he was “not at all satisfied” with his fill. He criticized manufacturers for shortsightedness in not anticipating the present level of the business, and he pointed out that record consumers are spontaneous purchasers who are intent on buying their favorite records without delay. In Dallas, Billy Emerson, general manager of Big State Record Distributors, called his fill situation “pitiful.” Citing deteriorating freight service and the labels' move to branch distribution as major causes, he said that the company’s fill was much worse than it was a year ago. Lieberman’s Sattler said he was “ab- solutely not satisfied” with the labels' response to his fill demands. He cited “30 to 40 percent back-orders from some labels” to back up his complaints. Some of the one-stops, however, took a more balanced view of the fill problem. Fathers & Sun’s’ Simpson, pointing to the high incidence of vacation days during the holiday season, said that his fill has been "holding up better than I expected.” Short- term gaps in Kenny Rogers and Jefferson Starship product were his only fill problems, Simpson said. Tone Distributors’ Held was critical of un- standardized procedures in the labels' fill response, but indicated that wholesalers should accept some of the responsibility. "Our buyers have to adjust to each manufacturer,” he said. “You have to pre- judge your sales." Return Policies Another issue of concern to the one- stops was the manufacturers’ institution of stringent new return policies. Wholesalers were divided over whether they stood to gain or lose from the strict limits on allowable returns. Those one-stops in a favorable position to garner important spot business from larger retailers were enthusiastic about the return policies’ potential effect. "I’m looking forward to a fantastic year because of the return policy,” said Tone’sHeld. He pointed out that more retailers, especially the smaller chains in the Miami area, will be tur- ning to the one-stops to meet their product needs, rather than risk over-stocking. Wholesalers like Cooper, however, who are highly dependent on inner-city Mom and Pop retailers for their business, are hardly optimistic. “The manufacturers are getting so stringent on their credit that they’re going to put every one-stop out of business,” Cooper warned. From his point of view, the new return policies can only have a negative effect. Citing the necessity to pass along the return restrictions to his own accounts, Cooper said: “They’re pushing the business towards us, but at eight percent, you can’t run your business too well. A ROYAL CHECK FROM THE TRIBUNAL — The Copyright Royalty Tribunal recently presented Edward Cramer, president of BMI, with a check in excess of $500,000 as BMI’s share of1978’s jukebox royalties. Pictured (l-r) are: Aian Smith, vice president of licensing for BMI; Theodora Zavin. senior vice president of performing rights for BMI; Cramer; and Larry Sweeney, controller for BMI. NARM Retail Training Program Set NEW YORK — NARlVfs five-day Retail Management Certification Program, designed for record store personnel, will nold its initial session at the Atlanta Dunfey Hotei Jan. 21-25. The faculty for the program, which will emphasize exercises keyed to the student’s real life experiences, will be led by Dr. Garland Wiggs, president of Association Educational Services and a professor of human resource development at George Washington University. Rounding out the faculty will be Van Webster of Hope Street Studio and Robert Benton, controller of the Los Angeles-based Music Plus chain. The program, described by Dr. Wiggs as “a fun but challenging learning ex- perience,” will feature a mixture of lectures and projects involving student participa- tion. Dr. Wiggs will teach the subject areas on the manager's responsibilities; person- nel management; motivation; communica- tion skills; interviewing and hiring; teaching; coaching and evaluation; time management; and sales theory and train- ing. Promo Material Van Webster will teach the merchan- dising/promotion sections of the course. Promotional materials, to be supplied by various labels, will be utilized by the stu- dents in the construction of in-store display material. Robert Benton’s lectures will cover the financial aspects of the retail operation, concentrating on financial management; inventory management; ordering and replenishment; and profit and loss con- cepts. The program schedule includes Chicago, April 21-25; Los Angeles, June 16-20; and Philadelphia, Aug. 11-15. For more information, contact the NARM office, 1060 Kings Highway, Suite 200, Cherry Hill, New Jersey 08034. Phone (609) 795-5555. Cautious Attitude This cautious attitude as a result of the new programs was echoed by buyers for the nine-store King Karol chain of New York City, the 90-store Budget Tapes & Records chain of Denver, the 1 27-store Wherehouse chain of southern California, the 30-store Sound Warehouse chain of Oklahoma City and the 16-store Waxie Maxie chain of Washington, D.C. “It’s going to make a radical change in buying,” said Kenny Dobin, LP and tape buyer for the Waxie Maxie chain. “I’m anx- ious to see how a lot of the companies are going to live with this. I don’t see how they can continue to solicit big quantities if they’re not going to take them back if we can’t sell them.” Aiso expressing caution, David Oliver, soul records buyer for the Sound Warehouse chain, explained, “It’ll have some effect on sou! buying, but we only buy in iittle chunks. However, well probably cut back on jazz buying and soul buying of new acts from 15-20%. We usually get an initial shipment of 25 pieces on a Lakeside or a Bar-Kays and wait for the reaction, but the new returns policies mean cutting the ship- ment to 20 pieces so we won’t be hurt if the sales don’t happen.” While most of the buyers noted that superstar product and releases by new and developing artists exempted from the return ceilings would be the least affected by the programs, all emphasized that those artists who are neither superstars nor new- comers would suffer the most. Passing New Acts “We're certaintly going to be buying light on these artists,” explained Roger Adcock, head buyer for Budget Tapes & Records. “We’re going to try and keep our buying tight, and in a lot of cases, it’sgoingto mean passing on a new act.” Emphasizing that the return ceilings for acts below superstar status makes support for such acts a considerable risk, Licorice Pizza's Brooks added, “As far as helping to break new acts, we can’t do that anymore, because we may end up suffering for trying to work with the labels. It (the returns ceil- ing) hampers what we can do in that area, and for that reason, we don’t like it.” Speaking even more strongly against this aspect of the returns programs, Ben Karol, president of the King Karol chain, added, “Sure, 100% returns is silly, but if the manufacturers don’t take the problems of the retailer into consideration, they’re looking for trouble. Manufacturers cannot set policies that retailers cannot live with. “It's going to be worse now than ever,” Karol continued, “because the lifeblood of this business is new releases. If we don’t get new artists who become stars and superstars, the business will wither and die.” This irritation with the apparent Sack of “proper” support for artists who are less than superstars was echoed by Alan Marker,- head buyer for the Record Shack one-stop of New York City. “The artists who will suffer the most will be the ones who’ve been plodding along with maybe three or four albums and a hit single,” Marker ex- plained. “When they have a new release, in- stead of maybe trying to initially blow it out, I’ll think twice. Pressure On Manufacturers “it puts the pressure on the manufac- turers,” Marker added. “They’ve set the standards, now they’ve got to promote the record and get airplay before we’ll jump on it. I can see just covering myself because we'll sell some anyway, but if there’s no feel around our market, I'll buy in very light.” In addition, Marker noted that one-stops face special problems with the new returns ceilings, “For us, having these return ceil- ings doesn’t hurt my initial buying as such, but when I sell in turn to retailers, then order more, then get returns, it does affect my buying patterns. “HI look twice at an LP before taking a chance on it now,” Marker concluded. “It will limit my re-ordering.” Also expressing concern over returns from customers, Aita Hayes, promotion director for the Big State one-stop of Dallas, added, “We’re going to buy according to the way the companies give us our returns. The companies always want you to stock everything, but now they won’t let you return it. It’s really going to be difficult and will keep you on your toes.” Wait-And-See Attitude “We are going to take a wait-and-see at- titude on everything,” added Todd Ramcke, buyer for the City 1 Stop of Los Angeles, who also emphasized the uncer- tainty felt at the one-stop level. “It will probably mean smaller orders more fre- quently, but I want to keep my options open (continued on page 31) STEPHANIE MILLS AT CIVIC CENTER IN ATLANTA — 20th Century-Fox Records recording artist Stephanie Mills recently performed at the Atlanta Civic Center. BMCK CONTEMPORARY Vs M VP — The New York chapter of The National Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences (NARAS) recently held its Most Valuable Player presentations for studio session musi- cians. Pictured at the presentations are (l-r): Arif Mardin, producer for Atlantic Records, and Valerie Simpson and Nick Ashford. THE RHYTHM SECTION BRUNSWICK RECORDS BACK ON CHARTS — Though Brunswick Records has been relatively inactive since 1976, it is coming back with a boom. The company recently released a single called “Bounce, Rock, Skate, Roll” by Vaughn Mason and Crew that is getting a great deal of radio attention across the country. Nat Tarnopol, president of the label, says the company is gearing up to come out with a stream of product over the next few months. RUMOR HAS IT ft After 10 years with Atlantic Records Aretha Franklin may be going to Arista Records . . . Ron Ellison will leave Mercury Records to become the new vice presi- dent at ARC Records . . . Ron Mosley will return to a prominent position. WILL CHICAGO RADIO EXPERIENCE MORE CHANGE IN THE ’80s — Earnest L. James, president and general manager at WVON/WGCI hinted that the ’80s will represent a time for change in black radio. “It is time that the old line black radio stations took a serious look at what they are doing, and start providing a real service to their community, rather than providing lip service. I have found that black people want more from a radio station than just music, which is the reason that the format on the AM has evolved into the total adult posture that it is. Not only have we instituted a talk show, but the entire station has changed. Certainly black people should have the option to be more involved in an adult formatted station, the same as general market audiences have. For quite some time, the station slogan has been ‘music and more,’ because black people do in fact want alter- natives,” said James. Commenting on whether or not this change is coming soon in black radio, he said, "The format is certainly a natural for AM black radio with an FM attached. I imagine if the format proves to be a successful one, it could become a trend since people always seem to follow success. Our last rating certainly showed we were gaining a larger audience, as did the re- cent media trend, so if we continue, we may be the first of a trend. Actually what we are do- ling at the stations is a total concept. We are involved in several community-related ac- tivities and being here has provided me with the unique opportunity to have a totally community-oriented station along with a total entertainment station with the FM. We have so many projects going —- bike-a-thons; fund-raising parties; each year our Christmas party is more successful; and our involvement with several church groups. We are design- ing the station to be totally responsible to the community.” RADIO ACTIVITY — Derek Clemens is the new operations manager at KDKO in Denver . . . The second annual Black College Radio Convention is tentatively scheduled for April 4-5, 1980 at the Paschal Hotel in Atlanta. For additional information contact Lo Jelks at (404) 525-2973 or (404) 523-6136. ARTIST ACTIVITY — Taste of Honey is in the studio recording with producers Norman Whitfield and George Duke . . . Keep an eye out for a pair of twins calling themselves Elephant Walk, who are just signing a recording contract . . . Prelude Records will be releasing two albums Jan. 15 with two new artists, Bobby Thurston and a group called Passion. ’80s CHANGES FOR THE RECORD COMPANY STANDPOINT — Larkin Arnold, senior vice president of the R&B division at Arista Records, says he sees more message music coming into focus. “The music changes as people change. There seems to be an upsurge in Third World music, such as the reggae of Bob Marley and the success we are experienc- ing with the Japanese group Hiroshima. Because of the fact that a lot of the younger peo- ple have grown up listening to many of the rock acts, there will also be an upswing in black rock groups like Prince. Whatever happens, at Arista, we are not looking to set any trends, or follow any. We will simply remain an artist-oriented label looking for good talent.” cookie amerson Store Buyers Express Caution (continued from page 27) at this time, especially when there is a good chance of getting stuck.” Also taking a wait-and-see attitude was Van Vanyo, vice president of national buy- ing for Lieberman Enterprises. “As a rack jobber,” Vanyo explained, “we reaiiy don't know right now how the returns policies will affect us. We’d like to be able to work with the ceilings, but we just don't know at this time. “The new groups, the guaranteed ones, we will use the same aggressiveness as in the past, trying to break them," Vanyo ex- plained, “and an established group, we’ll buy more or less the same, but not stockpile as much as in the past. However, on artists without hit singles, we will hold off for a couple of weeks until the single proves itself on the market.” Echoing this sentiment, Dwayne Witten, LP buyer for the Phoenix-based Alta rack operation, added, “It will mean a cut-down on the risks and chances we are able to take on new artists and new releases. Because of the returns policies, it’s going to be har- der for labels to convince us to buy on new artists. We’re looking at the return percen- tage and will be taking a much harder look at the new artist than we have before." No Difficulty However, Witten managed to end on an optimistic note, stating, “We can live with any policy as long as they let us clean up first and treat us fairly. Our returns have always been less than 20%, and that is right in line with the returns policies of the major manufacturers. We don’t anticipate any dif- ficulty with the future.” RESTLESS NIGHTS AT UCLA — Currently engaged in an extensive nationwide tour in support of her “Restless Nights" LP, Columbia recording artist Karla Bonoff performed recently at Royce Hall on the UCLA campus. London WC 2 England Phone: 01-836-1362/01-836-4188 In this, our annual MIDEM issue, we at Cash Box would first like to take this opportunity to salute and congratulate this fine organization and its upcoming convention. MIDEM officials predict record atten- dance figures for this year’s convention, and con- sidering what kind of year the international industry has just gone through, that in itself says a lot. As has often been said before, music is universal, it knows no boundaries. Perhaps one of the greatest strengths of MIDEM is the celebration of this univer- sality, where even national boundaries dissolve in the face of the music. But it goes even deeper than that. This week’s Cash Box also features stories about this year’s Grammy nominations and the recent Consumer Electronics Show (CES) in Las Vegas. Where national boundaries dissolve at MIDEM, a quick look at the nominations for the top Grammy awards will reveal a veritable melting pot of artists and genres — with disco, country, pop, rock and b/c all in the running for the top prizes. Musical boundaries are disappearing. And the CES. Hardware manufacturers and software producers came together for a common in- terest — music. On top of that, there was a glimpse of the future in the form of the rapidly developing video field. Hardware and software, state-of-the-art and future came together at CES. MIDEM . . . the Grammys . . . CES. Each in its own way shows us what music is about. No boundaries, but rather, a community built around a common musical interest. E/4ST COASTINGS PDs Have Mixed Feelings About Extended ARB Book by Marc Cetner and Mark Albert LOS ANGELES — The debut of Arbitron's extended measurement survey technique, which has been approved by the top three radio markets (Los Angeles, Chicago and New York) and will go into effect for 12 weeks beginning Feb. 25 in those major markets, has been met with mixed reaction from the program directors in the major markets, according to a Cash Box survey. The new measurement was designed by Arbitron to decrease “hypoing” — the runn- ing of an inordinate amount of promotions and contests during a ratings period — and N.Y. City Opera To Form National Touring Company by Ken Terry NEW YORK — A National Opera Touring Company is being formed under the aegis of the New York City Opera. The company, which will consist of 63 singers and a 27- member orchestra, is scheduled to tour for five weeks in the fall with the Frank Corsaro production of Verdi’s “La Traviata.” A three-week tour is also planned for the spring of 1981. At a press conference here last week, Beverly Sills, general director of the New York City Opera, said that the purpose of the touring company is to recruit, train and expose talent by unknown American singers. All the members of the National Opera Touring Company, she said, will be considered as part of the New York City Opera, and the cream of the crop will even- tually appear with the latter company in New York. In addition, she noted, the company will include singers who presently belong to the City Opera but who are not yet prepared to sing a major role at Lincoln Center. “Some of our singers are not ready to be Violettas in New York, but we’d like to give them a chance outside New York,” Sills stated. She added that she herself would fly into several cities along the tour route to watch the vocalists who will be performing in the role of Violetta. Forty Cities The initial tours of the National Opera Touring Company will consist of one- (continued on page 39) to more accurately gauge listenership, ac- cording to Rick Aurichio, vice president and general manager of Arbitron. 48 Week Measurement Arbitron has been testing the extended measurement technique in Seattle, New Orleans and Indianapolis, and it is the rating service’s contention that longer ratings sweeps are more beneficial to the radio medium. In December, the top three markets, plus San Diego, approved the continuous surveys, and the upcoming Spring quarterly sweep will be followed by Summer and Fall sweeps. A 48-week measurement will go into effect next year. While stations in major markets cited ex- tended measurement induced problems such as an immediate station philosophy re-evaluation, budget readjustment and* continuous ratings sweep pressure, a ma- jority of radio executives surveyed felt it was a move toward more accurate ratings and emphasized the quality of program- ming. “I think it’s a good idea," said John Gehron, program director at WLS/Chicago. “It will more accurately measure the station's total effort. A longer ratings sweep will take out problems of seasonal variation, holidays and crises, like the one we had last winter when the whole city was shut down for two of the four weeks during the sweep.” Echoing Gehron's sentiments was Joe Piasek, WPIX-FM/New York's PD. “Any new (continued on page 45) Limelight Complex Set To Open In Atlanta NEW YORK — A $5 million entertainment complex, the Limelight, will open this month at 333 Piedmont Road in Atlanta, Ga. The complex will feature disco dancing, en- tertainment, a screening room, numerous liquor bars and a health drink bar, a sound and light system and a second level balcony. According to club owner Pete Catien, the facility, whose capacity will be 1,200 will have a dance floor of polished stainless steel. The center of the floor will bea 16foot by 16 foot clear glass inset, which will also be the ceiling of a cage in which live tigers are kept. The club’s lighting system will accom- modate 40,000 watts, and sound will be channelled through 300 strategically mounted speakers. The hook is incredibly infectious and the melody is original enough to make this another Top 40 hit. TOM PETTY AND THE HEARTBREAKERS (Backstreet/MCA MCA-41169) Refugee (3:21) (Skyhiil Publishing Co., Inc. — BMI) (T. Petty, M. Campbell) With “Don’t Do Me LikeThat," the first single off of Petty’s “Damn The Torpedoes” LP, jumping into the Top 10 this week, this blistering rocker should keep him on the charts for some time to come. Growing interplay between guitar and organ, coupled with Petty’s forceful vocals, should make this a rock classic for Top 40. PINK FLOYD (Columbia 1-11187) Another Brick In The Wall (Pt. II) (3:11) (Pink Floyd Music Publishers, Ltd. — BMI) (R. Waters) As Pink Floyd's new album “The Wall" draws close to taking over the #1 spot on the Top 100 Albums chart, comes this catchy but foreboding selection, with its ominously steady drum work and angry lyrics. A chorus of English youngsters adds authenticity to the track, which will im- mediately appeal to AOR listeners. Pop lists should also take note. ROBERTA FLACK (Atlantic 3627) You Are My Heaven (4:10) (Black Bull — ASCAP) (S. Wonder, E. Mercury) The amazing Roberta Flack is back with this very stylish duet with the late Donny Hathaway on a tune co-written by Stevie Wonder and Eric Mer- cury, who also produces here. Harmonies are the highpoint on this incredibly accessible track, and although Flack doesn’t really get the chance to display her broad vocal range much, this will be a B/C, pop sleeper. RONNIE LAWS (United Artists UA-X1334-Y) Every Generation (3:45) (Fizz Music/At Home Music — ASCAP) (R. Laws) Jazz veteran Laws has always been considered a master sax player, but here he stretches out vocally and lyrically for a most impressive outing. Nice interplay between Laws' lead vocals and female backup singing, with the addition of some very smooth, swaying instrumentals, makes this a sleeper cut for many formats. Title cut from new LP. TOMMY JAMES (Millennium YB-11785) Three Times In Love (4:09) (Big Teeth Music Publishing Corp. /Tommy James Music, Inc. — BMI) (T. James, R. Serota) One of the great pop hitmakers of the '60s stages yet another comeback under a new deal with Millennium and the title track from his forthcoming LP. A delightful pop tune with a dash of folk, this track has already garnered healthy pop radio adds and should draw more with its light acoustic guitar strumming and bright vocals. WAYNE NEWTON (Aries II WA 108) Years (3:38) (Pi-Gem Music — BMI) (K. Fleming, D.W. • HIGHEST QUALITY COMPONENTS • FINEST QUALITY IN-HOUSE PRINTING OF INSERTS • DIRECT PRINTING OF VARIABLE • AUTOMATED ASSEMBLY AND PACKAGING • QUICK DELIVERY • LARGE CAPACITY • COMPETITIVE PRICING Takoma To Market Bukowski LP With Natl Bookstore Chain NEW YORK — Takoma Records, dis- tributed through Chrysalis, will market its first spoken word LP next month when it releases a live album by the renowned poet and author, Charles Bukowski. The disc, “Charles Bukowski Reads His Poetry,” was recorded in San Francisco by producer Joe Wolberg and features 12 two and three- minute selections from the writer’s many works, including his best-selling book, “Women.” Jon Monday, general manager of Takoma, said the label will coordinate the distribution of the LP with City Light Books, a national book supplier based in San Fran- cisco. Initially, he said, the label would con- centrate on the marketing of the album in U.S. book shops, aided by a poster cam- paign, because “the language is not par- ticularly conducive to commercial airplay. “Frankly speaking, we’re hoping to build a base in this country at the book store level first and then hope that commercial sta- tions catch on,” he explained. ‘This is not your ordinary pop record; well probably be working it six months from now.” He added that, because Bukowski has a respectable international following, he does not expect the label to have much difficulty marketing the album at the European record store level. “Bukowski’s name is instantly recognizable overseas by virtue of his television and radio appearances there,” said Monday. “I can’t honestly say that would be true at the record store level in this country.” The album, which will list for $7.98, is the first in a series of IPs for which Takoma has contracted Bukowski. “Our initial financial involvement in the project was not that great, so that we’ll be happy with whatever sales level we achieve,” said Monday. CBS, RCA Video Pact (continued from page 8) Corp., noted, “We regard this decision by CBS as a breakthrough in establishing a videodisc system, first in the U.S. market and subsequently abroad, that will set a standard of excellence for the electronics industry worldwide. ‘‘CBS’ outstanding programming, manufacturing, distribution and marketing capabilities make it an ideal participant in the introduction of the most significant new consumer product since color television. The fall tour will begin in Upstate New York and will proceed through the Middle West, closing in Southern California during late Novem- ber and early December. The latter part of the itinerary will coincide with the City Opera’s four weeks of appearance at the Dorothy Chandler Pavilion of the Music Center in Los Angeles. Among the locations which will be visited on the tour are Utica, Ithaca and Elmira, New York; Akron, Cincinnati and Columbus, Ohio; Purdue University and West Lafayette in Indiana; Decatur, Illinois; Madison, Wisconsin; Iowa City and Ames, Iowa; Omaha, Nebraska; Kansas City; Wichita, Kansas; Oklahoma City; Albuquer- que, New Mexico; Las Vegas; and Tempe, Arizona. The four engagements in Cincinnati, Omaha, Wichita and Oklahoma City will be presented under the auspices of Kool Super Nights, a concert series sponsored by the Brown & Williamson Tobacco Com- pany — USA. The spring, 1981 tour will cover the Southeast, including dates in South Carolina, Alabama, Florida and Louisiana. Steve Holowid, artistic coordinator of the City Ballet, will be the administrator of the new touring company. None of the singers’ names has been announced, and it is not yet clear who will conduct the tour orchestra. According to Holowid, the projected budget for the entire eight weeks of touring is $500,000, but the uncertainty of transpor- tation costs may affect this figure. Besides “T raviata,” said Sills, the touring company may eventurally perform such standard repertoire operas as “La Boheme,” “Madame Butterfly,” and “Rigoletto.” Sills also said that the City Opera will be holding regional and national auditions for the touring company. An announcementon this subject is expected shortly. The National Opera Touring Company is represented exclusively by Royal Artists Management Inc. Rogers And Summer Leading Nominees For 22nd Grammys CROPPER INKS PUBLISHING PACT WITH ATV/WOODED LAKE — Songwriter, musi- cian and record producer Steve Cropper recently signed an exclusive, long-term co- publishing deal with ATV/Wooded Lake Publishing. Pictured at the signing are (l-r): Jeff Franklin, president of Wooded Lake Music Publishing; Cropper; Steve Love, vice presi- dent of AT V Music; and Sam Trust, president ofATV Music, which will administer the Crop- per catalog. (continued from page 7) "Chuck E.'s In Love,” written by Jones, is one of eight tunes nominated for Song of the Year honors. This category also in- cludes such songs as Peaches & Herb’s “Reunited," which was written by Dino Fekaris and Freddie Perren; Gloria Gaynor's “I Will Survive” (also penned by Fekaris and Perren); Rogers’ "She Believes In Me,” written by Steve Gibb; Joel’s “Honesty,” which he wrote and performed; and Earth, Wind & Fire’s “After The Love Is Gone,” by David Foster, Jay Graydon, and Bill Champlin. Two songs performed by the Doobie Brothers and co-written by group member Michael McDonald complete the enteries. They are “Minute by Minute” (co- written by Lester Abrams), and “What A Fool Believes,” which McDonald penned with singer Kenny Loggins. Leading the list for best performances by a female artist in the pop, rock, R&B, and disco categories is Donna Summer, in the pop field, Summer's “Bad Girls” single was nominated as the best female pop perfor- mance along with Dionne Warwick’s “I’ll Never Love This Way Again,” Gaynor’s “I Will Survive,” Melissa Manchester’s “Don’t Cry Out Loud,” and Jones’ “Chuck E.’s In Love.” Summer's “Hot Stuff” has also been accorded a nomination in the rock category. Other nominees in this category include “You’ re Gonna Get What’s Coming” by Bonnie Raitt; "Vengence” by Carly Simon; “TNT" by Tanya Tucker; “Survivor” by Cindy Builens; and “The Last Chance Texaco” by Jones. In addition, Summer’s “Dim All The Lights” is one of five entries in the female R&B field, along with Warwick's “Deja Vu,” Natalie Cole’s “I Love You So,” Amii Stewart’s “Knock On Wood,” Anita Ward’s “Ring My Bell,” and the late Minnie Ripperton’s “Minnie.” The ‘‘Bad Girls” LP has also been nominated as the best disco recording. En- tries in this category aiso include the single, “Boogie Wonderland," by Earth, Wind & Fire and The Emotions (produced by Maurice White and A! McKay); “Do Ya Think I’m Sexy” by Rod Stewart (produced by Tom Dowd); "Don't Stop Til You Get Enough” by Michael Jackson (produced by Quincy Jones); and ‘‘I Will Survive” (produced by Dino Fekaris and Freddie Perren). ‘‘Do Ya Think I’m Sexy” was also nominated as the best pop song by a male performer. James Taylor’s “Up On The Roof” is one nominee in this category, as is "She Believes In Me” by Rogers; “Sad Eyes” by Robert John; and “52nd Street” by Joel. Best Male Vocal Nominees for the best male vocal perfor- mance in the rock field include the singles, “Is She Really Going Out With Him?” by Joe Jackson; “Gotta Serve Somebody” by Bob Dylan; “Dancin’ Fool” by Frank Zappa; “Blondes (Have More Fun)” by Stewart; and “Bad Case of Loving You (Doctor, Doctor)” by Robert Palmer. Entries in the category for best male R&B vocal performance are: “Cruisin’ ” by Smokey Robinson; “Don’t Let Go” by Isaac Hayes; “Don’t Stop ‘Til You Get Enough” by Michael Jackson; “Love Ballad" by George Benson; “Mama Can’t Buy You Love” by Elton John; and “Some Enchanted Even- ing” by Ray Charles. On the ballot for best pop group recordings are the albums “Minute By Minute” by The Doobie Brothers and “Breakfast in America” by Supertramp, as well as the singles “Lonesome Loser" by the Little River Band; “Sail On” by the Com- modores; and ‘‘You Don’t Bring Me Flowers” by Streisand and Diamond. Nominations for best recordings by a rock group go to The Blues Brothers for their album, "Briefcase Full of Blues;” to Styx for their “Cornerstone” record; to the Cars for the LP, “Candy-O;” and to The Eagles, The Knack, and Dire Straits for their singles, “Heartache Tonight,” “My Sharona,” and “Sultans of Swing,” respectively. Country Nominees in the country field, best female vocal performances will be decided between LPs by Emmylou Harris (“Blue Kentucky Girl”), Barbara Mandrell (“Just For The Record”), and Crystal Gayle (“We Should Be Together”), and singles by Billie Jo Spears (“I Will Survive”) and Brenda Lee (“T ell Me What It’s Like”). Nominees for the best male vocal perfor- mance in the country area are: Rogers’ single, “The Gambler;” Charley Pride’s album, “Burgers and Fries/When I Stop Leaving (I’ll Be Gone);” Hank Williams, Jr.’s LP, “Family Tradition; and singles by Eddie Rabbit (“Every Which Way Buy Loose”), and Willie Nelson (“Whiskey Fever”). In the classical music field, recordings by conductor Colin Davis garnered five nominations. His “Peter Grimes” LP, based on the opera by Benjamin Britten, received three nominations alone for best Classical Album, best Opera Recording, and best engineered LP. Other reknowned conduc- tors, including Lorin Maazel and Sir Georg Solti, as well as virtuosos Maurizio Pollini (piano) and Pinchas Zuckerman (violin), received three nominations each for their individual recordings. This year’s awards mark the introduction of a new category in the jazz field called Jazz Fusion. Entrants in this bracket are discs by Stanley Turrentine ("Betcha”), George Benson (‘‘Living Inside Your Love”), Weather Report (“8:30”), Chick Corea (“Secret Agent”), and Don Sebesky (‘‘Three Works for Jazz Soloists & Symphony Orchestra”). Ballots for the awards, which were mailed last week to the Academy’s 4,700 members, will also be cast in such fields as gospel, inspirational, Latin, comedy, children's, spoken word, Broadway show, instrumental composition and arrange- ment, motion picture score, album notes, album package, historical reissue, engineering, production, choral, and operatic. JAZZ ON JAZZ RETURN POLICY PUTS DAMPER ON CROSSOVER — Considering the slowdown of record sales in general, the stringent new return policies of most major labels seem likely to have an adverse effect on jazz-rock fusion and pop jazz. Many retailers have become less willing to order product by new acts, which, in the case of the major labels, often means crossover-type performers. All indications are that retailers are becoming much more conservative in their jazz buying. John Marmaduke of Western Merchandising told us that retailers who do a sizeable catalog business are also cutting back on orders, while Jim Grimes of National Record Mart reports a reduction in the number of stores with a broad- based selection of all jazz releases. Still, this doesn't represent an across-the-board trend, because the independent labels that distribute most of the jazz records don’t have a limit on returns. However, not all o.f the news is gloomy — merely cautious. Stu Schwartz of Har- mony Hut noted that 1979 marked a new interest in jazz, with sales of pop jazz and the new wave of jazz modernists on the upswing. He feels that, if this interest continues to grow, it will eventually be reflected in the sale of the more traditional forms. He added that, in the future, “we’ll be more careful in buying records by new artists. The bulk of our returns represent overbuying of new releases and records by untried acts. By cutting back here and buying new releases more wisely, we’ll reduce inventory but not overall representa- tion." So, for now, it appears that the inventory of many retailers will be fairly comprehen- sive. but their catalog depth will be shallow as they try to gauge buyer interest . . . Meanwhile, the retailers who will be least affected by this period of uncertainty are the specialty dealers who thrive on the sophisticated urban trade. Don Meckley of Chicago’s Jazz Record Mart says that their ordering has never been so large as to create a real overstock problem, and he adds that business is steadily increasing. FROM THE VAULTS — Dizzy Gillespie’s autobiography, "to BE or not to BOP" (with Al Fraser on Doubleday), is highly recommended as a bebop primer. This is a detailed and entertaining oral history told by those who made it, and serves to remind us just how great Gillespie's contributions were to both trumpet playing and composing, "To BE or not to BOP" traces Gillespie’s early years which, though full of hardship and prejudice, are fondly remembered — and follows his growth from trumpet disciple to leader. Gillespie is straightforward about his weaknesses (many of the musicians comment on his poor tone) and strengths (all credit Dizzy with the new harmonic conception of bop and with develop- ing a chordal style of trumpet, not to mention his remarkable facility). . . . For those who would like to build a Gillespie collection, there are many excellent catalog records to choose from. On Prestige there is “In The Beginning," which contains many of Dizzy's greatest small group performances and a number of classic compositions; “Paris 1948," which features powerful live recordings of his short-lived big band; and “TheGreatest Jazz Concert Ever," the legendary Massey Hall group from 1953 with Charlie Parker, Max Roach, Bud Powell and Charles Mingus. Verve offers “Diz And Roy," a classic 1954 shootout between Gillespie and his original inspiration Roy Eldridge. and “The Sonny Roliins/Sonny Still Sessions," wherein Dizzy teams up with two generations of tenor masters. Norman Granz’s Pablo label has given us many fine settings that showcase Dizzy Gillespie as elder statesman. If anything, the Pablos prove that Dizzy just gets better with age. “Dizzy Gillespie’s Big 4" is a no-holds-barred cooker with Joe Pass, Ray Brown and Mickey Roker; “Carter, Gillespie, Inc.” bridges the swing and bop eras by complementing Gillespie's brass flurries with the pear-shaped alto improvisations of Benny Carter; on "The Gifted Ones," Gillespie has a delightful encounter with the witty, taciturn Count Basie; and on “Free Ride," Lalo Schifrin frames the master’s trumpet in a contemporary- crossover setting that is tasty and propulsive. COMINGS AND GOINGS — Cecil Taylor’s epic duets with Max Roach at Columbia Un- iversity in December were recorded and videotaped, and all that now remains is to strike a bargain with an enterprising record company. The pianist has been attracting capacity audiences wherever he appears, and from January 15-19, he’ll come into Fat Tuesday's for a return engagement with altoist Jimmy Lyons, violinist Ramsey Ameen, cellist Alan Silva and percussionist Jerome Cooper (who plays drums like a string instrument). The last two nights will be recorded for a future album release . . . ECM recording artist Jack DeJohnette brought one of his Special Edition bands into Joseph Papp’s Public Theatre for a two-night stand. The drummer-keyboardist-composer was at the peak of kinetic powers, and a healthy sense of competition between reedmen Chico Freeman, David Murray and Julius Hemphill led to one of the most vivid saxophone decathalons in recent memory. DeJohnette’s Special Edition band, featuring Murray, bassist Peter Warren and altoist Arthur Blythe, is due out on ECM sometime this month, while Murray and Hemphill are currently touring the west coast with the World Saxophone Ouartet (due in at the Public Theatre on February 1 - 2.) Hemphill is also preparing a multi-media big band revue, which he hopes to stage at the Public Theatre sometime in the spring. Hemphill is one of our greatest composers and improvisers and a big band appearance is long overdue. . . I went to see James Blood’s punk jazz ensemble at N.Y.U.'s Loeb Student Center and was com- pletely blown away by the opening act, a five-man, a cappella doo-wop group called 14 Carat Soul. Watch out for these youngsters — you've never heard harmonizing like this in your life . . . Joseph Bowie, the trombone-playing brother of the Chicago Art Ensemble’s Lester Bowie, has been creating an exciting synthesis of avant garde jazz and straight- ahead dance rhythms at the Squat Theatre. I call it punk jazz, you can call it what you wanna — but make no mistake about it: Bowie’s Defunkt is one of the finest examples of a blossoming musical genre that is swiftly superceding so-called fusion music . . . The Bot- tom Line, Manhattan’s redoubtable rock showplace, is ushering in the new year with some exceptional mainstream jazz: Betty Carter will lead her trio there on January 18 - 19; Elektra/Asylum recording artists the Mingus Dynasty Band will be in January 25 & 26; and ECM recording artist Gary Burton will bring in his good vibes on February 1 - 2. VINYL PIPELINE — Among the latest releases are a goody by the excellent young trum- peter John Faddis, on Budda called “Good and Plenty" . . . Verve continues to unearth great records from the 1950s and is currently offering four new twofers: “The Duke Ellington Songbook," featuring Ella Fitzgerald with the Ellington Orchestra and special guest Dizzy Gillespie; "Soulville,” a sensual small group recording by the legendary tenorist Ben Webster, accompanied by an Oscar Peterson quartet; “Mulligan and Getz and Desmond," featuring the baritonist in settings that don’t include piano; and finally, a post-war set of Lester Young laments, “Mean To Me" . . . Timeless Muse has four new albums of swinging mainstream fare: guitarist Rodney Jones’ "Articulation," pianist Rein de Graaff’s "New York Jazz," tenorist George Adams' “Paradise Space Shuttle," and the latest from Art Blakey and his young Jazz Messengers, “Reflections In Blue chip stern TOP 40 1 Weeks On 1/12 Chart ONE ON ONE BOB JAMES & EARL KLUGH (Tappan Zee/Columbia FC 36241) 1 12 2 AMERICAN GARAGE PAT METHENY GROUP (ECM 1-1155) 2 9 3 ANGEL OF THE NIGHT ANGELA BOFILL (GRP/Arista 5501) 3 11 4 MASTER OF THE GAME GEORGE DUKE (Epic JE 36263) 4 9 5 RISE HERB ALPERT (A&M SP-4790) 5 14 6 STREET LIFE CRUSADERS (MCA 3094) 6 34 7 BEST OF FRIENDS LENNY WHITE (Elektra 6E-223) 8 19 8 A TASTE FOR PASSION JEAN LUC PONTY (Atlantic SB 19253) 7 14 9 8:30 WEATHER REPORT (ARC/Columbia PC2 36030) 9 17 10 NO STRANGER TO LOVE ROY AYERS (Polydor PD-1-6246) 11 6 11 STREET BEAT TOM SCOTT (Columbia JC 36137) 10 9 12 THE DANCE OF LIFE NARADA MICHAEL WALDEN (Atlantic SD 19259) 14 5 13 MORNING DANCE SPYRO GYRA (Infinity INF 9004) 12 42 14 THE WORLD WITHIN STIX HOOPER (MCA 3180) 13 14 15 AND 125TH STREET, N.Y.C. THE RHYTHM SECTION BROADCAST ENTERPRISE NETWORK, RE-ORGANIZES — Stan Raymond, head of the that organization's radio division, and Keith Adams, national program director for the chain, have resigned in the wake of a company reorganization. B.E.N.I. owns black- oriented WAOK/Atianta, WGIV/Chariotte and WCIN/Cincinnati. RUMORED CHANGES — David Banks has left RSO Records, Bob Ursery may be taking his place . . . Stan Bethel has left Unlimited Gold Records . . . Hank Talbert has left Arista Records . . . and there is a very heavy rumored change in the black division at Capitol Records, but this one has been around for quite some time ... Also hot on the wire is that Frankie Crocker has been offered a national P.D. slot with the RKO radio chain, where supposedly he would do the “Frankie Crocker Show" live to be aired through its network of stations. DETROIT ON THE MOVES AGAIN — Newly formed Rosanova Productions, based in Detroit, Michigan, has released a single called “I Need You" by John Freeman, who shares vocals with Almeta Latimore, who previously sang with and was managed by Aretha Franklin. Latimore will also have a single out with the label in a few months. Jay Butler, who has had an extensive career in the record business, will be handling promotion for the company. For further information contact Joseph Rosanova, Jr., president, at (31 3) 557- 4700. R&B PRODUCTIONS INITIATE BAY-KAYS TOUR — Renny Roker’s R&B Productions, based in Los Angeles, will be handling the 70-date Bar-Kays tour, which is scheduled to start towards the end of February. Jesus Garber, who is in charge of promotions for the company, mentioned, “We are a three-man operation that does not entertain the concept of having a contractor in a city simply throw up some posters and purchase a few radio spots. R&B Productions totally promotes an event, using all tie-ins available. We canvass all the area schools, set-up proclamations with the Mayor’s office if possible and generally do everything possible to bring the date alive." R&B Productions will be involved in promoting the dates with Roy Ayers, Prince, Cameo, Lenny White, Patrice Rushen and Chic this year, to name a few. Darryl Stewart recently joined the company after leaving Regency. Renny Roker, the company prinicpal, is expanding himself further, co-starring in an upcoming television series called "Nobody’s Perfect", a comical detective story. The program is the second of its kind from MCA. The first program, which was held last July, reportedly generated sales in excess of $4 million. The projected goal was $3 million for the approximately 65 albums in that program. Like the July program, consumer incen- tives and special dating are included in the “Country Time" campaign. MCA Distributing's vice president of national accounts, Neil Hartley, stressed that “this program is profitable for both the company and dealers. From our early reports, it looks like its going to be another Country Music Big In Grammy Race by Jennifer Bohler NASHVILLE — Spearheaded by UA recording artist Kenny Rogers, country music had quite an impact on the Grammy nominations for 1979. In addition to his domination of the country category, Rogers scored big in the pop category, with nominations in the single of the year and album of the year lists with “The Gambler" and his version of Steve Gibb's “She Believes In Me” in the running for song of the year. Further underlining country's growing across-the-board appeal, Rogers also gar- nered a nomination for best pop vocal per- formance, male, for “She Believes In Me." In the country category, Rogers led the way with three nominations — best country vocal performance, male, for “The Gam- bler"; best country vocal performance by a duo or group for “All I Ever Need Is You” with Dottie West; best country song for his version of Bob Morrison and Debbie Rupp's “You Decorated My Life.” Other artists scoring high in the nomina- tions department for country include Em- mylou Harris, Eddie Rabbitt, Willie Nelson, Larry Gatlin and The Bellamy Brothers, with two nominations each. Noticeably absent from this year's nominations were Anne Murray, last year's winner of a pop Grammy, and Dolly Parton. who last year won an award for "Here You Come Again." Predictably, Barbara Mandrell and (continued on page 56) extremely successful campaign. Hartley added, “Our intention is to give the general public the oppurtunity to buy the product they want. Many times an ac- count will not know he is out of a particular album until our people tell him. This program is designed to fill in the holes." New releases in the program include albums by Roy Clark, George Hamilton IV, Mel Tillis, Bill Monroe, Conway Twitty, Brenda Lee. Faron Young, Bill Anderson, and the Oak Ridge Boys; as well as current product (released after July) by John Co- nless, Conway Twitty and Loretta Lynn, Barbara Mandrell, the Oak Ridge Boys, Merle Haggard, John Wesley Ryles, Tanya Tucker and Don Willaims. Additionally, catalog items that have a proven track record of success will also be included, according to Chic Doherty, vice president of marketing, MCA/Nashville. "We were extremely pleased by the response to our country product promotion last summer. The strength of the MCA roster was verified in the tremendous sales we enjoyed,” said Doherty. Point of purchase materials featuring the “MCA Country Time" theme include a pocket catalog brochure that lists all coun- try catalog releases and the availability of tapes for these releases, as well as new album minis for the January and February releases: counter display/header cards with a brochure holder resembling a clock face; a four-color 4x4 montage of key MCA country artists listing the entire roste r in large type; and front boards to be provided on key artists to fit MCA in-store racks. Opryland Growth A Real Possibility NASHVILLE — The purchase of 57 acres of land adjacent to the Opryland Hotel by the NLT Corp. may lead to the expansion of the 600 room facility. The company closed the $2.75 million deal Jan 2. with Louis Draughon, a Springfield businessman and former owner of WSIX-TV in Nashville. “The purchase of this property enables NLT Corp. to control the integrity of the Opryland complex, which is recognized for its quality in both entertainment and lodg- ing," said NLT chairman Russell L. Wagner. “The purchase also provides NLT theop- portunity to begin immediately a feasibility study that we hope will ultimately lead to a major expansion of the Opryland Hotel.” he added. VOLUME XLI — NUMBER 37 — January 26, 1980 THE INTERNATIONAL MUSIC RECORD WEEKLY G4SH BOX GEORGE ALBERT President and Publisher MEL ALBERT Vice President and General Manager EDITORIAL Club Scene Heats Up NICK ALBARANO Marketing Director ALAN SUTTON Editor In Chief KEN TERRY Managing Editor J.B. CARMICLE General Manager, East Coast JIM SHARP Director. Nashville East Coast Editorial LEO SACKS AARON FUCHS RICHARD GOLD West Coast Editorial RICHARD IMAMURA. West Coast Editor MARK ALBERT. Radio Editor COOKIE AMERSON. Black Music Editor MARC CETNER MICHAEL GLYNN DENNIS GARRICK MICHAELMARTINEZ Research KEN KIRKWOOD. Manager BILL FEASTER — LEN CHODOSH JACK CHIPMAN — MIKE PLACHETKA HARALD TAUBENREUTHER - LES HONIG Nashville Editorial/Research DON CUSIC KEN WOODS JENNIFER BOHLER PATTI BRYANT Art Director GLENN 0 DAYTON The emergence of a nationwide network of dance oriented rock (DOR) clubs bodes well for the in- dustry, coming as it does during a time of continued tightening of radio station playlists. Once restricted soleiy to the east and the west coasts, DOR clubs are now beginning to crop up in the midwest and south, the last bastions of hard rock and heavy metal. At least one reason for the success DOR clubs are currently enjoying is that new wave, by any other name, is no longer a dirty word among club owners and record buyers. Although there is still resistance to extremes within new wave, as in the case with any musical genre, many new groups have been able to enter the mainstream under a single common denominator good rock ‘n’ roll. While confusion and caution toward the new rock will remain for awhile to come, DOR clubs should continue to swell in rank. And, the potential for artist development in the club scene is strong, as both local and name new wave acts play and tour regularly for modest fees, unlike many superstar rock or disco acts. Already a surplus of good talent has grown out of the DOR club scene, such as The Knack, Blondie and The B-52’s and now up-and-coming acts such as The Romantics. But for the DOR club scene to remain healthy and vital, it will have to avoid the pit- falls of trendiness. The recipe for success will remain good, simple rock. NEW MCES Sylvain Sylvain Syl Sylvain is, by his own admission, a unique type of rock star. The RCA recording artist, whose self-titled label debut has just been released, says that “it has nothing to do with the fact that I was born in Egypt, or that being a rock star is one step better than a go-go dancer. It’s just that I’d rather be recognized as a com- plete entertainer, like George Burns, who does a little bit of everything, or Sophie T ucker, whose credo was simply, ‘Don’t get bit by the same dog twice.' I’ll always love rock and roll, but only true entertainers live forever.” Sylvain’s career has always been marked by a sense of adventure. For star- ters, he was a founding member of the New York Dolls, who emerged from lower Manhattan’s vanguard arts community in the early 70s with a songbook of aurally nightmarish tales about men and women caught up in the terror of drugs, urban violence, and sexual paranoia. The focal point of the day was decadence, and while Lou Reed flaunted it and David Bowie ex- ploited it, only the Dolls made it sink in. The market for such music, however, was not yet there, and the Dolls broke up in 1975. Nevertheless, three of the band's mem- bers, Sylvain, David Johansen, and Johnny Thunders, have managed to launch and sustain solo careers. Sylvain was born in Cairo in 1953, the son of an executive for the National Bank of Egypt. He was raised there until he was six, after which the family moved to Paris, where Syl dressed in cowboy boots and pants, drank Coca-Cola outof shotglasses, and listened to Ray Charles, Little Richard, and Gene Vicent. The family moved to Buf- falo in 1961, but settled in Brooklyn shortly thereafter. In Brooklyn, Syl and the late Billy Murcia of the Dolls formed their first group, The Devils, after duping a pawn shop owner into thinking that one of the guitars he was selling had been stolen from them. The Devils then grew into The Pox, whose demise brought Syl and Murcia together with bassist Arthur Kane, guitarist Johnny Thunders, and Johansen. When the Dolls finally disbanded, Syl's first step was to form The Criminals, whose clean-cut energy yielded the now classic single, “The Kids Are Back.” He wrote and produced the track (recognized by the New Musical Express as the best American- made 45 of 1978) for Sing Sing Records, an independent label which he formed to manufacture and distribute the disc. The Criminals were short-lived, but an eight- track demo that they recorded was brought to Nancy Jeffries of RCA, and in June of last year, Sylvain was signed to the label as a solo artist. Last summer, he formed Teenage News (now known as The Texas Millionaires), consisting of Johnny Rao on guitar, Buz Verno on bass, Bobby Blain on piano, Jon Gerber on sax, and Lee Crystal on drums. Within weeks, thegroup entered The Power Station in New York with producers Lance Quinn and Tony Bongiovi and cut “Sylvain Sylvain.” “Musically, the album speaks for itself," says Syl, who is self-managed. “It may have a classic feel to it root-wise, but it’s definitely music for the ’80s. People who lean on it won’t be disappointed." TO W/4TCH Webster Lewis Quenching the-music thirst of the public was the prime motivation leading to “8 For The ’80s," the second Epic release by keyboardist Webster Lewis. Featuring the single “You Deserve T o Dance,” the album marks the first step toward Developing a multilithic sound for commercial consump- tion, according to Lewis. “Once I came out of the studio and the conservatory, I began to notice that people were begging for music," explained Lewis. “It seemed as though people had been beat over the head with, well, not mediocre, but repetitious music,” he added. Backed by a lineup that reads like a Who’s Who among jazz musicians, Lewis offers a tasteful brew of jazzy funk and finely tuned listening music. Among those notables on the disc are the T ower of Power Horns, Oscar Brashear, Bobby Bryant, Wah Wah Watson and three musicians Lewis has toured with recently, Paul Jackson, Bennie Maupin and fellow keyboardist Herbie Hancock, who co- produced the album with Lewis. Performing and recording with deep talent is nothing new for the effervescent Lewis. He grew up running with fast com- pany. Born in Baltimore, Lewis began his professional career playing organ for a nine-piece band known as the Soul Brothers, which backed major acts appear- ing in town, includingTheSupremes, Major Lance, Shep and The Limelights and Lloyd Price. Two years later, Lewis went on the road with Chuck Jackson and Tommy Hunt. A year later on his birthday, Lewis played at the renowned Apollo Theatre with King Curtis, followed by studio sessions for Spector Records. He then returned to Baltimore where he commenced study at Morgan State, which turned out to be his springboard into the jazz sound. After graduation from Morgan, Lewis returned to a revamped Soul Brothers Band at night and on weekends, while teaching during the day. Lewis then decided to study further, moving on to Boston where he met com- poser/musicologist Gunther Schuller, who helped him gain a presidential scholarship to the New England conservatory. After gaining his Masters in Musical Composition in 1969, Lewis launched a career that led him to conduct Lola Falana’s band for two years, then the Swedish and Norwegian Orchestras, and, finally the Houston Symphony Orchestra. He also has arranged tunes for The Jacksons, Bill Withers and Tom Jones during that time. Touring with Herbie Hancock and the Headhunters in 1978 was the turning point for Lewis. After moving from Boston to Los Angeles, the keyboardist began developing his current musical direction. "The tour with Herbie stimulated this new direction. Herbie helped me learn the use of electronic instruments and how to get the sounds I heard in my head on tape," Lewis' explained. He added that he hopes to further extend the ideas on the “8 For The 80’s" LP, break- ing music barriers by employing his mul- tilithic skills. "The more diverse the music, the more people the music reaches.” Lewis is currently preparing for a concert at the Shrine Auditorium in Los Angeles. ARTIST PROFILE Reedman Ronnie Laws On Brink Of Mainstream Success by Michael Glynn LOS ANGELES — Versatile reedman Ron- nie Laws, at the age of 30, is a highly- respected member of the jazz community and a six-year recording veteran with four well-received LPs to discredit on Blue Note and United Artists Records. His growth as a jazz artist has been astonishingly rapid since he first signed with Blue Note in 1974 and released “Pressure Sensitive,” which became the largest selling debut LP in the label’s 37-year history. Now, with the release of the single “Every Generation,” the title track from his forthcoming UA album, he is virtually knocking on the door of mainstream success as his career takes a new and highly-promising turn. “It’s the beginning of a new phase for me,” says the tail, affable Laws of the new LP and single. “It’s a little hard to project where it's going to go from here, but I believe they represent the direction I want to go into." ‘Song-Oriented’ Laws explains that his present direction in music has been towards a more “song- oriented approach” in both writing and playing, as the single "Every Generation” features Laws on both lead vocals, as well as saxophone. However, he is also quick to point out that although he sung on both his last album, “Flame,” and the current LP, he does not consider himself to be a singer. “I don’t really classify myself as a vocalist at all," stresses Laws. “In the process of try- ing to find someone to sing 'Every Genera- tion’ I just decided that I would be best suited to the job since I wrote it and knew, Ronnie Laws conceptually, just what I wanted to say. It also worked out because my vocal phras- ing is so similar to my instrumental phras- ing." The album, Laws explained, has “both a broad meaning and a specific message” in that it reflects every step of life from infancy to adulthood and old age. “In a sense, it also reflects my childhood, up until the point of my manhood and now my maturity as an ar- tist,” says Laws. Musical Family Growing up in Houston, Tex., Laws was part of a musically-oriented family. His mother, Miolla, was a gospel pianist, while his brother Hubert has gone on to become an equally well-known jazz and classical flutist. Two sisters, Debra and Eloise. are budding singers in their own right, with another Charlotte Laws Stroud, having contributed lyrics to the song "Love's Vic- tory" on the new album. “Unlike a lot of other families in music, we (continued on page 48) NARM, RIAA Start Counterfeit Hotline NEW YORK — In a joint action aimed at LP counterfeiters, RIAA and NARM have es- tablished a national toll-free number (800/223-2328) to report crimes in this area. Both organizations will encourage industry-wide use of the number to report offers to sell counterfeit discs and tapes, locations of offending retailers, and iden- tities of counterfeit manufacturers and graphics printers. The RIAA/NARM program will be an- nounced in full-page trade ads explaining the plan. The tollfree number provides a direct link to RIAA’s anti-piracy intelligence bureau, where investigators and attorneys will speed the flow of information to the FBI or other enforcement agencies. In making the announcement with RIAA President Stanley M. Gortikov, Joe Cohen, executive vice president of NARM, revealed that his organization will con- tribute approximately $50,000 to RIAA’s anti-piracy fund by the Spring of 1980. This will augment RIAA’s annual million dollar industry anti-crime project. RIAA and NARM seek participation in the telephone plan by employees of member companies, as well as non-members, sup- pliers and other industry constituencies. The new project is a response to the growing availability of counterfeit recordings at retail outlets. Annual losses are estimated in the hundreds of millions of dollars. PERMANENT WAVES — Rush-Mercury SRM 1-4001 — Producers: Rush and Terry Brown — List: 7.98 This thundering power trio from Maple Leaf country gets more ambitious and inventive with each successive outing. The bone crunching heavy metal is still a major factor in the group’s sound, but “Permanent Waves” is tempered with a progressive techno-rock influence. Geddy Lee’s munchkin-Iike vocals are improving with age, and the band’s uncompromising raunch and roll sounds best on “Jacob’s Ladder,” “The Spirit Of Radio" and “Natural Science.” NO BALLADS ~ The Rockets — RSO RS-1-3071 — Producer: Johnny Sandlin — List: 7.98 The ’80s are in full swing and The Rockets have a new album out to orchestrate it all. “No Ballads” is no idle boast; from start to finish it’s all “grab ’em by the collar” rock ‘n’ roll that never lets up until the needle is lifted from the groove. AOR should show a healthy interest in tracks like “Don’t Hold On,” “I Want You To Love Me,” “Time After Time” and a right on the money version of Lou Reed’s “Sally Can’t Dance.”. PRETENDERS — Sire SRK 6083 — Producer: Chris Thomas — List: 7.98 The new wave has developed some distinctive new wave vocalists (Deborah Harry, Lene Lovich and Pattie Smith), and the latest neurotic songstress to join the brash and rebellious bunch is Chrissie Hynde of the Pretenders. While the band delivers a punk sound that is catchy and fast paced, it is Hynde’s anguished vocals that bring the whole appealing sound together. Songs that pace this arresting debut LP include “The Wait,” “Private Life” and “Precious.” MUSIC FROM STAR TREK AND THE BLACK HOLE — Meco — Casablanca NBLP 7196 —- Producers: Monardo, Bogiovi and Wheeler — List: 7.98 The man who gave us the disco version of “Star Wars” brings more interstellar madness with his newest LP. The musicians from the “milky way” galaxy deliver exciting disco music with a big band influence, and Meco’s production and Wheeler’s arrangements turn the unusually large pop orchestra into a cohesive dancin' machine. The synthesizer also plays a promi- nent role. EMOTION — Merry Clayton — MCA-3200 — Producer: Steve Tyrell — List: 7.98 Merry Clayton, whose heart-wrenching voice, with seemingly infinite range is back with a solo album that combines the best of jazz, rock and R&B, producing a sound that is unmistakably hers. On cuts like “When the World Turns Blue” and “Let Me Cry A Little Longer,” Clayton is smooth but relentless in her delivery of the material on a cover of “Armed and Extremely Dangerous” and on a medley of Sly Stone tunes, Clayton’s voice sings, talks and almost dances, something the music certainly is geared to do. This album is a must for jazz, B/C and AOR programming. CHRSTOPHER CROSS — Warner Bros. BSK 3383 I Producer: Michael Omartian — List: 7.98 — Bar Coded Chris Cross has successfully merged the pop jail sound of the Dobbie Bros, and Steely Dan with southern California rock on his debut LP, and people are going to be talking about this young artist for a long time to come. There are a million in- fluences on this LP, but Cross emerges as a versatile performer, and one of the brightest hopes of 1980. The list of backing musi- cians on this fine first LP reads like a Who’s Who of rock and jazz. DANCING IN THE DRAGON’S JAW — Bruce Cockburn Millenium BXL 1-7747 — Producer: Eugene Martynec — List: 7.98 Canadian Bruce Cockburn now has his latest album available south of the border. Having already attained gold status in his homeland with “Dancing . . . ,” can this master acoustic guitarist duplicate the feat in the U.S.? By all standards the answer Is a resounding yes. Cockburn is a genius at weaving dense, moody patterns with his unwavering guitar expertise and a voice as strong and solid as Canadian timber. For A/C and AOR formats with faith in quality softness. MESSIN’ WITH THE BOYS — Cherie and Marie Currie — Capitol ST-12022 — Producer: Jai Winding — List: 7.98 — Bar Coded Who really knew that ex Runaway Cherie Currie had a twin sister named Marie? Who could have guessed that the two of them would release one of the best and strongest albums so far this year? Teamed with producer and keyboard wiz Jai Winding, the sister’s sterling sibling harmonies are showcased brilliantly on this collection of spine-tingling rockers and stirr- ing, credible ballads. For AOR receptive to hard rock ladies with an iron clad purpose. . . . LIVE AT LAST — Good Rats — Rat City Records/Jem RCR 998 — Producers: Mickey Marehello & Charlie Conrad — List: 7.98 Undoubtedly the most underrated band this country never made famous, the Good Rats have remained a quirky mystery for nearly a decade now. Virtually owning Long Island, New York, the band never strayed much from its home turf. Good Rats have always offered a unique brand of off-kilter hard rock that pre-dated new wave in its directness, yet could hold its own against any number of coliseum headliners. A must for AOR. pour LOVE STINKS — The J. Geils Band -- EMI-America SOO- 17016 —-^Producer: Seth Justman — List: 7.98 The J. Geils Band has been splitting ear-drums for sometime now, but instead of more deafening decibels, this current release borrows from the best of the band’s previous material and extends it into a tasty formula of new wave and funky rock tunes. “Just Can’t Wait” should satisfy old and new rockers alike. "Comeback" is a funkier song, complete with electronics and good guitar work. Both songs add strength and the LP could easily find its way into AOR programming. CITY — Roger McGuirm and Chris Hillman, featuring Gene Clark — Capitol ST-12043 — Producers: Ron and Howard Albert — List: 7.98 — Bar Coded Gene Clark has apparently de-emphasized his roll in the McGuinn, Clark & Hillman triumvirate, leaving Roger and Chris to hold the bag. And what an exciting cookin’ bag it is! “City” is the kind of album a new waver could envy, yet if tastes run toward the mainstream California, that’s okay, too. The cut “Skate Date” beautifully supersedes “Mr. Spaceman” for iden- tical listener impact, a definite winner for AOR playlists with more than one track able to make it to Top 40. “ROLLER BOOGIE” — Various Artists — Casablanca NBLP 2- 7194 — Producer: Bob Esty — List: 13.98 A torrid rock ‘n’ roll disco number by Cher, “Hell On Wheels," paces this double LP soundtrack to the film about a chubby little girl whose only ambition in life is to win a "Roller Boogie” con- test. “Boogie Wonderland” by the Emotions also highlights the album, but most of the dancin’ material was written, arranged and conducted by Bob Esty. This album is perfect for dance parties and should be especially pleasing to the knee pad crowd. NEVER BUY TEXAS FROM A COWBOY — The Brides Of Funkenstein — Atlantic SD 19261 — Producer: GeorgeClinton — List: 7.98 A high steppin’, low down Funk number about some of mama’s finest advice opens the latest LP from The Brides of Funkenstein. The first ladies of funk have a more mature sound now, and their ambitious, busy vocal marathons on this LP sound like a cross between a female choral group and Parlia- ment. The top cuts on this funky string-filled outing include “Party Up In Here” and “Smoke Signals.” HIGH ON YOUR LOVE — Debbie Jacobs — MCA-3202 — Producer: Paul Sabu —• List: 7.98 Tight arrangements and production characterize this album, which allows Jacobs to further extend her reputation as a dance vocalist. Although funky with her vocal stylings, the title track does not escape the euro-disco sound. Well syncopated per- cussions help divert attention from synthesizers that aren’t really needed. Another cut, “Lovin’ Spree,” fares better, as Jacobs shows on this tune that there is much more to her act than gutsy funk. This album would be appropriate for A/C and DOR programming. WHERE TO NOW — Charlie Dore — Island ILPS 9559 — Producers: Bruce Welch and Alan Tarney — List: 7.98 This is a surprising release for Island Records (known primarily for reggae and rock) as Charlie Dore is undeniably a country rock artist. Dore’s warm lilting vocals are augmented by the music of the Tarney Spencer Band and some of the finest session cats in Nashville, and Island can be proud of its first outing in this rather foreign genre. The best tunes on the LP are “Fear Of Flying,” “Sweetheart” and the title cut. CHISOLM & SPENCE — Columbia NJC 36345 — Producers: Chisolm & Spence — List: 7.98 — Bar Coded This debut album for Chisolm & Spence is laden with love lyrics backed by Texas blues and soft folksy rock sounds. “One Kiss” Is the tastiest original tune on the LP, with a cover of Steely Dan’s “Dirty Work" offering fine vocal harmony. “Your Last Let- ter,” the first single released from this LP, provides a fine and unique ballad for balance. BOLERO — Tomita — RCA ARLI-3412 — Producer: Plasma Music — List: 7.98 There have been some great electronic musicians to come along in the past decade — Jarre, Emerson, Carlos — but few have treated the great classical works with as much reverence as Isao Tomita. Tomita first burst onto the pop scene with “Snowflakes Are Dancing," and he can chock up another great achievement with his synthesizer tribute to Ravel. Tomita delivers “Bolero” and “Mother Goose Suite” with his usual elec- tronic panache. STUNTMAN — Edgar Froese — Virgin V2139 — Producer: Edgar Froese — List: 7.98 This Berliner mined unknown areas in electronic rock with Tangerine Dream, and on his own he has produced greater, even more musical works. The six swirling, whirling music scapes on “Stuntman” would be equally appropriate as a film score or the ambient music for daily household chores. Another synthesized triumph for Froese. The most interesting tracks are “It Would Be Like Samo" and "Drunken Mozart In The Desert." J Cash Box/January 26, 1980 11

Chrysalis Records’ Success Based On Solid Fundamentals (continued trom page 8) understand what has to be done. They don’t believe in quotas, as long as you’re developing an act. That is the most impor- tant thing, that you've covered every angle. If you do that, then everything will fall into place." This philosophy was instrumental in breaking Blondie's ‘‘Parallel Lines” LP and “Heart Of Glass" single, perhaps the biggest Chrysalis success story of 1979. “Blondie's ‘Parallel Lines’ was an album that we didn’t think would explode like it did," Licata noted. “The album was out for quite a while, then ‘Heart Of Glass' came out and everything took off. It broke wide open and opened the door for a lot of other things. It was a very important part of our success story." Album Oriented Getting its initial response from FM, “Parallel Lines" typifies much of Chrysalis' product, geared with a heavy emphasis toward strong albums. This direction is quite intentional, according to Licata. "You can’t be a record company on singles,” he explained. “You’ve got to build a catalog. You’ve got to have longevity, and the only way to do that is to get to the AOR area. The FM, AOR is what built Chrysalis Records.” “That’s why we have a lot of strength,” Licata continued. “That's why our catalog is so strong. Our catalog is unreal for its size. We do a tremendous amount of catalog business.” Nevertheless, the dual success of “Parallel Lines” and “Heart Of Glass" also pointed out that the only way to the top is through Top 40 play. Pointing out that Chrysalis is now getting more and more acts onto T op 40 playlists, Licata explained, “That’s the way you really get an act over the hump. You can sellX-amount of albums with AOR play, but in order to get one there, you have to have that hit single. We’ve been able to do that recently.” Blondie also typifies the Chrysalis at- Arista Appoints Smith VP, Nat’i R&B Promotion NEW YORK — Richard Smith has been ap- pointed vice president of national R&B promotion for Arista Records. In this capacity, Smith will assume all supervisory responsibilities in the area of R&B promo- tion, initiating and directing all national air- play policy on R&B album and singles product, and supervising the activities of Arista's reqional and local R&B promotion staff.
