Harmony Hut Announces Plans For ’80s Growth by Joanne Ostrow WASHINGTON — “In spite of what 1979 looked like, in the '70s we saw a growth of over 2,000%, said Stuart Schwartz, chair- man of Schwartz Brothers, the Washington-based record distributors and retail chain operators. In a press briefing following a meeting of 30 of the nation’s top record manufacturers and distributors, Schwartz and staff mem- bers highlighted the company's marketing plans for the 1980s. Schwartz Brothers is due to move to a new Lanham, Md., $3.5 million distribution and corporate office in September (pending construction delays). There the firm will have 65,000 square feet of warehouse space and another 30,000 for offices to accomodate 150 staffers. Harmony Hut, the record store chain, will see at least five new stores open in 1980, bringing the total to 25. An initial $200,000 has been earmarked for advertising to sup- plement the amount provided by manufac- turers. Two stores are due to open in March, located in Charlottsviile, Va., and Forrestville, Md. Then in October, one is slated to open in Frackville, Pa., another in Fredericksburg, Va, and after that, one in the Washington metro area. (Meanwhile, the downtown Harmony Hut in Washington will close at the end of January as the entire block is being razed). The company's marketing aims are geared to meet the “new maturity in the music market,” Schwartz said. Key ele- ments of the strategy are the move to mall stores and the emphasis on a broad selec- tion of product, instead of focusing on monster hits. The stores will stress the fact that “music is an excellent gift idea, the best entertainment buy, and that Harmony Hut has trained salespeople and an excellent selection across the board,” Schwartz told reporters. As the firm looks at changing demographics, the public's record buying habits seem to be changing to individual tastes and away from huge hits, according to Dan Pasley, vice president and creative director of the advertising firm handling Harmony Hut’s campaigns. Economic pressures mean people aren't parting with money easily, but, since they already have invested in home entertainment systems, collecting of catalog LPs is the logical next step, Palsey said. The company’s current ad theme, “Har- mony Hut has the music,” will be followed up in future ads with the slogan, “Recorded music is still your best entertainment buy.” Schwartz also noted that the stores sell a high proportion of tapes to LPs — roughly a 50-50 ratio. Eight-track is still slightly ahead of cassette, he said, but only because the auto industry is still making 8-track units. Classical LP Business (continued from page 40) market is primarily an economic one. The situation in Europe is still — I wouldn’t say economically healthier — but there’s more money available. That isn’t so in England, but it is on the Continent, in Holland, France, and particularly Germany. And that has a lot to do with the activities of the com- panies; it’s not for artistic reasons. This arti- cle pointed to the fact that a classical record company is primarily an artistic effort. I fully agree with the fact that it is an artistic and aesthetic effort; but it is also a commercial effort. And we should be able to stand on our own two feet.” Munao Relocates To New Headquarters LOS ANGELES — Susan Munao Manage- ment Co. and Summer Nights have an- nounced new headquarters located at 1 224 N. Vine St., Hollywood, Calif. 90038. The new phone is (213) 467-2227. The UA Music Launches Promotion Campaign NEW YORK — United Artists Music has launched a major promotional campaign to promote its professional services depart- ment. The drive will be backed by the in- troduction of a new logo and the presenta- tion of new materials detailing the songs contained in the various United Artists catalog. They include United Artists Music Co., Unart Music, Robbins Music, Miller Music, and Leo Feist Inc., among sub- sidiary catalogs. In the initial phase of the campaign, the new logo will be imprinted on five popular songbook samplers and five standard songbook samplers. In addition, the logo will be seen on an alphabetical and category catalog of UA songs, library slip- case packages, and information kits. These materials will be sent on a complimentary basis to key record company, television, radio, motion picture, and advertising ex- ecutives, beginning February 18. Commenting on the campaign, which was developed jointly by United Artists Music personnel and The Music Agency Ltd. of New York, Harold Seider, president of United Artists Music, said that it represented “a special committment by the company to building closer creative relationships with both traditional and newer groups or copyright users in the 1980s." According to the intense manager, Journey will be “spearheading the entire ad campaign” for North American Rockwell, the aerospace com- pany building the space shuttle. "We’re go- ing to be on this thing when it flies,” hesaid. “Journey is going to be the first rock group on the moon." Grammy Performers (continued from page 10) Dylan has been nominated for best rock vocal performance by a male for “Gotta Serve Somebody,” and flutist Galway is a nominee for best classic performance by a soloist for “Annie's Song & Other Galway Favorites.” Loggins is a nominee as a songwriter for the Doobie Brother's hit "What A Fool Believes,” co-written with Michael Mac- Donald. The Doobie Brothers are also nominated for best record of the year for the “What a Fool Believes” 45 and best album of the year for “Minute by Minute,” which is also nominated for the best pop vocal performance by a duo, group or chorus. The Charlie Daniels Band has been nominated for best country vocal perfor- mance by a duo or group for “The Devi! Went Down to Georgia,” while past multiple Grammy winner Dionne Warwick is nominated in the female pop vocal and R&B categories for "Deja Vu.” Grammy Award winners are chosen by votes of the active members of the Recording Academy. The 22nd Annual Grammy Award Show is a Pierre Cossette Production, produced by Ken Ehrlich. NARM To Honor Industry Vets For Their Service LOS ANGELES — George Albert, president and publisher of Cash Box, will be among music industry veterans honored at a special testimonial luncheon held by the National Assn, of Recording Merchan- disers (NARM) at its annual convention, which is scheduled for March 23 at the MGM Grand Hotel in Las Vegas. The luncheon will honor industry veterans who have been active over the past 25 years, many of whom have been charter members of NARM since 1958. According to a NARM spokesman, many of those to be honored are said to have “laid the groundwork” for the growth of the recorded music industry. Joseph A. Cohen, executive vice- president of NARM, said, "I have deep respect for the people who made this in- dustry happen. “We, in a so-called ‘young people’s business,’ must not forget that we can only operate on the base which they created." In addition to Albert, others to be honored include George Berry (Raccoon Records); George Souvall (Alta Dis- tributing); and associate member Cy Leslie (former owner of Pickwick Records), who heads a list of associate members who af- filiated with NARM in 1959. The associate membership list includes: RCA, Columbia, Capitol, Mercury, Warner Bros, and Disneyland. Worldwide Reaction To McCartney Arrest (continued from page 18) Katsuya Kobayashi of Radio Tokyo FM. “Some people feel that it could have been part of a concert promoters war, while others felt it may have been part of a newspaper. But most people, especially the young, felt that he was just unlucky." Kobayashi added that three of the major privately-owned radio stations, one private local station, the nationally-owned radio and the two FM outlets in Japan have agreed to cease playing Wings material for the next three months as a result of the bust. “Ordinarily, if it were a Japanese artist, such as Char or Yosui Inoue, the term would be oneyear,” added Kobayashi. “But we all agreed that with an international ar- tist the stature of McCartney, that would be impossible.” There have also been a number of demonstrations in Tokyo in support of McCartney. Over 500 teenage girls gathered for one demonstration outside of T okyo's Anti-Narcotics Center, chanting for the singer. ON JAZZ (continued from page 13) the String Trio of New York, composed of violinist Billy Bang, guitarist James Emery and bassist John Lindberg; and “Homage To Charles Parker” features such well- known figures as George Lewis, Anthony Davis, Douglas Ewart and Richard Teitelbaum . . . Biograph Records has purchased the Dawn catalog from the 1950s, and some of the most recent releases are guitarist Jimmy Raney’s “Too Marvelous For Words” and three good ones by major tenor players; “Lullaby In Rhythm" by Lucky Thompson, "One T o Blow On” by Zoot Sims, and “Be Loose” by Al Cohn . . . The major labels haven’t been quite so active, but RCA has just released "Genetic Walk" by keyboard innovator Ahmad Jamal, and Columbia gives us Arthur Blythe’s “In The Tradition” with Stanley Cowell, Fred Hopkins and Steve McCall and the latest collaboration from the fusion team of drummer Gerry Brown and bassist John Lee, “Chaser” . . . Blue Note Records has opened up the vaults for a major issue of ten previously unreleased masters by some of the greatest musicians of the 1960s: “The Soothsayer" by tenorist Wayne Shorter; "Sonic Boom” by the late trumpeter Lee Morgan; “Clubhouse" by tenorist Dexter Gordon; “Spiral” by vibist Bobby Hutcherson: “A Slice of the Top” by tenorist Hank Mobley; “New Time Shuffle” by tenorist Stanley Turrentine; “Confirmation" by organist Jimmy Smith; “Consequences" by altoist Jackie McLean; “Chant" by trumpeter Donald Byrd; and “Solid” by the late guitarist Grant Green. Blue Note will henceforth be releasing two albums of freshly minted masters every month, and spokesmen promise the label’s return to active participation in the contemporary jazz market. chip stern 44 Cash Box/February 2, 1980

EDITORIAL Definition Needed In the wake of recent rulings by the Federal Com- munications Commission (FCC) on the "fitness" of RKO General and Westinghouse Broadcasting to hold broadcast licenses, it is time for the Commis- sion to come up with a concrete set of standards to clarify the issue. It is no small matter to dismantle a large and prominent broadcast chain with a set of nebulous and apparently subjective standards. While the Commission's primary function of policing the airwaves to protect the public interest is certainly laudable, this duty should not be construed as a blank check to exercise power capriciously. In fact, the Commission should take special pains to see that none of its actions are ever even allowed to be interpreted in that light. Thus, it is imperative that the Commission clearly define its stance on this issue. As was revealed in the RKO hearings, Westinghouse Electric is but one of 15 companies that have situations with broadcast licenses similar to RKO's parent company, General Tire & Rubber. If RKO is "unfit" to hold licenses because it was apparently too close and too involved with the mis- deeds of General Tire and Rubber and Westinghouse Broadcasting is "fit" to hold licenses because it apparently was not close or involved enough with the misdeeds of Westinghouse Electric, what are the standards by which "too much" or "too little" is gauged? Are these standards sensible and fair? In the case of RKO, this distinction makes all the difference in the world for the future of a broadcast chain that has been valued anywhere from $300-600 million. This consideration alone would merit an im- mediate clarification of all applicable standards. Finally, it is just plain right that the FCC put all of its cards on the table. The Commission has been en- trusted with guarding the public interest in the broadcast field. It is time to prove it by giving the in- dustry a clear and fair set of guidelines to live by. EQUIPOISE - Stanley Cowell - Galaxy GXY-5125 - Producer: Ed Michel - List: 7.98 This extraordinary young pianist is among the most respected composer -arrangers in jazz and a veteran of some of the great groups of the 1960s, such as those of drummer Max Roach. This trio recording is engaging and masterful, as well it might be with players the caliber of bassist Cecil McBee and drummer Roy Haynes. I WILL SAY GOODBYE - The Bill Evans Trio - Fantasy - F- 9593 - Producer: Helen Keane - List: 7.98 Mellow and moody, the Bill Evans Trio, with Eddie Gomez on bass and Eliot Zigmund on drums, plays subdued music, devoid of rock and funk fusion elements. Evans shows extremely good taste in his piano stylings, which is most evident on the Bacharach-David tune "A House Is Not a Home." The music is more spirited on the trio's rendition of Herbie Han - cock's "Dolphin Dance." ON JAll COMINGS AND GOINGS - Detroit, Mich., a hot -bed of jazz talent which has produced such fine artists as Betty Carter, Milt Jackson, Kenny Burrell and the Jones boys (Elvin, Thad and Hank), is keeping the creative spirit of American music alive through the Detroit Jazz Center, a project of the Jazz Research Institute. With a big band led by Sam Sanders, a jazz gallery, rehearsal space, archives of books and records, and instruction in theory and arranging, tap dancing, big and small bands, rhythm section work and the music business, the Jazz Center (located at 2110 Park Avenue, Detroit, Mich. 48201) is keeping fans, community groups and musicians in touch with the most important trends and each other . . . Multi-instrumentalist/composer David Amram will return to the Brooklyn Academy of Music Feb. 4-8 to lead the Brooklyn Philharmonic in its annual Free Schooltime Series in a program of world folk musics .. . Soundscape, a fine loft on 500 West 52nd St. in Manhattan, will be featuring a full calendar of jazz happenings through the end of March. There will be performances by guitarist Steve Groves' Nightbridge, Cadmosca with cellist Muneer Abdul Fataah, drummer Eddie Blackwell with tenorist Charles Brackeen. and a provocative series of solo performances by reedmen George Bishop and Byard Lancaster, trumpeter/flugel hornist Leo Smith, drummers Rashid All and Sunny Murray. An extra bonus will be a solo marimba performance by timbale master Tito Puente (March 23). For further infor- mation contact Verna Gillis at (212) 581- 7032 . . . Little David Records distributed by Atlantic is buzzing with anticipation about an album of duets by pianists John Lewis and Hank Jones, slated for early February. A major tour will follow the LP's release . . . Elektra is just shipping an album by the Mingus Dynasty Band with Charlie Haden, Dannie Richmond, Joe Farrell, John Handy, Jimmy Owens, Jimmy Knepper and Don Pullen . The Blackbyrds, having ended all affiliations with founder and teacher Donald Byrd, have signed an exclusive, long-term contract with Fantasy Records. Hoping to regain the form that garnered them three gold records and several hit singles, the Blackbyrds will be team- ing up with producer Deodato to begin work on an album in early February. The Blackbyrds are Keith Killgo on drums. Kevin Tonev on keyboards, Joe Hall on bass and Orville Saunders on guitar . .. Drummer Phillip Wison, who has done it all, from the original Art Ensemble of Chicago to the Paul Butterfield Blues Band, told me about two ex- citing projects he's involved in with trumpeter Lester Bowie. Phillip and Lester teamed with Fontella Bass ("Rescue Me") and Martha Bass to make a gospel album for Black Saint, and they'll be going into the studios with Amina Claudine Myers, Malachi Favors and Arthur Blythe in late February to record with Manfred Eicher for ECM . . . Speaking of Arthur Blythe, the greatest altoist has a superb new album on Columbia and has been making equally superb music at his favorite stomping grounds, the Tin Palace. A few weeks back he did some stunning duets with acoustic bass master Art Davis, which in- cluded everything from chamber -like dialogs to bluesy free improvisations. This past week, with his recording band on "In The Tradition" - bassist Fred Hopkins, drummer Steve McCall and pianist Stanley Cowell - he romped through a selection of jazz classics with the fury of a modernist and the devotion of a traditionalist .. . The young reedman, Marty Ehrlich, a fine writer and session player, recently co -led an intriguing modern quar- tet with guitarist Jerome Harris (best known for his bass work with Sonny Rollins) at the in- timate Folk City, the original stomping ground for Dylan. The music was lyrical but (continued on page 28) SPACE MAN - Sun Ra, who recently led his Jet Set Arkestra at the Bottom Line, is shown here relaxing after the Arkestra's in- terstellar jam session. For two shows he led the audience on a sojourn of intergalactic jazz only charted by his own Jet Set. JAZZ ALBUM PICKS HOMAGE TO CHARLES PARKER - George Lewis - Black Saint BSR 0029 - Producer: Giacomo Pellicciotti - List: 9.98 George Lewis is probably the most expressive, intelligent trombonist to have emerged in the past decade. A gifted improviser, comfortable in any idiom, his own compositions and group ideas lean in the direction of third system conceptualizations, drawing on electronics, classical and Afro- American forms. One side of this LP is given over to a very formal reading of blues -based materials, while the title side is a peaceful, touching ode to the life and death of the twentieth century's greatest musician. SOUNDSCAPES - Cedar Walton - Columbia - JC - 36285 - Producer: George Butler and Cedar Walton - List: $7.98 In a word. funky jazz characterizes this album by the former Jazz Messenger. While cuts like "Warm To the Touch" and "The Early Generation" do not forsake their jazz roots, the percus- sions by Rubins Bassini and Ray Mantilla provide additional dimension to already very full-bodied music. Walton's electric piano technique is best on "N.P.S.," where the feedback is def- tly controlled to provide a gritty tonal quality. FLUTE TALK - Sam Most with Joe Farrell - Xanadu 173 - Producer: Don Schlitten - List Price: 8.98 Sam Most is one of the seminal figures in the history of jazz flute, widely acknowledged to be among the first great soloists on the instrument. Here Most is joined by Joe Farrell on flute for a fanciful, upbeat selection of sambas, swingers and mood pieces, with a typically excellent mainstream production from Xanadu, the cooking "Hot House" and the improvised flute duet. "Leaves," are the standout performances. Cash Box/February 9. 1980 11

EAST COASTINGS Artist Development Is Being Redefined By Record Labels (continued from page 7) that "if an artist is capable of exciting crowds through live performances, we're still going to come to the party when necessary to break the artist through." Concert Attendance Down The fact that there are fewer ticket - buying dollars available has led the record companies to re -appraise the importance of concert tours in developing the careers of new artists. "Everybody is taking a second look at touring," said Perry Cooper, director of artist relations, development and product management for Atlantic Records. "To put an act on the road just to showcase tiem really doesn't make sense in most cases." Rather than expending their budgets en- tirely on tours with questionable prospects of success, artist development planners are channeling more funds into the crucial areas of marketing and promotion. Even a confirmed believer in the viability of selec- tive touring like Jerry Jaffe, vice president of artist development for Polydor Records, pointed out: "We've been putting out money into the direct marketing of acts. We show them the marketing campaign and say, 'This is what we're doing for you, this is directly related to your career, it's not mak- ing it more comfortable for you on the road - maybe even harder - but the money is going to get you over the top.' " The use of film, television and new video technologies is becoming an attractive alternative to the complete dependence upon touring for breaking new acts. Ac- cording to Regeher, the addition of a full TV department is "the biggest change" in War- ner Bros.' artist development program over the past two years. Although he insisted that the label is not de-emphasizing tour- ing. Regeher said that promotional films and videotapes - like those produced for the Pretenders by the new Warner Bros. department - will receive increased funding as the audio-visual presentations increasingly "supplement" live ap- pearances. Media Promotion As the labels shift the focus of their development programs, they are up- grading the value of media promotion as a means of establishing recognition for their new artists. According to Davis, Capitol has arranged successful, two-week, non- performing promotional tours for Bob Welch and Cherie & Marie Currie "specifically for the purpose of introduing them to the press and radio program direc- tors." At some companies, economic measures have led to the dissolution of ar- tist development programs and their re- incorporation into the overall functions of marketing, promotion and publicity. "Our artist development is going to be through airplay, advertising and publicity," said Joan Bullard, vice president of artist rela- tions and publicity for MCA Records. Rogers Gets First #1 Pop Single LOS ANGELES - Kenny Rogers reaffir- med his stature as the leading country crossover artist this week when his "Coward Of The County" single from the "Kenny" LP captured the top spot on the Cash Box Top 100 Singles chart. The feat marks the first time Rogers has held the #1 position on the Pop Singles chart as a solo artist. Rogers is also riding high on the album charts. His "Kenny" album is currently riding at the #1 slot on the Coun- try LP chart, and at the #6 spot on the Pop Album chart. "Press is going to be more important than it has been for a number of years," she ad- ded. In spite of the austere economic environ- ment, artist development executives are still adhering to the basic principle on which the function has been based since the mid - 70s; the need for a strong liaison between the performing artists and the complex web of marketing and promotional activities un- dertaken on their behalf by the labels. The underlying theory that a customized plan developed for each individual artist will help the act achieve a quicker success is still a key operating guideline. Woolley Plan Andon and Fred Humphrey, director of AOR promotion for Columbia Records, mapped out an "unusual" strategy for in- troducing singer/songwriter Bruce Woolley to the United States in December. Although his album was set for February release, the decision was made to bring Woolley to New York, where he played a number of show- case dates which, Andon said, "gave the company the chance to see what this guy was all about." Airplay exposure was arranged for the import LP, "Bruce Woolley & The Camera Club," with special emphasis given to the British hit single, (continued on page 28) Illegal Records Cost Industry $50 Million In '79 NEW YORK - In 1979, the FBI and local law enforcement agencies, working with the Recording Industry Assn. of America's anti - piracy intelligence unit, confiscated more than $50 million worth of illegal record counterfeiting and tape duplicating equip- ment, counterfeit LPs, pirate eight -tracks and cassettes, and related materials. The estimated value of the confiscated hardware and software represents just a sampling of 28 major actions in 16 states, according to Jules Yarnell, RIAA Special counsel on antipiracy. Among the software retrieved in the various raids is more than 208,000 pirate and bootleg eight -tracks and cassettes, 27,000 counterfeit LPs, some 500,000 counterfeit and pirate Spanish language eight -track labels, 60,000 counterfeit sleeves and thousands of additional LPs and tapes taken in large tonnage seizures that are not broken down by item. Materials Destroyed At the same time, more than $5 million worth of raw materials, machinery, coun- terfeit LPs and eight -tracks were destroyed under court orders in connection with previous confiscations. Included were 173,000 counterfeit LPs and eight -tracks in the seizure from John LaMonte d/b/a House of Sounds in June; thousands of eight -tracks, machinery and raw materials in the R&A Audio (Ramon Gutierrez) raid in July, and 4,300 eight -tracks in the action against Elton and David Sewell d/b/a David's Novelties in September. There were also several important criminal prosecutions and adjudications that strengthened anti -piracy statutes in states such as New York and California. David Heilman, for example, was found guilty of 18 counts of copyright infringe- ment and sentenced to a six-month jail sen- tence, with a $9,000 fine, currently under appeal, in the U.S. District Court, Northern District of Illinois. Heilman and E.C. Tape were also hit with a summary judgement of more than $4 million in Milwaukee County Circuit Court in December, following a two- week civil trial. In the first conviction resulting from FBI (continued on page 16) REGGAE ROBIN HOOD - Although Michael Butler's Broadway production of "Reggae" has been garnering the media buzz, my bets are on the movie "Rockers" to be the vehicle that will take reggae to its next phase of popularity. Directed by Theodoros Bafaloukos, the Jamaican -based film, which has been playing in England since mid -September, could be subtitled "The Harder They Come Gets Religion." The similarity of "Rockers" to "Harder" lies in its focus on an Everyman's rise to heroism, us- ing reggae as a musical Richter scale. But while the former was what one might call a goats -head western, "Rockers" is the story of a Rastafarian Robin Hood, Leroy "Hor- semouth" Wallace, who robs from the (westernized) rich and gives to the poor. If the movie has any shortcoming, it is Wallace's character: His somber, somewhat stoned egalitarianism doesn't create the excite- ment of Cliff's down -and -dirty charisma. Ultimately, though, this film offers us valuable access to Jamaican culture, even as it entertains, and it comes at a time when it will help reggae music in this country. Finally, the soundtrack album, which will be out on Island in June, coinciding with the film's American release, will do its own share of good for reggae. The 16 -track LP offers a rich cross-section of music, including songs by Peter Tosh, Bunny Wailer, Junior Murvin, Gregory Isaacs, Justin Hines, and the Jaes. The latter. by the way, recorded one of my favorite Jamaican albums of 1979, an incredibly traditional mix of reggae -inflected doo- wop called "Unforgettable Times" on the E&K label. REVIEWS ALBUM REVIEWS FUN AND GAMES - Chuck Mangione - A&M SP -3715 - Producer: Chuck Mangione - List: 8.98 Mangione offers clean sounds on this album with ample help from the likes of guitarist Grant Geissman, who keeps the horns and rhythm sections on an even keel. The cut "Give It All You Got" has an urgency in the pace, but does not seem rushed at all. The title track is indeed aptly named, complete with Mangione's inimitable singing horn. Very good for B/C and Pop programming. VOYAGER - Roger Whittaker - RCA AFL1-3518 - Producers: Eric Robertson & John Mackswith - List: 7.98 Roger Whittaker has been lending his deep resonant vocal style to wax for 14 albums now, and he seems to improve with age. His latest adult -pop oriented album is rife with string -filled ballads like "I See You In The Sunrise" and uptempo toe tap- pers like "I Was Born." Whittaker puts a lot of folk influence into his material and it comes to the forefront on songs such as "Sail Away" and "Song For The Captain." For A/C lists. THE BEST SIDE OF GOODBYE - Jane Olivor - Columbia JC 36335 - Producers: Shelton, Masser & Darrow - List: 7.98 - - Bar Coded Olivor possesses one of the most distinctive female voices in contemporary music, and although her sound is a little slickly produced on this waxing, she serves up her finest collection to date. At times her voice is reminiscent of a mellow Barbra Strei- sand. but her shimmering tones have that memorable Olivor trademark. She is as at home on a Broadway stage as the recording studio, and the most affecting moments on this LP can be found on "Weeping Willows, Cattails" and the title cut. THIS DAY AND AGE - D.L. Byron - Arista AB 4258 - Producer: Jimmy lovine - List: 7.98 This volatile east coast rocker puts a lot of the savage bite into his music that Elvis Costello and Bruce Springsteen are renown for. Byron's lyrical themes have to do with the young and res- tless, and his new wavish musical attack is equally exciting. Production ace Jimmy lovine handles the direction on this star- tlingly good debut. Best cuts include "Am I Falling In Love Again." "Listen To The Heartbeat" and "Backstage Girl." Check out the drum mix on this album. TEMPTATION - Marc Tanner Band - Elektra 6E-240 - Producers: Nat Jeffrey & Fred Mollin - List: 7.98 Tanner has matured quite a bit since his debut LP last year. He is no longer afraid to let the wild boy creep into his clean streamlined rock sound on "Temptation," and the bold step consistently pays off. His hook -laden California rock style is propelled by a young band that is now accustomed to his style and rocks with conviction. The LP's fine moments are on the title track, "Don't Say No (Surrender)" and "Hot And Cold." FREEZE FRAME - Godley & Creme - Polydor PD -1-6257 - Producers: Godley & Creme - List: 7.98 Godley & Creme were always responsible for the moodier. more cerebral moments in yesteryear's 10cc. "Freeze Frame" finds these two pop maverick wizards once again in top form, stretching the boundaries of traditional pop arrangements by unleashing a plethora of percussive gymnastics and multi - layered lyrical mind games that tickle the funny bone, excite the intellect and even manage to get the feet tapping. Godley & Creme have come up with one of the most challenging AOR commodities since Hot Legs thought school stank. FRANKIE ELDORADO - Epic NJE 36291 - Producer: Frankie Eldorado - List: 7.98 - Bar Coded Frankie Eldorado is an expert at producing slick, space age, bubble gum rock. The sugary vocals are often wrapped around a hard rocking disco beat. but the songs are perfect for Top 40 car radio listening. If bands like 1910 Fruit Gum Company and The Ohio Express were around today, they'd sound just like Eldorado. Top tracks on this fun waxing are "Good Thing," "Ain't That Peculiar" and "Dancin' To Me." PHILLIPS/MACLEOD - Polydor PD -1-6255 - Producer: Tony Peluso - List: 7.98 The Phillips Macleod aggregation takes a grittier rock ap- proach here than on their last few albums. The power rock guitar rhythms are driven home with authority. and the boys' harmonies are on the money as usual. There are lots of strong AOR tracks on the LP. but the most immediately memorable are "Young Girls." "East Side. West Side" and "Down By The River." Pure pop/rock for AOR. THE TRANSFIGURATION OF BLIND JOE DEATH -:John Fahey - Takoma TAK-7015 - Producer: John Fahey - List: 7.98 - Bar Coded Fahey is a master of the acoustic 12 -string guitar, and he puts his finger picking expertise to 15 songs on this quality recording. He handles a mixture of genres - lilting ballads. old folk songs and freewheelin' bluegrass numbers - on "The Transfiguration Of Blind Joe Death." The songs from this calm- ing collection are equally suited to film scores and for listening during those lazy Saturday afternoons in the hammock. it..,-,..,,,....., THE FLYING LIZARDS - Virgin VA 13137 - Producer: David Cunningham - List: 7.98 If there was ever an album that could be considered Dadaist, this has to be it. David Cunningham is the mastermind of this pseudo -band, and although many will find the music on this avant -minimalist LP offensive, it borrows directly on the John Cage school. The sterile spoken -sung vocals are supplied by Cunningham's art school friend, Deborah, and the recording techniques are all based on chance, mistakes and technological incongruities. Still, the recordings of "Money" and "Summertime Blues" are ingenious in their ridiculousness. Well, they laughed at Dali. GALLAGHER - United Artists LT -1019 - Producers: Ken Kragen & Jim Mazza - List: 7.98 The line on the back cover of this off the wall comedy album reads "... you people ain't thinkin' about this stuff," and it hits the essence of Gallagher's humor right on the head. This LP captures the weird and riotous hypothetical routines of Gallagher in a live situation. Although much of his humor is visual, he has put together a nice mirth -filled waxing. This jester has both a fine vinyl and television future ahead of him. SUE SAAD AND THE NEXT - Planet P-4 - Producers: Richard Perry & James Lance - List: 7.98 While this album has a new wave veneer, Sue Saad and the Next's debut packs a strong.mainstream rock punch. The songs on the record are frantically paced rockers, and the lyrics are of the rebellious teenage variety, but the music is more in the mold of newcomers like Ellen Shipley and Pat Benatar. The power rockers that highlight this beautifully produced waxing are: "It's Gotcha," "I Want Him," "I I Me Me" and "Danger Love." THUG OF LOVE - Dirk Hamilton - Elektra 6E-249 - Producers: Dirk Hamilton & Don Evans - List: 7.98 Some day Dirk Hamilton's going to be a star. His lyrics have the wry wit of a Zevon, and he sings with the abandon of Van the Man. While his music isn't as strong on "Thug Of A Love" as it was on "Met Me At The Crux." there are still Hamilton classics such as "Out To Unroll The Wheel World," "Colder Than Mex- ican Snow," "Change In A Child's Hand" and "In A Miracle." Hamilton is a forceful rock 'n' roll talent, and AOR should jump on this finely crafted effort. A DIFFERENT KIND OF TENSION - Buzzcocks - 1.R.S./A&M SP 009 - Producer: Martin Rushent - List: 7.98 This is the official, unadulterated third album from one of England's finest now available domestically. The Buzzcocks re- cent "Singles Going Steady" LP served as an intense primer for newcomers to the band's unique brand of singles -oriented melodic relentlessness. The result this time around is nearly identical in that, once again, it is an album rife with a tight. well - honed barrage of singles. Fans of spirited, proletarian love songs should greet this newest offering by the Buzzcocks with gusto. SURVIVOR - Scotti Brothers SB 7107 - Producers: various - List: 7.98 This is a fine debut by a hard driving mainstream rock band that should be around for awhile. Led by well-known Chicago - based guitar player Jim Peterik, the group has a lot of the midwest influence in its style. The sound is clean, the hooks are consistent and the musical dynamics astonishing. This talented fivesome looks like it has a fine future ahead. Best tracks on wax include "Youngblood," "Love Has Got Me." "Somewhere In America" and "Whatever It Takes." WINNERS - Kleeer - Atlantic SD 19262 - Producers: Dennis King and Kleeer - List: 7.98 This accomplished R&B/Funk quartet possesses an easy moving rhythm guitar/bass sound surrounded by a swirling keyboard. The smooth, dynamic vocals fit the bouncy beat per- fectly, and added female harmonies add luster to the proceedings. The band moves into changes at a more proficient speed than most laid back B/C bands. Best cuts are "Open Your Mind." "Rollin' On" and the title cut. ya AFRICAN SUITE - MCA MCA -3205 - Producer: Richie Rome - List: 7.98 This LP is laden with the euro-disco-monorhythmic beat, with a bit of African and Latin percussion thrown in to spice the ac- tion. Pneumatic vocals by Carolyn Mitchell and Brenda Hill, es- pecially on cuts like "Grass" and "In The Pocket," offer a soothing reprieve from the thumb popping bass play and the heavy footed bass drum mantra. The synthesizer is persuasive as a rock element lent to African disco. For AOR and B/C. LIVE MAGNETIC AIR ,400, 41 2 LIVE MAGNETIC AIR - Max Webster - Capitol ST -12042 - Producers: Max Webster & Terry Brown - List: 7.98 - Bar Coded This LP, recorded live in southern Ontario in 1979. will in- troduce this stellar Canadian rock band to a lot of AOR programmers. Its hard rock attack is pleasantly offset by some interesting jazz and blues breaks, and is slightly reminiscent of the old Brian Auger assemblage. Look for "America's Veins." "Hangover" and "Here Among The Cats" to get lot of FM play. Cash Box/February 9. 1980 15

In addition to termination of the agree - Contraband Records Total $50 Million In '79 (continued from page 14) raids on December 19, 1978 in five east coast states, Frank Martino, principal of Ramart Publishing Corp., Central Islip, N.Y., pled guilty to a two -count information charging him with wire fraud and copyright infringement in U.S. District Court, Eastern District of New York. The plea was accepted conditional on his agreement to cooperate with the government against the individuals involved in the scheme, and he was senten- ced to three months in jail and fined $15,- 000 in May. New Laws In New York and California, substantially strengthened anti -piracy statutes went into effect in 1979. In New York, manufacture of pirate recordings is now a felony punishable by imprisonment for at least one and up to three years and/or a fine of up to $1,000. The manufacture or sale of recordings made from a live broadcast per- formance without the artist's permission is treated as a felony with the same penalties as manufacture of pirate recordings. The sale of such recordings is the same grade of offense as the sale of a pirate recording. In California, anti -bootlegging provisions similar to those in New York were enacted. The manufacture and sale of recordings made from live or broadcast performances without the artist's consent is also now prohibited. Korvettes To Sublet 13% Of Store Space NEW YORK - Korvettes has revealed that it plans to sublease approximately 13% of the store space in its 50 outlets to other retailers in an effort to improve its profitability. However, David Rothfeld, vice president and divisional merchandise manager for Korvettes, reaffirmed that the conversion of space would not affect any of the chain's existing record departments (Cash Box, Jan. 19). Nevertheless, he did allow for the possibility that a few of the chain's outlets may be closed. The conversion move, which was an- nounced last week by the chain's owners, the Agache-Willot Group of France, would be equivalent to the closing of five or six Korvettes stores, according to John Magee, vice president of real estate. Of the chain's total occupancy of nine million square feet, he said, Korvettes occupies two million more square feet than it needs. Blackbyrds Sign New Contract With Fantasy LOS ANGELES -A long-term, exclusive recording contract with Fantasy Records has been signed by the Blackbyrds, who will begin work on the first album of the new deal in early February. Deodato is slated to produce the album with the Blackbyrds. ABKCO Reports Loss NEW YORK - ABKCO Industries Inc. reported last week that its revenues for the fiscal year ended September 30, 1979 fell to $8.1 million from $16.3 million in 1978. The company also reported a net income loss of $99,585, compared to a profit of $44,208 for the previous year. In addition, the company's revenues in the fourth fiscal quarter, ended September 30, fell to $2.3 million from $10 million in 1978. ABKCO's earnings for the period resulted in a loss of $9,438, compared to a $176,571 drop for the comparable 1978 period. Roth doesn't have any bizarre statements to make about the poster inside the new Van Halen LP, "Women And Children First," which is due out in early March. The poster was taken by photographer Helmut Newton, whose book "White Women" and fashion work in "The Eyes Of Laura Mars" film have stirred public con- troversy in the past. ANARCHY IN THE FILM CAN - For those in need of a Sex Pistols fix and can't afford the import copy of the latest Public Image album "Metal Box," vindication is on the way. The two -record set, which currently comes in a metal film cannister, will be released on Warner Bros. under the title "Second Edition" on March 1. BEFORE AND AFTER SCIENCE - The Manhattan Transfer will be the feaVred per- formers at the 8th annual Histocompatibility Convention at the Bonaventure Hotel in Los Angeles on Feb. 8. The performance will cap a week long event that will play host to leading biologists from all over the world who will come together to discuss new field developments in such areas as organ transplants, genetic disorders and diseases, and bloodbanking. "An Evening of Appropriate Entertainment," which the Feb. 8 show is being tagged, will also boast such talent as new wave dandies Interpol, Tally Brown and master of ceremonies Timothy Leary. S.F. DISCO GOES DOR - Once a bastion of disco in the Bay Area, The City has shifted gears, and on Jan. 31 the club opened its doors as San Francisco's newest new wave/rock 'n' roll dance club complex. DJ hosts Beverly Wilshire, Richard Gossett and Howie Klein (all formerly of X's new wave disco) will spin. RIVIERA RECORD - Tony Orlando's SRO performance at Las Vegas' Riviera Hotel showroom on Jan. 19 set a house record for attendance. The previous record was join- tly set by Kenny Rogers, Olivia Newton -John, Liza Minnelli and Steve Martin. MCDONALD MONOPOLY - Although he can't be sued for anti-trust, blue ey9d soul singer Michael McDonald can be heard on no less than five recently released aleums. His velvety vocals can be heard on current releases by Nicolette Larson, Lauren Wood, Chris Cross, as well as the "Together" soundtrack and the Kenny Loggins smash "This Is It." McDonald, who will also be producing the new LP by Capitol recording artist Amy Holland, could be one of the reasons why the Loggins single has gone so high on the black contemporary chart .. . Paddy Faralla has departed her post of director of national press for Casablanca Records and Filmworks to pursue interests in music and film. She can be reached at (213) 761-1310. GRAHAM PURCHASES OLD WALDORF - Rock impressario Bill Graham has exten- ded his music business empire by buying one of San Francisco's most successful nightclubs, The Old Waldorf. The 600 -seat venue was opened three years ago by Jeff Pollock. Graham said he plans no basic changes in the way the club has been managed, and Pollock and his staff will continue to run the famous Bay Area nitery. marc cetner 16 Cash Box/February 9, 1980

REVIEWS SINGLESREVIEWS FEATURE PICKS THE KNACK (Capitol 4822) Baby Talks Dirty (3:40) (Eighties Music/Small Hill Music - ASCAP) (D. Fieger, B. Averre) Ready for 'The Big Knack Attack', Part II? Well, this first single from the band's forthcoming LP .. but the little girls understand" continues the same infectious staccato guitar rock groove as on "My Sharona," as well as the thundering drum rolls. Again, the lyrical content is imbued with sex- ual connotation, so preview before playing. FOREIGNER (Atlantic 3651) Women (3:25) (Somerset Songs Publishing In- c./Evansongs Ltd. - ASCAP) (M. Jones) Foreigner should score its third direct single hit from the "Head Games" LP with this uncom- promising piledriver of a rock song. Slashing lead guitars, courtesy of writer Mick Jones and Ian McDonald, lead the way into the hardcore boogie beat, with Lou Gramm's rough 'n' tumble vocals, for another pop, AOR winner. HEART (Epic 9-50847) Even It Up (3:45) (Strange Euphoria Music/Know Music - ASCAP) (A. Wilson, S. Ennis, N. Wilson) Steamy lead guitar riffs pace the first single from Heart's upcoming "Bebe Le Strange" LP, punctuating the aggressively sensual lead vocals of Ann Wilson in fine fashion. The band's rhythm section holds the heavy bottom down nicely on this straight ahead boogie number, complemen- ted by vigorous horn work on the finale. Hot rock for AOR, pop action. PRINCE (Warner Bros. WBS 49178) Why You Wanna Treat Me So Bad (Ecnirp Music Inc. - BMI) (Prince) With "I Wanna Be Your Lover" still firmly ensconced in the Top 15 of the pop singles chart, multi -instrumentalist Prince comes with this swirl- ing electronic pop/dance concoction. A multi - format killer, this number showcases falsetto lead vocals in front of powerful electric crescendos. Combo of hot lead guitar and striking keyboards makes this a winner. CRYSTAL GAYLE (Columbia 1-11198) It's Like We Never Said Goodbye (3:32) (Cookaway Music, Inc./Dejamus Music, Inc. - ASCAP) (R. Greenway, G. Stephens) A strong, melodius hook and Gayle's sweet, supple vocals are the key elements here - which could make this track another crossover success along the lines of her last Top 20 single "Half The Way." Resonant piano and acoustic guitar roll along at a mid -tempo gait, backed by pop - symphonic strings. A solid pop A/C, C&W pick. UTOPIA (Bearsville BSS 49180) Set Me Free (3:09) (Unearthly Music, Inc./Fiction Music, Inc. - BMI) (Utopia) Utopia, with techno wiz Todd Rundgren at the helm, has come up with its strongest pop single entry to date here. A bouncy keyboard and bass dominated beat rolls along at a catchy clip, as Kasim Sulton leads the strong vocals with sterling harmonies and backup assistance from the rest of the band. A frothy concoction aimed at Top 40. PRETENDERS (Sire SRE 49181) Brass In Pocket (I'm Special) (3:01) (Modern Publishing Ltd./Hynde House of Hits/ATV Music U.K.) (C. Hynde, J.H. Scott) Pretenders lead vocalist Chrissie Hynde is quickly emerging as one of the bright new singer/stylists of 1980 and one listen to this track will show why. Her sly, sexy warbling and tremen- dous control on this distinctive R&B-infused pop - /rock tune should make this #1 UK hit a pop, AOR smash on these shores as well. THE GAP BAND (Mercury 76037) I Don't Believe You Want To Get Up And Dance (Oops, Up Side Your Head) (3:29) (Total Ex- perience Music Pub. Co. - BMI) (L. Simmons, R. Wilson, C. Wilson, R. Wilson, R. Taylor) A swaying, downbeat instrumental groove, with a lilting, clicking backbeat, is joined by a truly catchy rap on this track from "The Gap Band II." Already receiving heavy B/C radio activity off the LP track, this is destined for crossover status. Watch for this one. SINGLES TO WATCH. THE ROMANTICS (Nemperor ZS9 7527) What I Like About You (2:56) (Forever Endeavor Music, Inc. - ASCAP) (Palmer, Marinos, Skill) The Detroit -based Romantics blend the raw urgency of '60s rock groups, a la The Standells with the quick en- semble pop of contemporaries like The Knack. Here, rough guitar chording is nicely mingled with new wavish vocals for a vibrant pop, AOR pick. THE SEARCHERS (Sire SRE 49175) It's Too Late (3:27) (Rockfield Music/Almo Music Corp. - ASCAP) (J. David) After a long absence, The Searchers have re -grouped with two of the original members remaining. What they have delivered here is a truly contemporary pop -rock number with a breezy, infectious hook, aided by shakin' tambourine, zesty piano and guitar and tasty vocal trade- offs. A pop sleeper. KEITH HERMAN (Radio RR 419) Body Body (She Knows What To Do) (3:09) (Noble Son Music Corp. Ltd./Renmal - ASCAP) (K. Herman) Herman's last single, "She's Got A Whole Number," from "the Next Song Is . ." LP came on the low end of the Top 100 but this snakey, sexy rocker should take him even further. Herman's tough, gritty vocals will undoub- tedly bring more AOR, pop play. TARNEY/SPENCER BAND (A&M 2214) Cathy's Clown (3:23) (Acuff -Rose Pub. Inc. - BMI) (D. Everly, P. Everly) An eerie electronic opening moves into a unique elec- trified re -working of the Everly Brothers' classic hit. Arrangements here bear a startling resemblance to Cliff Richard's "We Don't Talk Anymore," penned by Allan Tarney. Choice pop, AOR pick. JEFF CONAWAY (Columbia AE7-1196) City Boy (3:58) (Laurel Canyon Music Ltd. - ASCAP) (P. Floyd, C.J. Ellis, M. Appel) Jeff Conaway, co-star of the popular television series "Taxi," comes up with a bouncy urban pop/rock selec- tion for the first single from his self -titled debut LP. The strong Springsteen influence here is supplied by Bruce's former manager, Mike Appel, who co -wrote and co - produced the record. THE STONE CITY BAND (Gordy G 7179F) Strut Your Stuff (4:00) (Stone City Music Company - ASCAP) (L. Ruffin, Jr.) Rick James' Stone City Band steps out front on this single from their upcoming "In N' Out" LP. Polished funk is the order of the day with a bright chorus of female singers up front and gruff male vocalizing com- plementing. Horns, percussives and snakey bass and lead guitar make this exceptional B/C fare. CLIFTON DYSON (Motown M 1482F) Body In Motion (Want Your Body In Motion With Mine) (3:59) (Magic Lamp Music/Pretty P Music - ASCAP) (L. Harrington, C. Dyson, P. Harrington) Previously released on the independent All-American label, this pulsating dance/R&B selection features the urgent vocals of Ronnie Dyson's brother Clifton, with scintillating female backup assistance. A powerful dance cut for B/C lists. THE CONTROLLERS (Juana/TK JUX-3426) We Don't (3:55) (Groovesville/Everynight - BMI) (J. Sahmwell, T. Tate) A bright bed of strings, horns and easy drumming back this glossy ballad from The Controllers' "Next In Line" LP. Harold Melvin and The Blue Notes come to mind here, but this superior vocal ensemble is most definitely in a class of its own. For B/C lists. RAINBOW (Polydor PD 2060) All Night Long (3:49) (Thames Talent Pub., Ltd. - BMI) (R. Blackmore, R. Glover) Blackmore and company crank it up loud on this hard 'n' heavy rocker from the "Down To Earth" LP. Guitar and bass attack on the hook and the gruff lead vocals will at- tack AOR play. RUSH (Mercury 76044) The Spirit Of Radio (3:00) (Core Music Publishing - CAPAC/ASCAP) (N. Peart, G. Lee, A. Lifeson) Canadian power trio Rush is back with a tumultuous rocker from its recently released "Permanent Waves" LP that should strike an immediate chord within the radio community. Geddy Lee's high vocals and the band's electrically charged instrumental should click on AOR lists. BEN E. KING (Atlantic 3635) Music Trance (3:40) (Smiling Clown Music Pub. - BMI) (Ben E. King) Veteran pop/R&B hitmaker Ben E. King strikes a highly danceable, funk -infested groove here, maintained by congas and various percussives as well as a thick bass line. Writer David Adelstein's lush keyboard work and Welch's soft, sinewy lead vocals could make this a pop, A/C sleeper. RITCHIE ADAMS (MCA MCA -41182) The Best Of The Rest Of Our Lives (3:51) (Silver Blue Music, Ltd.) (R. Adams, G. Nissenson) Glistening piano and a crying guitar line open up this pop/A/C entry from newcomer Ritchie Adams, with a full, glossy production by veteran Joel Diamond. Adams' big tenor is given full rein on the heavily orchestrated crescendos. LITTLE FEAT (Warner Bros. WBS 49169) Wake Up Dreaming (3:40) (Streelights Music - ASCAP/Ayn Animus Music - BMI) (B. Payne, F. Payne) The legacy of Little Feat lives on and this single from the latest and final LP, "Down On The Farm," is a testa- ment to the group's talents at making lively, distinctive rock. Sharp guitar work meshes with bright piano for a sure pop, AOR pick. KARLA BONOFF (Columbia 1-11206) Baby Don't Go (3:17) (Seagrape Music/Valgovind Music BMI) (K. Bonoff, K. Edwards) Invigorating a cappella harmonies open up the third single from Bonoff's "Restless Nights" LP, moving into an easily paced, country -tinged pop number. Bonoff's rich vocals are accompanied by twangy guitar work. Recom- mended for pop, A/C and Country lists. Cash Box/February 9. 1980 17

Publishers Look To The Future (continued from page 10) Screen Gems' first projects of 1980 are already well underway with the addition of the songs of Off Broadway usa , a new band in the Cheap Trick mold, to a rock catalog that also features Boston, Queen, Bob Welch and Journey. In addition to Off Broadway usa, Screen Gems has also signed two other acts, Lisa Garber and Beth Nielsen, and Sill feels that the female singer/songwriters are the exception to the usual self-contained act rule. "My feeling is that both of these girls write material that is strong enough to be covered," says Sill. Also projected for mid -1980 is a new album by The Rolling Stones, who have been publishing with Screen Gems since the'"Sticky Fingers" LP. "The Stones have always been a consistent song seller for us," explained Sill. "And that's what the business needs to get back on its feet right now, a couple of supergroups like the Stones or The Beatles. It needs that kind of shot in the arm." DANCE TOP 40 DISCO Wks. U, Wks. HILLMAN & CLARK ROCKETS SHOTGUN STEVE WALSH TOP SINGLE BREAKOUT OF THE WEEK REFUGEE - TOM PETTY - BACKSTREET/MCA TOPALBUM BREAKOUT OF THE WEEK PERMANENT WAVES - RUSH - MERCURY WHAT'S IN-STORE TAPE NEWS - Fuji Corporation has announced its marketing plans for the new year. The company will be offering selective dealerships 5% co-op advertising and point of purchase promotion materials. Advertising will also be expanded beyond hi-fi periodicals to general interest publications. A special deal will be offered whereby the purchaser of two FL -90 minute audio cassettes will also receive a free push-button storage case that holds eight tapes (normally $6.95). In the area of blank video tape, Fuji will offer a complete set of point of purchase materials, including a plexiglass display case designed to sit on or behind the counter and hold 150 video cassettes. Each cassette will feature a plastic case and label, which should help to eliminate shedding problems. The company's slogan, "One brand fits all," forms the key thrust of the campaign which is aimed at demonstrating that customers who purchase quality audio tape from Fuji should also purchase video tape products from the same source. CBS PROMOTIONS - A check with the CBS office in New York uncovered these promotional activities now in progress: WNEW-FM and J. & R. Music World conducting a Romantics contest in support of the groups' appearance at the Bottom Line on Valentine's Day. Contestants must submit a Valentine card to the store or radio station describing what they consider their most romantic thought. The contest will run from Feb. 1 to Feb. 8 with the winners chosen on the basis of originality. Grand prize will be a "romantic weekend" at the Playboy Club in Great Gorge, N.J. and a pair of tickets to the group's concert. Second prize will be a holiday dinner, again with free tickets to the show. There will also be 100 runner-up prizes of Romantics LPs . . . Another contest is being run by WKTU and the seven Discomat stores to promote the latest George Duke album, "Master of the Game." In this case, entrants must guess how many keyboards Duke plays on his album. The grand prize here is a weekend trip for two to Game City in Atlantic City, N.J. Twenty-five runners- up will receive the latest CBS albums by Duke, Cheryl Lynn, Jean Carn and Webster Lewis. RCA -MILLENNIUM PUSH - Millennium Records is now involved in a major thrust behind the latest Bruce Cockburn LP and single. The first phase of the campaign was aimed at pre-release awareness. Five thousand teaser postcards were printed for distribution to the press, radio, colleges and retailers. The cards featured the question, "Who is Canada's best kept secret?" with the retail cards' answer reading, "Ask your local RCA sales representative." Other merchandising and marketing aids include a large poster of Cockburn and a special bio on the artist. The second stage of the promotion is now un- derway. Two half-hour radio specials, also in LP form, have been produced featuring the album and interview with Cockburn. The specials, which are being aired in early February over the Thirsty Ear syndicate of 50 college radio stations, will be supported by some 10,- 000 posters and flyers. Budweiser, which is sponsoring the broadcasts, will also participate in the third marketing phase - listening parties at colleges in the top 20 U.S. markets. While MIM is at- tracting interest from within the music in- dustry, festivals scheduled for August are drawing attention to Memphis' past and at- tracting thousands of fans to the music -rich City. MIM was formed in March 1979 to promote the various music interests in Memphis. Cash Box recently talked with David Porter, president of MIM, about the organization and its goals to re-establish Memphis as one of the hubs of the music industry. "We have definitely noticed an increased interest in the Memphis music industry since the formation of MIM," noted Porter. "Since last year there have been a lot of positive things happening. Memphis is the home of Anita Ward (who scored big in 1979 with her disco/pop hit, "Ring My Bell"). Of course the organization didn't cause the record to be a hit, but we made a concerted effort to support it in any way we could. Our organization is a base of support for the music industry here. The feeling is more positive now than it has been in some years." Demise Of Stax The demise of Stax Records in the early '70s was something of a setback for the Memphis music industry. According to Porter, the general feeling was that there was nothing musically happening in Memphis. "People took their beds and walked, so to speak," Porter said of the folding of the legendary Stax label. "For a while, it was a big shock - nobody was doing anything. But it wasn't long before people started working at it again. Now the feeling is we can do it - all over again - we will do it all over again. People are creating again. You've got talents like the Bar -Kays saying 'we're not going anywhere else because it's all here in Memphis.' I think what Memphis once represented is only a fraction of what it will come to represent. "There's a new breed of talent happen- ing, and the old breed of talent is more dedicated than it has ever been. There is a definite, positive attitude that we can recap- ture what Memphis once represented in the music field." Historically, Memphis is known as a predominantly R&B city, but Porter con- tends that the new industry will be representative of all facets of music - from pop to R&B to country. Educating the music industry in Memphis to these different fields of music is part of MIM's function. The organization holds monthly meetings, which feature speakers from different areas of the industry. Porter added that the organiza- tion is also planning a variety of educational seminars, which are presently in the for- mative stages. A nationwide membership drive is also on the agenda. The MIM currently boasts some 100 members, as well as a 15 - member board of governors, including: Porter, David Porter Productions; Cordell Jackson, president of Moon Records; John Fry, owner, Ardent Studios; Lester Snell, arranger/producer; Edgar Mathews, music director for Evelyn "Champagne" King; Warren Wagner, Shoe Productions; Bill Frulla, attorney; Rusty Jones, ASCAP; Jerry Smith, BMI; Harold Streibich, attor- ney/publisher; Evelyn Graves, publisher; Estelle Axton, past owner of Stax Records, president of Fretone Records; Judd Phillips, Sunshine Management; Bob (continued on page 32) Jones, Wynette Together Again NASHVILLE - George Jones and Tammy Wynette are back together again, at least on record, according to an announcement made at a press conference held at Wynette's home last week. Present at the announcement were Wynette, Jones, Paul Richey (Jones' manager) and George Richey, Wynette's husband. It was also announced that Jones has signed with the Jim Halsey Agency in Tulsa and his future performances include duets with Wynette on the Tonight Show and in concert and appearances by the duo on Johnny Cash's upcoming "25th Anniver- sary Special." It has been over two years since Jones and Wynette recorded together. The single just recorded, written by Wynette, was recorded in Muscle Shoals, Ala. and is scheduled for immediate release with an album to follow. Jones will also return to the studio shortly for more recording as a solo artist. - ASCAP GETS PASSLE OF PARTONS - ASCAP recently signed several members of the Parton family to writer membership agreements. THE RHYTHM SECTION SOLAR AT THE TOP - Solar Records' "Second Time Around" by Shalamar is that com- pany's first #1 record, which at the same time was its first certified gold single. Solar recording artists The Whispers, Lakeside, Dynasty and Shalamar will be going on a 70 - date tour starting next month. Dick Griffey, president of the company said, "This will be the first time since the old Motown days that four acts from one company will tour together. The tour will be billed The Solar Galaxy of Stars, and will be a production with several of the acts doing things with each other as opposed to a group doing just its own thing and leaving." THE CONTOURS TO ROCKET - Veteran recording group The Contours have signed with Rocket Records and will release its first single for the label entitled "I'm A Winner" in early February. The group is being produced by Michael Valvano, who has previously been involved with Stevie Wonder, The Supremes, Meat Loaf, Edwin Starr and others. The group was signed to the label by president Barney Ales, who was involved with the group during its first major hits. HOLLAND, DOZIER, HOLLAND AND PINK LADY - The Songwriting/producing team of Holland, Dozier, Holland are in the studio laying down tracks for an upcoming album pro- ject with Japanese recording duo Pink Lady. POP GORDY'S MOVIN UP - Harper & Row Publishers have published the life story of Pop Gordy, who passed away in November of 1978. The autobiography of Pop Gordy's life is entitled "Movin Up," with features and introduction by Alex Haley. RICK JAMES STARTS 50 -CITY TOUR - Motown/Gordy recording artist Rick James will commence a major 50 -city performing tour, which is scheduled to be completed in less than 21'2 months. During the tour, James will be showcasing his back-up band, The Stone City Band, whose debut album entitled "In 'N' Out" will be released before the tour starts. Prince will open the show for James during the tour, which will start Feb. 22 in Ft. Worth, Tex. WLLE IN RALEIGH OFF AIR - The FCC demanded that Raleigh, North Carolina's only black radio station, WLLE, cease all programming last week. The station had had its license revoked in 1976 for fraudulent practices and double billing, and the FCC had gran- ted the station several extensions of its license while management negotiated for a buyer. When no agreement came to pass, the FCC sent the station a telegram last week, ordering it to stop all programming. COIN MACHINE Marofske, Midway President, Broadway Arcade Enjoying Names Executive Committee Eight Percent Annual Growth CHICAGO - David Marofske has been named president of Midway Mfg. Co. of Franklin Park, Ill., a wholly owned sub- sidiary of Bally Manufacturing Corporation of Chicago. Marofske, a 20 -year Midway veteran who served as vice president of manufacturing since 1972, succeeds president Marcine Wolverton, one of the founders of the coin - operated electronic games manufacturing firm. Upon assuming his new post, Marofske announced the formation of an executive committee and named officers to serve on that committee. Dr. Martin Keane, (Ph.D., Engineering) associated with Midway since 1976, joins the executive committee and continues in his capacity as vice president of engineer- ing. Paul Vesper, a 20 -year Midway veteran most recently in charge of the Printed Cir- cuit Department and Electronic Compo- nent Division, was promoted to vice presi- dent of manufacturing. Open House SAN FRANCISCO - Bay Area operators recently gathered at Portale Automatic Sales here to attend a combination open house and new product showing. The occa- sion marked the premier of the new Rock- Ola "Techna" phonograph for Northern California customers and the formal in- troduction of the new Gottlieb pinball line, Exidy Releases New Player Piano SUNNYVALE - Exidy Inc. of Sunnyvale. Calif. is currently in the process of produc- ing and distributing its new pneumatically operated Player Piano series. Three dif- ferent models of the antique piano are be- ing marketed ranging in price and style. All of the new pianos feature the follow- ing: real stained glass panels, player rolls that easily snap in and out for changing, automatic rewind on rolls and completely sealed bearings. Other features such as 180 rolls (10 songs per roll), plastic keyboard covers and special wood are available on the maintenance free pianos. The pianos are not reproductions, but actual pianos converted to air operated player pianos. Production is limited and or- ders are processed as received. which was recently acquired by the dis- tributor in this market. "We are pleased to be representing the Gottlieb products in our San Francisco office," remarked Por- tale president Peter Betti, "and after previewing their upcoming new products I am certain that Gottlieb games will have a strong impact in the 1980 pinball market." Other new products were also shown at the open house and these included Exidy's new sitdown "Tailgunner 2," Game Plan's "Coney Island," Atari's "Asteroids" and a new balloon vendor, "Fanky Malloon" by Vending International. Tom Adams, opera- tions manager of Araven in Santa Clara, was among the enthusiastic attendees who commented about the impressive equip- ment lineup on view. "The Fanky Malloon may have interesting applications in our area," he said, "and we are looking forward Photo coverage appears on page 42. to trying it here." Adams also had high praise for Atari's Asteroids, rating it as "one of the best video games" on the market. Among manufacturer representatives who were on hand to meet with the operators and answer questions were Lila Zinter (Exidy), Tom Petit (Atari), Bill Rickett (Dynamo), Stan Levin (Game Plan), John Holtz (Rock -01a), Don Hutmeyer (Gametronics) and Jerry Vick (Vending In- ternational). Inda Trinwith, games ad- ministration manager for Pizza Time Theater, expressed delight at the oppor- tunity to "meet the manufacturer reps as well as Jerry (Monday) and Peter (Betti) in a congenial atmosphere to learn more about the equipment." Commenting on the products featured, she said, "I was par- ticularly impressed with Tailgunner 2. The sitdown cabinet design and mode of play is especially good for our clientele and this is the type of game that will have high appeal in our locations." (continued on page 42) by Leo Sacks NEW YORK - "There was a time when it was hard to justify the hours we would spend here each day," recalled Steve Epstein, manager and co-owner of the Broadway Arcade, New York's oldest and largest coin -operated amusement center. "Traffic would fluctuate wildly, making it a very long haul at times. But then the City Council legalized the pins in '76, and sud- denly they had achieved a sense of legitimacy. It was as if the market had opened to millions of people - artists, musicians, lawyers, kids from Hells Kitchen, management, prostitutes. Everybody came here. It was a big melting pot." Epstein, 32, has been working at the Ar- cade, located on W. 52nd St., ever since his father, David, and a partner, Albert Simon, purchased the 8,000 -square -foot, split- level facility in 1964. "The store was a white elephant for a long time," he remembered. "Since we're not in the mainstream of the Times Square area, we've always tried to bring the best possible service to our customers. I know what it means to get a fair shake on a machine, because I'm a player myself. I un- derstand the animal; I can relate to it. We're very sensitive to that here." This sort of experience recently guided the multi -operational Arcade to its fourth consecutive eight percent profit increase. According to Epstein, who has won a place among elite American pinball executives for his innovative management, fast, open playfields, and knowledgeable clientele, each one of the Arcade's 50 pinball machines generates approximately $75 a week; an additional 45 video games gross an average of $115 a week, he said. He ex- pects to add another 55 machines by the end of the year. While the company's primary business is coin -operated, it also leases space to Circle Magic, a souvenir and trick shop, and Broadway Billiards, which occupies the building's ground floor and has 27 pool and ping pong tables. The businesses, which are individually owned, were part of the original Arcade when it was built by the amusement corporation of Schork and Schaffer in 1941. A third enterprise, Broadway Nuts, a candy concession, is wholly -owned by the Broadway Arcade. Maintaining Premises Epstein has great personal and professional admiration for his father, who has spent over 30 years in the industry. "I learned about the business from him, and the rules he taught me still stand today," says young Epstein. "Number one is that the playfield must be cleaned every two weeks. THE INTERNATIONAL MUSIC RECORD WEEKLY GEORGE ALBERT President and Publisher MEL ALBERT Vice President and General Manager EDITORIAL VOLUME XLI — NUMBER 40 — February 16, 1980 C4SH BOX Better Days Ahead Just over one month into the ’80s, it is encourag- ing to see the industry once again pursuing a policy of aggressively making the music happen . . . tem- pered by the lessons of the 70s, particularly 1979. With most of the returns programs formulated last year now in effect, as well as more prudent business practices, it appears as though the in- dustry is well on the way to complete recovery from the economic ills of 1979. Most encouraging, though, is the performance of the plethora of new artists who debuted or first broke through during lastyear’ssiump. If a silver lin- ing can be found in the problems of 1979, it must be the numerous new acts that are now ready to release second or third albums. There is now an abundance of new talent in the wings, and this can only be healthy for the industry in the long run. Ranging from new wave to ska to the rise of adult contemporary and country, music is showing a variety and vitality that brings back memories of bet- ter days. In a short while, the industry won’t have to rely on a few “superstar” acts to support whole com- panies. There is quality up and down the rosters of every company, and this can only mean prosperity, both for the short and long runs. 1979 taught the industry some valuable lessons. Having learned these lessons well, the industry can now look forward to a bright future. Asher Discusses Wide Range Of Topics At B’Nai B’rith Meeting by Aaron Fuchs NEW YORK — During a program titled "An Evening With Dick Asher,” the deputy president of CBS Records Group, urged members of the Music and Performing Arts Lodge of the B’Nai B’rith to perceive other facets of the leisure time business as the music industry’s real competition; to con- sider that the axiom that “records are our best entertainment value” may no longer hold true; and to be more selective in choosing artists and material. Asher, who was introduced by Cy Leslie president of CBS Video Enterprises, recalled aspects of his tenure with CBS UK in 1973. At that time, he said, the British MCA Replies To Alexenburg Suit, Files Own Claim LOS ANGELES — MCA, Inc. has filed a reply and a counter claim in a New York federal court to a suit filed by former Infinity Records president Ron Alexenburg asking dismissal of the suit and award of damages resulting from management of the label which was formerly affiliated with the cor- poration. Responding to the $2 million damage de- mand by Alexenburg, which was filed Nov. 28, MCA said that it became apparent that Infinity was not aviableand profitable entity when it was unable to repay more than $1 5 million in advancements from the parent company. Infinity was created by MCA in April, 1978. The Alexenburg suit claimed multiple breach of contract, resulting from moves by MCA to assign infinity artists to the MCA Records label and to terminate much of In- finity’s non-contract staff. The MCA/Alexenburg agreement, of- fered as an exhibit in the original suit, called for advancement of $15 million to Alexen- burg’s management firm (RAA Productions Ltd.) during the management period, which was from June 1, 1978 to Dec. 31, 1984. The MCA reply to Alexenburg’s charges was that Infinity breached its obligation to the company by “grossly mismanaging the business affairs of Infinity.” The counter claim asks the court to award losses in- curred as a result of the alleged mis- management and also the costs of the legal action. MCA contends that Alexenburg rejected attempts by the company “to explore alter- natives designed to reduce expenses and preserve assets of Infinity.” The MCA reply also said that additional attempts by the company to prevent the demise of Infinity met with further resistance from Alexenburg, who, MCA said, offered no viable suggestions of his own. NARM Surveys Status Of Computerization NEW YORK — In an effort to determine the current extent of computerization in the retail and wholesale segment of the record industry, NARM has sent a questionnaire to its regular membership requesting perti- nent information. Information gathered by the question- naire, which was prepared by Michael San- difer, president of ADVCOM, and the NARM staff, will be used in planning future NARM educational workshops on com- puterization. In addition, the questionnaire is intended to provide specific, quantitative information to bolster NARM's campaign to have all recorded product bar coded by the manufacturers. The 1980 NARM convention will hold a seminar on computerization in the 1980s on March 25 at the MGM Grand Hotel in Las Vegas. government reduced the work week to three days because of the country’s ailing economy. “Nevertheless,” Asher pointed out, “within three years we were able to in- crease our sales and profits by 200 to 300 per cent. Using this as an example, Asher urged that “at a time when disposable in- come is shrinking at an alarming rate,” the industry must come to terms with the fact that “we’re not in the music business. We’re in the leisure time business,” and that “our competition is Star Wars, the Yankees, and Spaulding.” Asher warned the audience not to be like the 19th Century railroad ty- coons, “who perceived themselves in the railroad business rather than the transpor- tation business, and wound up being left with vestigial empires.” Asher also advised the industry to try to give the consumer more value for his money. “Our premise has always been that recorded music is the best entertainment buy. Is it true?” He warned that in today’s marketplace, “records are not an obvious best buy.” ‘Edit Out Waste’ The imperative need of the business, ac- cording to Asher, is to “edit out waste, and we haven’t been doing it. Shown at the taping (l-r) are: Nugent and Klein. E/4ST COASTINGS— IT’S MY PARTY AND ... If immodesty may be permitted, Cash Box’s "Dawn of the Decade Bash” was by all accounts the most well received and widely attended party the music business has seen this season. Held Feb. 5 at the Upper East Side club Manhat- tan, the party was attended by such record company notables as Allan Davis, Joe Mansfield, Dick Kline, Larry Palmacci, Paul Smith, Mike Martinovitch, Henry Allen, Nat Weiss, Stuart Siegal, Jerry Jaffe, Mike Leon, Stan Hoffman, Bob Altschuler, Tunc Erim, Randy Roberts, Fred Fioto, Keith Jackson, and Sammy Vargas. Among the celebrities who turned out were Manhattan Borough President Andrew Stein, the Spinners, the Four Tops, Evelyn “Champagne” King, Bernard Edwards and Nile Rogers of Chic, Warded Piper, Carol Douglas and Beverly Johnson. One of the even- ing's highlights was witnessing Doc Pomus and Don Covay, two of rock history’s greatest songwriters, meet and discuss the possibility of collaborating. I also got the chance to tell Jerry Love and Mike Zager, who produced the Spinners’ “Working My Way Back to You,” and John Edwards, who sang lead on it, how glad I was to see this fine singer so sympathetically produced. Special thanks must also be given to club owners Victor and Jay Alfasa and to publicists John Carmen and David Granoff. Finally, though, what I found most gratifying, after more than a decade of being accommodated by record company publicists, was getting the chance to host and accommodate them in return. Another progressive rock station, WSHE in Florida, has joined the long list of stations consulted by Lee Abrams . . . The Know, the group fronted by ex-Blondie Gary Valentine, turns up on a Planet Records ten-track LP sampler . . . Charlie Rich had three gold records stolen from his home in Memphis . . . Jimmy Rogers, who played guitar for the Muddy Waters band when Little Walter played harp, is coming to T ramps on Feb. 22 . . . the Press Office will represent David Bowie . . . Legendary R&B shouter Nappy Brown, who did the original version of Ray Charles' “The Night Time Is the Right Time,” would like to resume performing and recording. He can be reached at (803) 276-8826 . . . Lorimar/CBS will release the soundtrack to “Cruisin,” which will feature new material by Willy Deville (whose third Capitol album will only be released overseas) and Rough Trade. This new group will also back up Warhol star Divine when she debuts “Restless Underwear,” a “rock and roll musical revue,” at the Beacon Theatre Feb. 14 . . . I’ll beat Symphony Hall in Newark on March 9 when Stan Krausse, the man who discovered the Persuasions, puts on a “progressive doo-wop” concert with acts ranging from his house- stopping young protegees, Fourteen Karat Soul, to classic harmonizers like the Clovers and the Charts and headlin- ing neo-doo-woppers the Manhattans. The show will be hosted by Bobby Jay, WELCH HONORED BY RIAA —Neil Welch, the assistant director in charge of the FBI’s New York Division, was presented with an honorary gold record last week for his investigations into record piracy opera- tions. The presentation was made by Jules Yarnell (right), the RIAA’s special anti- piracy counsel. whose excellent Saturday morning doo-wop show on WWRL pulls the station's highest ratings. CELEBRITY BLUES — You would think that legendary guitarist-song writer Steve Cropper had called in enough favors, with the likes of Keith Richards, Mick Jagger, Eric Clapton, and Rod Stewart contributing to his first solo album in over ten years. But the album’s release is being held up indefinitely, pending the vocal contribution on two tracks by the men who brought Cropper back on the road, blues brothers John Belushi and Dan Ackroyd . . . Bravo to MCA’s Nashville office for signing neo-country swingers Asleep at the Wheel. CALLING MISS INFORMATION — Carl Perkins did not have cancer, as was reported here last issue. Perkins was, however, hospitalized for a sinus infection that was ex- erting pressure on the brain, and the situation was scary for a while. Fortunately, medication broke up the infection and, incredibly, Perkins has already resumed tour- ing. Interested parties may take note of the fact that ”01’ Blue Suede” is no longer with Jet Records ... in addition, although last week’s column siaieo that for my money Island president Chris Blackwell has the best “Cars” of any exec in the business, my original copy read best “ears.” aaron fuchs 14 Cash Box/February 16, 1980
