REVIEWS ^LBUM REVIEWS AUTOGRAPH — John Denver ~ RCA AQL 1-3449 — Producer: Milt Okum — List: 7.98 Denver dedicates most of the material on “Autograph" to the mountains and Alaska. The mellow troubadour, who put Colorado on the map as far as the music is concerned, has tur- ned his folkie style into a more streamlined country/MOR style in recent years, and this LP is reflective of that change. There are lots of joyful up-tempo tunes on this album but the finest tunes are the ones of reverence like “Whalebones And Crosses” and the title cut. THE CALL OF THE WILD — Max Demian — RCA AFL1-3525 — Producer: Al Garrison — List: 7.98 Max Demian put out its debut album to a lot of critical acclaim and spotty sales, but this new LP should remedy that problem. The band plays clean, inventive contemporary rock ‘n’ roll that's filled with inventive hooks and witty lyrics. Although the band is rooted in the mainstream, the music is offset by an aloof, Car- sish sound on songs like “Call Of The Wild” and “Slip Away.” This LP is a winner for AOR and the best songs are “Born Senile” and “Bundle ‘A’ Nerves.” SHOOTING STAR — Virgin VA 13133 — Producer: Gus Dudgeon — List: 7.98 While Virgin Records' past has been identified with the rock avant garde (Mike Oldfield and Tangerine Dream) and its pre- sent is characterized by the new wave (XTC and Fingerprintz), the label has never been known for producing a tight, commer- cial mainstream rock act. But that stigma ends with debut LP from Shooting Star. This tightly controlled rock unit has an af- finity for great 4/4 hooks, as well as full bodied ballads. AOR programmers should really sink their teeth into this one. L.A. BOPPERS — Mercury SRM 1-3816 — Producer: Augie Johnson — List: 7.98 The L.A. Boppers are as slick as they come as far as R&B bands are concerned. The bands bouncy, bop doo wop vocal sound is velvety smooth and should catch on fire on the B/C charts. Whether your black contemporary taste runs from street corner symphony to funk to straight ahead R&B this classy L.A. aggregation has all the chops. The boppiest tracks are “Is This The Best," and “Life Is What You Make It.” FLEX — Lene Lovich - Stiff/Epic NJE 36308 — Producers: various — List: 7.98 — Bar Coded This eccentric new wave queen with the bulging eyeballs and pigtails first gained international acclaim in 1978 on Stiff's World Tour, which also gave us Rachel Sweet. Last year’s "Stateless" album was regarded by many to be one of the finest debuts of 1979, and her neurotic, affected vocals are at their peak once again on "Flex.” This time around, Les Chappell (rock’s answer to Mr. Clean) and the boys treat Lovich’s spooky compositions with all the reverence of a synthesized seance. HEARTS UNDER FIRE — Dann Rogers — International Artists I.A. 5000 — Producer: Ian Gardiner List: 7.98 Rogers has put out a rollicking good debut album with "Hearts Under Fire.” He possesses a style that is somewhat reminiscent of Kenny Loggins in its versatility and intensity. He approaches a lot of styles on the album including dramatic folk, streamlined rock, perky R&B, and silky adult contemporary. Both AOR and A/C programmers should like this finely crafted LP. Special guests like Burton Cummings and Delaney and Bonnie help out on this record, which is highlighted by "China,” "Old Mexico" and “I Got The Fever.” DARTS — Polydor PD-1-6250 — Producers: various — List: 7.98 The Darts sell quite well in Europe and there is no reason why this group of ‘50s revivalists can’t capitalize on the current DOR craze in the States. The fine vocal group puts a contemporary sheen on old chestnuts like “Cool Jerk," “It’s Raining” and “Duke Of Earl,” and gives the tunes its own special identity in the process. For those who long to take a stroll down memory lane, but not too far, the Darts are the perfect prescription. MERCURY SHOES — Jesse Barish — RCA AFL 1-3420 — Producers: John Hug and Marty Balin — • List: 7.98 This is the second LP from this fine Bay Area artist, and he has improved a hundredfold since last year's debut. Barrish is a Marty Balin find and has written some songs for the Starship, but he really puts on his rock 'n' roll boots with “Mercury Shoes.” His good time rock sound is FM infectious and com- mercial at the same time, so both AOR and adventuresome Top 40 programmers should pick up on songs like the title cut, “Too Hip To Be Happy” and “Street Music.” WILLIAM OZ — Capitol ST-1205 — Producer: Stewart Levine — List: 7.98 — Bar Coded This brilliantly produced act has the stability and intensity of such Top 40 melodic metal bands as Boston and Foreigner. Oz has a strong rock voice, and his band fuels his material with the power chord fury that we have come to expect from the best ur- ban rock bands. Oz and company do a brilliant heavy metal ver- sion of Holland -Dozier- Holland’s “Stop! In The Name Of Love,” but Oz’s own compositions are also noteworthy. For AOR. AFTER DARK — Andy Gibb — RSO Records RS-1-3069 — Producers: various — List: 7.98 Although this darling of the AM airwaves has a softer vocal style than that of his infamous brothers, it is hard to tell the dif- ference between Andy's LP and a Bee Gees album. However, one can’t deny the accessibility of the platinum, orchestrated pop sound. All of the songs on the LP were written, predictably, by Barry Gibb and the usual RSO session men are on hand for the occasion. The best cuts include “Desire" and an Olivia Newton-John duet, “I Can’t Help It." THE AGE OF PLASTIC — The Buggies — Island ILPS 9585 — Producer: The Buggies — List: 7.98 The Buggies, Trevor Horn and Geofferey Downes, are pur- veyors of the new techno-pop sound. The duo employs intricate production techniques, space age lyrical themes, and possesses a keen pop sensibility. While skeptics might con- demn the Buggies as Alan Parsons with a backbeat, the group has a yen for commercial song hooks and the LP proves to be as much fun as a ride on a space shuttle. VICTIMS OF FURY — Robin Trower — Chrysalis CHR 1215 — Producers: Emerick and Trower — List: 7.98 — Bar Coded Trower has always been considered one of the most dis- tinctive guitar stylists in rock, and his thunder and lightning axe technique makes “Victims Of Fury” his most superbly realized work since the groundbreaking “Bridge Of Sighs” LP. Bill Lor- dan’s kinetic drumming and the haunting vocals of James Dewar are an integral part of the sound, but it is Trower’s fret- board pyrotechnics that are clearly the center of attraction here. END OF THE CENTURY — The Ramones — Sire SRK 6077 — Producer: Phil Spector — List: 7.98 There have been a dozen copy bands, but no one can reproduce the pile-driving punk sound of the Gabba Gabba Hey boys. The Ramones sound better than ever on “End Of The Century,” and this time the pogo power is given even more of a lift by legendary producer Phil Spector. The band’s music is becoming a staple at DOR clubs around the country, and the jackhammer rock attack on this LP is paced by “Danny Says,” “This Ain't Havana” and “Rock ‘n’ Roll High School." YOU CAN GET CRAZY — Bellamy Brothers — Warner Bros. BSK 3408 — Producer: Michael Lloyd — List: 7.98 The Bellamy Brothers are quickly turning into one of the most appealing contemporary country acts around. The duo has the perfect feel for laid back drifting ballads that are as comfortable on country stations as they are on A/C outlets. The twosome is refining the sound that Jimmy Buffett pioneered with his soothing Latin and Caribbean acoustic rhythms. Top cuts in- clude “Sugar Daddy,” “Dead Aim” and "I Could Be Makin’ Love To You.” AIR POCKET — Roger Powell — Bearsville BRK 6994 — Producer: Roger Powell — List: 7.98 — Bar Coded The supersonic rocket Roger Powell normally travels on, Utopia, apparently has a space shuttle attached to it that Powell has hopped into and shot away from the mother ship. On his own, Utopia’s keyboardist nimbly swoops and soars his way through the full gamut of keyboard product available for com- mercial use. An AOR gem and, yes, Todd kept out of the booth on this one. TAROT SUITE — Mike Batt & Friends — Epic NJE 36312 — Producer: Mike Batt — List: 7.98 For over a decade, Mike Batt has been a hit making producer/arranger about (London) town, keeping a very low profile while in the process. His name is now on the front of an album cover and it’s his brainchild alone. The premise of this awesome rock symphonic production is a musical interpreta- tion of various T arot card characters. A more ambitious, talent- heavy production has yet to emerge this year. Guest shots range from the London Symphony Orchestra to Rory Gallagher. I’M A ROCKER — Mike Berry — Epic/Cieveland International — Producer: Miki Dallon — List: 7.98 Mike Berry's heart is in ‘50s leather and he possesses a sound that recalls Roy Wood and the early ELO days, but he emphasizes the Buddy Holly half more than the Beethoven. The songs on "I’m A Rocker” are chain gang tough in drive, but he tempers the sound with sleek harmonies and strings. The first side of this waxing has a contemporary hard rock feel, but side two is filled with roots rock ‘n’ roll covers and biographical tunes. PLANET OF LOVE YOU CAN GET OFF ON THE MUSIC — Le Pamplemousse — AVI 6080 — List: 7.98 Le Pamplemousse (“Grapefruit” in French) found success with last years "Le Spank” and it should fare well on the B/C charts with its new effort. The group has a bright funky sound that is filled with synthesizer meanderings and surprise horn blasts, and it is perfect music for the dancin' crowd. While the band won't win any contest for originality, the spirited vocals of Carmen Twillie and the girls are irresistible. j Cash Box/February 16, 1980 15

Generating on-the-spot sales, plus helpful exposure for the artist, label and retailer, in-stores can have both short and long-term benefits for all involved parties. “Some of the benefits are obvious,” said Ira Heilicher, whose Great American Music Company in Minneapolis, Minn, has spon- sored several successful in-stores featur- ing country artists, including one by Con- way Twitty that attracted 3,500 people and resulted in approximately 700 sales. “A good in-store brings people to the store who may have never been there before. “You put your best foot forward, and the people may say, ‘Hey, this is a unique place.’ Hopefully they’ll store this impres- sion somewhere in the back of their minds, and when they want a record, they’ll come to us again.” Nevertheless, with the recent economic pinch in the record industry, many record labels have begun to reevalute the effec- tiveness of in-stores. With auxiliary ex- penses being trimmed by the labels, more selective processes for justifying in-stores are being used. Retailers Cautious In addition, retailers are no longer ran- domly participating in in-store functions. They, too, are approaching the promotional ploy with a more pragmatic, economic eye. “In-stores for everyone seem to be on the decline,” noted David Counter, area manager for the Disc Records chain in Dallas. “It’s getting too complicated to get artists to do them — you have to involve managers and so many people. I guess the labels are also afraid that there won’t be a good turnout and that the artist’s manage- ment will jump on them.” Thus, to insure a successful in-store promotion, a cohesive flow between the retailer and label is an obvious step. While most retailers queried suggested that labels offer more advertising support, label representatives suggested that retailers be more aggressive in putting together their own promotional tactics, beyond what sup- port the label offers. “Aggressive accounts (retailers) sponsor the most successful in-store appearances,” noted Stan Byrd, national promotion, War- ner Bros. Country. “Accounts that go a few steps beyond the advertising support a label offers are accounts that are going to have a successful in-store. Advance publicity is one of the most important aspects of any in-store appearance.” Labels Must Help Heilicher agreed with that summation, but added, “the manufacturer should always support an in-store with the proper amount of media advertising, whether it be print or radio. In alot of cases, the manufac- turers should drop a lot of their rules. The object of an in-store is to get as many peo- ple as possible to the store — to expose them to the acts and product.” Advanced publicity includes all media exposure possible, including radio and print advertising. Signs posted in the store as well as in the surrounding neighborhood prior to the event are invaluable. Some retailers and labels even venture so far as to work with local radio in doing a remote from the store during the artist’s appearance. Selecting the correct venue for a par- ticular artist is also an important considera- tion. John Jump, sales manager with MCA Records, Minneapolis, suggested that (continued on page 31) CMF Library Opens Audio-Restoration Lab NASHVILLE — A new audio restoration facility has been opened at the Country Music Foundation Library and Media Cen- ter, making it possible to restore the sound on pre-stereo recordings to their original quality. The Audio Restoration Laboratory built by Art Shifrin, is the most sophisticated facility in the United States for restoring sound on pre-stereo recordings to top quality, according to spokesmen at the Foundation. The laboratory is the result of over 18 months of planning and construc- tion. In addition to handling Country Music Foundation sound restoration projects, the Laboratory will be especially useful to record companies involved in reissuing historical recordings. "Our laboratory is capable of producing master tapes from original recordings, test pressings, transcriptions, and early tape master,” said Danny Hatcher, the founda- tion’s deputy director for library operations. The Audio Restoration Laboratory has complete variable speed, two-track recording capabilities for quarter-inch tape. Its basic mastering machines are full- track mono. The lab contains over 30 pieces of equipment, including two master- ing machines, sound filtering and equaliza- tion equipment, special styluses for dif- ferent record groove, sizes, turntables and noise suppression units designed es- pecially for audio restoration work. The first was a silver album for William 's current album, "Portrait, " reaching sales of 250,000 pounds sterling and the second was for Most Popular Artist of The Decade as a result from a poll in "Country Music People," a top country publication in Europe. Better Utilization Of Artist In-Stores (continued from page 29) retailers as well as label representatives working on in-stores should befamiliar with the demographics of the host-store’s neighborhood. Specifically, if a country ar- tist is going to appear in a store, that store should be located in a neighborhood or area that supports country music. “People will drive a distance for a con- cert, but it is better to have an artist appear in a store that has a built-in audience — fans within the neighborhood,” noted Jump. The artist can also be the key to a suc- cessful in-store. Heilicher noted that the most successful in-stores are done with ar- tists who are easily recognizable as popular singles artists, citing the previously men- tioned example of Conway Twitty’s ap- pearance. Still, there is also room for those who are not so well known. “It seems to me that the labels are not taking the time to help new and up-and-coming artists the way they should," said Lee Perron, manager of Friends Two Records in Oklahoma City. “This is unfortunate, especially for the new acts, because they are not getting the extra exposure that would help them along in their careers. New Artists "We like working with a new artist because it makes us look better,” Perron added. “It shows that we are pulling for them. There's more satisfaction in seeing a new artist sell." Nevertheless, while attracting potential customers to the store is the most impor- tant aspect of an in-store, having enough product on hand to fill those customers needs is probably second on the priority list. An adequate representation of the ar- tist’s entire catalog is preferable. THE COUNTRY COLUMN There’s no denying that Crystal Gayle is one of those universal artists who enjoy across the board success. But what does she think about the “popular” sound that seems so prevalent in so much of today's country music? Of course she appreciates the success. (What artist wouldn’t?) She is quoted as saying she would like to see more “country” in country television shows. Reportedly after last year’s CMA Awards, (which was one of the most popular television shows on that night), Gayle felt that the show “could have involved more of the country- roots, instead of just all crossover artists. That seems to be all that performs anymore — myself or Dolly, or you know ... I see that makes for good television publicity or whatever, but I think (the other way) would be more entertaining. I really think it would be nice to have some of the old sounds on here, the roots, and let people get an all- around picture of country music.” Perhaps the '80s will be the decade that country music returns to its roots. By the way, Gayle and Barbara Mandrell are reportedly two of the top contenders for the lead role in “Best Little Whore House In Texas.” Winning that role would cause quite a change of images for either woman. Last week Kenny Rogers claimed the top spot in the Cash Box Top 100 Singles chart, and made a bit of history for Jack Clement Studio in Nashville. The Larry Butler-produced, Billy Sherrill- Crystal Gayle engineered single marks the first time a single cut at Clement’s studio has reached the#1 position in the pop charts. We must note, it certainly isn’t unusual for the country chart. It is interesting to also note that two other singles that were mixed or recorded in Nashville are firmly seated in the pop charts — Dan Fogelberg’s "Longer” and Steve For- bert’s “Romeo’s Tune.” John Conlee is preparing for the ’80s with a new Silver Eagle Bus, and a new five-piece band to go with it. Joining Conlee will be Steve Sechlar, Willie Hall, Terry Crisp, Gregg Sides and Mickey Grimm. Conlee just completed a new album, and is preparing to begin a tour with Marty Robbins and the Kendalls in late February. Conlee's not the only one adding new members to a band. The Oak Ridge Boys recently welcomed three new members: Pete Cummings, Fred Satterfield and Ron Fairchild, who is a second generation Oak. His father, Tommy, had a 14-year tenure with the group as pianist. The rest of the band is comprised of Don Breland, Skip Mitchell and Garland. Ending his fifth year as host of “Grand Ole Country” in Toronto, Ronnie Prophet has been named Male Performer of the Year by RPM. He also captured the Juno Country Male Vocalist of the Year award twice, including 1979. Prophet’s show has won the RPM Big Country Award for the past three consecutive years as TV Show of the Year. The Oak Ridge Boys will soon be making an IT&T radio commercial. To celebrate the sixth birthday of their granddaughter Stephanie, Kitty Wells and Johnny Wright bussed the child’s entire kindergarten class to McDonalds. Mike Moss, owner of the 900-seat Plantation Dinner Theatre and the 600-seat Barn Din- ner Theatre, was recently presented a special commendation from Tandy Rice, Top Bill- ing, on behalf on the CMA. The commendation cited Moss for his extraordinary support of country music. In the past, Dolly Parton, Crystal Gayle, Porter Wagoner, Brenda Lee, The Oak Ridge Boys, among others, have appeared at his establishments. Brenda Lee will be recording a portion of the soundtrack for “Smokey and the Bandit II” as well as try her hand at acting. She’s not sure how big her role will be, but sh e expects to have a good time working on the film. With Burt Reynolds as star, who could help but have a good time. When you get involved with politics, you better be prepared for the consequences. Storyteller Tom T. Hall has been actively campaigning for President Carter during the two- month hiatus from his own touring. But Hall has learned that politicking has its ups and downs. After the Iowa caucus, Hall left immediately for the Huntsville, Ala. Carter kick-off. In Columbia, T enn., however, the weather got a bit testy, causing Hall’s limo to skid into a four foot ditch. No one was hurt, but it took the wrecker so long to remove the lengthy limo from the ditch, Hall missed out on that kick-off. jennifer bohler Tom T. ON JAZZ WENT DOWN TO ST. JAMES INFIRMARY — It saddens all of us at Cash Box to note the passing of one of America’s most ebullient and influential musicians, pianist Professor Longhair (aka Henry Roeland Byrd). Professor Longhair was one of the seminal figures in the origins of the New Orleans sound. By combining barrelhouse blues and boogie woogie with Caribbean rhythms, Professor Longhair helped initiate a new kind of R&B, which in turn had an enormous effect on the birth of rock and roll — what Muddy Waters was to the Chicago blues, Longhair was to New Orleans R&B. The Professor’s good-time music and rollicking piano syncopations were an important influence on such people as drummer Earl Palmer (one of the first men to play the trademark New Orleans rhythms), saxophonist Lee Allen, and keyboardists Fats Domino, Huey “Piano” Smith, Mac “Dr. John” Rebennack and Allen Toussaint. Longhair, who first started recording in 1949, had been in fine spirits during his Saturday night gig at the Tipitina in New Orleans, but he died in his sleep on Jan 30 at the age of 61 , only one day after the release of his last recording, “Crawfish Fiesta" on Alligator. “It was horribly ironic,” said Bruce Iglauer, the producer of “Crawfish Fiesta.” “To record Professor Longhair was a longstanding dream of mine, and during the months of preparation together we’d become good friends. It’s a wonderful album, and Professor Longhair felt it ex- pressed everything he wanted to do on a record, so for him to die like this, at this time, is terribly upsetting.” New Orleans gave one of their own a bittersweet send- off, with two brass bands, a 3,000-person parade, piano playing by Toussaint and a eulogy by Jerry Wexler. Though Professor Longhair’s death is a particularly cruel winter wind, the celebratory nature of a New Orleans funeral reminds us not to mourn his departure but to celebrate the life dance he set in motion. As Toussaint put it, “he’s the Bach of Rock.” Thank you Prof., and so long. COMINGS AND GOINGS — A pair of weekend gigs by Weather Report and The World Saxophone Quartet demonstrated that the state of both electric and acoustic jazz is healthy and growing. In their spectacular Beacon Theatre performance, Weather Report showed that the widely circulated stories of their demise are vastly exaggerated. I’ve never heard this band play with as much power and grace. They synthesized both the electronic freedom and symmetry of the "I Sing The Body Electric” period and the pan-ethnic funk of their post-“Sweetnighter” music in an astonishing presentation of new compositions, special lighting effects and a historical slide show (using Duke Ellington’s venerable “Rocking In Rhythm” as the musical foreground). Yes, but is it jazz? It most assuredly is. Jazz can no longer be neatly categorized and filed away, artificially separated from other musics. Instead jazz is like a great musical umbrella that can translate and transform all musical genres into a cohesive whole. From the swift, hard bop of their opening number, Weather Report proved that they were greater than the sum of their parts, each individual offering a different musical and cultural perspective: Peter Erskine, a powerful modern jazz-rock drummer, gave the group the drive of a big band, sometimes sounding like Buddy Rich paraphrasing Harry Partch; the new percussionist, Robert Thomas was ex- ceptionally sensitive, providing both pan-ethnic folk rhythms and a kinetic visual dimen- sion with his cobra-wristed conga drumming; Jaco Pastorius kept his theatrical postur- ings to a minimum, and contributed scintillating counterpoint and rumbling bass modula- (contirwed on page 44) TURRENTINE AT WRVR - Elek- tra/Asylum's Stanley Turrentine recently played at Carnegie Hall in New York. While in town he stopped by radio station WRVR for an on-the-air interview. Pictured are (l-r): Herschel. DJ. WRVR; Pat Prescott. DJ. WRVR; Stanley Turrentine. and Jim Platt, program director, WRVR. BSK-3379 — Producer: Michael Colina — List: $7.98 David Sanborn offers more potential crossover product here, with the title cut and “Creeper” as purely dance music. “Carly’s Song" and “Lisa" are appropriately more mellow songs, best suited for dinner and cocktails with the spouse. Sanborn's sax- ophone work never ceases to be lyrical, which is the common fiber linking the LP's material to more pop oriented pieces like “Anything You Want,” co-written by Sanborn and the Doobies’ Mike McDonald. SPECIAL EDITION — Jack Dejohnette — ECM 1-1152 — Producer: Jack DeJohnette — List: $7.98 This album makes a space case for traditional jazz, as De- johnette, with help from altoist Arthur Blythe and tenorist David Murray, makes cuts like “Zoot Suite” and “One For Eric” sound like fully-textured standards. “Journey to the Twin Planet” is a tasteful space excursion best described as intertextured sounds, tied to playfully atonal counterpoint. A cover of John Coltrane's "Central Park West” provides an appropriate diver- sion from the space race. SPIRIT CHASER — Leo Smith — Nessa N-19 — Producer: Chuck Nessa — List: $7.98 Leo Smith is a powerful trumpet and flugelhorn master with deep roots in both ethnic musics and modern classicism; he is developing his own unique brand of sound, a free-form folk music. The music here ranges from an exquisite piece for three harps and trumpet to the staggered, asymetrical rhythms of drummer Pheeroan ak Laff and bassist Wes Brown on the title tune’s open-ended discussion. Cuts like "Acufunkture,” “CMS," and“Flip City” are strictly for movement, while “Commuter Rab- bit (For Folon),” “After,” and “Nice ‘N’ Sleazy" provide easy listening funk. All the music is endlessly punctuated by the sassy sax of David Woodford. “Blue Lodge” is the mellowest of- fering on this disc. WHALE CITY — Dry Jack — Inner City IC-1075 — Producer: Dry Jack — List: $7.98 The second Inner City LP from this band is more of the com- petent, unobtrusive music characterizing previous efforts. David Lamb’s keyboards act as a hitching post for the fusion sounds, which range from electronic space to be-bop to con- tempo jazz. “Neener Nawner (pts. I&ll)” is for relaxation; “Wimpy Thing” stirs up some funk; and the title cut is for deep thought. SPIRAL — Bobby Hutcherson — Blute Note LT-996 — Producers: Alfred Lion, Francis Wolff and Duke Pearson — List: $7.98 The innovative vibist’s 1965 recording sounds as bold and fresh as anything called modern jazz in 1980. These elliptical, melodic compositions fall halfway between the bop of Bird, Rollins and Miles and the "new thing” of Coltrane, Coleman and T aylor. Hutcherson sounds like a ballerina dancing on glass, es- pecially on his dreamy ballad, “Visions." The unheralded Joe Chambers and Stanley Cowell are brilliant throughout, and on the climactic “Jasper,” Sam Rivers, Freddie Hubbard, Andrew Hill, and Richard Davis burn the joint down. 36 Cash Box/February 16. 1980

THE RHYTHM SECTION MORE TELEVISION FOR THE BAR-KAYS — In Los Angeles taping some television shows, The Bar-Kays are laying down a new game plan for their career. James Alexander, spokesperson from the group, says, "We had always been on the road so much that we never had time to do any television shows. Last year the group did over 125 dates. This year, we will do 35 dates during the summer, 35 during the fall, cutting our touring time way down. We are extending time for producing other groups and are presently involved with our manager/producer Allen Jones, who is producing a group called Quick.” SOUNDTRACKS — Linda Clifford will be recording a single for upcoming film called “Fame". The storyline of the film surrounds a children's school of acting, music and dance. The soundtrack will be on RSO Records with other participants to be announced soon. RECORDASWESNORE — Veteran guitarist Tony Drake discovered a new twist when he recorded his uncle sleeping and put music to it. The single is called "Uncle Nate’s Dream” on Sonny Graver’s Stanson Records. The record is starting to get some national attention, and Graver commented that he has received letters from radio people discussing the uni- queness of the record. The title of the album is “Me and My Drums” and is actually a product of Paul Humphrey (Lawrence Welk’s drummer) and Drake, with the two of them playing all the instruments. For more information call (213) 874-6204. GAYNOR AROUND THE WORLD — Gloria Gaynor is embarking on a worldwide tour of 37 countries, starting at the South American Music Festival in Chile, Feb. 10-11. Gaynor will also go to Tokyo, southeast Asia, the Middle East, England, Rumania and Bulgaria. She is presently finishing her new album with Dino Fekaris, in association with Freddie Perren, and will be back in the States to support the release of the new album, which is scheduled for late April. RUFFIN/GIBB COLLABORATION — The single “Hold On To My Love,” by Jimmy Ruffin was produced by Robin Gibb and will be released on RSO Feb. 13. Ruffin and Gibb are presently in the studio completing the remainder of the album. TEDDY GUEST AT MEDICAL BENEFIT — Teddy Pendergrass will be a guest at a party benefitting the Atlantic City Medical Center Minority Appeals Committee during his first appearance at an Atlantic City hotel Casino. TRIBUTE TO WAR — Soul Train recently taped a tribute to the group War, honoring the ten years they have been in the business. The show, which included film clips and special choreography done by the Soul T rain Dancers, paid tribute to the longevity the group has had in the recording industry. It will be shown throughout the country at different times. “Q” and BENSON WRITING — Wanting to take George Benson’s upcoming album in a totally new direction, producer Quincy Jones has decided that all the searching for the right songs may have been in vain. i/iLtN r SANTA MONICA CIVIC — Parliament/ Funkadelic do no more harm with their highly orchestrated lunacy than do TV com- mercials. But after their show, your enure body (and if you follow their instructions, especially your booty) will be tired and you may have to be carried out. Tuesday, Jan. 29, the first of a four-day concert set at the Santa Monica Civic Auditorium, was no exception, as the entire cast of zany, funked-up characters created by P/F mastermind George Clinton pinned the tail on the funky during the group’s “Gloryhaliastoopid” show. While a few overzealous funkers had to be ejected from the proceedings, the P- Funk movement music had the audience rockin’ and funkin' for nearly four hours with a balanced mixture of new and used funk. The first half of the show featured for- mer Spinners lead singer Philippe Wynn, who sang the lead role in the ‘‘Uncle Jam Wants You” episode. Later, P/F keyboard master Bernie Worrell, along with young guitarist Mike ‘‘Magic'' Hampton, burned the cotton out of artificial funkers’ ears with the now classic ‘‘Maggot Brain.” Dr. Funkenstein himself did not appear until the second half of the show. Arriving on stage, resplendent in glittering cowboy hat and chaps, over a black body shirt, Clin- ton pranced about, exhorting the audience to quit fakin’ the funk, and to stay on their feet. While the tactic worked, the spon- taneity of previous Parliament/Funkadelic outings, which include a variety of visual ef- fects (most popular of which is the landing of the Mothership) seemed lacking. Philippe Wynn's contribution throughout the show was well-received, but during his presence on stage, especially during his rendition of the Spinners' hit “Sadie," hardcore funk gave way to more subdued showmanship. michael martinez B ob James & Earl Klugh DOROTHY CHANDLER PAVILION, L. A. — The second in this year's “Jazz Series” program, this presentation of the team that came up with the "One On One" LP ( Tap- pan Zee/Columbia ) provided a pleasant and well-executed show on this winter's eve. Bob James' keyboards and Earl Klugh's guitar have collaborated enough times in the past and both jazzists’ styles comple- ments the other so completely that the audience knew more or less what to expect, and that is exactly what it got. Though hindered at times by rather amateurish lighting, James and Klugh paced the show well, moving through cuts from their own individual albums as well as from “One On One.” The show opened with an exciting version of the “Theme From Taxi," which generated a rousing reception that got the set off on the right foot. From then on, the show was comprised almost equally of Klugh's and James' songs. On “Vanetta," Klugh got serious and played some top-notch jazz, and James ' stretched out on “Westchester Lady," collaborating with the keyboards to get the audience moving. Another highlight of the evening was the drumming of Harvey Mason. A solid professional, Mason displayed a lot of style and flair throughout the set and, combined with Perry Hughes' rhythm guitar, Gary King’s bass and Dr. Gibbs’ percussion, provided a solid and exhilarating rhythm throughout for the headliners. Veteran reedman Ray Pizzi opened the show with a truly inspired performance spotlighting his new Discovery LP, “The Love Letter.” Highlight of the set was “Willow Creek,” featuring a wild bassoon solo by Pizzi. Pizzi should be around for some time to come. richard imamura K ris Kristofferson & Willie Nelson THE FORUM, L.A. — One could tell by the bloated beer lines atThe Forum during Kris Kristofferson’s performance that most of the L.A. cowboy contingentwastheretosee the chief outlaw himself — Willie Nelson. The Forum concert marked the first time the two country-western music legends have been paired in concert. The mini-tour seemed inevitable since Nelson decided to record an album of Kristofferson's tunes. Though warmly received initially, Kristof- ferson failed to generate much energy dur- ing his performance, which was largely due to the melancholy nature of his songs, many of which were not suited for the singer's vocal qualities. During the set, the audience seemed to take as much interest in people wearing unique cowboy garb. But when Willie hit the set, The Forum’s beer and bathroom lines evaporated, leav- ing the Forum foyer looking like a ghost town. Nelson and his Family Band made the crowd yelp, stomp boot-clad feet and wave enough cowboy hats to qualify for a card stunt section at the Rose Bowl game. Adding to the excitement were guitarist Grady Martin and fiddle player Johnny Gimble, both much-respected Nashville sessionists, whose galvanizing solos raised yelp and hoot decibels tremendously. Eventually, members of the group, celebrity fans and other musicians joined Nelson on stage to close the show. Jane Fonda and Dyan Cannon graboed tam- bourines and strutted about the stage as Nelson closed the show with two famous outlaw songs, "Mamas, Don't Let Your Babies Grow Up to Be Cowboys” and “My Heroes Have Always Been Cowboys,” which Nelson sings in the film “The Electric Horseman. ” Despite the hoopla on stage, nothing could detract from Willie’s show, which was the reason all those would-be-cowboys assembled in the city-slicked Forum. michael martinez THE ROXY, L.A. — If anyone could transform the art deco ambience of this Hollywood nightspot into the raucous at- mosphere of a Chicago blues bar, it would be Muddy Waters. Although the sweat, sawdust and pitchers of cold Old Style beer were noticeably missing during Waters' re- cent series of SRO shows here, the blues master's folksy rapport and raw-edged slide guitar brought a bit of State Street to the Sunset Strip. Perhaps more than any other performer this side of Milwaukee, Waters’ stage reper- toire offers a perfect primer of Chicago blues for the uninitiated. After a trio of rollicking instrumentsls by his six-piece backing band, highlighted by some fine harmonica work by Jerry Portnoy and lead guitar picking by Bob Margolin, the Blue Sky recording artist strode onstage amid hoots and howls and worked his way into Big Joe Williams’ “Baby, Please Don’t Go.” A rendition of Sonny Boy Williamson’s "Nine Below Zero” continued the smoideringly gritty groove, perfectly evok- ing the hard Chicago winters. “They Call Me Muddy Waters," the bluesman’s signature piece, developed the call and response between Waters and the crowd even further. Things really started getting hot after “Rock Me, Baby" and “Everything’s Gonna Be Alright,” with its rousing, spiritual chorus. Hoochie coochie man Waters tur- ned on the gas, though, with his final num- ber, “Mannish Boy,” as he leapt off his stool and stalked the lip of the stage, shaking the microphone stand and bringing the crowd to near-fever pitch. An encore of “Got My Mojo Workin’ ” was equally as effective and Waters left the stage with the entire audience on its feet screaming for more. A finer display of traditional Chicago blues mixed with bits of contemporary instrumentation and show- manship would be hard to find . . . anywhere. Opening the show was perhaps one of the most underrated and little known ladies of the blues, Etta James. James is a belter of considerable vocal prowess, as she ex- hibited with some improvising sans microphone. However, her choice of material, with the exception of “T ell Mama” and her closing number, “I’d Rather Be Blind," left something to be desired. Covers of mainstream pop tunes such as the Eagles' “Take It To The Limit,” Janis Joplin's “Piece Of My Heart” and Kiki Dee’s “Sugar On The Floor” seemed ill-suited to her wailing blues style. mike glynn THE WHISKY, L.A. — Still reeling from receiving her very firstGrammy nomination days earlier, petite powerhouse Cindy Bullens totally exhausted a packed house of fans with a healthy set of exemplary rock 'n' roll. Opening up with the one-two punch of “Anxious Heart” from her first and only United Artists LP, "Desire Wire,” the dirty blonde-haired, androgynous Bullens, decked in a black jumpsuit, leapt into her performance with an aggressive fervor rarely matched by a female rock artist. Although her show hasn’t changed much since the last time she played this venue, both her loyal following and the uninitiated hung on her every stage movement, whether pouncing atop the piano during the sexually provocative “Willie All-Night" or demonstrating her two-step boogie shuffle during “Real To Reel.” Her stage mannerisms, a blend between Mick Jagger and Suzi Quatro, underscored a natural self-confidence in her equally strong reper- toire of original compositions. Dedicating one number to her new label, Casablanca, she ripped through a number of tunes from her current LP, “Steal The Night,” including the title cut and her char- ted single, the jumpy pop-rocker “Trust Me." However, the high point of the set was undoubtedly the title cut from her first aibum and a razor sharp version of “Sur- vivor," the song that has earned her the Grammy nomination. Aided by the standout performance of her four-member backup unit, with special special mention to the slick guitar playing of Mark Doyle and the excellent drum work of Thom Mooney, both also members of David Werner's group, she sent the crowd home with a series of smart encores, in- ON SMGE eluding the much-requested “Finally Rockin’.” Once again, Bullens proved her- self to be a legitimate contender for the female heavyweight rock crown. mike giynn WHISKEY A GO GO, CANNES - Amongst the many live showcase performances at MIDEM this year, one of the most in- teresting and refreshingly original acts to be seen was the Icelandic Fireband. Spawned from a very small country and initially aimed at an equally tiny market (gold disc is 5,000), the Fireband revealed some fresh northern talent that deserves to infiltrate other larger territories around the world. The group’s record company, Icelandic Recordings & Music Inc., spon- sored Fireband’s three-night Cannes stint in a substantial bid for international atten- tion and recognition. And they got it, for although Iceland is small, Fireband proved that its talent can be large and dynamic. The nine-piece group, consisting of four female vocalists and five musicians, performed a sophisticated and endearing set of Icelandic material mainly sung in English, with the occasional well- known rock standard thrown in to prove all- round virtuosity. The musical platform was basically funk R&B, interspersed with a mixture of Anglo- American pop-rock. And though their music showed an interesting cross- pollination of foreign styles, an overall Icelandic ethnic-folk stamp gave the music depth and freshness and an original appeal that could never be duplicated. The songs delivered some poignant melodies backed up with a fine musical thrust, which included some outstanding brasswork and a lot of devious intricate basswork. Visually, the group’s high- fashion camp stance is nothing less than aesthetically stylish — all four of the female vocalists would look at home in the highest Paris fashion house. The group's male contingent also held a jet set elegance befitting any major rock star, and with the all-round intrinsic talent to back up the projected visuals, Fireband’s well-groomed musical and visual approach seems strong enough to crack larger foreign markets. nick underwood BOTTOM LINE, N.Y.C. — This grouping of former sidemen of Charles Mingus's Jazz Workshops has been playing in the Apple, and elsewhere, since being formed by Mingus’s widow, Sue Graham Mingus, to perpetuate the late bassist’s music. There have been some personnel changes, but things seemed to have settled on Ted Cur- son, trumpet, Jimmy Knepper, trombone, John Handy, alto sax, Dannie Richmond, drums, and Mike Richmond, bass. Pianist Hugh Lawson, and tenor sax man George Adams were last minute subs for this date. The band is much tighter than it has been on other occasions. The leadership seems to have been firmly (and wisely) taken by Richmond, a longtime Mingus alter-ego. The arrangements are by Sy Johnson, for the most part, as delineated on the band's first Elektra album. "Chair In The Sky." Interestingly, the audience remained through the entire late-night marathon, of- fering a standing ovation at its conclusion. arnold jay smith

Monk Managing Van Halen On Road To Inf I Success (continued from page 10) a record these days, a company will not put you out for more than three to five weeks.” Monk explains that in the future it’s going to be a test for the industry to try to break new acts with a single, as tours are being cut extensively. He insists that the labels desperately need to strengthen their artist development departments and promotion staffs because of this dilemma. Although Monk says that recession has not hurt Van Halen in the area of tour sup- port, it has created the group’s biggest current problem — finding a strong open- ing act. It has also affected the quartet in other small ways. “If the label can’t afford to give us alimoand a photographer to go visit radio stations or the trades, then we’ll go anyway," offers Monk. “It’s up to us to pick up the slack. In addition, they used to buy a tremendous amount of tickets for each show in L.A., and this year we’re giving them the tickets. It helps Warner Bros, loosen up the budget so they can concen- trate on the new talent.” Recessionary moves aside, Monk main- tains that the business of touring has changed drastically since hefirst broke into the business as Blue Cheer's road manager in 1967. "When they first started out Blue Cheer got killed on the road," recalls Monk. “Their label (Phillips) put them out on tour with a lot of money and no real guidance. Two of the members developed real bad (drug) habits, and the albums sold less and less. Now, a company !ikeWarnerBros.,for instance, have people like Carl Scott and Henry Gere to look after these acts, and that's why they put me on the case.” After his stint with Blue Cheer, Monk, who came out of Franklin Marshall College and the legitimate theater as a lighting designer, joined Bill Graham and the staff at the newly opened Fillmore East in 1968. The New York born and raised manager ran the legendary venue’s sound department in 1968 and became stage manager in 1969. He also took the crew up to Woodstock for that legendary three-day affair. In 1970 he left the Fillmore staff and jour- neyed to England where he worked for The Moody Blues. Later he handled security on several Rolling Stones European tours, then returned to the U.S. to become Johnny Cash's sound man. In recent years he has worked as road manager for Tom Waits and in an artist development capacity for Warner Bros. Prior to his becoming overseer of Van Halen, Monk was the road manager on the controversial Sex Pistols tour of America. The energetic manager is adamant about the idea that Van Halen's world wide acclaim has not led to ego absorption, and insists that the band's down to earth quality is the key to successful promotional cam- paigns. “We will never become a snot- nosed platinum band,” states Monk. “We do in-stores because an in-store means that the kids who are 12 and 13, an age where mom and dad won’t let them go to the show, can come and say hello and get autographs. There is a real intimacy there. They also love to go into radio stations and play DJ and relate to their fans. The band likes doing these promotions, so we don’t feel it is pimping the group in any way.” Although it is a bonafide platinum act in the U.S. and Canada, Van Halen (currently gearing up for a national tour that begins April 1 in Vancouver), will be concentrating on the weaker international markets in 1980. "We're trying to break in new areas like South America and Scandinavia, and someday we hope to crack South Africa," says Monk, who travelled to Africa last year on a promotional tour with lead singer David Lee Roth and drummer Alex Van Halen. “With the new album (‘Women And Children First' due out March 1) and ten months of touring ahead. Van Halen is go- ing after the world.” FBI Seizes Equipment In Georgia Pirate Raid NEW YORK — A four-month investigation by the FBI into the alleged manufacture and distribution of tapes in DeKalb County, Ga., has led to the seizure of approximately $3 million worth of manufacturing equipment. Using Federal search warrants obtained from a U.S. Magistrate in Atlanta, raids were conducted by FBI agents at four loca- tions in DeKalb County, including a tape supply company and two warehouses in Decatur and a residence in Stone Moun- tain. Among the materials seized, ac- cording to Benjamin Cooke, special agent in charge of the FBI’s Atlanta office, were a master duplicator, 235 master recordings, 70 cartons of eight-track tapes, labels af- fixed to tape cartridges, and three vans used to transport the goods. Although no arrests were made, the material was turned over to a Federal grand jury now convening in Atlanta. Later in the same even- ing, we went downtown to catch the World Saxophone Quartet, comprising four of the premier saxophone virtuosos in modern jazz, David Murray, Hamiet Bluiett, Oliver Lake and Julius Hemphill. Special note must be made of Hemphill, who is the group’s main com- poser and arranger. As one musician observed to me, “Julius understands the implica- tions of every note he writes, and he has a very sophisticated ear for modern harmony and counterpoint. Also, he’s one of the few composers in jazz who really understand extended form. His writing has a real sense of development and variation.” We couldn’t agree more, and we might even go one step further and suggest that Hemphill could be the Duke Ellington of the 1 980s. His writing shows an appreciation of the most sophisiticated aspects of modern classicism as well as the essence of low-down, sanctified bluesiness. In his alto, tenor and soprano improvisations, he has transformed the work of Ornette Coleman, Eric Dolphy and Charlie Parker into a personal language. Multi-reedman Oliver Lake comple- ments Hemphill’s bluesiness with his own oblique reveries and spiralling flourishes, and tenorist David Murray is probably the most muscular, melodic tenorist to have emerged in many years — both Lake and Murray also contribute excellent compositions to the band’s book. And baritone saxophonist Bluiett holds everything together with sinuous counter- melodies and excoriating lyricism. The highpoints of the show were some super-bop en- sembles that escalated into four-way explosions and a concluding series of duets and solos that showcased the contrasting styles and cohesiveness of each player. The best recorded example of the World Saxophone Quartet’s art is on “Steppin,” an exemplary Black Saint import which gives a taste of blues, bop, free jazz, classicism and theatrical flourishes. But seeing is believing, so check them out next time they’re in your local jazz den. CO N IvMCHINE ‘Space Invaders II’ Samples Released CHICAGO — Taito America Corp. recently serviced its newly appointed distributors with samples of “Space Invaders — Part II,” the color cocktail table premiered by the company at the November AMOA conven- tion. It is contained in a streamlined cabinet design that is new to the U.S. market. Based on Taito’s original “Space In- vaders” theme, the new model is an adap- tation designed to offer additional challenge to the more skillful player, while affording the average player the same challenge found in “Space Invaders — Part I.” The first screen of targets is exactly the same as in the original Space Invaders. The invaders appear on the screen moving in a steady left to right motion, with a laser base and four fortresses in the left hand corner. The laser base is moved left and right with the control lever and the lasers are fired by pressing the fire button. New to Space Invaders — Part II is a Mystery UFO, which flashes on and off as it travels across the screen and will intermit- tantly drop invaders into vacant areas where previous invaders have already been eliminated. When one of these invaders is hit, it will randomly divide into two attacking invaders, increasing the complexity and tension of the game. BODY IN MOTION CLIFTON DYSON (Motown M1482F) AMOA’s Notre Dame Seminar Scheduled For March 14-15 CHICAGO — The eighth annual AMOA Notre Dame Seminar will take place March 14-15 at the O’Hare Hilton in Chicago. Registration is limited to 70 people and the cost is $120.00 per person. The event is sponsored each year by the national association in cooperation with the College of Business Administration and Center for Continuing Education of Notre Dame University, and the seminar program is conducted by members of the faculty staff. The three-man operator panel dis- cussion, which was successfully launched at the 1 979 seminar, will be repeated this year with Fred Collins of South Carolina, Wesley S. Lawson of Florida and P.J. Storino of New Jersey on the panel. All three are highly qualified, experienced operators and, in addition to presiding overtheformal presentation, each will participate in small discussion groups as a further accom- modation for those attending. Dr. Gerry Sequin will serve as seminar coordinator, and the opening discussion on Friday morning will deal with “Behavior Modification," applicable to interviewing, hiring and training employees and related areas, conducted by Dr. D. Chris Anderson. The remainder of the day,- following a lunch break, will be devoted to the operator panel and small group discussions on the subject “How To Increase Your Income $10,000 This Year.” Saturday morning’s topic will be “Tax Considerations For Operators,” with General Vending Sales GM Block Retires CHICAGO — Coin industry veteran Irving Block has retired from his post of general manager for General Vending Sales Corp. of Baltimore, Md., after a 37-year associa- tion with the firm. Joel M. Smeyne, president of the firm, made the announcement with regret, stressing Mr. Block’s “unselfish dedication to the coin-operated amusement industry” and to General Vending, in particular. emphasis on tax planning, business deduc- tions, capital gains and losses, investment tax credit, etc. This session will be conduc- ted by Dr. James L. Wittenbach (CPA). Dr. William P. Sexton, who has par- ticipated in three previous seminars, will conduct the afternoon session on the sub- ject “Delegation of Authority: Why, How and When.” Taito America’s ‘Space Chaser’ Set For Delivery CHICAGO — Scheduled for delivery in early February is the new 2-player “Space Chaser” video game from Taito. This is the first model to be manufactured by Taito America Corporation in its new Elk Grove Village (Illinois) factory. (continued on page 46) ‘Space Chaser’ Tournament Soccer Enters New Market With Coin-Op Pool Table SEATTLE — Tournament Soccer of Seat- tle, Wash, has widened its horizons in the coin machine business with the recent un- veiling of its “Tournament Eight Ball” pool table. The new product marks the first time that the soccer table company has ven- tured into the realm of the coin operated pool table. The Tournament Eight Ball product will be manufactured under contract by U.S. Billiards and will come in a “get down brown” color and feature the rainbow stripe of Tournament Soccer as well as a reworked and improved interior. After con- versations with many manufacturers, the U.S. Billiards team of Al Simon, Dick Simon and Len Schneller presented the combina- tion of a product with long-term reliability and an open minded management to the Tournament Soccer staff. “We feel it’s the most natural extension of our company,” explains Lee Peppard, president of Tournament Soccer. “Our proven methods, applied to pool, can revitalize a product that has lost its impor- tance in the operator’s mind and pocket. In far too many areas of the country, the pool tables are on 25<t play — and too many are location owned." The Tournament Eight Ball pool table and promotion are designed to benefit the operator in the business of operating pool tables. The promotion will require operator ownership and will provide the tools for the operator to put the new table on 50<t play. “We will approach the marketing of coin pool tables with the same commitment to total follow through, to make the operator and location more money because of their involvement with our product,” said Pep- pard. The key to the success of the new program is the strong rapport that Tourna- ment Soccer presently enjoys with its dis- tributor network. The distributors have been actively involved .over the past eight months as a source of invaluable informa- tion as the pool table product and promo- tion have been fine tuned. As in the table soccer program, locations with operator-owned tables will be provided tournament kits that include eight weeks of qualifying in their location for ma- jor Tournament Eight Ball events. N.Y. 10019 EDITORIAL Formula For Profit As the home video market continues to grow and expand, with new highs in VCR sales predicted for this year and videodisc players to be nationally marketed by the start of 1981, now, more than ever, is the time for the full-line record retailers and wholesalers to get in on the ground floor of this burgeoning home entertainment industry. Record merchandisers should note that initial in- vestments in stocking video cassette software are currently very low, with most of the major suppliers and manufacturers requiring little or no minimum order requirements to start up. Large inventories are unnecessary as well, since many companies have one-to-two day order turnaround policies. Additionally, suppliers’ credit terms are es- pecially attractive now, with extended credit, state- ment dating and stock adjustments a part of most contracts. And video software will require little or no major store modification since the cassettes fit in conventional 8-track cases. Also, locked display stands are available at nominal costs, while exten- sive point-of-purchase displays are being offered free of charge. With some software lines now being shipped through conventional record distribution channels, such as WCI Home Video through WEA, Inc., and many more to follow suit in the near future, product will become extremely accessible to the record merchandiser. New distribution patterns will also delay the sale of major films to pay TV for 6-12 months, so if a customer wants a film he will most likely have to buy it. According to Joe Cohen, executive vice president of NARM, the upcoming 22nd Annual NARM Con- vention in Las Vegas “will devote an entire day to discussing the home video marketplace for the first time in the history of the organization.” With the sup- port of NARM, now all that is needed is the support of the record merchandiser. Welk Re-Acquires Ranwood, Sells To Teleklew Prods. LOS ANGELES — Larry Welk, the presi- dent of Ranwood Records, recently re- acquired the label from the now-defunct GRT Corp. and almost immediately re-sold the company to Lawrence Welk’s Telklew Productions, Inc. Ranwood founder Randolph C. Wood and label principals Christine Hamilton, Morry Goldman and Larry Welk sold their company to GRT in 1978. GRT went bankrupt in mid-1979 and the original associates re-acquired the label through a foreclosure sale by the Bank of America. Larry Welk will continue to act as presi- dent with Hamilton as executive vice presi- dent and Goldman as vice president in charge of national sales. Ranwood is now back in its original location at 9034 Sunset Bivd., Hollywood, Calif. 90089. Warner To Head Creative Music Publishing Group LOS ANGELES — Jay Warner has been named to the position of president of The Creative Music Group, a new publishing organization in association with K-tel Inter- national. Warner, a member of the ASCAP advisory board, was formerly the vice president of the Entertainment Company. Prior to coming to the Entertainment Com- pany, he was vice president of the Wes Farrell Organization in New York and Los Angeles. Company Philosophy "The company’s philosophy will be to have an active and creative atmosphetefor writer-artists and writer-producers to work in," said Warner. “The establishment of the songwriter is as important to us as the es- tablishment of a song. The Creative Music Group will also actively pursue the acqusi- tion of catalogs that would benefit from our kind of exposure and usage in everything from sheet music to film music.” The headquarters for the Creative Music Group will be located at 6430 Sunset Blvd., Suite 716, Hollywood, Calif. 90028. Bache Appointed VP Of Finance, CBS Records NEW YORK — Theodore S. Bache has been named vice president of finance and administration for CBS Records. Bache joined CBS in 1964 and was appointed assistant controller of CBS television networks in 1969. He was named assistant controller of CBS Inc. in 1971, and vice president and controller of CBS specialty stores division in 1976. Theodore Bache -EXECUTIVES ON THE MOVE— Ferrante Named at Atlantic — Vito Ferrante has been named as director of business affairs for Atlantic Records. Ferrante, a lawyer, is a graduate of New York University Law School. While still in law school, he began working for Arista Records, where he remained for three years, most recently serving as contracts manager. Reed Appointed At C BS — CBS Records has announced the appointment of Stephen D. Reed as executive assistant to the president, CBS Records Division. Since 1978 he has held the position of director, development, CBS Records. He joined CBS in 1976 as a planning analyst in the corporate planning office, and in 1977 was named manager, planning. Reflection Names Marks — Reflection Records has announced the appointment of Amy Marks as director of business affairs. In addition to coordinating with each of the departments of the company, she will also supervise all advertising. Changes At WEA — The following appointments have been announced by War- ner/Elektra/ Atlantic. Skid Weiss, currently national director of advertising and public relations, has been appointed to national director of communications; Alan Perper, currently national advertising manager, has been appointed national director of adver- tising; Barbara Burns, currently national advertising coordinator, has been appointed national advertising manager. Before joining WEA in 1971, Weiss had lengthy ex- perience in book publishing, headed his own public relations firm, and was vice presi- dent of United Syndications, Inc. Prior to joining WEA in May of 1977, Perper had, since 1970, been national director of creative services for the J.L. Marsh Co. (predecessor of Pickwick International). Formerly with ABC/Dunhill Records, Burns joined WEA's Cleveland Branch sales order department in 1974. After a short tenure in sales, she was promoted to the position of media buyer/promotion secretary in the expanding advertising/promotion department. She was promoted to national advertising coor- dinator for WEA in August, 1978. Most recently, he was associate director, national promotion at Infinity Records. For example, we must now open the doors for an 8 o’clock concert by 6:30 P.M., and at least two hours before that in the event of a problem with the crowd. _ Booking Problems ‘‘Obviously, we’re going to have a problem in booking tours to meet that sort of time schedule,” he continued. “A group would have to complete their equipment check by 4:30 in the event that the doors were to open at that hour. Now we must ask ourselves whether we can run a concert business under those type of restrictions. Obviously, we're not going to trade off dollars for public safety, and only time will tell what sort of success we will ultimately have in adhering to these new guidelines." j 12 Cash Box/February 23. 1980

WCI’s Music Group Reports 12% Earnings Drop For 1979 (continued from page 8) operations rose 33% to $109,058,000 from $82,197,000 in the preceeding year. This figure does not include an additional $91.7 million realized from the sale of 50% of WCI’s cable operations to the American Ex- press Company. With this gain included, WCI’s net income for 1979 totalled $200,- 747,000. In the fourth quarter, income and revenues were the highest for any quarter in WCI’shistory. lncome(beforethegainon the sale) was up 28% to $33,706,000 from $26,339,000 in the same period last year. Revenues for the quarter rose 8% to $468,139,000 from $387,038,000 in the final quarter of 1978. WCI’s board of directors voted to split the existing common shares by distributing one additional share for each three shares currently held. The board also voted a 33- 1/3% increase in the quarterly cash divi- dend by declaring a dividend of 25<t per share on all shares outstanding, including the newly issued shares. The new shares Late Night Show To Feature New Wave Video Acts LOS ANGELES — The seven-week old show Rock World marks the return of the “radio on TV” concept to late night televi- sion. While not the first such program, one of the show’s co-producers said that the program would be the first show “geared to be exclusively new wave-oriented programming.” The program, produced for Fire Sign, Ltd. by the company’s president, Billy Ar- nell, and Steve Loeb, is comprised of video promos from record labels and video footage from various foreign markets. The show airs in late night programming in 18 major markets. The program is broadcast twice a week at an earlier time in the Atlanta market. Arnell said, “A lot of acts don’t get ex- posure on radio and television and this is an alternative. We like to consider this a visual radio station.” He said because of the late time slot and the show being syndicated, there was more freedom to use programs previously un- aired in the U.S., such as Germany’s Musikiaden. All of NBC’s owned and operated sta- tions and some NBC and ABC affiliates, carry the program while NTN Entertain- ment, the show’s developer, handles in- dependent syndication. Butterfly Files Suit Against MCA (continued from page 8) to provide advancements, accountings and payments based on the accountings, and to promote and distribute Butterfly product. When contacted last week, Butterfly president A.J. Cervantes told Cash Box that MCA contracted with Butterfly to develop disco product in order for MCA to wedge into that music market. According to Cervantes, when the disco market began to soften, Butterfly officials’ attempted to persuade MCA to let the com- pany expand Butterfly product to other music markets and received little or no response. Cervantes said that Butterfly is now in the process of negotiating agreements with other labels that would call for Butterfly to develop new artists and to provide marketing and promotion support to such artists in exchange for distribution and marketing support of the product (Cash Box, Feb. 9 ). MCA declined to comment on the suit. POINTS WEST THINK PINK — Pink Floyd brought its “The Wall” production to the L.A. Sports Arena Feb. 7-13, and staged one of the most ambitious multi-media events that L.A. rock fans have ever seen. Whether one enjoys the group’s music or not, there is no denying that the band has a unique artistic vision. Based on Roger Waters’ album concept, the 2% hour show involved the building and tearing down of a 31 ft. high, 160 ft. wide, 420 brick wall. "The Wall,” representative of the paranoia and psychological entrapments of the modern day malleable masses, was composed of polystyrene bricks and also acted as a screen for four 35mm projectors, which showed slides and three independent films that were constantly being overlapped. Hats off to Gerald Scarfe for his Salvador Dali meets Ralph Steadman animation, design and direction, and to production manager Graham Fleming, who incorporated the various inflatable puppets that emerged from the wall in sync with the music’s story line during the course of the show. A special men- tion should be made of Brittania Row Liahtinq's stunning work and Brittania Row Audio, which mixed 108 channels of phenomenal sound. The show’s end was signaled by the great crash of “The Wall,” which was activated by a special computerized system. A 70- member stage crew was employed for the mammoth production, and 15 semi-trailers will be used to transport the psychedelic extravaganza to New York. JA ON JAZZ COMINGS AND GOINGS — At Fat Tuesday's you enter an old-fashioned steak and ale restaurant with checkered tablecloths and elegant woodwork. Then, passing through an unobtrusive closet door, you descend a twisting staircase which leads to the jazz room — a surrealistic Pullman parlor car with a small, mirrored performance space. The combina- tion of muted, glistening lighting and good acoustics makes Fat Tuesday's among the most intimate jazz rooms in New York. Of course it wouldn't be a real jazz room without great musicians, but Fat T uesday's has had its share recently. One of the most devastating per- formances came from pianist Cecil Taylor’s Double Trio. Taylor may be the finest pianist in the world. He has synthesized his influences from classical music (Henry Cowell, Igor Stravinsky, Bela Bartok) and jazz (Thelonious Monk, Bud Powell, Charlie Parker, Miles Davis and Duke Ellington) into polymorphous group improvisations that are completely unique in American music. Short, bursting phrases and ensemble passages are the jumping-off point for a floating, round-robin dialog of call and response. At Fat Tuesday's, this resulted in a modern improvised chamber music of immense power and gossamer delicacy — a kind of stratospheric ballet. At the center of the maelstrom was Taylor's piano and Jimmy Lyons' heraldic alto saxophone, providing roving clusters of motion and melodic focus. On either side of Taylor and Lyons were Ramsey Ameen on violin and Alan Silva on cello and contrabass, who contributed an undercurrent of motion and counterpoint. Finally, on opposite ends of the bandstand were drummers Jerome Cooper and Sunny Murray, who took the low road and high roads respectively; Cooper created a steady drone and implied several tempi on his tom-toms and bass drums, while Murray was like a force of nature, answering Taylor's flurry of pianistic figures with a barrage of broken accents and cymbal flourishes. Together, they created a music of pure motion and ecstasy. The last two nights were recor- ded for a future album release, and at press time we learned that one of the major labels is negotiating for the tapes of Taylor's epic duets with Max Roach at Columbia University last December . . . OUT OF THE WOODS — Fteedman-composer Henry Threadgill has gained world-wide recognition as a member of Air, one of the most vita! improvising trios in modern jazz, and, with last year's Arista solo album, "X-75, Volume 1," he established himself as a major moaern composer with his writing for voice, four woodwinds and four basses. With his re- cent appearance at the Tin Palace — Manhattan's premier showplace for jazz innovation — Threadgill further added to his credentials as a woodwind improviser and arranger. His new sextet was a house-rocking delight, whether offering inferences of the dance or going off into space with full-throttle free blowing. Threadgill's group is a modern version of an old-fashioned brass band, achieving a futuristic New Orleans polyphony and real low- down bluesiness. Performing on alto and tenor saxophone and occasionally on flute, Threadgill makes music that is as notable for what he edits out of his solos as for what he plays — a pontillistic. gut-bucket sound. On one joyous calpyso. Threadgill sounded even more like Sonny Rollins then Newk himself. Trumpeter Olu Dara is the most underrated brassman in New York, with a style of phrasing that recalls the growling special effects of Buber Miley. the lyrical subtlety of Miles Davis and the pungent sarcasm and rhythmic drive of Lee Morgan (Dara leads an impressive brass band of his own, the Okra Orchestra). Trombonist Joseph Bowie has the guttural vocal power of Tricky Sam Manton and a (continued on page 48) LOUISIANA LEGEND — Professor Longhair has died (Cash Box, Feb. 16), but the music of New Orleans’ R&B king will survive for some time to come. Ironically, his last album “Crayfish Fiesta,” (see review) was released just the day before his death. CRAWFISH FIESTA — Professor Longhair —- Alligator AL 4718 — Producers: Bruce Iglauer, Andy Kaslow and Allison Kaslow — List: 7.98 "Crawfish Fiesta" is Professor Longhair's last, and possibly his greatest album. With sympathetic production, a tight pulsating rhythm section, biting horn work and Fess’s own house-rocking piano and yodeling vocals. “Crawfish Fiesta" has all of the joy and funk that made Professor Longhair one of the founding fathers of progressive R&B. Sounds of the Carib- bean. the sanctified church and jazz boil in Longhair’s musical gumbo on "Red Beans," "Willie Fugal’s Blues." “In The We Wee Hours" and the title tune — all danceable and airplay bound. BL/4CK CONTEMPORARY THE COMMODORES SAIL ONTO DINAH! — Motown recording group the Commodores recently appeared on a segment of Dinah performing their Grammy nominated song, "Sail On. " as well as displaying their latest gold and platinum achievements. Pictured are (l-r): Walter "Clyde" Orange, Thomas McClary and William King of the group; Shore; Paul Williams, co-hostfor the show; Lionel Richie, Jr.; Ronald LaPread and Milan Williams of the THE RHYTHM SECTION LOLA FALANA TO MOTOWN/BERRY GORDY HONORED — Lola Falana has been signed to a recording contract at Motown Records. Falana will be the featured guest per- former at upcoming Urban League fundraiser dinner honoring Motown Records’ Berry Gordy at the Century Plaza Hotel in Los Angeles, March 5. Gordy will be the recipient of that organization’s seventh annual Whitney M. Young Jr. Award. Vernon E. Jordan, Jr., president of the National Urban League will be the featured guest speaker, and actress Jayne Kennedy will serve as Mistress of Ceremonies. Over 1,000 civic, industry and business people are expected to attend the event, and proceeds from the dinner will be used to help finance the advocacy programs organized by the Urban League, which have placed several hundred people in jobs, and provided service during the past year. SAMMY DAVIS AT WATTS BENEFIT — The third annual Neighbors of Watts Benefit will be held March 22 at the Biltmore Hotel in Los Angeles. The event is being billed as “An Evening With Sammy," and is a tribute to the entertainer’s lengthy career and his involve- ment as a contributor to child care. The organization was founded to expand the scope of development for low income families in Watts, California. ISLEYS ON THE ROAD — T-Neck/Epic recording artists The Isley Brothers will start on a 40-city tour that will begin in May and continue through August. The group has not toured since September, 1978. This tour will be timed to follow the release of the group’s album, “Go All The Way,” which will be released at the end of March. A single from that album, "Don’t Say Goodnight,” was released this week. Star Entertainment in Memphis will promote this event. For further information contact Fred Jones at (901) 942-1507. GIL SCOTT SAYS ‘SHUT ’EM DOWN’ — Keeping with his reputation of being very out- spoken on political matters in his music, Scott-Heron’s recent single, “Shut 'Em Down,” il- lustrates his stand against nuclear energy. The song is already being considered for of- ficial use by organizations campaigning for safer energy usage. Scott-Heron is currently planning appearances at various benefit concerts with Jackson Browne, Bonnie Raitt and other artists committed to safe energy. BARRY MANILOW TO SOUL — Soul Magazine is expanding its coverage, with Barry Manilow, its first non-black artist to be featured as a cover story in the March issue. Manilow will be the subject of an in-depth interview, featuring conversations with Dionne Warwick and Phyllis Hyman, both of whom have records produced by Manilow. Clive Davis, president of Arista Records, will also make some surprising statements during the interview. ARTIST TIDBITS — Producer Jeff Lane has been scheduled to produce several cuts on the next Teddy Pendergrass and Lou Rawls albums ... A new Brothers Johnson album was released this week, entitled “Light Up The Night.” . . . The Jacksons are in the studio producing their next album ... It has been rumored that Michael Jackson is producing his sister LaToya for Polydor Records . . . Barry White is coming out with a very interesting song called “Young America,” which is a medley of “Yankee Doodle Dandy,” “America The Beautiful,” and “The Battle Hymn of the Republic.” The song is by the Love Unlimited Orchestra and features the Barry White Singers. In keeping with his previous style, White will release his album in early April, which is entitled “Sheet Music.” . . . The first cut from the next Ndugu Chancier album is a cover of the Andy Gibb song “Shadow Dancing.” The surprise is that this song was cut in one day, and features The O’Jays, George Duke, Hubert Laws and Wah Wah Watson. . . . Patti LaBelie just finished her new single called “Release,” which is being released in about three weeks.
