NTERN/mON/IL EMI Tops U.K. Sales In 1979; WEA, CBS, Indies Close Gap by Nick Underwood T^TiHSERSTOASt SUCCESS — WEA UK’s new wave stars The Pretenders recently visited the company depot at Alperton, just outside of London, to show its appreciation to members of the sales force and allied workers for help in putting the single Brass In Pocket" and the group’s self-titled LP atop the national charts. Pictured are (l-r). Pete Farndon of the group; Mike Hitches, director of Alperton operations; Chnssie^ nde . James Honeyman-Scott and Martin Chambers of the group; Moira Bellas, WEA A&R and press director, and Jonathon Clyde, Warner Bros, general manager. INTERN /1TION/4L DATELINE Canada TORONTO — Perhaps the company’s strongest commercial domestic foray in years, and most certainly the most exciting recording project to emerge in this very young decade is A&M’s Bryan Adams’ self- titled debut. Rarely has a Canadian artist expressed such maturity and aggressive assuredness in an initial recording. Early programming reaction is highly accep- table, and the Feb. 12 North American release is definitely one to watch on both sides of the border. Adams, ex-Sweeny Tod alumnus (the band that spawned Nick Gilder), is based in Vancouver, and managed by Bruce Allen (Prism, GTO, Randy Bachman). If his disc isn’t the finest Canadian recording issued this year, it ought to be one remarkable rejuvenating year for locally-raised talent. Another band with immense potential is Epic’s Harlequin, a Winnipeg-based rock outfit with an impressively palatable first album, “Victim Of A Song.’’ Group spokesman is guitarist Ralph James, one of the more articulate interview subjects on the trail today. As James puts it, the band took its time in issuing its first pressing in order to get what they considered to be the focussed attention of executive producer Jack Douglas (of Aerosmith fame). They put together “a complete package," he says, including another strong artwork con- tribution from Hipgnosis ("who didn’t know anything about us, except that we had no money and wanted them to take time out of doing the Wings album for ours”). One of the grittiest, hard-working touring outfits in the country, they brought their show into a receptive El Mocambo, where several execs had a look-see. Thus far, the first disc is well beyond halfway to gold, and should reach certified status on the strength of potential AM singles. James is confident of an American release of the group's product. “We’ll delay the next album until we know for sure whether they’re willing to put the first one out in the U.S. We don’t want to be working two different albums on two sides of the border. But after all the delays the past two years, we can wait awhile to put another project together.” In this column a few weeks back, we mentioned the results of the Canadian Recording Industry Association poll for the most popular male and female artist of the decade in Canada, those-being Gordon Lightfoot and Anne Murray. Forgotten was the group of the ’70s. Of course, it was the Guess Who. Their early-decade RCA material still rang truest among the natives. Already, flaks and prophets alike are touting the label’s recent domestic acquisi- tion, Stonebolt. as potentially the next supergroup in the country. Such predic- tions can be often more harmful than beneficial. Their first disc for RCA (having issued one on the now-defunct Parachute label last year) was scooped up at MIDEM, and will be issued practically anywhere the next few months. kirk lapointe United Kingdom LONDON — BBC Radio One is planning an audio history program spanning 25 years of rock music in the U.K. Titled 25 Years Of Rock, the program series will start airing in (continued on page 36) LONDON — EMI Records has again come out on top in the overall market share posi- tions, despite the acute problems it has un- dergone and the sale of the company to Thorn Electrical in the past year. The latest British Market Research Bureau (BMRB) figures for the record industry market shares show that, although EMI suffered a reduced majority in both singles and LP sales, the company still leads. EMI rivals CBS and WEA, along with the ever-growing independents A&M, Chrysalis and Virgin, all improved their shares of the U.K. market. The survey, published in conjunction Knack, Capitol Top January ’80 CRIA Awards TORONTO - Capitol recording group The Knack topped the Canadian Recording In- dustry Association (CRIA) January cer- tifications with a quadruple platinum album award (400,000 units) for the "Get The Knack" LP and a platinum single award (150,000 units) for the single, “My Sharona." Other CRIA album certifications in- cluded five double platinums (200,000 units), seven platinums (100,000 units) and ten golds (50,000 units). Singles certifica- tions included one platinum (150,000 units) and four golds (75.000 units). Double platinum album certifications went to the “Bee Gees' Greatest on Polygram and Blondie’s “Eat To The Beat,’ Little River Band's "First Under The Wire,” Anne Murray’s “Let’s Keep It That Way. and Kenny Rogers' "Kenny,” all on Capitol. Platinum album certifications were awar- ded to Frank Mills’ “Sunday Morning Suite" on Polygram, Joe Jackson’s "I’m A Man” on A&M, and Murray's “I’ll Always Love You,” the Kinks’ “Low Budget," Barry Manilow’s “One Voice,” "Eat To The Beat and “Kenny," all on Capitol. Gold album certifications went to Zachary Richard's “Migration” on CBS, “The Best Of Rod Stewart" on Polygram, Herb Alpert’s “Rise" on A&M and Jethro Tull’s “Stormwatch,” Murray’s “I’ll Always Love You,” Manilow’s "One Voice." "Kenny," Dr. Hook’s “Sometimes You Win," Crystal Gayle’s "Classic Crystal” and "Eat To The Beat," all on Capitol. Gold singles for January were Mirielle Mathieu’s “Santa Maria de la Mer” on Polygram, Styx’ “Babe” on A&M, and Robert John’s “Sad Eyes" and The Knack s "Good Girls Don’t,” both on Capitol. with BMRB by Music Week, the largest U.K trade magazine, showed that for 1979, EMI came in first position with 18.7% of the album market and 18.9% of the singles share. Closely behind EMI with IPs came CBS with 16.3%; followed by WEA with 13.5%; Polydor. 7.8%; Phonogram, 5.7%; Chrysalis, 4.8%; A&M, 4.7%; RCA, 4.1%: Decca, 3.6%; K-tel, 3.3%; Pye, 2.7%; Virgin. 2.7%; Arista, 2.3%; MCA I nt. . 1.4%; MSD. 1.2%; Stiff. 1.2%, and others, 6.0%. Singles Action In the singles field, WEA took second place behind EMI with 17% of the singles market share. Next came CBS with 15.5%; Polydor, 8.1%; Pye. 6.8%; Phonogram, 5.9%; A&M, 4.6%; Virgin, 4.3%; Chrysalis, 4.2%; RCA, 3.6%; Stiff, 2.1%; Arista, 1.3% Decca. 1.3%; MCA Int., 1.2%, and others, 5.2%. Though both CBS and WEA upped their share in 1979, EMI took a battering with 1979 figures substantially lower than 1978. In 1978, EMI had a 21.7% album share (down to 18.7%) and 20.2% single (down to 18.9%). The thriving independents, Chrysalis, A&M and Virgin, on the other hand, all showed a substantial increase in the market shares, despite the recession that hit hard in 1979. Chrysalis’ LP share was up on 1 978 figures with LPs from 1.9% to 4. 8%. A&M also increased from 2.4% to 4.7%, and Virgin jumped from 1.6% to 2.7%. For the prosperous independents, the singles story was the same. COIN MACHINE Exhibit Space Sold Out For 1980 NAMA Western Meet CHICAGO — Six weeks before the opening of the 1980 NAMA Western Convention in Anaheim, Calif., the association's sales director Jack Rielley announced a sellout of all available space and a new record in number of exhibitors and space used. “We have signed more than 140 ex- hibitors and all available booths have been sold, even after we expanded the original floor plan," according to Rielley. He said 30 companies will be first time exhibitors at the convention. Comparing this year’s show with the two previous western conventions Rielley noted that a record 138 exhibitors participated last year, which was a increase West Coast Reps Comment On ATE by Marc Cetner LOS ANGELES — The great numbers of foreign copies of American games and the dominance of video were the two most noteworthy trends spotted by West Coast manufacturers at the ATE show in London, according to a recent Cash Box survey. All coin executives sounded also agreed that the June 22-24 event at Alexandra Palace was also the best attended event in recent memory. The problem of foreign copies of American machines has been of great con- cern to manufacturers of late, and the abundance of duplications at the ATE brought this disconcerting trend to a head. “Japanese copies of American games in Europe are cause for serious concern,” said Lila Zinter of Exidy. “They have an ex- pertise in copying any straight raster game, and XY monitor games are also being copied. You can make a case of copyright infringement here, but it doesn't hold water in Japan or Europe. It’s getting so there’s no (continued on page 43) from the 112 in 1978. The convention and trade show will be held at the Anaheim Convention Center March 14-16. Wayne Hood, president of Hood Service, Inc. of Bellflower, Calif., has been named convention chairman and Mrs. Harold Steuber of Long Beach, Calif, will serve as chairperson of the Ladies’ Activities Program. Walter L. Koch of Rowe Inter- national, Inc. in Whippany, N.J., is chair- man of the trade show advisory committee. Program sessions, scheduled on Friday and Saturday morning, will deal with vending company security measures and achieving employee productivity goals. Concurrent Sunday morning sessions will highlight employee training, sanitation and safety, establishing company policies for employees and external communications. Keynote Speakers Allan P. Lucht, president and chairman of Servomation Corporation of Greenwich, Conn., and Patrick L. O’Malley, chairman of Canteen Corporation of Chicago, will be keynote speakers on Friday and Saturday. Lucht is 1980 chairman of NAMA and O'Malley is a past chairman of the associa- tion. The convention banquet on Saturday night will feature singer Jody Donovan and comedian George West, announced G.H. Tansey, NAMA’s director of conventions. Members of NAMA may register for the convention free of charge and represen- tatives of non-member operating com- panies will be required to pay a $15 per per- son fee. The registration cost for non- member manufacturers is $75 for the first person and $50 each for any additional per- sonnel from the same company. Further information and hotel reserva- tions may be obtained through the NAMA office at 7 South Dearborn St., Chicago ill 60603. Exciting Sounds And Visual Effects Enhance Williams’ New ‘Laser Ball’ CHICAGO — Williams Electronics, Inc. an- nounced thecommencementof production on “Laser Ball,” which is the factory’s latest 4-player, wide-body pinball game. The dynamism of the machine’s cabinet design is complemented by exciting sounds and visual effects such as atom smashing lights emitting beams from the backglass spec- trum; and throughout the game throbbing intergalactic sound surrounds the player as scoring builds. Laser Ball offers three flipper play with double flippers at the bottom of the playfield and a “powerhouse flipper” placed in the middle to challenge the ability and dexterity of the player. To accomplish high point scoring, the Laser Ball skids through the top lances activating the star- studded force field. Triggering all ten stars lights a “laser beam” for 10,000 points. To add to the scoring excitement there are a series of drop targets labeled L-A-S-E-R B- A-L-L as well as a super-charged hole kicker and “laser lane” spinners. In stressing the total appeal of the game Williams' marketing director Ron Crouse stated, "Laser Ball has enhanced player at- titude to wide body pinball by generating the fast moving excitement of standard body games with the added skill- challenging performance possibilities of a wider playfield. Once you play Laser Ball,” he added, “you’ll become a wide body pin- bail fan.” The new game utilizes Williams’ total front end programming which was in- troduced on “Stellar Wars” to facilitate ad- justments without the necessity of remov- ing the top glass. As Crouse noted further, Laser Ball is Williams’ answer to the need for an action-packed visually exciting, futuristic sound, sight and light show in a wide body game. The model is available through Williams' distributor network. t^ S J<SSh Singer One-Stop For Ops principals. Pictured are (l-r): Michael Gae, MCA salesman ; Ciasnocha; Holmes and Tar- Int’l Coin Machine Trade Show Set For April 18-20 In New York City CHICAGO — Exhibit contracts for the 2nd annual International Coin Machine Trade Show have been mailed, according to Ben Chicofsky, the show’s producer, and special arrangements have been made to provide excursion fares on U.S. and over- seas flights, as an accommodation for con- ventioners. Show dates are April 18-20 at the New York Statler Hotel in New York City. Billed as an “all-inclusive vending machine trade show,” the products being featured will encompass merchandise vending, amusement games, jukeboxes, coffee service, bulk, cigarettes, drink machines and trade supplies. Exhibit rates start at $450 for a single booth and the convention will focus ex- clusively on equipment displays, with no seminars or other planned activities being offered. All exhibits will remain open for a total of 21 hours, as follows: 1 1 a.m.-6 p.m. on Friday, 10 a.m.-5 p.m. on Saturday and 10 a.m.-3 p.m. on Sunday. As an added inducement for convention visitors ICMTS is offering special package tours which include hotel accommodations at either the New York Statler Hotel or Sheraton Center, as well as meals, theater tickets and other services, at special rates. COIN MACHINE West Coast Reps Comment On ATE (continued from page 38) way we can compete over there.” Paul Jacobs, who recently acquired the position of executive vice president at Un- iversal U.S.A., was sympathetic with Zin- ter’s statements about copies. “There were lots of copies of the American hits by Italian and Japanese manufacturers,” stated Jacobs. “The copies aren’t filtering back into the U.S., but they do muddy up the European market." Another manufacturing representative who was aware of the copy dilemma was Cinematronics salesman Jim Stroud. He mentioned that there must have been 20 copies of “Galaxian” at the show and con- fusion over which manufacturer was mak- ing what. However, he was quick to point out that video was starting to make a big impact in Europe. “The Europeans have video fever now,” said Stroud. “The video game is finally becomming a worldwide phenomenon.” Sutash Bhutani, vice president of Namco America, also seemed excited about video's dominance at the London show. "People seemed to be zealous about the video games,” offered Bhutani, “and the cocktail table market is also getting very strong.” While the majority of the manufacturers surveyed reported that the show was crow- ded beyond expectation and that business moved at a brisk pace, some of the manufacturers felt that the show was too well attended and that Alexandra Palace was not a suitable venue for the ATE. One such manufacturing representative was Paul Jacobs. “I am not sure that I’m in agreement with letting the public in the way they did,” said Jacobs. “There was so many people in the aisles that it became very dif- ficult to conduct business.” Jim Stroud was also overwhelmed by the crowd's size. "The Palace was just too small to hold everybody," commented Stroud. “You couldn't even walk where you wanted to go. You simply were pushed by the crowd." Although the crowds and the overabun- dance of copies caused most of the con- troversy at the three-day affair, all of the manufacturers agreed that the show was profitable. Perhaps Gremlin Enterprises marketing director Bob Harmon best expressed the sentiments of his fellow manufacturers by saying, “The acceptance of video and favorable weather conditions made this year's ATE one of the most successful ever." PERSONALITY PROFILE Cinematronics’ Sayers Rises In Male-Dominated Industry ‘Torch’ Gottlieb Ships Its New ‘Torch’ 4-Player Pinball CHICAGO — Jack H. Mittel, vice president and general manager of D. Gottlieb & Co., announced the release of the factory’s new pinball game, "Torch." Describing the new model, Mittel said, “Torch, appropriately, has an athletic theme and the release of this game was timed to coincide with the excitement that is building for the Summer Olympics games. The flashy playfield glass reflects the inten- sity of international athletic competition,” he added, "and its timeliness and colorful display will immediately attract players." The central feature of the game is a “tic- tac-toe" bonus multiplier which challenges the player to activate the lights in vertical, horizontal and diagonal patterns, multiply- ing the bonus progressively from two to ten times when all numbers are lighted. The game also has “hit" lights to indicate which roto targets are struck plus a double "shoot-again" feature which scores extra balls in two areas of the playfield. “We call Torch the champion of the games,” Mittel concluded, “and we are predicting that pinball players everywhere will be intrigued by the new features if of- fers." The newgameiscurrently being shipped to domestic distributors. CHICAGO — When a woman rises to a vice presidency in the male dominated coin machine industry, it’s news. When the woman is Lenore Sayers, vice president of marketing at Cinematronics, it’s good news. The saga of Lenore Sayers begins in California and remains there. Raised in a small northern farm community of Woodland, she attended San Jose State College in the late '60s and early 70s. She majored in the biological sciences, in- tending to become a doctor, but suffered the characteristic late '60s disillusionment with college and left for San Diego to recon- sider her future. Eventually Lenore got a job in retail sales in a shopping mall until December 1973, when a friend said that the company she worked for needed help in the purchasing department; the company was Kee Games. Previously, Lenore had only known thecoin business as a consumer; now, in sixth months, she rapidly ascended from clerk to expediter to junior buyer of machine com- ponents to marketing administrator for Kee president Joe Keenan. As administrator, she handled customer service, processed game orders, and, when J. Keenan was out of the office, received her first taste of talk- ing to distributors. After Kee merged with Atari, she retained the same respon- sibilities. Enters Marketing In March 1975 Lenore assisted Gene Lipkin in Atari’s marketing department. She was knighted with the enviable title S.O.P.S. — sales order processing super- visor, and her rapport with distributors bloomed. One week when Gene Lipkin was out of town, her baptism in sales began. He had asked her to call some distributors, and they responded well to her low-key, un- derstated approach. In fact, Lenore emphasizes the importance of Lipkin’s tutelage. It was the prime influence in her continued involvement and fascination with the coin industry. After a successful initiation in game sales, Lenore gradually received a couple of accounts at a time, then a couple more, but with the advent of messieurs Ballouz, Osborne and Rubin in sales, she temporarily returned to S.O.P.S. She still maintained contact with distributors, providing information on scheduling and shipments; however, she longed for sales. She persisted, cajoled, asked for a try, and would not be dissuaded by warnings about the roughness of some distributors. Lipkin consented to a trial by fire, gave her com- plete responsibility for one national ac- count for 90 days. She passed the ordeal, and in 1976 became a full fledged sales person. After Howie Rubin established Atari’s east coast office, Lenore used it as her home base. She and Rubin split the territory between Chicago and the Coast. Lenore, after careful consideration, made a major decision in July 1979: She left Atari to become vice president of marketing at Cinematronics. The new com- pany offered her an opportunity to expand her career. According to Lenore, “At Cinematronics I am more involved in dif- ferent aspects of manufacturing. Working (continued on page 44) ‘Asteroids’ Becomes Best Selling Video Game In Atari History SUNNYVALE — “To date we’ve produced more ’Asteroids’ than any other game in our history, and orders are still piling up,” reported Don Osborne, Atari’s national sales manager. “It's our biggest hit yet, surpassing even some of our classic hits like ‘Tank’, ‘Breakout’ and ‘Atari Football’. The un- usually high response to this game is a testimonial to the fact that it is returning ex- tremely high profits to operators all over the world." Osborne continued. “Asteroids has the kind of play appeal and reliability that gives it good location versatility. It con- tinues to be highly successful in game rooms as well as street locations of every type." Osborne pointed out that typical com- ments from operators include those of Jim McIntyre, who operates Lakewood Gar- dens Miniature Golf in Lakewood, Calif. In a letter to the factory he noted that “Asteroids is a fantastic game with earning potential equal to or above ‘Space Invaders’,” adding that Asteroids has expanded his base of players, pulling in new clientele that in- cludes 25-30 year old players. Asteroids is a unique space action game with explosive rapid-fire action in which one or two players are challenged to destroy asteroids and enemy spacecraft. The new Atari-designed QuadraScan video display system, which offers highly realistic visual effects, space age sound effects and a new High Score Table round out some of the features of this game. GEILS BAND CHUCK MANGIONE NAZARETH TOP SINGLE BREAKOUT OF THE WEEK EVEN IT UP — HEART — EPIC TOPABUM BREAKOUT OF THE WEEK FUN & GAMES — CHUCK MANGIONE — A&M WH4TS IN-STORE NUMAN CONTEST — Atlantic Records is currently conducting a nationwide Gary Numan display contest for WEA personnel. The competition will take place with WEA branches in 1 1 cities and will utilize a special edition poster designed by the New York office. The con- test. which runs from Feb. 11-March 14, will be judged on the basis of creativity and quan- tity of placement. First prize will be $400. There will be five other prizes as well ... In addi- tion. other promotional Numan materials have been developed, including an eight minute in-store video of two cuts from the LP “Replicas." Large quantities of a 25 ”x38" tour per- sonality posters are also available. These posters will be shipped to stores, concert promoters and the press. TAPE NEWS — Sony Corporation recently revealed its new promotion package for 1980. It combines discounts, heavy co-op advertising, extendable terms and convenient inven- tory material. Also available during the promotion is the new “Full Color Sound" tape dis- play. (Last year’s “Sound" advertising campaign resulted in a 114% increase in Sony blank audio tape sales. The new advertising program has been budgeted at S6.5 million.) The current display will utilize graphics from the first “Full Color Sound" print ad and will be designed to hold 192 tapes. It will easily convert from a stand-alone to a counter display. There will also be special promotions for individual cassette series. The EHF tape, a high bias cassette, will be featured on a “buy two and get one free" basis. Purchasers of three HFX series cassettes will receive a carrying case. SHF tapes will be sold with a special offer of a free “Full Color Sound” poster with the purchase of two tapes. Finally, purchasers of three L NX low-noise cassettes will receive a deck of “Full Color Sound" playing cards. Premiums consisting of umbrellas, T-shirts, and other promotional items utilizing ad- campaign artwork will be made available to dealers and distributors as a means of utilizing co-op dollars. MORE VALENTINE PROMOS — The 20 Music Plus stores are running a Valentine’s Day promotion highlighted by the slogan. “Our hearts are in the right place with the Valentine's Day gift pack.” The pack consists of an $8.98 list LP, a love pin normally $4.99. a Valentine card and T-shirt, all for the price of $10 . . . Peaches, Dallas, Oklahoma City and Tulsa are conducting a contest tied in with the opening of the film “Foolin' Around. "Along with free passes to the premiere on Feb. 14. customers received movie posters. T-shirts and were eligible for a drawing in which each store gave away three limited edition heart-shaped Seals and Crofts picture discs . . . Peaches, Indianapolis, held a Heart contest on Valen- tine's Day, where customers had to guess how many red-hot heart-shaped candies were contained in a jar in the store. The winner received the jar as well as the CBS catalog of Heart LPs . . . Finally. Peaches, Cleveland, gave away a rose with the purchase of each Tom Petty album sold, while Licorice Pizza held a Valentine’s Day drawing to win a dozen roses. OTHER ACTIVITIES — Polygram has awarded first place in its “Sonic Energy Sweepstakes" to its Los Angeles branch. This was based on three events: a skate-athon. in conjunction with KHJ radio; a basketball game with the Seattle Supersonics and L A. Lakers (in which the branch played KRLA radio during half-time); and another game with the L.A. Lakers and the San Diego Chargers . . . Disc Records of Texas is holding an MCA country catalog in-store display contest with a $300 first prize for the winning outlet Peaches, Cincinnati, hit with an unusual Steve Forbert “Jackrabbit Run." There was a drawing on Feb. 13 in which 10 names were selected. These contestants than ran through the store on a 100-second record run grabbing as many of the 100 album-sized jackrabbit posters as they could. For each jackrabbit captured, the participant received one LP or tape from the current CBS catalog. There was also a premium for the first 100 spectators, good for one CBS promo cassette, one rock poster and $1.00 off any CBS LP or tape in stock . . . Spec’s, Miami and radio station “Love 94" conducted a Rupert Holmes “Perfect Him For A Night” contest. The winner of the drawing had 94 seconds to call the station after his name was announced to win $94 in cash and limousine service for two to the Bodega Restaurant in Miami . . . Finally, Licorice Pizza, scored with a “Star Trek Look-alike Photo Contest,” Feb. 7-24. with a grand prize of a Bushnell Spacemaster II Telescope. CUSTOMER QUOTE OF THE WEEK: “I’ve looked all through the “Fs ". and I can’t find a single Pink Floyd album!” REGIONAL ACTION — American Gigolo soundtrack and new Chuck Mangione selling well in the west . . . 3-D album selling well in the midwest . . . Mickey Mouse Disco album breaking out of the south . . . New Ramones powerful in the south and west . Searchers with sales in the east. EDITORIAL A Matter Of Giving At the recent membership meeting of the American Society of Composers, Authors & Publishers, better known as ASCAP, the treasurer’s annual report revealed that record levels had been achieved in total receipts and domestic receipts. Both figures exceeded $100 million, the domestic receipts topping that level for the first time ever. However, it was also noted that inflation had “tar- nished” the Society’s true revenues and that there had been little true growth. Perhaps that is a sign of the times. In a utilitarian sense, music surely occupies one of the lower rungs on the ladder. After all, you can’t eat a song, drive a commercial jingle to work or wear the score for a television drama. Still, music occupies an important part of our lives. It offers comfort and inspiration, as well as pure entertainment. In such troubled times as we are living in now — with turmoil on the international political level and chaos within the worldwide economic community — perhaps what we need is more of the human and creative side of life. ASCAP members should feel proud for that reason. All financial aspects aside (after all, who other than oil shieks abroad and oil magnates at home can genuinely claim economic growth today?), the members of the music community are among the few who give more to society than they can ever ask in return. EXECUTIVES ON THE MOVE Signal Tenders Bid To Acquire Ampex Corp. LOS ANGELES — Signal Cos. Inc., a manufacturer of aerospace and industrial products, has tendered an offer to acquire Ampex Corp., the Redwood City, Calif. based firm that manufactures and markets professional equipment for the audio, video and computer industries. The offer involves an exchange of common stock valued between $347.6 million and $511.7 million. Under the terms of the agreement, Signal would exchange 0.79 shares of its common stock for each share of Ampex Corp. common stock. Ampex currently has approximately 11 million common shares outstanding and 1.7 million shares reser- ved upon exercise of employee stock op- tions and conversion of convertible deben- tures. The proposed merger between the two companies is subject to termination by either party if, at any time up to 10 days before becoming effective, the average closing price of Signal common stock on the New York Stock Exchange for any con- secutive five-day period is above $51 per share or below $40 per share. The merger is also subject to approval by the boards of directors and shareholders of each company, various government regulatory agencies and a favorable tax rul- ing. The two companies said that the ac- quisition should be completed by the mid- dle of this year. A spokesman for Signal Cos. said that the firm does not “contemplate any changes” in Ampex’ operating philosophies or in “its existing manage- ment.” Signal’s subsidiaries, which include Garrett Corp., Mack Trucks, Inc., Dunham- Bush and UOP, Inc., are allowed to operate independently, while the parent company retains legal and financial controls. Ampex Corp., which suffered heavy losses when involved in the recorded music business, has rebounded solidly. Most recently, earnings before tax credits for the three-month period ended Jan. 26, 1980, increased to $6.4 million, up 34% from the $4.8 million reported during the same period of the previous year, while net sales and other revenues jumped 28% from $92.9 million to $118.9 million. Net earnings increased 70% from $6.2 to $10.6 million for the same three month period, including a $4.2 million benefit from utilization of tax carryforwards as com- pared to a similar benefit of $1 .5 million for the same period a year previously. Sales of audio-video and magnetic tape product lines were cited as being par- ticularly strong during the quarter, as or- ders were reported to be up 1 2% during the last quarter. V.R. Records Formed LOS ANGELES—loe Rosanova, Jr., presi- dent of Rosanova Productions, Inc., has an- nounced formation of the V.R. Record label, which will be located in the Rosanova Productions building in Southfield, Mich. Gordon Price, Jay Butler and Etta St. James have joined the label to establish national distribution and promotion. V.R. Records will deal primarily with R&B and pop oriented music. The label will also include its own publishing and manage- ment divisions. ABKCO Posts First Quarter Revenues NEW YORK — ABKCO Industries Inc. reported last week that its revenues for the first quarter ended Dec. 31, 1979 rose to $3.3 million from $2.3 million in the first quarter of 1978. This resulted in a profit of $35,865, compared to a loss of $14,647 in 1978. ASCAP Monies Up Again In ’79 (continued from page 8) total distribution of $100,639,000. The figure represents an increase of $9, 1 73,000 over last year’s $91,466,000. The sum represents the amount left after salaries and office expenses of $24,349,000 were subtracted. In 1978 those expenses totalled $21,349,000. Domestic distribution of the $79,427,000 — up from $75,586,000 in 1978 — was made in four quarterly installments, all higher than the previous year. By quarters, the payouts were $14,695,000 for the three months ended in March (up from $14,315,- 000), $16,646,000 in the second quarter(up from $15,104,000), $22,070,000 in the third quarter (up from $20,127,000), and $26,- 016,000 in the fourth quarter (up from $22,159,000). Domestic receipts for 1979 increased to $103,473,000 from $97,577,000 the previous year. Included in the breakdown are: licensees, including symphonic and concert, $99,765,000 (up from $95,033,000 in 1978); interest on investments, $3,319,- 000 (up from $2,178,000); and membership dues, $389,000 (up from $366,000). Receipts from foreign societies showed an increase over 1978 to $24,462,000 from $1 9,074,000. (continued on page 46) Integrity Reports Losses LOS ANGELES — Disc retailer Integrity En- tertainment has announced first-half losses and a second quarter profit slump, blaming the decline on “the general depressed con- ditions in the industry.” For the six months ended Dec. 31, In- tegrity, Big Ben’s and The Wherehouse reported a net loss of $535,000 (18 cents per share) compared to a net profit of $1,- 127,000 (36 cents per share) the previous year on 6% less revenue of $39,300,000 against $41,700,000. The company’s profits dropped in the second quarter to $621,000 (21 cents per share) from $932,000 (30 cents per share) as revenue was flat at $24,300,000 for both periods. Glankoff And Wishner CommunicationsFormed NEW YORK — Peter P. Glankoff and Howard E. Wishner have formed Glankoff and Wishner Communications, Ltd., a public relations firm servicing corporations involved in product, services and com- munications endeavors. Among the firm’s clients are the Don Kirshner Entertainment Corporation and the Chajet Design Group marketing, a firm specializing in package design and corporate identity. The firm is located at 342 Madison Ave., New York, N.Y. 10017. Phone number is (212) 883-0001. K-tel Posts Figures NEW YORK — K-Tel International reported that operating income for the second fiscal quarter of 1980 was $1,974,000, a drop from $2,071,000 for the same period in 1979. In addition, operating revenues for this quarter were $65,288,000, up from $61,999,000 for the same period last year. For the first half of fiscal 1980, K-Tei reported profits of $2,167,000 on sales of $97,439,000, up from a profit of $1 ,427,000 on sales of $91,569,000 from the same period last year. Boutwell Starts Own Merchandising Firm NEW YORK — Ron Boutwell has resigned as chairman of the board of Boutwell In- c./Niocua Merchandising Ltd. in order to start his own merchandising firm in Hollywood’s Berwirr Entertainment Com- plex. Burdsal Ramsey Friedman Remer Burdsal Promoted At 20th — Bill Burdsal has been promoted to director of administra- tion, 20th Century-Fox Records Corp. He has held similar positions at Motown Records and Capitol Records. He served six years at MGM Records Corp. and was vice presi- dent of administration, leaving to form his own firm, Burdsal Enterprises. Lider Named At Polygram — Polygram Distribution, Inc. has announced the appoint- ment of Dorothy Lider as regional credit manager-west for PDI. Most recently, she was national credit manager for 20th Century-Fox. Prior to that she worked at ABC as regional credit manager. Ramsey Promoted At MCA — Roger Ramsey has been appointed southwestern regional country promotion manager for MCA Records. He joined MCA Records last March as Houston’s local promotion manager, working with MCA’s pop, R&B and country artists. Blundo Promoted At Polygram — Polygram Distribution has announced the appoint- ment of Lisa Biundo as national advertising administrator. She joined PDI in May of 1979 as advertising coordinator. Prior to that she worked as advertising director of a retail record chain in New York. Friedman Named At Arista — Arista Records has announced that Michael Friedman has been appointed director, product management, associated labels, as well asdirec-' tor, video services for the label. Prior to this appointment, he was assistant to the presi- dent of Arista, and before joining the label he was a personal manager for a number of recording artists. Archibald To Marvin Josephson — John C. Archibald has been appointed vice chair- man of Marvin Josephson Associates, Inc. where he will be in charge of corporate plan- ning and development. He comes to his new position from The Chase Manhattan Bank, where he was senior vice president and group executive responsible for six lending divisions that dealt with major U.S. corporations. Remer Appointed — Doc Remer has been named national promotion director for Mirus Music, Inc. Prior to his appointment he was midwest regional promotion manager for Ariola America Records and has been involved in marketing, management, writing, production, and publishing. Changes At T.E.C. — Billy Hendricks, executive vice president of T.E.C. Records an- nounces the appointment of Cynthia Jeffers to national promotion director; Gene Burleson as regional director of promotion/southeast; Darryl Williams as local promo- tion manager/southwest. Prior to joining T.E.C., the above personel were with Arista Records; Hendricks as regional director east coast; Burleson as regional director southeast; Williams as local promotion/southwest, and Jeffers as national R&B promo- tion coordinator/New York. Rosenberg Named — Silver Blue Productions has announced the appointment of Roy Rosenberg to director of national promotion. Most recently, he was northeast pop promotion director for Atlantic Records. Previously he was local New York promotion manager for Atlantic Records and Mercury Records. Cheech appointed — Record Plant Studios in New York has announced the appoint- ment of Cheech Lero as traffic manager and Randi Greenstein as production coor- dinator. Most recently Lero was associate editor of “Modern Drummer" Magazine. Greenstein was in production area at Masterdisk Inc. and most recently at Infinity Records. NEGRON SIGNS WITH B-LINE — Chuck Negron, founding member of the group Three Dog Night, has signed an exclusive contract with B-Line Productions/Management, Inc. and is currently in the studio with producer Tony Martin, Jr. after a three-year hiatus. MASS ACTION — Casablanca executives turned out in force to support the label’s recording artists, the Skatt Brothers, during a recent engagement at the Starwood club in Los Angeles. Pictured standing are (l-r): Phyllis Chotin, Casablanca; Christy Hill, Casablanca; Bill Aucoin, Skatt Brothers manager; Dick Sherman, Casablanca vice presi- dent, marketing; Ernie I Petrone, Polygram; Danny Davis, Casablanca vice president, promotion; Al di Noble, Casablanca vice president, product development; Bruce Bird, president of Casablanca; Kevin Keogh, Casablanca and Sean Delaney, Ritchie Fontana and Craig Krampf of the group. Pictured seated are (l-r): Mauri Lathower, Casablanca vice president, international; Bobby Applegate, Casablanca; Roberta Skopp, Casablanca vice president, press; David Andez, Richard Martin-Ross and Pieter Sweval of the group; and T.J. Lambert, Casablanca. Capitol/EMI/UA Group Revamps Promotion Units By Consolidation (continued from page 7) now handle R&B promotion for the Capitol, United Artists and EMI America labels; while the United Artists Nashville team will assume country promotion duties for Capitol and United Artists. In the new set-up, Mack will continue to report to Bruce Wendell, Capitol vice presi- dent of promotion, and Shults will report to Zimmermann. In addition, crossover product in both divisions will be the respon- sibility of Wendell for Capitol acts and Charlie Minor, UA/EMI America vice presi- dent of promotion, for his labels’ acts. In the R&B unit, the acts that fall under the aegis of the consolidated promotion team include Natalie Cole, Peabo Bryson, Tavares, Maze, Nancy Wilson, Sun, Mystic Merlin, Pyrymyd, Angela & Rene, Donna Washington and Eddie Henderson on the Capitol label; Ronnie Laws, Earl Klugh, Noel Pointer, Brass Construction, Southroad Connection, Quick and Dayton on United Artists; and Wilson Pickett on EMI America. In the country division, the acts that will be covered by the consolidated Nashville team are Kenny Rogers, Charlie Rich, NARM Will Award 21 Scholarships NEW YORK — Twenty-one scholarships will be awarded at the 1980 Scholarship Foundation Dinner on Monday, March 24, at the annual NARM Convention at the MGM Grand Hotel in Las Vegas, Nevada. This is the greatest number of scholarships ever presented in the foundation’s thirteen- year history. Kenneth Gamble, Chairman of Philadelphia International Records and president of the Black Music Association, has contributed a $6,000 scholarship in honor of BMA. CBS has contributed a $6,000 scholarship in memory of Andre Kostelanetz. The Kostelanetz Memorial Scholarship brings the total of CBS scholarships to three, including the God- dard Lieberson Memorial Scholarship and one in the name of the corporation. Cristy Lane, Billie Jo Spears, Dottie West, Bobby Smith, Saundra Steele, David Willis and Bobby Wright on United Artists; and Glen Campbell, Anne Murray, Jessi Colter, Dr. Hook, Deborah Allen, Lee Clayton, Billy “Crash” Craddock, Kenny Dale, LaCosta, Mel McDaniel, Diane Pfiefer, Don Schlitz, Keith Stegall, Chip Taylor and Gene Watson on Capitol. Zimmermann denied rumors that a further consolidation of the R&B units of Capitol and United Artists/EMI America was in the works. Industry speculation centered on a total merging of the R&B divisions of the labels, with the new entity to be headed by Dr. Cecil Hale, currently head of Capitol’s R&B unit. Zimmermann emphatically stated that no further consolidations in any divisions of the Group are planned in the foreseeable future. Zimmerman did confirm, however, the closing of “a small distribution branch” in Miami. He added that the southeast region will now be serviced by Capitol’s Atlanta branch. Jazz Consortium Open As Non-Profit Group NEW YORK — The Consortium of Jazz Organizations and Artists (CJOA), has opened. The CJOA is a not-for-profit ser- vice organization whose purpose will be to hold funding seminars for jazz projects with visiting experts from city, state and national funding organizations, private corporations and utilities. According to Mari-Jo Johnson, the organization’s executive director.” One of CJOA’s interests lies in the revitalization of jazz in general and of the Harlem com- munity in particular.” The consortium is located at 2090 Adam Clayton Powell, Jr. Boulevard. Phone number is (212) 866- 9000. Jackson 45 Is Gold NEW YORK — Epic recording artist Michael Jackson’s single “Rock With You,” has been certified gold by the RIAA. REVIEWS SINGLES REVIEWS FEATURE PICKS i II II IHIMIIII——H^——— — JOURNEY (Columbia 1-11213) Any Way You Want It (3:20) (Weed High Nightmare Music — BMI) (S. Perry, N. Schon) Short, smart drum shots and quick, choppy guitar licks pace the first single from the upcoming “Departure” LP. If this record is any indication, the Bay Area platinum powerhouse quartet hasn’t so much shifted direction as it has re-structured its musical stance and tightened up the rhythm sec- tion. This new economy should see them achieve new pop, APR heights. JIMMY RUFFIN (RSO RS-1021) Hold On To My Love (3:36) (Stigwood Music, Inc., admin, by Uni-chappell Music — BMI) (R. Gibb, B. Weaver) David Ruffin’s younger brother Jimmy should receive massive B/C and pop attention with this track co-written and produced by Bee Gee Robin Gibb and Blue Weaver. Ruffin gives the glistening melody a tough vocal workout and Gibb adds one of his patented high vocal swoops just for good measure. Already grabbing numerous adds. STEVE WALSH (Kirshner ZS9 4287) Schemer-Dreamer (3:20) (Don Kirshner Music/Blackwood Music Publishing/Rightsong Music — BMI) (S. Walsh, A. Crudup) Kansas’ lead singer and keyboard man Steve Walsh steps into the solo spotlight with the title track from his recently released debut LP. Com- bining a re-working of Arthur Crudup’s early rock classic “That’s All Right” with a neatly fitting boogie beat intro. ISAAC HAYES (Polydor PD 2068) A Few More Kisses To Go (4:05) (Rightsong Music — BMI) (I. Hayes) Following the surpriseTop 20 success of “Don’t Let Go," the hot buttered soulster lets his sexy crooning talents loose on this jazzy R&B ballad and the result is a solid crossover effort for pop and A/C, as well as B/C lists. Hayes’ distinctive breathy bass vocal is balanced by subtle female backup work and the thick mid-tempo instrumen- tal is just right. DARYL HALL & JOHN OATES (RCA PB-11920) Who Said The World Was Fair (3:30) (Hot-Cha Music Co. /Six Continents Music Publishing, Inc. — BMI) (D. Hall, S. Allen) A pounding, Latin-tinged dance beat kicks off the bright, tumbling second single from Hall & Oates’ “X-Static” LP. This is an extremely lively af- fair, and the swinging percussives are nicely com- plemented by clicking guitar and jumpy keyboard fills, making for a finger snappin’ pop-dance addi- tion. THE ISLEY BROTHERS (T-Neck ZS9 2290) Don’t Say Goodnight (It’s Time For Love) ( part 1 & 2) (4:32) (Bovine Music, Inc. — ASCAP) (E. Isley, M. Isley, C. Jasper, R. Isley, O. Isley, R. Isley) A most fitting first single from the Isley Brothers’ forthcoming “Go All The Way” LP, this sinewy R&B-flavored ballad is virtually brimming with sensuality, aided by the silky, luxuriant lead vocals of Ron Isley. A feathery instrumental bed buoys this sturdy multi-format effort. CLIFF RICHARD (EMI America 8035) Carrie (3:42) (Unart Music Corp./Cookaway Music, Inc. — BMI/ASCAP) (T. Britten, B. Robertson) A foreboding opening sets the playfully menac- ing tone for this offbeat single from the "We Don’t T alk Anymore” LP. A brooding bass line and eerie synthesizer bring out the ghostly charm in this tune, which has a strong reference to the Brian DePalma film thriller. Already charting, look for more pop adds. AIRPLAY (RCA PB-11738) Should We Carry On (3:43) (Garden Rake Music/Foster Frees Music/Irving Music — BMI/Cotaba Music-PRO) (D. Foster, J. Graydon, B.J. Cook Foster) Producer/songwriter David Foster steps out from behind the boards with Jay Graydon, and the first single from the duo's self-titled debut LP shows that they have the sort of commercial pop/A/C-oriented musical sensibility to justify their name. SINGLES TO W4TCH ELLEN FOLEY (Epic 9-50839) Sad Song (3:30) (April Music, Inc. /Heath Leavy Music/WB Music Corp. — ASCAP) (M. Middler, P. Mason) Foley’s last single, “What’s A Matter, Baby,” scored well on international charts and playlists but this early '60s styled pop ballad should help build her audience further at home. Phil Spector-like production. SANTANA (Columbia 1-11218) All I Ever Wanted (3:26) (Light Music-BMI/Urmila Music — ASCAP) (D.C. Santana, C. Solberg, A. Ligertwood) The second single from Santana’s “Marathon” LP finds him and his crew in perhaps the hardest rocking groove ever, as a pummelling drum beat and supersonic guitars cut through the song like a blowtorch. An ex- tremely hot AOR track. PATTI LABELLE (Epic 9-50852) Release (The Tension) (3:01) (Warner-Tamerlane Publishing Corp./Marsaint Music, Inc. — BMI) (A.R. Toussaint) Allen Toussaint wrote this most timely track for Labelle’s upcoming “Released” LP and the funky New Orleans musical flavor suits the soulful Labelle well, as it has in the past with the Labelle hit, “Lady Marmalade.” Look for B/C, dance play. SLAVE (Cotillion 45011) Foxy Lady (Funky Lady) (3:23) (Cotillion Music, In- c./Wayne Watts Music — BMI) (J.R. Wilson) Slave scored heavily on B/C lists the last time out with the title track from its "Just A Touch Of Love” LP and this equally funky follow-up should gain quick adds right out of the box. Heavy bottom and steady dance beat could also spell crossover success. ROY SUNDHOLM (Polydor PD 2065) Waiting For The Night (3:07) (Dizzy Heights Music Publishing Ltd.-PRS) (R. Sundholm) This track from Sundholm’s current LP, “The Chinese Method.” has the kind of breathless vocal edge and tumultuous musical intensity that rock ‘n’ roll dreams are made of. A wall of rock for AOR, pop lists. SUE SAAD AND THE NEXT (Planet P-45912) Won’t Give It Up (3:33) (WB Music Corp. — ASCAP) (S. Saad, T. Riparetti, J. Lance, B. Anstatt) Planet rookies Sue Saad and the Next rank high among the recent bumper crop of new rockers to watch, and this single shows they have both the style and power to back that recommendation up. Fast but not flashy, this has the drive and substance to make it on AOR and pop lists. CROWN HEIGHTS AFFAIR (De-Lite DE-803) You Gave Me Love (3:38) (Delightful Music/Crown Heights Affair Publ. Co., Inc. — BMI) (I. Reid) This record, from CHA's “Sure Shot" LP, was recorded very loud, presumably for the benefit of disco/dance play, but this should suit the tastes of B/C programmers and audiences as well. NANCY WILSON (Capitol 4839) Let’s Hold On To Love (4:35) (Funky Caroline Music — BMI) (C. Johns, L. Farrow) Longtime Capitol R&B veteran Nancy Wilson is back with a unique mid-tempo ballad harkening back somewhat to Dionne Warwick’s earlier hits. From “Take My Love," her 41st LP for the label, this could cross to pop lists. ZAMFIR (Mercury 76045) The Lonely Sherherd (3:09) (Happy Music-Verlag) (J. Last) Internationally known orchestra ieader/com- poser/producer James Last has come up with a very uni- que track for an artist known only as Zamfir, who plays the unconventional Pan pipe of Greek extraction. A bit- tersweet, oddly affecting melody could make this a novelty sleeper. QUIET STORM (Tamla T 54310F) Only You — Part 1 (3:47) (Bertram Music Co. — ASCAP) (R. Rancifer) This Smokey Robinson-produced R&B/dance outing is long on rhythm with rock steady bass and conga work behind jazzy female harmonies. A tasty sax break fits right in the pocket. B/C and dance programmers are urged to give this a listen. MARC TANNER BAND (Elektra E-46614) Hot And Cold (3:27) (Otherwise Publishing — ASCAP) (M. Tanner, R. Edwards, J. Romersa) E/A has quickly followed “Hold Your Head Up." Tan- ner's last outing from his new “T emptation" LP, with this muscular rocker. Crackling guitar work weaves throughout the big power chords here, as Tanner's vocal cuts deep. A pleasure for AOR, pop lists. JOAN ARMATRADING (A&M 2224) He Wants Her (3:15) (Rondor Music, London, Ltd., ad- min. in the U.S. and Canada by Irving Music, Inc. — BMI) (J. Armatrading) The second single from Armatrading's “How Cruel" EP strikes a most distinctive balance between a lazy reggae beat and a lyric filled with the sexual tension of the male on the hunt. Well-handled by the English-Jamaican songstress, this deserves AOR, B/C and pop play. NAZARETH (A&M 2219) Holiday (3:35) (Panache Music Inc. — ASCAP) (Me Caf- ferty, Cleminson, Charlton, Agnew, Sweet) The first single from Nazareth's new “Malice In Won- derland” LP is truly a group effort, with each member contributing to the composition. The band's new pop- oriented approach also owes a debt to such original pop- sters as T-Rex here. Slick enough for pop, but not too light for AOR. THE CLASH (Epic 9-50851) Train In Vain (Stand By Me) (3:00) (Riva Music, Inc. — ASCAP) (J. Strummer, M. Jones) This is without a doubt the most commercial effort The Clash has released to date, but it hardly represents a sell- out to attain mass appeal by the punk veterans. An infec- tious rhythm has supplanted the three chord guitar at- tack and Joe Strummer is more restained but equally as effective. An AOR, pop sleeper. KENNY DOSS (Bearsville BSS 49197) Sugar (3:26) (Every Knight Music/Unichappel Music — BMI) (M. H. Bryant) The first fruit of a production pact between Bearsville and blues great Willie Mitchell, this track from Doss’ up- coming “Movin’ On A Feeling” LP is highly infectious. 18 Cash Box/March 1, 1980

MERCHANDISING wmrs IN-STORE TOWER PROMOTIONS — A check with the Tower Records stores in the San Francisco Bay area turned up these activities. A Pearl Harbor contest is in progress at the Berkeley, Concord, San Francisco, Mountain View, Fresno and Campbell stores. There wili be a drawing that will result in ten couples being awarded a “Pearl Harbor cruise” on the Blue and Gold Fleet around San Francisco Bay ... A second contest is being held in conjunction with KKHI radio, Columbia Masterworks and United Airlines. The grand prize will be a weekend for two in New York, March 24-31, with accomodations at the Plaza Hotel. The couple will be given tickets to see “Don Pasquale” at the Metropolitan House and “Mefistofeles” at the New York City Opera. NEW YORK PROMOTIONS — Some new activity has been reported from the New York CBS office. The 28 Record World/T.S.S. locations and WLIR-FM are conducting a major Molly Hatchet promotion. A drawing will be held in which there will be 21 consumer prizes. The grand prize will be a “Flirtin With Disaster” gold record, picture discs and autographed Hatchet albums. Ten second prizes will also be awarded: picture discs and autographed LPs, with ten third prizes of picture discs and Hatchet albums. In addition, there is a merchandising contest for the chain. The store manager who does the best job of display- ing the LP will receive a gold record with five runner-up prizes of picture discs. . . A second promotion involving the Romantics album is being conducted with the seven Crazy Eddie’s stereo outlets and three college radio stations, NYU, Fordham and Rutgers. A New York City “Weekend Spree” is being offered to the winner. This will consist of tickets to a play, dinner and a horse and buggy ride for each night of the weekend. MORE STAR TREK NEWS — Several more chains have announced promotional activity involving the Star Trek LP. Korvette’s in New York is displaying a pinball machine in its 34th Street store that forms the basis of the promotion. The contest, tied in with WKTU radio (92 AM), will work as follows: Contestants will mail entries to WKTU or fill out forms at the Korvettes stores. Ninety-two winners will be selected at random, each receiving a Star Trek album. They then will be allowed to compete in a pinball playoff during the following week. The 20 highest scorers will receive customized tote bags designed at the New York CBS office. They will then participate in the finals, with the winner receiving the machine it- self, valued at $1,800 . . . The Music Plus stores are conducting a Star Trek and Pink Floyd promotion under the slogan, “Even the Walls Have Ears.” A drawing on Nov. 26 wili deter- mine the four winners, each of whom will receive pairs of RSL Formula 30 speakers. OTHER ACTIVITY — Peaches, Kansas City, conducting a large push for Nutts and Butts, a local group. The LP is being given a heavy storeplay along with distribution of buttons and sale of t-shirts . . . Some creative merchandising of the new Heart album. Sound Warehouse, San Antonio, is having customers complete entry forms with three trivia ques- tions about the group. There then will be a drawing with a grand prize of free membership to the International Fitness Center; and Peaches, Oklahoma City, with a charity push, is donating $1 to the Heart Association for every Heart album sold between Feb. 14 and Feb. 28 . . . Radio Doctors, Milwaukee, is holding a promotion along with WPLX. The station has formed a “Rock ‘n’ Roll Air Force” club and any patron who comes into the store on a Wed- nesday and shows the club’s emblem will receive a discount . . .Peaches, Indianapolis, has a Bruce Cockburn “Dancing in the Dragon’s Jaws" kite contest. Entrants will register dur- ing February to be eligible to win six Chinese kites. CUSTOMER QUOTE OF THE WEEK: “I’d like to exchange this album. I listened to it, and frankly, I don't like it at all,” IN-STORE — Toto made an informal appearance at Charts, Phoenix, Feb. 4 . . . Jane Oiivor, with a huge in-store, Feb. 8, at the new Sam Goody store at Moorestown, New Jer- sey, drew close to 1,000 patrons . . . Whispers showed up at National Record Mart, Oakland, Penn., Feb. 23 . . Lydia Lunch was at Tower, Seattle, Feb, 29. REGIONAL ACTIVITY — New Heart is strong everywhere, particularly in the midwest and west. . . Latest John Denver has strong reports from the midwest and west. . .New Warren Zevon is powerful in the west, with new Sister Sledge selling best in the east . . . Lene Lovich is strong on both coasts, and Brothers Johnson are breaking out of the east and south. ENDS AND ODDS — More saies and openings: Gary’s Records, Virginia, is holding a special saie to celebrate the 25th anniversary of Motown Records. All the “Greatest Hits” packages will be run on special saie during the last weekend in February. . . Disc Records, Texas, is going with a “Leap into the 80’s with the best music of the 7G’s” sale at its 13 stores. Albums from the 7% WEA program wili be sold at reduced prices . . . Radio Doctors scored with a four-day “Honest George Washington” sale in which all albums were featured at $1.00 off the normal price . , . National Record Mart ran a grand opening sale at its new Columbus, Ohio outlet, Feb. 21-24. THE RHYTHM SECTION NEWS FROM ARISTA — At the recent Arista Records regional meetings held in Los Angeles, label president Clive Davis announced that Aretha Franklin had been signed to a contract. Other highlights of the meeting included presentations of upcoming product from Raydlo, The Three Degrees, The Average White Band, Gene Page (featuring Charlene Sylvers) and Dionne Warwick. Warwick’s new effort was produced by Steve Buckingham. NEW ARRIVAL — Casablanca's Jehryl Busby and his wife Carolyn are the proud parents of a bouncy baby girl named LaVonne Frances. BLACK OPINION COMPANY FORMED — Data Black Public Opinion Polls Inc. isthefirst black-owned national survey and research organization devoted entirely to the study of the black American public. Data Black will focus on conducting four scientific local and national surveys annually for distribution to subscribers. Data Black is jointly owned by Dr. Kenneth Clark, president of the Clark, Phillips, Clark, Harris research consulting firm, and Percy Sutton, chairman of the board of Inner City Broadcasting Corporation. For more in- formation call James E. Booker Associates. Inc. at (212) 755-0842. FCC CHANGE EEO RULING — After April 1, the FCC will start to review stations with five or more employees, to determine whether minorities or women are employed at a ratio of 50% of their availability within the local work force. Stations that have 11 or more em- ployees will be required to have a 50% ratio of minority and/or women in its top four job categories. All stations with 50 or more employees will be subject to a complete EEO review. RANDY BROWN TAKES OFF WITH CHOCOLATE CITY — Randy Brown’s first album for Cecil Holmes’Ghocolate City Records, “Midnight Desire,” is really off to an excellent start as several major stations including WOL, WWRL, KGFJ, WWIN, KATZ, WGIV and others have added the single “We OughtTo Be Doin’ It." Gearing up for a heavy push on Brown’s career, the company is organizing a showcase to make more of the public aware of what a fine performer he is. BOOTH CHALLENGES FCC — Booth American Company informed the FCC that it will fight to keep its broadcast license and not succumb to the easy out with a “distress sale." The two organizations will meet April 1 5 at a hearing that has been set by the FCC to deter- mine whether this organization will keep its broadcast license and the two Detroit stations, WJLB and WMZK. John L. Booth II has been quoted as saying that the company is confi- dent that when that organization’s total record is reviewed, the FCC will agree that Booth America Company is indeed qualified to hold the licenses of its two Detroit stations. Booth has owned WJLB since 1941, and it was the first station in Detroit to program specifically for the black community. THE ENTERTAINMENT COMPANY MAGIC — The Entertainment Company, which has worked its magic on such top artists as Cher, Captain and Tennille, Tom Jones, and Thelma Houston, to name a few, is now waving that wand over a new group on MCA Records called Heat. The album was produced by Tom Savianoand David Wolfert and will be released in early March in an album cover that is mirror black, embossed with burning letters that spell out H-E-A-T. ROAD WILLIE & LEON (Columbia KC2 36064) 67 38 COMPASS POINT DAVID ALLAN COE (Columbia JC 36277) 68 13 ROSE COLORED GLASSES JOHN CONLEE (MCA AY-1105) 69 67 SPECIAL DELIVERY DOTTIE WEST (United Artists LT-1000) 70 11 Capitol And UA Consolidate Country Promotion Staffs by Don Cusic NASHVILLE — The United Artists and Capitol labels combined their country promotion staffs Feb. 19 in Nashville. In a consolidation move that also affected the R&B promotion teams for the labels in Hollywood (See separate story, page 7), Capitol/United Artists/EMI America presi- dent Don Zimmermann announced that Lynn Shults will head the Group's Nashville operation, with Jerry Seabolt in charge of country promotion. As explained by Zimmermann, the con- solidation under Shults, head of Capitol's Nashville operations, and Seabolt, head of United Artists' Nashvilie unit, means that the UA promotion team will now handle acts on both labels. As a result of the consolidation and UA’s assumption of country promotion duties, four employees were terminated on Feb. 19. Among the staffers terminated were Ed Keeley, head of Capitol’s country promo- tion unit, Jack Pride and Chuck Flood, also with Capitol; and Pat King from UA. ‘Better Focus’ Zimmermann stated that the consolida- tion would provide a “better focus and bet- ter direction” for country promotion. A total of 24 acts will fall under the wing of the new promotion set-up. These acts in- clude Kenny Rogers, Charlie Rich, Christy Lane, Billie Jo Spears, Dottie West, Bobby Smith, Saundra Steele, David Willis and Bobby Wright on the United Artists label; and Glen Campbell, Anne Murray, Jessi Coulter, Dr. Hook, Deborah Allen, Lee Clayton, Billy “Crash” Craddock, Kenny Dale, LaCosta, Mel McDaniel, Diane Pfiefer, Don Schlitz, Keith Stegall, Chip Taylor and Gene Watson on Captiol. Capitol-EMI manufactures and dis- tributes both Capitol and United Artists product and the labels share a common sales force. Also, since January 1980, both labels have shared offices at 29 Music Square East in Nashville in a building ow- ned by Kenny Rogers. Cates, Hagen Open Production Co. NASHVILLE — Producers Joseph Cates and Chet Hagan have announced the for- mation of Cates/Hagan, Inc., a Nashville- based production company. Located at 25 Music Square West, the firm will be headed by Barbara Hill, a native of Nashville who is an associate of the parent company, Joseph Cates Co., Inc., of New York and Los Angeles. According to the producers, the facility is an indication of their involvement with and commitment to the Nashville music and en- tertainment community. Cates and Hagan have in the past worked on such television specials as the CBS Johnny Cash specials; “Fifty Years of Country Music,” with hosts Dolly Parton, Glen Campbell and Roy dark; “Country Night of Stars,” with hosts Crystal Gayle, Eddy Arnold, Tennessee Ernie Ford and Chariey Pride; and most recently, “Country Superstars of the Seventies,” a program for President and Mrs. Carter which aired from historic Ford’s Theatre in Washington, D.C. Cates and Hagan have also scored big with separate production ventures. Cates lined up some impressive credits for his work on the motion picture, “The Last Married Couple In America,” and many television specials, including “George M" and “ ‘S Wonderful, 'S Marvelous, S Gershwin.” Hagan was the producer of “instant specials” for 20 years with NBC News, which included "American Revolution of '63” and “The Cuban Missile Crisis." Hagan was also the first producer of the Country Music Association Awards Show. Thunderbird Signs Three Artists To Roster TULSA — Thunderbird Artists, a division of the Jim Halsey Company, has added Kenny Dale. Sequestered off to the side of the ac- tion on a bandstand, often playing for inattentive audiences, a real musician is challenged to pull the people into the spirit of the music. Visiting the charming Seventh Avenue bar, the Angry Squire, one night recently for a quick snort, Cash Box was sur- prised to see pianist/vocalist Amina Claudine Myers holding forth with a trio on the elevated bandstand. Though she’s usually associated with the avant garde through her work with people like Lester Bowie, Muhal Richard Abrams and Leroy Jenkins, Amina’s grasp of the jazz tradition and her regal, dignified beauty recall the great Mary Lou Williams. We came in on the heels of Ellington’s “Take The A T rain,” which Meyers invested with a rich bluesiness and driv- ing two-handed harmonies. On “Sum- mertime,” bassist Bob Cunningham’s immaculate arco melodies steered clear of the usual cliches, propelling the tune from deep melancholy to exultant swing; and guest drummer Phillip Wilson provided gossamer colors and intricate accents at a dynamic level so soft it felt like the human breath . . . Trombonist Joseph Bowie is no stranger to the bar blues either, his early mid-western musical experiences hav- ing been dotted with carnivals, rock and roll and late night R&B. His new punk jazz band, Defunkt, is dedicated to the dance impulse, and their performance at the rock disco Hurrah reflected both the rolling rave-ups of seminal Detroit rock bands like the MC5 and the very rawest of pre-“Are You Experienced” Jimi Hendrix. The dance elements in Dekunkt’s music are still evolving, and more often than not they work up to loping, violent ex- changes between guitarists Kelvin Bell and Vernon Reid and bassist Melvin Gibbs. Bowie’s singing was a triumph of style over content, but his trombone playing — both acoustic and electronically altered — was muscular, highly vocalized and humorous. If Defunkt is dutch for, the St. Louis Ensemble — • Bowie's collaboration with funky-buff altoist Luther Thomas — is a complete delight right now. Featuring Alex Blake’s quicksilver Alembic bass lines, Donald Smith’s sanctified piano and vocals (his ecstatic solo rendition of Billy Strayhorn’s “Lush Life" was one of the evening’s high points), and the Cajun rhythms of drummer Phillip Wilson, the St. Louis Ensemble’s Public Theatre performance was an ebullient historical progression from cottonfields and country churches of the deep South to the swaggering hiposity of the urban blues and jazz traditions. Bowie seemed more comfortable with the old-timev R&B of the En- semble, evoking images of Miles in his solos, while Luther Thomas sounded like Lou Donaldson being pistol-whipped in the bathroom of an East St. Louis precinct. Their free jazz explorations were also worthy, but the theatrical gesturing and deep gospel overtones of their church parody (“Won’t you accept Jesus, brother?”) made everything else pale by comparison . . . HELPING HANDS —- The Universal Jazz Coalition, Inc. (UJC), under the leadership of executive director Cobi Narita, has been providing guidance and practical assistance to New York jazz musicians for many years, with an emphasis on opening up a dialog between the creative and business ends of the music industry. Last month at the Jazz Gallery (55 W. 19th Street), the UJC held a conference on the jazz record industry with panelists Vernon Slaughter (CBS), Elliot Horne, (RCA), Bob Hurwitz (ECM), Andre THE ROXY GENERATION — United Artists Records recording-artist Ronnie Laws recently performed at L.A.’s Roxy. MAGICO — Haden, Garbarek and Gismonti — ECM ECM-7- 7757 — Producer: Manfred Eicher — List: 8.98 There is much drama on this LPfrom these three journeyman jazzmen. Jan Garbarek’s mournful sax, Charlie Haden’s responsive bass work and Egberto Gismonti's flavorful guitars and piano set a mood and never let go. There is nothing obvious about the music, but the sound flows from tempo and melodic phrases effortlessly. “Bailarina” and “Palhaco” are powerful enough to demand more than casual listening, while the rest of the LP becomes a single, haunting mood piece. WITH ALL MY LOVE — Wilbert Longmire — Tappan Zee/Columbia JC-36342 — Producers: Bob James and Jay Chataway — List: 7.98 — Bar Coded Easy-going, building inevitable conclusions, Wilbert Longmire’s quality for musical understatement lends much character to this often melodic LP. With the help of producer Bob James on keyboards, Longmire delivers a sensitive product with mass appeal potential. “But I Love You," “Crystal Clear,” “Take Your Time,” the theme from the TV show Taxi, and “Strawberry Sunset” are the best tunes on this disc. YOU’LL NEVER KNOW — Rodney Franklin — Columbia NJC- 36122 — Producer: Paul Buckmaster — List: 7.98 — Bar Coded Progressive ensemble jazz, spiced with unobtrusive, yet lux- urious orchestration, makes this LP a jazz-pop must. Never hurried, Rodney Franklin manages to touch base with nearly all established facets of jazz interpretation, while forging ahead into his distinct style. "Felix Leo," “The Watcher," “The Groove,” and the title track are prime cuts from this fine album. JAZZABUM PICKS grnraBSwnTr i continued on p,iqe 42) DUKE ELLINGTON/SONG BOOK ONE - Sarah Vaughn — PabloToday 2312-111 — Producer: Norman Granz — List: 8.98 The rich, dusky singing of jazz diva Sarah Vaughn is show- cased in a variety of ensembles and moods on this excellent new Norman Granz production. The Divine One shines in lux- uriant string settings like "In A Sentimental Mood” and “Lush Life"; rich, pensive ballads like “Solitude" and the amazing "Day Dream”; and heavy swingers like “In A Mellow Tone.” Excellent jazzmen like J.J. Johnson, Joe Pass, Jimmy Rowles and Zoot Sims offer homage to Duke and Strayhorn and orchestrate every vocal slur and moan to perfection. THE DUKE ELLINGTON SONGBOOK — Ella Fitzgerald — Verve VE-2-2535 — Producer: Norman Granz — List: 8.98 This is a vital, vibrant jazz recording. Fitzgerald's impeccable swing, and trombone — like intonation are perfectly couched in the matrix of voices and counterpoint which Duke Ellington con- jures from this powerhouse 1957 orchestra. The selection of tunes illustrates just how totally Ellington dominates the American song form, and the “Portrait of Ella Fitzgerald” is a magisterial example of his prowess with extended forms. Ella is particularly sweet and slashing on “Rockin’ In Rhythm," and "The E And D Blues,” a blue suede coo on “I Didn't Know About You." ALIVE! — Alive — Urana Records/Wisc Women Enterprises ST WWE 84 — Producer: Althea Waites — List: 7.98 A spirited romp by this five-woman jazz group comprised of drummer Barbara Borden, percussionist Carolyn Brandy, bassist/cellist Suzanne Vincenza, pianist Janet Small and vocalist Rhiannon. The music recalls the insistent modal designs of the '60s with fine, lyrical playing and Afro-Latin over- tones, not to mention some fine vocal arrangements with A/C radio promise. Smurf Sales Up In Scandinavia COPENHAGEN — Following a trend that first took hold in Scandinavia two years ago in Norway, Smurf albums have become a significant outlet for local talent. Initiated by Geir Borresen’s debut on Ole Sorli’s Decibel label, the Smurf craze has accoun- ted for more than one miliion album sales in Sweden, Norway and Denmark. The originator of the Smurf trend on the continent was the German artist Fader Abraham, who in turn, was influenced by the Wombles on the UK. The Wombles, which featured Mike Batt (who currently records for Epic), was an ecology-minded fad group of the late-‘60s and early-‘70s that popularized “silly” pop music along the lines of the Banana Splits of the USA. Smurf sales have been the strongest in Norway, where, in the last two years, Borresen’s releases on the Decibel label have accounted for more than 500,000 sales. Smurf sales in Denmark have also been significant in the last two years, with Johnny Reimar’s releases on his own Starbox label accounting for more than 200,000 sales. In Sweden, which was the last of the Scandinavian countries to pick up the smurf trend, Klasse Moiberg and Stefan Ruden have accounted for more than 250,- 000 sales in the last year. ASCAP Monies Up Again In ‘79 (continued from page 12) For the sixth straight year, ASCAP repor- ted on advances made to members to be recovered from future distributions due these members. As of Dec. 31, 1979, total outstanding advances to members were $4,512,000, up from $3,467,000 a year earlier. According to ASCAP, the manage- ment reviewed the status of expanded ad- vances and an amount totalling $112,000 was considered as non-recoupable. However, $70,000 from advances written off in prior years was recovered. ASCAP's cost of operating for 1979, based on domestic and foreign receipts amounted to 19.03% in 1979. Foreign Installments Foreign distributions were made in two installments. A July 31 disbursement of $9,- 716,000 was distributed as follows: England, $4,176,000; France, $2,472,000; Germany $2,355,000; Sweden, $529,000; and South Africa, $184,000. On Dec. 28 another foreign installment was made totalling $11,496,000 for the following countries: Australia, $1,372,000; Austria, $516,000; Belgium, $461,000; Canada, $3,645,000; Denmark, $303,000, Holland, $1 ,082,000; Italy, $933,000; Japan, $848,000; Spain, $237,000; and Swit- zerland $523,000. Adams also formally announced that he would retire as president of ASCAP in April. Although he said he would continue “to remain a boyfriend,” the announcement ends a 17-year reign as the society's head. Networks Battle Radio Syndicators (continued from page 19) cited Westwood One as his #1 competitor for short form features. Westwood One, a major syndication firm that relies on the barter system, distributes Star Trak, a 90-second rock news show; an interview feature hosted by Candy Tusken called Off The Record; a rock interview show hosted by Mary Turner; and the Dr. Demento show. Westwood One founder and president, Norm Pattiz said, "The situation is com- petitive in the strictest sense. The only dif- ference is in distribution." It was felt by everyone surveyed that the bottom-line beneficiary of increased com- petitive quality programming is the listener. “When the listener is the winner,” Golden Egg's Cutler said, “then radio has suc- cessfully done its job." Consumer Electronic Imports Decline In ’79 NEW YORK — United States imports of most consumer electronics goods declined in 1979, according to the marketing ser- vices department of the Electronic In- dustries Association’s Consumer Elec- tronics Group. Imports of record players, record changers, and turntables for the year drop- ped to 6,995,627, a decline of 36.7% from the 1 1,057,646 units brought into the U.S. in 1978. Imports for this product category in the fourth quarter of 1979 also declined to 1,761,027, a 37.4% decrease from the 2,- 81 2,598 figure reported in the same period of 1978. In the video tape recorder/player category, U.S. imports increased to 629,- 280 units, representing a 23.6% increase from the 509,155 total reported in 1978. Fourth quarter video tape recorder/player imports also rose, jumping to 221,942 units from 133,723 units in the same period last year. Heilman Loses Appeal NEW YORK — A Federal judge has upheld the conviction of David Heilman, former president of E-C Tape Service, on charges of criminal copyright infringement. In a decision issued on Feb. 8 by Judge John F. Grady of U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, the Court rejec- ted Heilman’s contention that the U.S. Copyright Act is “constitutionally vague” and that he was selectively prosecuted. Liable For $4 Million Heilman was convicted of 18 counts of copyright infringement in February, 1979. More recently, a Federal judge in Milwaukee ruled that Heilman and E-C Tape were liable for more than $4 million in damages to record companies whose product was illegally duplicated by the company. In his decision, Judge Grady stated that Heilman’s knowledge of numerous civil ac- tions taken against illegal duplicators in- validated his contention that his infringe- ments were not willful. “Instead of conform- ing his conduct to the bounds of the law, (the) defendant chose to persist in conduct which he knew had a ‘high likelihood of be- ing held by a court of competent jurisdic- tion to be a violation of a criminal statute.’ That is surely sufficient to meet the accep- ted definition of willfullness.” ASCAP Sets Deadline For Writing Awards NEW YORK - ASCAP has set March 1 as the deadline for the receipt of entries in the 14th Annual ASGAP-Deems Taylor Awards. Prizes of $500 each will go to the authors of the best non-fiction books about music and/or its creators published in English in the U.S. A. during 1979. Prizes of $250 each will be awarded to writers of newspapers and/or magazine articles on similar subjects. Publishers of the winning works will be honored with plaques at the annual awards ceremony at ASCAP’s New York head- quarters. Writers, editors and publishers may enter works, and four copies of each entry are required. An entry in the articles category may be between one and ten arti- cles. Entries should be addressed to ASCAP-Deems Taylor Awards, American Society of Composers, Authors, and Publishers, One Lincoln Plaza, New York, New York 10023.
