The presentation of System 80 elec- tronics and Dimension 80 followed with an on-stage dialog between Dick Finger, direc- tor of engineering, and George Offshack, field service engineer, who began by detail- ing the variety of new features that were made possible through advanced (continued on page 48) NAMA President Hits New USDA Regulation CHICAGO — Charging that the U.S. Department of Agriculture regulation of competitive foods in schools “won't do a thing to help increase participation in the school food program or to discourage the plate waste criticized by members of the Congress", G. Richard Schreiber, presi- dent of the National Automatic Merchan- dising Association, predicted that the issue "may well wind up in the courts." The regulation, which is expected to go into effect by July 1 of this year, prohibits the sale of all soft drinks and items of “minimal nutritional value” until after the last lunch period throughout the school grounds, as noted by NAMA. Schreiber cited USDA’s own documen- tation, issued Nov. 28, 1979, as a curious contradiction since it went to great lengths to show that the regulation would have vir- tually no effect on the dollar volume of con- fections and soft drinks sold in schools. “This regulation is an obvious attempt to split the opposition,” Schreiber said. “Most candies and snacks can be sold from kin- dergarten through high school but soft drinks are prohibited completely, whether they meet the nutrient density test or not." (continued on page 48 1 Futuristic Design Highlights Bally’s New ‘Silverball Mania’ Pinball Game CHICAGO — Bally has taken pinball a step beyond with the creation of “Silverball Mania,” the factory’s newest and uniquely attractive conventional flipper. In this new model the Bally art department has provided an outstanding visual experience for players with dramatic artwork and graphics depicting a futuristic pinball world in a large silver pinball. Combined with the physical appeal of the game is the exciting play action it offers and the various scoring options to match the visual effects. Players must try to light all letters of the words SILVER-BALL MANIA on the playfield; each letter is worth 1,000 points with additional points for each com- pleted sequence. The first completion lights the Wizard Bonus for 15,000 points; the second lights the Supreme Wizard Bonus for 30,000 points and the third awards a special and lights a letter in the backglass SILVERBALL carryover feature. Any lit letter in the carryover feature (whether activated by player or operator adjustment) will remain lit from game to game to attract player interest. The game also has a center hoop feature with two rollovers and one target which help to light the playfield letters. The rollovers also increase the bonus up to 5x and the target can also award an extra ball. Ad- ditionally, there is a disappearing kicker beneath the flipper which can be activated by the top center lane or the center hoop as well as a kicker special light that can be lit. Further information about the new machine may be obtained by contacting a Bally distributor or the Bally Pinball Division at 90 O'Leary Drive, Bensenville, ill. 60106. ‘Silverball Mania’ Cash Box/March 1, 1980 47

THE INTERNATIONAL MUSIC RECORD WEEKLY VOLUME XLI — NUMBER 43 — March 8, 1980 G4SH BOX GEORGE ALBERT President and Publisher MEL ALBERT Vice President and General Manager EDITORIAL Who Do We NICK ALBARANO Marketing Director ALAN SUTTON Editor In Chief KEN TERRY Managing Editor J.B. CARMICLE General Manager, East Coast Cash Box would like to be the first to congratulate the RIAA, the FBI and all of the others for their con- tinuing efforts to control the pirates, counterfeiters and bootleggers in the record industry. If ever there was a cancer in the industry, it is certainly those who would steal the legitimate work of others. The theft of copyrighted works is a plague around JIM SHARP Director, Nashville East Coast Editorial LEO SACKS — AARON FUCHS RICHARD GOLD West Coast Editorial RICHARD IMAMURA, West Coast Editor MARK ALBERT, Radio Editor COOKIE AMERSON, Black Music Editor MARC CETNER — MICHAEL GLYNN DENNIS GARRICK — MICHAEL MARTINEZ Research KEN KIRKWOOD. Manager BILL FEASTER — LEN CHODOSH JACK CHIPMAN — MIKE PLACHETKA HARALD TAUBENREUTHER — LES HONIG the world, and it is good to see that steps can be taken to alleviate this problem. Everyone, from the artist to the label president to the retailer on the cor- ner, suffers from the actions of the pirate. However, as shown by the recent revelations on the east coast, one of the most disturbing things is the apparent involvement of legitimate record in- dustry people in the pirate schemes that law enfor- cement officials discovered. If our own industry par- ticipates in and perpetuates the problem, how will it Have To Blame? be possible to clean up the situation? If those who make their living and draw their creative satisfaction from the industry participate in the very actions that will ultimately destroy it, what hope is there for the future? If the music industry is to eventually triumph over those who would destroy it for personal gain, it must be a concerted effort. To borrow from Alexander Dumas, it must be “all for one, and one for all.” The music industry lives and dies as a single entity. If we are to all prosper in the coming years, we must all look outfor each other and stand up for what’s right. After all, if the music industry is allowed to go down the drain for the personal interests of a few non-thinking individuals, who do we have to blame but ourselves? Doobie Brothers, Billy Joel Local Polygram Capture Top Grammy Honors KuSUS'tSpS By by Alan Sutton LOS ANGELES — Artists whose careers have withstood the test of time — including Bob Dylan, the Doobie Brothers, Herb Alpert and Dionne Warwick — made a strong showing atthe 22nd annual Grammy Awards telecast live over CBS from the Shrine Auditorium here Feb. 27. The Doobies celebrated their 10th an- niversary by winning Grammys for best record (“What A Fool Believes”) and best pop group vocal, while the band's Michael McDonald was cited for best vocal arrange- ment and shared a Grammy with Kenny Loggins for writing “What A Fool Believes.” Dionne Warwick, a two-time Grammy winner, was again voted best female pop Up To 60 Record Staffers Dropped Casablanca by Richard Imamura LOS ANGELES — Up to 60 employees were terminated last week by Casablanca Record and FilmWorks as a result of the recently announced reorganization and belt-tightening at the Polygram Records Group (Cash Box, Feb. 23). The shake-up, which also included the shifting of Casablanca’s accounting department to the Polygram operation in New York, was particularly heavy in the editorial, publishing and publicity units. “The only thing we’re doing here is restructuring,” said Bruce Bird, Casablanca president. “We’re cutting back in the fringe areas, but the core of Casablanca, the strength, is still here." Nevertheless, while Bird stated that the figure of 60 employees terminated was “completely ridiculous,” various sources both within and outside the company con- firmed that total. Hardest hit by the terminations were the editorial, publishing and publicity units, with editorial head Ellen Wolf and publishing head Steve Biddell among those cut. Publishing duties will now be handled by Polygram’s Chappell Music, and ac- counting for the whole group will be han- dled by the conglomerate’s central office in New York. Nevertheless, said Bird, “some of the people” from Casablanca’s ac- counting unit will join the Polygram staff in New York. Bird also denied reports regarding the closing of Casablanca’s New York offices. (continued on page 44) singer by the 4,500 members of the National Academy of Recording Arts & Sciences. While Narada Michael Walden is best noted for his dazzling drum work with such eminent jazz/rock forces as John McLaughlin’s Mahavishnu Orchestra, The Jeff Beck band and Santana, his fourth solo album proves he has abilities elsewhere. Walden’s new “Dance Of Life” LP is at #15 on the Cash Box B/C LP chart and his single, “I Shoulda Loved Ya,” has goneTop 5 on the Black Contemporary Singles chart. The stats are proof positive that Walden has come out of the closet and exposed himself as a fine R&B vocalist. Narada showed that he was capable of handling other genres outside of rock and jazz with early 1979’s “Awakening” LP. The record was chock full of pop/disco cuts. However up until that time, Walden opted for a more cerebral sound. In 1972, Walden, anotoriousfreakforthe volatile jazz fusion sound of John McLaughlin, met the guitarist back stage at a gig in Connecticut. Walden expressed the desire to meet McLaughlin’s guru, and within days the man had set up a meeting that would turn out to be the turning point in Walden’s life. Sri Ghimnoy accepted Walden as a disciple and gave him the name Narada, meaning he who “brings light, delight and compassion from heaven to earth and takes back to heaven from earth all of her sufferings.” Shortly thereafter, McLaughlin asked the kinetic drummer to play in his band. Gigs with Jean-Luc Ponty and The London Symphony followed, and in ’74 Walden was guest drummer on Jeff Beck’s “Wired” LP. Walden left his beloved Mahavishnu in 1975 to pursue a solo career with Atlantic, sandwiching his solo efforts in between projects with Weather Report and Alphonse Johnson. Walden took his maiden voyage in 1976 with “Garden Of Love Light.” Since that time, he has recorded three more albums, “I Cry, I Smile” \n ’77, “Awakening" in early ’79 and this year’s R&B infused effort, “Dance Of Life." MCA ’79 Profits Up Despite Disc, Publishing Drop LOS ANGELES — Bolstered by a strong fourth quarter showing, MCA, Inc. reported record revenue and profit levels for the fiscal year ending Dec. 31, 1979. Revenues of $1.27 billion and profits of $178 million represented 13% and 39% jumps over 1978 fjgures, respectively. A lower tax rate (30% vs. 37% In 1978), plus peak Universal Studios and videodisk profits, more than offset record company losses and Sower profits in the Spencer Gifts subsidiary. Profits of $178 million, or $5.95 per share, achieved a record high for the second consecutive year. 1978 profits totalled $128 million, or $5.52 per share. Revenues of $1.27 billion broke com- pany standards for the third consecutive year. 1978 revenues, a record at the time, totalled $1.12 billion. In the records and music publishing areas, losses of $9.62 million represented a drastic drop from 1978 figures, which, showed a $14.2 million profit. The losses occurred despite a 25% increase in revenue from $131 million in 1978 to nearly $164 million. RIAA To Honor FBI For Its Disc Anti-piracy Work LOS ANGELES — The Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) will honor the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) for its efforts in combating recording piracy and counterfeiting with the 12th annual Cultural Award at a dinner in Washington, D.C. March 4, Director William Webster is scheduled to accept the award on behalf of the FBI at the RIAA function. In selecting the FBI, the RIAA noted that the Bureau’s enforcement program protects the creators of sound recordings, movies, books and plays from un- authorized exploitation of their works by pirates, bootleggers and counterfeiters. The selection of the FBI as Cultural Award recipients was made by the RIAA Board of Directors at its December meeting. Nets $50 Million In ‘79 Last year alone, the FBI, working with the RIAA’s anti-piracy intelligence unit and local law enforcement agencies, was responsible for confiscating more than $50 million worth of illegal record counterfeiting and tape duplicating equipment, counter- feit records, pirate eight-track and cassette tapes and related materials. In announcing the award, the RIAA said the FBI is “helping to preserve an environ- ment in which creativity and the arts can flourish, and the creative artist can prosper.” Recording industry executives will host approximately 1,000 guests at the annual dinner, including members of Congress, the Administration and the independent agencies. Entertainment is scheduled to be provided by Helen Reddy and Larry Gatlin and the Gatlin Brothers Band. REVIEWS DEPARTURE — Journey — Columbia FC 36339 — Producers: Geoff Workman and Kevin Elson — List: 8.98 — Bar Coded Journey has changed drastically from its early days as San Francisco’s premier progressive rock band. While its sound is still custom made for AOR, Journey is quickly becoming the Three Dog Night of the FM airwaves. Along with Styx and Foreigner, the band is probably the most listenable and com- mercial concert hall attraction around. The album is a lightweight rock stunner and is a must add for both FM and Top 40 programmers. Top tracks are “Any Way You Want It,” “Someday Soon” and “I’m Gryin’.” THE BLUE ALBUM — Harold Melvin and the Blue Notes — Source/MCA SOR-3197 — Producer: Harold Melvin — List: 7.98 Featuring vocals by songstress Sharon Paige, “The Blue Album” is a signal that there’s no time to be sad and blue. It’s time to dance, and “Tonight's The Night” leads the way. “Prayin’ ” is a cut from the traditional Blue Note doth, in style and vocal counterpoint. “If You're Looking For Somebody to Love" is a classy offering that features the writing of hit duo McFadden and Whitehead. Pop and B/C formats can get turntable mileage from this LP. PROTECT THE INNOCENT — Rachel Sweet — Stiff/Colum- bia NJC 36337 — Producers: Martin Rushent and Alan Wistanley — List: 7.98 —- Bar Coded Sweet turned a lot of heads with last year’s “Fool Around” LP, as she deftly mixed and matched country and punk stylings. While there is nothing as startling as “Who Does Lisa Like” or “What’s In The Cuckoo Clock,” on “Protect The Innocent,” Sweet shows off more of her straight ahead rock personality. Her new band hasn’t got the guts of Fingerprint!, but still rocks with intensity. A respectable follow-up LP. For AOR and adven- turesome Top 40. SYMPATHY — John Miles -lArista AB 4261 - Producer: Alan Parsons — List: 7.96 Miles is the lead singer on most of Alan Parsons’ projects, and on “Sympathy” he demonstrates, once again, that he is a most versatile singer. The songs on the album range from am- bitious progressive rock opuses, “We All Fall Down,” to light R&B/pop songs like the title tune. Parsons’ production is close to faultless, and the album showcases Miles’ vocal dynamics. Best Cuts are “Good Man Down” and “Fella In The Cellar.” BUGS TOMMOROW — Casablanca NBLP 7199 1 Producers: various — List: 7.98 The debut album by Bugs Tommorow represents Casablanca’s first venture into the new wave. Bugs and his band have an urgent, clean new rock sound that is augmented by catchy, erudite vocals and some of the wittiest lyrics around. The album has a Costello feel to it, but the band's music is more in the name of fun than Elvis’ work. This is a polished debut LP, and Bugs should have a bright future ahead. For AOR. PERISCOPE LIFE — Kayak — Mercury SRM 13824 — Producers: John Tilly and Kayak —- List: 7.98 This fine seven piece Dutch band has a layered guitar/synthesizer sound that conjures up images of a progressive rock ABBA. The lead vocals of Edward Reekers and the female chorus (Irene Linders and Katherine Lapthorn) meld into a spirited harmony. Songs such as “What’s In A Name” and “Beggars Can’t Be Choosers” have a European feel, but should appeal to the American FM audience. This is the group’s first effort on Mercury and it should finally break the band in the U.S. FORTRESS — Roadmaster — Mercury SRM1-3814 — Producers: Flo & Eddie and John Stronach — List: 7.98 This hard-rocking band from the midwest has always put out a hard-driving, fast-paced sound that is reminiscent of REO Speedwagon. However, this time out, producers Flo & Eddie and John Stronach have pulled in the reins, and heavily influen- ced the five-piece group with their pop sensibilities. The result is Roadmaster's most controlled and commercially viable effort to date. “Ride The Wind Away” and “Someday” are perfect for AOR. ANN-MARGARET — MCA MCA-3226 — Producer: Paul Sabu — List: 7.98 It’s been a long time between records for this alluring Las Vegas showstopper, but now she’s back with a strong rock ‘n’ roll/disco album. Sabu's production is unmistakable. The thundering percussion and his searing guitar are the perfect vehicle for Ann-Margaret’s growling, tigress-like vocals. The freewheeling “Never Gonna Let You Go” and the snarling “Mid- night Message” are the album’s best moments. SKYWAY — Skyy — Salsoul — SA-8532 — Producers: Randy Muller and Solomon Roberts — List: 7.98 “Dance, Dance, Dance,” a song of obvious intentions, best characterizes the music on this LP. The sound ranges from the Euro-disco mode to straight-ahead funk. The three ladies providing vocals on this disc make fine harmony, backed by consistent tempos. “Skyy Zoo” is the most inventive offering on this LP, while “High” and “Music” are tailor-made for happy feet. B/C programmer’s delight. THREE TIMES IN LOVE — Tommy James — Millennium BXL1 -- Producer: Tommy James — List: 7.98 On first listen, “Three Times In Love” suggests those hallowed 1967 bubblegum days of “Crimson and Clover" and “Crystal Blue Persuasion.” But a closer inspection will reveal that James’ music has truly matured. Songs such as “It's All Right Now” and “I Just Wanna Play The Music” show a contem- porary and tough Top 40 sound, while “Everything I Am” has a David Gates-like flavor. A nice comeback for A/C and Top 40. /""N AGAINST THE WIND — Bob Seger & The Silver Bullet Band — Capitol SOO-12Q41 — List: 8.98 — Bar Coded The man from Natbush City returns with “Against The Wind,” and happily, the LP was worth the wait. Court Documents Suggest Counterfeiter, Retailer Ties (continued from page 5) identified as Norton Verner of Rexdale, Canada. Verner, according to a four-count federal indictment returned against Tucker last month (Cash Box, Feb. 16), is said to have purchased approximately 60,000 counter- feit eight-track tapes from T ucker for an es- timated $80,00 in cash during 1978. The in- dictment also charges Tucker with at- tempting to “influence, construct and im- pede the due administration of justice” by telling Verner not to reveal the identities of parties engaged in the sale of counterfeit goods to the FBI, as well as attempting to extort $2,500 from Verner to protect the confidentiality of their relationship. Undercover Operation To obtain evidence of the illicit manufac- ture and distribution of counterfeit product, undercover agents opened up a record store called Modular Sounds in Westbury, N.Y., in mid-1978. At the shop, agents videotaped and recorded conversations with more than 50 individuals involved in the sale of counterfeit product. The objec- tive of the investigation, according to court documents, was to present the operation to “suspect music industry individuals, com- panies and corporations as another il- legitimate outfit involved in the purchase, manufacture and sale of counterfeit and pirate sound recordings." According to the deposition of one of the agents that ran the store, many of the in- dividuals with whom he associated during the course of the investigation had an "in- depth knowledge of each other’s opera- tions” and “openly competed against each other to filter their product through dis- tributors for final resale on the retail market.” The agent noted that, in his under- cover capacity, he spent approximately $8.25 million on counterfeit and pirate product. His purchases included approx- imately 117,000 counterfeit and pirate labels; 40,000 counterfeit sleeves; approx- imately 20,000 counterfeit and pirate eight- track tapes; 3,000 counterfeit cassettes; more than 400 masters; 400 duplicated pancakes; and assorted raw materials, in- cluding blank pancakes, shrink wrap, win- ders and blank cartridges. A well-placed Justice Department source last week allowed for the possibility that counterfeit product may have passed through both independent and branch dis- tribution organizations in large quantities. "We do not know of distributors dealing ex- clusively in counterfeit goods,” said the source, who added that whether counter- feiters deal directly with members of the legitimate industry is a matter for specula- tion. ‘Peppered’ Shipments However, an agent involved in the Modular Sounds operation told Cash Box in September 1979, that one-stops repeatedly delivered “peppered” ship- ments of goods to the location. “Once the il- licit product was manufactured,” said the agent, “it was sold directly to the one-stop or to an intermediary who in turn sold to the one-stop, and in some cases, directly to some major retail stores in the New York City area.” He added, “These inter- mediaries could be directly traced to organized crime.” The investigation, said the agent, in- dicated that organized crime’s involvement in the counterfeiting business begins at the distribution level, “because the real money comes from the sale of the goods. Manufacturing the product is too much of a risk, because you have to take into con- fidence the people that supply you the raw material, as well as the people who package the goods. As soon as the business becomes less of a high risk ven- ture, that’s when organized crime steps in.” List 01 Titles Counterfeit product seized as a result of the Modular Sounds investigation included many popular recordings by such artists as Fleetwood Mac (“Rumours”), Rod Stewart (“Foot Loose and Fancy Free") and Linda Ronstadt (“Simple Dreams”). In addition, product by Elvis Presley ("Moody Blue”), Donna Summer (“Alive and More”), Chicago (“Chicago XI”), as well as K-Tel In- ternational’s “Dance Machine” compila- tion, was also allegedly counterfeited and then distributed to retail stores in the New York metropolitan area, as well as other points in the east. Spokesmen from the various record companies whose goods were counterfeited declined to say whether they had discovered any of the aforemen- tioned titles in their returns. Many of the titles, according to court transcripts, were sold in the form of coun- terfeit pancakes and finished eight-track product by Tucker to undercover agents. Court records indicated that Tucker nor- mally wholesaled single discs for $1.50. In the case of “Saturday Night Fever,” however, the two-record set sold for $3.50. STEPPING DOWN — ASCAP president Stanley Adams recently announced that he would not seek re-election as president of the society after 17 years. However, he will remain a member of the ASCAP board. His announcement came during the ASCAP Los Angeles General Membership meeting. POINTS WEST GROWING UP IS HARD TO DO — While it is hopelessly trite in spots and unwieldy at times for director Adrian Lyne, Casablanca Record and FilmWorks’ latest film Foxes, is a bold and affecting film. Set against the seamier, neon side of Los Angeles’ San Fer- nando Valley, the film attempts to take a realistic look at the hectic life style of the modern-day teenage girl. While the ad campaign, advises that the movie’s four central characters are “daring to do it,” the film treats the female leads with the utmost respect. Jody Foster, who playes Jeannie, is the film’s most complete and believable character. Foster is the emotional anchor for Mary (Sally Kellerman), who plays a neurotic child- like mother, Madge (Maryln Kagan), her friend who so desperately wants to lose her virtue; Diedre (Kandice Stroh), a friend who possesses a rather robust sexual appetite; Annie (Cherie Currie), who plays the classic pill popping runaway, and Brad (Scott Baio), who plays a sort of skateboarding Dear Abraham. Although the character sketches seem ridiculously stereotypical, winning performances by the principal stars and some deft direction save the movie from becoming the average teenage exploita- tion film. Such contemporary issues as the dissolution of the nuclear family, and the new sexual freedom are also examined in a film that runs at a rock ‘n’ roll pace. The sub- ject matter and the dramatic synthesizer-oriented score by Giorgio Moroder work beautifully together, and his deft interweaving of Donna Summer’s “On The Radio” theme throughout the film also works as a nice cinematic device. Songs by Janis Ian, Angel, Brooklyn Dreams and Cher are also part of the thought provoking film’s soundtrack. The United Artists Film was produced by David Puttnam and Gerald Ayres. THE STRANGE CASE OF MR. MURPHY — Shoes bass player/vocalist John Murphy woke up one morning recently and found himself seeing funny black spots. A few days later his eye doctor diagnosed the visual impairment as detached retinas, and he was rushed to the Evanston, III. (The Shoes hometown) hospital. The Feb. 17 operation left the bewildered bass player lying flat on his back in total darkness for four days. Doctors were at a loss to explain why the freak injury (it usually plagues whiplash victims) hap- pened to Murphy. Murphy is now resting comfortably at brother/guitarist Jeff's house after the delicate operation, which requires removal of the eyeball. Murphy is required to wear bandages over both eyes, but there is a good chance that he will fully recover his eyesight. Well-wishers can call John at (312) 746-8213. marc cetner 14 Cash Box/March 8. 1980

Present were a number of CBS executives, retail account representatives, local radio program and music directors, and recording artist Larry Gatlin, who performed that night at the Houston Livestock Show and Rodeo. The marketing campaign is a take-off from the political campaign this election year that promises to give America “the people's choice.” CBS Records is using this slogan to capitalize on an already widespread and popular slogan to attract attention to its country product. Houston was chosen because of the tremendous volume of country sales in the southwest area of the country, particularly the Texas market. CBS artists who will be spotlighted during the campaign are Larry Gatlin, Mickey Gilley, George Jones, Willie Nelson, Johnny Paycheck, Bobby Bare, Johnny Cash, Moe Bandy, Charlie Daniels, Freddy Fender, Crystal Gayle, Johnny Rodriguez, David Allan Coe, Freddy Weller and Joe Stampley. COUNTRY CBS Bows CountryCampaign (continued from page 17) Paycheck and Bobby Bare. Retail sales will be supplemented with radio spots and a television spot. There will be five 60-second radio spots, four of which will feature three artists each and one which will highlight the entire Willie Nelson catalog. The tv spot will be a 30-second multi-artist presentation available for ac- count customization. CBS will also have a complete advertis- ing kit available for the product, including a sheet of logos; a sheet of ovals; 150 line drop-ins with a listing of artists’ names; 600 and 1,200 line blank space ads with headline and logo inside; 300 line Willie Nelson catalog layouts; mini sheets for 600 and 1 ,200 line reproductions; 600 line tape ad with design and a sheet of tape slugs for the 600 line ad. Additionally, a 2” x 2” sticker logo has been developed, which, when affixed to the product included in this program, will iden- tify it at retail. The consumer will have the chance to see this logo in print and/or on tv, again on the display material in the stores and then again on the actual product Retail Survey Retailers surveyed by Cash Box were generally favorable to the program. Lee Perron, manager of Friend’s Two Records in Oklahoma City, stated “A program like this is beneficial in two ways. First, it’s nice to have the marketing tools to use in-store and second, the use of the media will hopefully attract more traffic and cause more interest in new product” Perron added, “The whole idea behind this is that they want us to buy more product and they feel that by giving us the free radio spots and the marketing tools, we will in turn beef up our inventory for the expected increase in traffic. How much the retailer beefs up his inventory will depend on how well the label salesman presents his program.” Dutch Cramblitt of Circles Records in Phoenix added, “A program like this is definitely helpful to me as a retailer, par- ticularly the television advertising. It hits a market that is more easily swayed than the radio audience.” Advertising A Big Part Pete Steed of Radio Doctors in Atlanta agreed. He explained, “If the name of my store is tagged with the advertising, then it is helpful to me. If they don’t let people know I have the records here, normally it isn't. “Advertising should be a bigger part of the major merchandising campaign. We will use posters and other marketing tools to make a display for a centra! area where it can be seen because people do stop and look. It does attract customers,” Steed con- cluded. “I do like to use marketing tools.” Perron added, “The CBS approach seems like they’re going to help us with the traffic and in-store marketing, which will cause an up- surge in product sales. That seems like a positive approach, more so than the program approach where if you buy the product first, then you get the tools.” Artists Covered Product included in this special cam- paign includes the fourth quarter, 1979, releases from Willie Nelson, Crystal Gayle, Larry Gatlin, George Jones, Johnny Paycheck, Charlie Daniels, Mickey Gilley, Johnny Duncan, Moe Bandy/Joe Stam- pley, David Allan Coe, Rosanne Cash, Johnny Cash, Moe Bandy and Kris Kristof- ferson. First quarter, 1980, releases in the program include Willie Nelson, Janie Fricke, Freddy Fender, Johnny Rodriguez, Lacy J. Dalton, Freddy Weller and Bobby Bare product. Product in the mid-line series, priced at $5.98 includes albums by artists Willie Nelson, Johnny Paycheck, Moe Bandy, Johnny Duncan, Tanya Tucker, Marty Rob- bins, George Jones, George & Tammy, Johnny Cash, the Oak Ridge Boys, Charlie Rich, Tammy Wynette, David Allan Coe, Sonny James, Joe Stampley and Ray Price. Rick Blackburn Blackburn, Sherrill Center Of Nashville CBS Restructuring NASHVILLE — In a major restructuring of the CBS Records Nashville office, Rick Blackburn has been appointed vice presi- dent and general manager, and Billy Sherrill has been named vice president and executive producer. In addition, Sherrill will have his own production firm aligned with CBS. The announcement was made in New York by Bruce Lundvall, president of CBS Records. Blackburn will now be responsible for all marketing and A&R activities at CBS’ Nashville offices and will oversee all promotion, product management, artist development, publicity and creative ser- vices. He will also deal extensively with in- dependent producers. Sherrill has signed an exclusive, long- term production deal that will provide him the opportunity to sign new artists for CBS Records under his own production logo. The first artist to be recorded through this new arrangement will be Lacy J. Dalton. Additionally, Sherrill will continue to produce George Jones, Tammy Wynette, Johnny Paycheck, Johnny Rodriguez, Johnny Duncan and David Allan Coe for CBS, Blackburn joined CBS Records in 1966 as midwest regional sales manager for Epic, following a brief stint in radio in Cin- cinnati. in 1968, he was named director of merchandising for Epic and Associated labels. Blackburn joined Ode Records as vice president and genera! manager in 1970, later returning to Epic as director of national sales. He moved to Nashville in 1974 as vice president and general manager of Monument Records, which was affiliated with CBS at the time. In 1976 he returned to CBS as vice president, marketing. Sherrill joined CBS Records in Nashville in 1963 as a producer and in 1966 was named executive producer. In 1967 Sherrill was named director, Epic A&R, in Nashville and a year later, assumed the position of director of A&R for Columbia and Epic. In 1972 he was named vice president of Nashville A&R for CBS Records. ON J/4ZZ COLEMAN LANTERN — Saxophone giant Ornette Coleman has been rehearsing his remarkable electric band, Prime Time, for an Italian tour later this month. Prime Time — comprised of Jamaladeen Tacuma (Rickenbacker electric bass), Bern Nix and Charlie Elierbee (electric guitars), Denardo Coleman and Calvin Weston — also recorded a digital album last April that is creating a buzz of interest in the industry. Nix plays behind the beat like a JSmm Hall; Elierbee plays ahead of the beat with choppy James Brown figures and Hendrixian vamps; Weston lays down a firm funk groove that is right in the pocket as Denardo provides African fills and accents; and Tacuma— easily the most innovative elec- tric bassist in jazz today — holds everything together with his swiftly modulating lines and engages in a continuous dialog with Coleman's alto saxophone preachings. Tentatively en- titled “Fashion Face,” Coleman's album has impressed all who’ve heard it as the most revolutionary synthesis of dance music and jazz extant — one industry figure told me he thought it could definteiy get on the WBLS rotation. Need we say more? Coleman is also preparing to perform his symphonic work, “Skies Of America,” in Italy later this year, and has been arranging some compositions by the excellent singer, Roberta Baum. One of Baum’s songs, “Is This Creation?”, has airplay written ail over it, and they'll be going into the studios after Coleman’s return from Italy to cut a single. Coleman has been the most important American musican of the past 20 years, touching upon ethnic music, string and reed chamber works, small group swing, free jazz, blues, funk and rock. He has defined all manner of musical directions and it looks like we’ve finally caught up to where Ornette has been all along — the ‘80s is go- ing to be Ornette Coleman’s decade, so check it out or move over. BLOOD ON THE TRACKS — Blood Ulmer, a long-time collaborator of Coleman's, has recently been getting a lot of press attention on the basis of his live appearances and his Ar- tists House album, “Talas of Captain Black.” He recently recorded a new album with Oliver Lake on alto, David Murray on tenor, Olu Dara on trumpet, Amin All on Fender bass, and Calvin Weston and Ron Shannon Jackson on drums that more accurately reflects the funk directions that have delighted New York audiences. Rumors of a major label signing have circulated daily, with Warner Brothers given an inside track, and Columbia and Arista also in contention. At press time, the latest rumor had Ulmer signed to Warners, but we couldn’t confirm this, so we’ll have to keep you posted. INDEPENDENTS ON THE RISE — ECM Records’ successful distribution arrangement with Warner Brothers has inspired other jazz labels to take a look at similar deals. Ac- cording to Dr. George Butler, vice president of A&R , jazz/progressive music, for Colum- bia, his label is discussing the possibilities of such an arrangement with John Snyder of Ar- tists House Records. Could this be a trend? Weli, in an incisive industry article for an up- coming issue of Musician, Player & Listener British guitarist-producer Robert Fripp cites Polydor President Freddie Haayen’s insightful forecast that a large record company will shortly have a small roster of its own acts and function mainly as an administrative agency for several small labels ... In another observation that bodes well for jazz, Fripp points out that “what is now considered to be a marginal sales figure will be attractive within two and vital within five years.” Given the current state of the economy and the low cost of produc- (continued on page 37) ASCAP JOINS TRIBUTE — ASCAP mem- bership rep Eric McCaskill (c) joined E/A ’s Patrice Rushen (!) and Motown 's Syreeta at the "Tribute To The Black Child" sponsored by the Brotherhood Crusade at L.A.’s Shrine Auditorium. (Arista AB 4234) 20 28 DONALD BYRD (Elektra 6E-247) 32 17 CATCHING THE SUN ; Spyro Gyra — MCA MCA 5108 — Producers: Jay Beckenstein and Richard Calandra — List: 7.98 Smooth music here, with few frills. This LP will delight those captured by the lush music on the "Morning Dance” album. Spyro Gyra has managed to develop a distinct sound that may very well make them a contemporary jazz staple. There is something for all jazz tastes here. The title track is easy listen- ing, while “Laser Material” provokes contemplation about where jazz might be going. “Percolater” and “Safari” are also tasty tunes. EXCURSION BEYOND — Flight — Motown — M7-932R1 — Producer: Lee Young, Sr. — List: 7.98 From the title track on, this biend of electronics and stan- dard jazz travels to-and-fro between yesterday and, perhaps, tomorrow. Pat Vidas’ polytrumpet on the title cut and on “The Rumble” is refreshing and does not denigrate the idiom. Much of the music here is inventive, with Jim Yaeger’s synthesizer work leading the way. But a cover of the Jacksons’ “Shake Your Body (Down to the Ground)” will probably stimulate both jazz and B/C listeners. PICK ’EM — Ron Carter — Milestone M-9092— Producer: Ron Carter — List: 7.98 Graceful chamber music stylings that borrow from classical music in the use of a four-piece cello section, but which put the emphasis on a discreet form of bluesiness that Garter's followers have come to expect. Carter’s piccolo bass is the main melodic voice, along with Kenny Barron’s serene piano on a selection of tunes that range from the reflective ballad “Tran- quil” to the pungenttitletune(with Hugh McCracken's tasty har- monica and guitar). Adult Contemporary potential here. J4ZZABUM PICKS THREE WORKS FOR JAZZ SOLOISTS & SYMPHONY ORCHESTRA — Don Sebesky — Gryphon Records G-Z-791 — Producer: Norman Schwartz — List: 13.98 Sebesky’s orchestral synthesis is a brilliant coup that suc- ceeds against all odds in unifying the harmonic gravity of Bach. Stravinsky and Bartok with the uncanny rhythmic and melodic spontanaeity of a Charlie Parmer — a rite of swing instead of the usual ponderous mish-mosh. Stravinsky’s metric boldness is particularly well-suited to jazz interpretation, and the re- working of Bartok's Concerto tor Orchestra to include Bird’s spirit is a particular pleasure. FIRST STRING — String Trio of New York — Black Saint BSR 0031 — Producer: Giacomo Pellicciotti — List: 9.98 Bold, imaginative compositions and improvisations from this sensitive, exploratory axis of Billy Bang (violin), James Emery (guitar), and John Lindberg (bass). The influence of Anthony i Braxton and Ornette Coleman is strongly felt in the pointillistic timbres, angular melodies and freely inflected swing. TheString Trio’s exceptional group interplay benefits greatly from the i crystalline recording quality that one has come to expect from Black Saint Records. OUTSTANDING IN HIS FIELD — Bobby Shew — Inner City 1C 1077 — Producer: Bobby Shew — List: 7.98 West Coast musicians can swing their collective asses off, as this powefui quintet demonstrates. Shew is an exceptionally swinging trumpeter with a pure, beautiful tone, whose playing suggests Freddie Hubbard, Miles Davis and Blue Mitchell. The music on this record is reminiscent of the best Blue Note ses- sions of the 1960s in the way that it merges modern modal im- provising with the most essential elements of bebop. i 32 Cash Box/March 8. 1980

THE RHYTHM SECTION NARM MANAGEMENT PROGRAM •••• MARM’s Retail Management Certification Program is now gearing up for a second presentation, which will beheld in Chicago, April 21-25. The first presentation, held in Atlanta was very successful, according to Gerald Richardson, president of R&R Records and general manager of The Music Scene, and Thomas Ziegler, ' manager of the record division at Ziegler Enterprises. Richardson and Ziegler were spon- sored by the BMA at the first presentation, a five-day affair. “I was very happy that the BM A chose me to get involved in this program,” Ziegler explained. “I fee! that it allowed me to sharpen my management skills. It put me in a better position to deal with setting up dis- plays that sell records, and gave me a better approach to training new sales employees.” Richardson added to those comments, saying, “The seminar was like a crash course in management. ! was exposed to financial and corporate people who had expertise that I wanted to know about. I feel that the merchandising class is a must for anybody in that area of the business, being that there were exceptional ideas presented. My experience with the seminar led me to do a complete turnaround in my buying habits, and I think I am already seeing positive results.” More seminars will be in Los Angeles, June 16-20, and in Philadelphia, Aug. 4-8. The BMA will sponsor two black retailers per seminar. If you would like to attend these meetings when it comes to your city, contact the NARM office at (609) 795-5555. Members are charged $300 and non-members $400 for the 5-day sessions. COMMODORES TO TOKYO — The Commodores will be this year’s special guests at the | March 30 Tokyo Music Festival, which is one of the most important music events in Japan. The group will appear at the Tokyo Prince Hotel, where tickets for the event will sell for $100 a ticket. The group will leave March 26 and will return to the U.S. April 3, following a mini- tour performing at Budokan and the Exhibition Hail in Osaka. PRINCE TOUR — Prince has just embarked on a three-month tour that will take him to over 50 cities. The major portion of the tour will involve southern and east coast cities. The tour will start in Chicago and end in New York in May. WEATHERING THE STORM IN DETROIT — There have been estimates that there are ap- proximately 300,000 people out of work in the Detroit area, with approximately 75% of that number being blacks. 90% of the black unemployed are under 30, and that translates into many record buyers being out of work. Calvin Simpson, head of Simpson’s Records In that area says, “We are weathering the problems in this area by simply applying a more aggressive cost control program. Unfortunately the problems in this area are only com- pounded because the manufacturers are having problems and are not able to assist retailers in this market. Though it has never been as severe as it now is, the record buying ] habits of the black consumer will keep us alive though we are not doing business as usual.” I ARTIST ACTIVITY — Cameo will be one of the featured groups in the upcoming Kool Jazz I Festival, to be followed by a nine-city engagement . . . Parliament recently donated 25 | cents from each ticket sold during its concert at the Apollo Theatre to the United Harlem j Growth Foundation. Sunstorm Taps Conway LOS ANGELES — Ed Conway has been named head of Sunstorm Management Consulting, a division of Sunstorm Enter- tainment Services, Inc. He is leaving the post as financial director of Sunstorm Recording Studios. Business managment, music publishing and production will be his responsiblities. Before joining Sunstorm, Conway was vice president of finance for Casablanca Record and FilmWorks and was previously affiliated with ABC Records and MCA, Inc. Arrangers Sue For Royalty Monies LOS ANGELES — A complaint has been filed with the Copyright Royalty Tribunal by the American Society of Music Arrangers, asking that arrangers receive royalty monies for creative contributions to copyrighted musical material. The applicable Copyright Law currently Skyliners’ Vogel-Rapp Commits Suicide NEW YORK — Janet Vogel-Rapp, an original member of the Skyliners, recently committed suicide by asphyxiation from carbon monoxide. Vogel-Rapp, 37, had a history of severe depression and repor- tedly left the group a year earlier for that reason. Vogel-Rapp is perhaps best remem- bered for helping write the group’s “oldie” standard, “Since I Don’t Have You,” and for her soaring background vocal contribution to the frequently covered tune. Vogel-Rapp is survived by a husband and three children. groups arrangers in the work-for-hire category with orchestrators and musicians as employees who are hired by composers to work for a fee on a musical work. Disagreeing with such a grouping, Eddy L. Manson, president of the society, said, “Arrangers are not employees but in- dependent contractors who work for a fee." His comments were includedHn a letter to Tribunal Chairman Mary Lou Burg. Manson also contends that arrangers are responsible for making records more saleable. His group is demanding that arrangers be cut in on the record companies’ royalty take, and that a separate mechanical royalty be paid arrangers on each record sold which includes their work. The Tribunal is now soliciting comments from the Recording Industry Association of America, (RIAA), the National Music Publishers Association, the American Guild of Authors and Composers, as well as other interested parties. Nominees Named For Las Vegas Award Program LOS ANGELES — In an event to be named in honor of the late Jimmy Durante, the top five nominees in 15 categories of the first “Best of Las Vegas" award program were announced last week. Some of those nominated include Liberace, Shirley MacLaine, Frank Sinatra, Kenny Rogers. Wayne Newton, Lola Falana, Diana Ross, Johnny Carson, Bill Cosby, Joan Rivers, Willie Nelson, Chicago, Sister Sledge, The Village People, David Brenner, Bernadette Peters and Rip T aylor. A 21-member panel made the announ- cement following an all-day session at the Riviera Hotel, where the panel members discussed the categories, nominations, ballotting and tabulation by a certified public accountant. The panel is comprised of three mem- bers from each of the seven facets representing the Las Vegas entertainment community. Each of the panelists polled their respective groups to develop the list of nominees. The winners will be announced at the Tropicana Hotel on March 21, and the program will be taped as a television special. The show will be co-produced by Knight Productions with PM Theatrical Productions of Las Vegas. The categories include Las Vegas Star of the Year; Male Musical Star; Female Musical Star; Comedy Star; Coun- try/Western Star; Rock Performance; Sup- porting Star; Lounge Star; Best Production Show; Best Revue; Best Principal Perfor- mer; Best Gypsy; Specialty Act; Choreographer of the Year; and Orchestra of the Year. Two additional categories, Special Achievement Honors and Most Promising Newcomer will be announced just prior to the awards ceremony. Star hosts, hostesses, guest stars and presenters will be announced at a future date. Having seized financial docu- ments, Constable Langley says several charges may be laid, which, when com- pounded, could lead to a sizeable convic- Magnet Records Changes Global Licensing Pacts LONDON — Following its switch last year from EMI to Rye Records, the Magnet label has drastically altered its international licensing deals. Formerly under the EMI umbrella for most areas outside of the UK, the label has changed to separate com- panies for individual territories. Magnet’s new licensees for overseas territories will now be Teldec for Germany, Austria and Switzerland; Polydor for France; Discos Columbia for Spain; RCA for Argentina and Brazil; Festival for Australia and New Zealand; Peerless Fabrica de Discos for Mexico; Polygram for Eire and CBS for Canada. In the U.S., Magnet has decided to place its artists with various companies in- dividually due to the size of the American market. Currently, the Darts are with Polydor, Chris Rea with CBS and Matchbox with Sire. The remaining roster has not been placed. Magnet, however, has not dropped EMI licensing altogether. Successful relationships with EMI in Scandinavia and Benelux (Belgium, Netherlands and Lux- embourg) have been extended, along with another current deal with RPM in South Africa. In the area of publishing, Magnet Music has extended its deal with Intersong Ar- temis for the majority of overseas territories. Commenting on the new worldwide licensing strategy, Magnet chairman and managing director Michael Levy said, “I felt it would be more beneficial to have in- dividual partners in each territory. The companies would be totally committed to the Magnet label, instead of an overall deal where certain markets weren’t as commit- ted as they should have been. We, therefore, looked carefully at each market to pick the partner we felt was right tor us." Crack Bootleg U.S., Canada tion if proven. Tokyo Music Festival To Feature Infi Lineup TOKYO — An international lineup of con- testants and a special guest performance by Motown recording group The Com- modores will highlight the ninth annual Tokyo Music Festival, March 30 at the Nip- pon Budokan Hall there. To date, 11 entries from seven nations have been selected, including Karla Bonoff, Dionne Warwick, Gloria Gaynor and The Stylistics from the U.S.; Patsy Gallant and Claudja Barry from Canada; Amii Stewart from Germany; The Dooleys from the U.K.; Park-Kyung Al from the Republic of Korea; Elisa Chan from Hong Kong, and Passionata from the Phillippines. Additional entries representing other na- tions will be announced in the near future, as well as a Japanese contingent to be selected by a national competition. One of the fop musical events in Japan, the Tokyo Music Festival is broadcast throughout the nation via the national television network. A&M recording artist Rita Coolidge won the Grand Prize at last year’s festival, which also featured a guest performance by Casablanca recording artist Donna Summer. INTERNATIONAL DATELINE Argentina BUENOS AIRES — The Carnival (Mardi Gras) festivities in Argentina are usually one of the major booking events for local and foreign artists, with many sports and social clubs featuring dance parties and shows. The fall of the dollar in the past three years has increased the share of this seasonal market for foreign artists, since for local impresarios it has been easy to match their fees, and usually an Inter- national artist has been helpful to fill a dance hall to capacity. However, the increasing internal costs during the past year and severe losses suf- fered by some of the clubs in 1979 caused a change of attitude this time: instead of BO- SS artists coming from other countries, only half a dozen have been strong enough as to convince local promoters to bring them during a risky period. The main attraction, once again, has been Spanish-born Julio Iglesias, who had already spent several months here. Iglesias currently lives in Miami but retains a strong backing here. Other artists from Spain have been Manolo Otero, Dyango, Manolo Galvan; from Italy, Franco Simone and Al Bano, with Romina Power; from Brazil; Jose Augusto and Terry Winter. From the States arrived Gloria Gaynor, but after two days in Buenos Aires she sud- denly decided to return home, leaving con- tracts unfilled. In a few days Tom Jones is expected here, and he will tour the interior of the country. Folk artists have also obtained good box office results in several cities of the interior, while local rock stars also proved to be good crowd gatherers; Leon Gieco, who has developed a blend of rock, pop and folk rhythms, has been leading the pack, with Charly Garcia, Nito Mestre and others also ranking high. For the record companies, the results of these Carnival festivities may be another sign of the revival of local pop, which for a couple of years was smashed in percen- tage of sales by pop products. The high costs of local recordings and the shrinking of the market also helped, but at this mo- ment it may be sensible to start rebuilding local casts. It is too early to suppose that this trend will strengthen in the near future, but it may change the expectations of many in the record and entertainment industries during this year. The idea of Government-imposed restrictions on the air play of foreign music (an 80% minimum of local product has been expected since a few months ago) would also help to the development of quite a few local pop artists, who are currently deeply worried about radio promotion and consider that the ongoing craze of foreign music hurts them very much. miguel smirnoff Italy MILAN — Total record sales in Italy during 1979 rose 20% over 1978 to $230 million, according to the trade publication Musica e Dischi. EMI Electrola In Massive Push For Rock Acts by Harald Taubenreuther MUNICH — EMI Electrola is currently in the midst of a major promotional campaign en- titled “The German Way Of Rock.” In sup- port of new EMI Electrola LPs by Scorpions, Eloy, Triumvirat, Eberhard Schoener, Kraan and Wallenstein, plus a new Kraftwerk album on the group's Kling- Klang label, the campaign will encompass massive promotion along traditional lines, plus a few new innovations. A comprehensive radio campaign has already been implemented, as has a massive print blitz encompassing both trade and consumer publications. In addition, EMI Electrola is providing heavy tour support for the bands, who will all tour Germany sometime during the promotional campaign. The new wrinkle in record promotion has been the incorporation of motion picture theatre spots. Somewhat along the lines of American video clips of various bands, EMI Electrola has booked approximately 300 theatres to show the promotional films. While advertising consumer goods in motion picture theatres is not new in Ger- many, EMI Electrola is the first to use this medium on such a massive scale for promotion of records. Personnel Cuts At Casablanca In Wake Of Polygram Buyout SoundViews (continued from page 6) and an alleged ultimatum from Polygram brass to trim the company’s personnel to no more than 45 persons. While admitting that Casablanca's current offices in New York will be vacated by the record people, Bird stated that the staff will be trimmed and moved to another location in the city. In addition, he said that the film personnel would remain at the old location. “Casablanca will continue to have an east coast office,” Bird said. “We are still a separate company (within the Polygram structure), and it will still be the same as it was.” Bird then noted that while the editorial, publishing and publicity units had been trimmed, the promotion, marketing and ad- vertising units had actually been strengthened by the restructuring. In the area of promotion, Bird noted, “Where we used to have eight local and six Polygram Shifts Promotion Reps (continued from page 6) trate that area which is primarily singles- oriented — the local promotion group — under one umbrella, and, at the same time, to provide a stronger specialist organiza- tion at each of the record companies.” The spokesman declined to comment on reports that as many as 30 Polygram field people had been laid off recently. He noted, however, that even if there are cutbacks on a local level, a number of new regional and national promotion positions will be created at the same time. Consequently, he said, it’s too early to estimate the number of people who will be affected by the organizational changes. Frisoli pointed out that the new structure will enable Polygram to launch two- pronged promotion campaigns utilizing local and regional personnel. There will be close coordination between Bleiweiss and the label promotion heads, added Frisoli, and a promotion plan for a particular record may be initiated either by PDI or by one of the Polygram labels. regional people, we have added six R&B and ten national people. Altogether, we’ve added nine Polydor people and seven Mer- cury people.” Bird also noted that Casablanca senior vice president Cecil Holmes and his Chocolate City Records staff add further strength in promotion. On another issue, the “key man” clauses in the contracts with Donna Summer, Kiss and Parliament, Bird declined to comment when asked if any of the artists had invoked the escape clause. Under the “key man” clause of a con- tract, artists may terminate their contracts with a company if a “key man” (former president Neil Bogart, in the case of Casablanca) exits the company. Summer’s representatives declined to comment on the issue, while represen- tatives for Kiss and Parliament were un- available for comment. (continued from page 16) NTSC systems. DIGITAL DEVELOPMENTS 3M reports that the first digital multi-track recording of an opera has been made by Herbert von Karajan for PolyGram, using the 3M 32-track digital mastering system. The subject of the sessions was the Berlin Philharmonic Orchestra’s recording of Richard Wagner's 4Vt hour opera Parsifal with the chorus of the Berlin Opera. The tapes will be mixed down and then edited on 3M's new electronic editing system . . . Telarc's ninth digitally-mastered album, featuring the St. Louis Symphony Orchestra, directed by Leonard Slatkin, comprises Georges Bizet’s “Carmen Suites Numbers 1 and 2” and Edvard Grieg's “Suite From Peer Gynt, Op. 55, 46.” It was recorded on the Soundstream Digital Recording System . . . REVIEWS SINGLES REVIEWS FEATURE PICKS BILLY JOEL (Columbia 1-11231) You May Be Right (3:58) (Impulsive Music/April Music Inc.—ASCAP) (B. Joel) Joel makes the transition from piano man to all- out rocker on the first single from his new "Glass Houses” LP, throwing a few vocal stones of his own while using a hard guitar-oriented instrumen- tal that is highly reminiscent of Chuck Berry and the Rolling Stones. Witty, urbane and energetic, this is great for pop, AOR. STYX (A&M 2228) Borrowed Time (4:14) (Stygian Songs, admin, by Almo Music Corp.—ASCAP) (D. DeYoung, T. Shaw) “Don’t look now, here comes the Eighties!” is the opening cry on this AOR favorite, the third single from the "Cornerstone” LP. Styx backs it up with a hard rock attack guaranteed to make pop programmers take notice. Tommy Shaw leads the way with hisfiery lead guitar work, while Dennis De Young and the band add crack harmonies. THE WHISPERS (Solar YB-1 1928) Lady (5:05) (Spectrum Vll/Yours, Mine & Ours— ASCAP) (N. Caldwell) As The Whispers continue to climb the pop chart with “And The Beat Goes On,” this bluesy second single from the vocal group's Top 10 LP features an additional helping of its outstanding harmonies and the light but sexy lead vocals of Wallace Scott. Organ-dominated instrumental neatly ties everything together for B/C and pop. THE CRETONES (Planet P-45911) Real Love (3:15) (Twist Party International—BMI) (M. Goldenberg) The Cretones’ Mark Goldenberg, who previously assisted Linda Ronstadt on her “Mad Love” LP, turns in a taut and driving rocker for the band’s first single from its debut Planet LP, “Thin Red Line." Ringing guitars underscore the sharp harmonies on the chorus, mixing both English and American rock influences. A distinctive AOR, pop sleeper. SMOKEY ROBINSON (Tamla T 5431 IF) Let Me Be The Clock (3:47) (Bertam Music Co. ASCAP) (W. Robinson) Smokey cruises along on a beautifully arranged instrumental track, combining rolling timpani and bell chimes with a swaying pop/R&B melody, on this first single from his new “Warm Thoughts” LP. A supple, subtle string section, clicking guitar and a high backup chorus contribute to the easy feel of this multi-format winner. DIONNE WARWICK (Arista AS0498) After You (3:37) (Sumac Music, Inc.— BMI) (D. Frank, D. James) Recent Grammy Award winner Warwick should continue her current hot streak with the quietly building third single from her “Dionne” LP. The pace increases gradually from a soft opening to a full-blown crescendo at the close, with swelling strings, a full background chorus and a regal flourish of strings. Lush A/C, pop material. HEAT (MCA MCA 41203) Baby (This Is Love That We’ve Found) (3:59) (Koppelman-Bandier Music Corp.— BMI) (T. Saviano, J.M. Arnold) A sweet combo of piano, light woodblock and bluesy sax introduces the first single for Heat’s self-titled debut LP. Jean Marie Arnold wraps her multi-octave vocals around the lyrics here with an operatic flair, while the well-integrated harmonies complement the lushly textured R&B instrumen- tals. Look for heavy B/C action to break. GRACE SLICK (RCA PB-11939) Seasons (3:23) (Cheeks Publishing—BMI) (G. Slick) Slick has been missed since her departure from the Jefferson Starship, but this first and highly dis- tinctive single from her forthcoming “Dreams” LP proves that the wait was not in vain. The folk- oriented melody, which brings to mind Mary Hopkin’s ‘‘Those Were The Days,” fits her arresting vocals like a glove. For AOR and pop lists. H € A T SINGLES TO W4TCH THE BEACH BOYS (Caribou ZS9 9032) Goin’ On (2:58) (New Executive Music/Chailove Music— BMI) (B. Wilson, M. Love) The Beach Boys’ summery music has an eternal quality about it that has stood the test of time, and this track, from the upcoming “Keepin’ The Summer Alive” LP, shows the band's instincts for a great melody are as keen as ever. The harmonies are top-notch, as always. Purely pop. RONNIE LANE (RCA PB-11914) Kuschty Rye (3:10) (Warner Brothers Music Corp.— ASCAP) (R. Lane-Lambert) Former Face Ronnie Lane has returned, this time as a solo act, and this Pete Townshend-produced track finds Lane blending English folk elements with pop instrumen- tals. Lane’s vocals owes a debt to Dylan here and should attract heavy AOR and some pop play. SHALAMAR (Solar YB-1 1929) Right In The Socket (3:40) (Spectrum Vll/Rosy Music ASCAP) (K. Spencer, L. Sylvers, D. Griffey) Shalamar scored heavily with “Second Time Around,” but this pulsing dancer scored equally as well in disco clubs as the other half of that previous single. A thick, propulsive beat, aided by handclaps, keeps things mov- ing, while the vocal trade-offs and keyboard work add zest. A B/C, pop sleeper. JAMES LAST BAND (Polydor PD-2071) The Seduction (Love Theme) (3:35) (Ensign Music Corp.—BMI) (G. Moroder) Internationally known James Last turns in a mellifluous cover of the “seduction” theme from the mo- tion picture soundtrack for American Gigolo. From the warm, intimate sax soloing to the panting synthesizer, this is a pop instrumental sleeper. ELVIS COSTELLO AND THE ATTRACTIONS (Columbia 1-11194) I Can’t Stand Up For Falling Down (2:05) (East Memphis Music/Cotillion Music— BMI) (H. Banks, A. Jones) Costello and crew soup up the old Sam and Dave rave- up here, as the rhythm section keeps the pace short and snappy, while the Farfisa organ pumps out over Elvis’ echoed vocal. Look for AOR to break this one. DAMION & DENITA (Rocket PIG-41206) Is It Still Warm (3:56) (Blue Standard Music/Stevenson Music/British Rocket Music Pub. Co.—ASCAP) (C. Shadrach, W. Duncan, D. Hardy, T. DePierro) An extremely polished R&B duet between newcomers Damion & Denita, the milk and honey vocal blend and un- hurried instrumental here should gain immediate B/C radio attention. SHOOTING STAR (Virgin VA 67005) You’ve Got What I Need (3:46) (Mad Ted Music Inc.— BMI) (G. West, V. McClain) Kansas City-based Shooting Star serves up crackling midwest power rock with a marching hook that is positively infectious on the band’s first single from the “Wild In The Streets” LP. Guitar and keyboards provide fireworks for pop, AOR. THE METEORS (PVC PVC-1000) It’s You, Only You (4:18) (publisher not listed) (Sinzheimer and Bakker) Dutch new wavers The Meteors create a futuristic blend of spiraling guitar notes and cascading syn- thesizers on this Cars-ish cut from the “Teenage Heart” LP. FUN WITH ANIMALS (A&M 2223) The Test Of Love And Sex (2:37) (Haxtoons Music/Sealovesongs — BMI) (R. Haxtons, C. Sealove) Fun With Animals display an off-beat, tongue-in- cheek approach to new wave rock that puts them in a league with Devo here. Blips, whirs and pulsing elec- tronic keyboards are right for DOR, AOR play. DOLLAR (Carrere CAR 7214) I Wanna Hold Your Hand (2:56) (Duchess Music Corp. (MCA) — BMI) (J. Lennon, P. McCartney) The early Beatles classic is given a most enticing euro- pop treatment on this single from the French Carrere label. Crystalline choral work is fused to a steady, mid- tempo beat replete with handclaps. Sweet, neat pop. LEIF GARRETT (Scotti Bros. SB 516) I Was Looking For Someone To Love (2:53) (Michael Music — ASCAP/Don Kirshner Music/Blackwood Music, Inc. — BMI) (M. Lloyd, H. Greenfield.) This MOR-ish ballad from Garrett’s forthcoming “Same Goes For You” LP will undoubtedly please Leif’s many teen fans with its string-laden, uncomplicated melody and breathy vocals. There is strong A/C poten- tial, as well as pop. TRIUMPH (RCA PB-11945) I Can Survive (3:45) (Triumph Songs-CAPAC) (G. Moore, M. Levine, R. Emmett) Canadian power trio Triumph returns with this teen- oriented rocker from the “Progressions of Power" LP, moving from a soft acoustic opening to a crackling, guitar-dominated slice of boogie. Excellent for AOR, pop play. GOTHAM (Aurum S-0004) Put Your Money Where Your Mouth Is (3:14) (Don Kirshner Music/Blackwood Music Pub. — BMI/Kirshner Songs/April Music — ASCAP) (G. Allan, G. Retailers Note Role Of Imports In Creating American Market (continued from page 8) AtSpec’s Music, a 12-storechain located in Florida, vice president Bayard Spector credits import-buying fans of the Boom- town Rats with laying the foundation for the success of the domestic release of “The Fine Art Of Surfacing.” Opining that the group had not “scratched the surface of their potential” in America as an import item, he says that his stores dropped the import once Columbia Records had issued the domestic version. Greg Specyal, import buyer for Turtle Records, which has 12 outlets in the Atlanta area, drew a clear distinction between im- port buyers “who love to keep up with what's happening overseas” and the “American mainstream buyer” who will hear about a new British group from import-buying friends and purchase the record "by the time it hits America." Delay Hurts Sales Sometimes, however, a long delay bet- ween the availability of an import and the release of its domestic counterpart can hurt the sales of the American version. “Of course, if an import comes out two or three months before it's going to kill the domestic version — it wipes it right out,” asserts Howard Krumholtz, buyer for the Tower Music chain, which has 27 stores on the west coast. Krumholtz notes that sales of imports by Gary Numan and The Jam at Tower’s Sunset Strip outlet had a marked negative impact on the movement of the American releases when they appeared in the bins several months later. Jeep Holland, chief import buyer for the Boston-based Music Sales company, which has ten Music World and two Music City stores in New England, reports a similar problem with the American issue of Gary Numan’s “The Pleasure Principle.” Although he cautions that assessments of the affect of imports on domestic sales must be made on a case-by-case basis, Holland claims that “the market was gone” for albums by XTC and Fingerprintz because of the time gap between their availability as imports and their domestic release. Nevertheless, the steadily rising prices of import LPs — retailers reported price hikes ranging from 75$ to two dollars per record over the past two years — are helping to in- sure the existence of a budget-conscious (continued on page 61) CMNCE TOP 40 DISCO Wks. MERCHANDISING WFWT’S IN-STORE Atlantic Action — A national display contest, dubbed the “Great Atlantic Soul Explosion,” is currently underway. The competition, open to all WEA field merchandisers, sales per- sonnel and Atlantic promotion reps is designed to feature new releases by Slave, Narada Michael Walden, the Spinners and the Brides of Funkenstein. There will be a $1 ,000 grand prize and 10 runner-up prizes of $50 each. Each participant must submit a minimum of five displays in five different accounts. Prizes will be based on the most creative inclusion of all four pieces of product in or around the display . . . Three Tower stores in the Los Angeles Area, working with Atlantic, recently held a Manhattan Transfer contest with the grand prize of a key to the Playboy Club. The drawings were held at the chain’s Westwood, Pan- orama City and Hollywood stores, with the winner in each outlet receiving passes to the Playboy 25th anniversary party. The Manhattan Transfer were featured performers at the gala. RECORD BAR HAPPENINGS — The 98-store Record Bar chain recently announced the following promotions: A “Guess the Grammy Award Winners” contest was conducted at the three Raleigh, North Carolina stores. Winners were awarded the catalog of either Supertramp, Billy Joel or Donna Summer ... A Toto promotion was held at Record Bar, Gadsden, Ala., in conjunction with CBS Records. Here the three finalists tried stacking 99 pounds of albums in two minutes. The winner was given $99 worth of CBS product . . . The three Atlanta stores are having a “Happy Hour” weekdays during the month of March from 5-6 p.m. All front rack product will be featured for one dollar off the regular selling price. These outlets will also sponsor an “Early Bird Gets the T-shirt” promotion. The first five customers each Saturday purchasing a regularly priced LP or tape will get a free Record Bar T-shirt. TAPE SEMINAR — Dog Ear Records of Illinois reports participation in a recent seminar held at the offices of the Irv Rose Group, marketers and distributors for Maxell Products. The meeting, conducted on Feb. 24, concentrated on merchandising and uses of Dis- cwasher and Maxell merchandise. This is being followed by a chain-wide display contest, March 1 -April 14, in which cash prizes will be given for the best presentation of these items. There will be cash awards based on visibility, as well as others based on sales. WARNER BROS. PROMOTIONS — A B-52’s “Rock Lobster Derby” is being held, March 15-19, at First Book and Record Shop in Dayton, Ohio, and Bullfrog Records in Kittering, Ohio. Each of the four winners of a drawing held at the stores will be given his own live lobster which will participate in a race at the Dayton Convention Center. These lobsters will first be submerged in a vat of cold water, with melted butter added for inspiration. The en- trant with the winning lobster will be awarded a dinner at the Tropics Restaurant in Dayton. Runners-up will receive B-52’s albums ... Second prize will consist of limo service to the show and dinner-for-two . . . Finally, a display contest in support of the Ramones, Pretenders and Pearl Harbor albums is being conducted by the eight Everybody’s stores in the Northwest. There will be a $100 first prize, a $50 second prize and third and fourth prizes consisting of free records. Throckmorton, Gibb Take Top Honors in Songwriters’ Association Awards by Don Cusic NASHVILLE — The Nashville Songwriters Assn., International (NSAI) honored Sonny Throckmorton as its Songwriter of the Year and “She Believes In Me” by Steve Gibb as the Song of the Year at its 13th annual din- ner and awards show, held March 1 at the Hyatt Regency here. The banquet and awards show highlighted a two-day event sponsored by the NSAI that featured a songwriter's show- case on Friday night, Feb. 29. Performing at the showcase were Sonny Throckmorton, Tom T. Hall, Randy Goodrum and Gail Davies with a special performance by Felice and Boudleaux Bryant. The Bryants, writers of such hits as “Bye Bye Love,” “Wake Up Little Susie,” “Ail I Have To Do Is Dream,” “Rocky Top” and numerous others have seen their songs sell approx- imately 200 million records. It was only the second time in 30 years they have perfor- med in public and the audience gave them an enthusiastic and warm welcome. On Saturday, March 1, the NSA! held a symposium with panelists and workshops on the various aspects of songwriting. Es- pecially popular was a critiquing session where songwriters and publishers com- mented on songs submitted by participants in the symposium. In addition to “She Believes In Me” by Gibb, there were 15 other songs and their writers honored with Songwriter Achieve- ment Awards, which are voted on by the songwriters. (Songwriter of the Year is determined by chart success.) Songs and songwriters honored with the special achievement awards were “All the Gold In California" by Larry Gatlin; “Amanda” by Bob McDill; “Coward Of The County” by Roger Bowling and Billy Edd Wheeler; “The Devil Went Down To Georgia” by Charlie Daniels, Tom Crane, Fred Edwards, Jim Marshall, Taz Digregerio and Charlie Hayward; “Every Which Way But Loose” by Milton Brown, Steve Dorff and Snuff Garrett; “Family Tradition” by Hank Williams, Jr.; “I Know A Heartache When I See One” by Rory Bourke, Charlie Black and Kenny Chater; “If I Said You Had A Beautiful Body” by David Bellamy; “Just When I Needed You Most” by Randy Vanwarmer; “Last Cheater’s Waltz” by Sonny Throckmorton and Curly Putman; “Lay Down Beside Me” by Don Williams; “Shadows In The Moonlight” by Rory Bourke and Charlie Black; “Texas When I Die” by Patsy and Ed Bruce and Bobby Borchers; “When I Dream” by Sandy Mason; and “You Decorated My Life” by Bob Morrison and Debbie Hupp. Belmont College Hosts Seminar On The Performance Rights Amendment by Angela Ball NASHVILLE — The controversial Sound Recording Performance Rights Amend- ment (HR 997) currently before Congress, was the subject of a seminar conducted by the Music Business and Commercial Music Divisions of Belmont College on Feb. 27 here. The bill would initiate royalties for all creative personnel involved in the produc- tion of an album with a 50-50 split between record companies and musicians. Victor W. Fuentealba, president of the American Federation of Musicians, (AFM) and Robert F. Guthrie, assistant director, Department for Professional Employees, AFL/CIO, were guest speakers representing musicians in the debate. James J. Popham, assistant general counsel of the National Association of Broadcasters (NAB) and Len Hensel, general manager of WSM represented broadcasters in the panel. Broadcasters oppose the congressional bill because they would be required to pay a licensing fee to broadcast music. They claim that by making broadcasters pay a license fee, they would in effect be subsidiz- ing performers. Countering claims that the licensing is similar to that of songwriters, Poppel said, “Performers have means to other modes of income as authors and composers do not.” Fuentealba pointed out that the recording industry is the only industry where the worker makes a product that in turn displaces the worker. Once the musi- cian has been paid recording monies, he gets no monetary return whether the album sells 50 or 50,000 copies. According to Fuentealba, “Musicians feel that we are be- ing exploited whenever records are being used for profit. If records were not used, musicians would be employed.” Music Industry Banquet The seminar was followed by a banquet for the Music Industry Advisory Council which includes many prominent industry people. Newton J. Collins, director of the Music Business and Commercial Music Divisions of Belmont College said, “It’s the first of many opportunities for the music in- dustry programs at Belmont to serve the in- dustry. Student as well as industry response has been excellent.” Belmont is planning another seminar March 19, focusing on “Survival and Out- look for the Record Industry.” Richard Asher, deputy president of CBS Records Group, will be tne guest speaker. Representatives of other Nashville record companies will participate in a panel discussion Cash Box/March 15, 1980 51

Well, not officially. But it could very well be. The long awaited Eddie Rabbitt television special has finally been set to air over NBC July 11. Rocker Jerry Lee Lewis, actress Stockard Channing, 14-year-old banjo virtuoso Wendy Holcombe, Emmylou Harris and Henny Youngman will all be on hand to help Rabbitt create a music/variety/comedy hour. The following day, Rabbitt will be the topic of an ABC radio special, which will air on 400 affiliated stations. Both of these goodies will take place after the release of Rabbitt’s seventh Elektra/Asylum album, which he has already begun work on at Caribou studios in Colorado. Congratulations to Vince Kickerillo and Mary K. Miller, who married Feb. 16 in Houston, Tex. And speaking of nuptial bliss . . . Mel Tillis and his new bride Judy have moved into a specially designed log cabin in Asheville, Tenn. WELLER BOWS POWER COUNTRY — Kiss did it with rock. Is Freddy Weller planning to do it with country? Maybe so. Weller debuted his “power country” show featuring his new band, Spurzz, in Tulsa Feb. 28, and we hear tell that Spurzz is the first theatrical country music band. Weller and the band spent more than three months preparing for the kick-off date, while staging, lighting and special effects were in the works. Costumes for the group were Eddie Rabbitt designed by Pete Menefee, who has worked with Kiss. Reportedly, the look is that of Galactic cowboys. Spurzz consists of Tony Ingram, Lee Newell, D. Anthony Valentine, Gary Dibenedetto and Travis Lewis. BLACK CONTEMPORARY POLYDOR ACTS JAM IN CHICAGO — Polydor recording artists Peaches & Herb and Ray, Goodman & Brown recently met in Chicago, where the groups were performing selec- tions from their respective LPs, "Twice The Fire" and "Ray, Goodman & Brown.” Shown (I- r) are: Herb Fame; Maurice White, Chicago promotion representative for Polydor; Sonny Taylor, vice president of special markets for Polydor; Linda "Peaches" Green; Billy Brown; Al Goodman; and Harry Ray. THE RHYTHM SECTION BLACK MUSIC AMERICA — Lou Rawls and Don Cornelius have become involved in a radio special called Black Music America. The duo co-hosted what will be a six-hour show produced by a grant for the United Negro College Fund from the Anheuser-Busch Com- pany. The show will trace the history of black music and artists from turn of the century ragtime to modern disco. The show will be aired on approximately 100 black-oriented radio stations across the country. This special is the second part of a Rawls-Budweiser program to raise money for the 41 colleges and 50,000 students who are within the United Negro College Fund network. Last October, he taped a three-hour television show with top entertainers to kick-off this program. The radio and television specials will be supported by a marketing campaign featuring displays and special advertising assistance provided by Anheuser-Busch. For information on how to obtain the radio specials, contact Melvin B. Shaw at The United Negro College Fund office, (214) 630-2511. SOUTH FLORIDA STREET JOCKS — The South Florida Street Jocks have organized as an off-shoot of the Florida Record Pool to distribute and break black-oriented product. Bo Crane, founder of The Florida Record Pool has appointed Jerry Jarvis director of Street Jocks. For further information, they can be contacted at (305) 665-2605. BEVERLY HILLS HONORS ELLA — Ella Fitzgerald was honored by the Beverly Hills Chamber of Commerce at its annual ball, which was held last week at the Beverly Hilton Hotel. She received The Will Rogers Memorial Award, noting her outstanding contribution to the world of entertainment. Previous recipients have been Merv Griffin, Bob Hope, Carol Burnett, and George Burns, to name a few. DAVID AXELROD “MARCHIN’ ” — Producer/composer David Axelrod, who is best known for his works with Cannonball Adderley and Lou Rawls, is touring in support of his latest album, "Marchin' ” on MCA Records. Axelrod, who has his fingers in several different pots, will be producing Latin-rock band Tierra. He is also presently researching Arab/Egyptian and Israeli music for a project he may be contracted for involving the Mt. Sinai Peace Festival, scheduled for Israel in November. WAR/BLOOD, SWEAT & TEARS — War and Blood, Sweat & Tears featuring David Clayton-Thomas will embark on a month-long European tour. The bands will perform together and separately, and they will record material to be used later on live albums.
