Record Buyers Are Bogart Gives Keynote Speech Quality Conscious, Says NARM Panel (continued from page 16) Crystal Clear's Wodenjak said that record stores now account for nearly 50% of his company’s sales. This compares with a 95% to 5% sales ratio in favor of stereo hardware outlets only a few years ago. “In 1976, there were only a limited num- ber of titles available,” noted Wodenjak. “Now hi-fi retailers can’t handle the large number of titles so we and other manufac- turers are leaning heavily toward record stores.” Cohen of Licorice Pizza, in response to a question about who buys audiophile recordings, replied “everybody. The audiophile market has expanded beyond just jazz and classical buyers,” he said. Educate The Consumer Cohen went on to say that “educating the customer” is the most important factor in successfully marketing and merchandising audiophile product. He cited in-store play, employee awareness and special promo- tions and displays as proven sales boosters. In addition, he suggested that merchandisers set up special information centers with charts or posters explaining the various types of audiophile product. In closing, Marmaduke implored the ma- jor record companies to improve the quality of their prerecorded 8-track and cassettes. He claimed that poor quality control at the manufacturer level has made it possible for consumers “to make a better sounding cassette at home on a $100 system than they can buy at my store." Saying that greater manufacturer diligence in this area would go a long way toward alleviating the industry's current dilemma over hometaping, Marmaduke in- troduced a NARM resolution calling for im- proved quality control. It reads: "Be is resolved that the NARM board of directors unanimously implores the recording industry to increase the quality of tape used in its high speed duplication of 8 tracks and cassettes. “Having a prerecorded product inferior to what the consumer can tape at home has spawned the blank tape explosion that is significantly harming artists, merchan- disers and manufacturers.” (continued from page 20) about all the different facets of our business . . . people who are all-around music industry people. Maybe we haven't encouraged each other — nobody can learn to hear a record, or feel a record, but you can learn the business from the people who do know. How many lawyers and managers and business managers who make their living from this industry don’t even bother to come to NARM, to understand what we’re selling? How many artists are in this room right now? How many of them care to understand what it takes to market their product? Aren’t they our partners? As partners we are responsible for educating our- selves, because only then can we fully realize that we are not adversaries . . . that we’re in it, for better and worse, togehter. The new decade will be a time for the survival of the fittest. The new partnerships that evolve during this time, that adapt to the challenges of our changing business, will be the ones that survive. And I for one know that there are new businesses — major corporations — being formed as I speak. Perhaps our partnerships would be helped if there was a sisterhood of the RIAA for the artists. It should be possi- ble for them to have their own convention or be invited to our NARM convention. NARM: The National Association of Recording Merchandisers. Maybe we've been too narrow-minded Maybe what we should really have is an organization called the National Association of People Who Make Money From Records. Not a real catchy title, but perhaps a true one. We’ve become, after all, so very interdepen- dent. Radio stations make money from records; trade publications make money from records. We are inter- twined and no one has anything to gain from a business that doesn’t live up to its potential. Maybe if artists talked to retailers, the retailers could help the artist market their image properly. Maybe then the artist wouldn’t want a quadruple-fold pop-up jacket, because they’d realize that their records could easily warp in a package like that. If you retailers could actually com- municate that to an artist, maybe you wouldn't have all those unhappy customers bringing back defective records. It's bad public relations for everybody. Bad vibes . . . they're rampant. Pick up any paper that writes about music and you will find doomsday predic- tions: disco is dying, the bottom is falling out, the sky is falling in ... we are surrounded by Chicken Littles. Some of them seem anxious to predict the end is near if only to say: "I told you so." Why so much negativity? Why do we need to sound our own death knell? Do we have a death wish? Consumer publications like the Wall Street Journal get their information from these papers. No wonder our image on the street is fading; if we don't believe in our industry’s future, why on earth should anyone else? And yet, you won’t have to listen very hard to the con- versations in the halls of this convention to hear a lot of moaning and complaining. People are scared. People are angry. People want answers — now — as if answers were something you could order like room service. The fact is. no one person has got all the answers, but in this very room is enough collective wisdom to help pull us out of the hole we're in. There are people in this room who have done it already. We just recently had an old timers day I missed being eligible by two years. Can you believe it? The kid missed an old timers day by only two years? What do the old timers say about our present predicament? They’ve live’d in this business and have seen it grow, and grow, and grow. And all of a sudden it seemed as if someone popped the balloon. Did they really pop it? . . . Of course not. Nobody is killing us; some of our deepest wounds are self-inflicted. So only we can save ourselves. It’s called self-reliance. It’s an old American characteristic, and maybe it’s time we took it down from the attic and dusted it off. "In this twilight of power, there is no quick path to a con- venient light switch," wrote Adlai Stevenson. Look at the person sitting next to you. Like it or not, you're in this thing with that person. It's one thing to talk a united front. It's something else to create the means to a new survival But the opportunity arrived on our doorsteps. I’ve got a letter here, just like the letter all of you received, too. Within it lies a challenge, a challenge to unite behind an industry campaign that NARM is organizing, a campaign urging consumers to "Give The Gift Of Music." Back in 1972, we were told how the milk industry united for the mutual benefit of its members. That was eight years ago. Eight years or more talk and no action. Finally, NARM is calling our bluff. They are calling us to put our best minds to it; to share marketing ideas that we think are "winners;" to give freely of our imagination. Are we going to respond with openness or mistrust? Will we cooperate or compete? Will we be selfish? Because if we choose to be, and if we fail to take this opportunity seriously, we might not get another chance like it. This is a test. This is no gimmick This is our survival we are talking about. It is not enough to combat the negativity, to police our- selves against those who cheat and counterfeit. There must also be positive influences that come from within our business. "Give The Gift Of Music" can be a positive in- fluence, but only if we let it. If we ignore it, or think it doesn’t have a chance, before we even try, then, of course it won’t. Indifference will destroy it just as surely as sabotage. It’s really amazing that we're wondering whether we as an industry are ready to get behind a unified campaign. Because the public is certainly ready, and that should be all the incentive we need. In the newest marketing report from Warner Com- munications, on buying records and tapes as gifts, the consumer indicators are totally positive. It showed that three years ago as many as 47 million people spent 330 million dollars just on records to be given as gifts. No mat- ter what their musical taste, consumers of records buy records for others It’s real simple. They think it’s a great buy. And it is. If we truly believe that, the NARM campaign should be a cakewalk. Will it be? Let’s take it as a sign, as an idea long overdue. I expressed a similar thought the last time I stood before this convention in 1976. 1 chose then to close my mid-year NARM speech with a quote from Das Energi, by Paul Williams. I choose now to read it again, because it is more appropriate than ever: "A few men realizing the obvious and communicating with each other can create a chain reaction. There is nothing so potent as an idea whose time has come. "We are on the verge of The New Age, a whole new world. Mankind's consciousness, our mutual awareness, is going to make a quantum leap. Everything will change; you will never be the same. Ail this will happen as soon as you are ready." In this room are the people who can make it happen. I say to all of you: give the industry a chance. I love it. I am back in it And I will help change it But you've got to start thinking about today. It won’t happen today. Let it happen tomorrow. Make it happen by next week. But make it hap- pen. George Bernard Shaw once remarked that "The peo- ple who get on in this world are the people who get up and look for circumstances they want, and if they can’t find them, they make them." I am a born-again music man. I believe that we can make them together Thank you Video Problems Cited At 4th Int’l Conference (continued from page 36) director, Chrysalis Records. Brown aired the view that the recent technological video explosion had, in his opinion, taken most of the record companies by surprise and after showcasing to delegates the Blondie video album “Eat To The Beat,” told the audience, "There seems to be a lack of original video programming for consumers to purchase and record companies feel that this is an opportunity to offer the public something unique. Most record companies are ready now, and all we need to do is expand the conceptual idea of video programming, keep the budgets tight, and there is money in it for us all.” Brown also asserted that the com- parative low production costs and stereo capabilities of the videodisk will make an attractive new venture for many record companies: “We think our business is well- geared to handling the complete flow- through of video programming through to the consumer. We have the ability to relate to creative people and we have the budget consciousness, manufacturing capability, and distribution capability because we’re doing it already with records. And we have the marketing and promotion ability. The record business has to go into video, because the video album is going to be the replacement for the audio LP." Brown concluded by reiterating that Chrysalis Records and the music business in general is wholly and firmly committed to the development of video programming and sales. The music and video session continued to evolve with a talk on the video potential for classical music, given by Neil Mundy, director of programs, RM productions; a scathingly satirical and critical attack on the present sound technology of video and the need to improve quality of sound for video by Adrian Hope, audio-visual correspon- dent of “New Scientist;” and a concluding talk, given by Howard Siegal, lawyer for Pryor, Cashman & Flynn, U.S.A., entitled “Criteria For The Music Business." Siegal defined the present situation of the music business, where in his view he felt most record companies had only the ex- perience of video-promotional material. Direct Artist Involvement “The promotional video approach will no longer do if the record companies wish to be at the center of the video boom,” said Siegal. “They should now be looking to their own artists to provide the creative im- petus for video. The best commercial video software at present is from direct artist in- volvement and production, likethematerial produced so far by people like Todd Rundgren, Billy Joel and Devo.” Siegal continued to point out that though many record companies do not have the production facilities necessary for pure video ventures they should not be hesitating in investing in such. On the legal aspect of video software copyright laws, Siegal issued a warning that the lack of policing by the publishing industry is now history. "Without accommodating the copyright aspect, companies should proceed with caution as they are in jeopardy at their own risk,” he added. Lagoya Recalls Career Triumphs Despite Tragedy (continued from page 32) smash?” According to Lagoya, his part in Bolling’s "Concerto For Classic Guitar and Jazz Piano" was completely written out, despite the role of jazz in the composition. "Since Claude wanted the flute and the guitar to have a classical role in his ensemble," recalls Lagoya, “he left the improvisation for the pianist and the others.” Nevertheless, says the guitarist, he wanted to open himself up to the swing feeling of Bolling’s ensemble. “There were even times when he told me, 'You'reswinging too much,”’ remembers Lagoya. While both the double live album with Rampal and Lagoya’s first album with Boll- ing were recorded for RCA, the guitarist never signed a contract with that label. Previous to his interim association with RCA, he was a Philips recording artist; now he is exclusively signed to Columbia. Expanding Repertoire Since the guitar repertoire is somewhat limited compared to that for the piano or the violin, for example, guitarists must rely to some extent on transcriptions to round out their concerts. But Lagoya feels that it is very important to select only those non- guitar works that lend themselves to transcription. “I’m somewhat of a purist," he says. “I'm always looking for original works, and when I look for a work to transcribe, it's usually a piece that doesn’t work too well on the in- strument for which it is written, but could work better on the guitar. I wouldn’t transcribe Chopin or Liszt, because their music is too pianistic. If a piece is well- composed for a particular instrument. I'll leave it alone." He cites a set of variations for harp by Beethoven as a good candidate for transcription because “the harp is a plucked string instrument that's inex- pressive in terms of dynamics compared to the guitar.’ Similarly, he points out, most music by Bach can be transcribed, “because Bach wasn’t thinking of the in- struments, he was thinking of the music.” Besides transcribing some pieces, Lagoya has also re-orchestrated concertos by Giuliani and Carulli in order to make the guitar part stand out better. “Back when those composers were around,” he ex- plains. "concertos for guitar were unusual, and the people who wrote them didn't really know which instruments blended well with guitar and which instruments didn't. So they tended to write mostly for string orchestra; whereas, today, we know that guitar really mixes well with an oboe or a flute or a bassoon. I have re-orchestrated these works in the light of the experience of the past 150 years.” ON JAZZ wanted to do the "Pinnacles” project to satisfy myself. That s why I spent so long writing the music and arrangements, and that's why I wanted to choose very special musicians for the session — a fantastic group, the best. And I must say I’m very pleased with the results. With stalwart assistance from tenorist Joe Henderson, bassist Ron Carter, pianist Tommy Flannagan, drummer Billy Higgins, trumpeter Oscar Brashear and percussionist Kenneth Nash. Johnson has fashioned some of the most tasteful pop-jazz flourishes since Freddie Hubbard’s “Red Clay” and "Straight Life." As a matter of fact, there's even a funky perfor- mance of Weldon Irvine’s “Mr. Clean," which was featured on "Straight Life." Johnson’s witty, multi-faceted arrangements amplify the uncompromising integrity of each soloist while somehow rendering things accessible. Johnson makes particularly good use of funk syncopations and electronics such as Flannagan's luminous keyboards and the trom- bonist's synthesizer attachments, pitch followers and echo effects, balancing them with a good dose of straight-ahead you-know-what (swing!). J.J.’s excellent collaboration with Nat Adder ley on Pablo (“Yokohama Suite") is also well worth your while, so all we can say is "welcome back" to a master. In our continuing efforts to better serve the music industry, Cash Box has introduced a new feature — a comprehensive radio chart detailing airplay and sales action for the Top 100 singles. Debuted in the March 29, 1980 issue, the Cash Box Radio Chart is proving to be the most advanced radio program- ming guide devised to date. Not only does the chart detail which stations are adding and jumping each record on a weekly basis, it also notes which stations are day parting the hits. This information is tied in with any regional sales patterns that emerge during the week, thus giving a clear picture of how a record is doing on an overall basis. In addition, the chart identifies those records below the Top 30 that have displayed exceptionally strong action during the week. “PrimeMover” isthat record with the most radio activity; “Hit Bound” is the record with the most adds; and “Cash Smash” is the one with the strongest sales action. Altogether, these categories identify those records that are moving up the charts the fastest. It is our hope that this new chart will provide the most accurate information upon which decisions can be made. On a weekly basis, Cash Box will strive to provide current and precise data to aid the in- dustry. Service is the name of the game for a trade journal, and Cash Box is proud to say that you read it here first. (United Artists LT 1026) — 1 (Columbia FC 36374) — 1 © YOU’LL NEVER KNOW RODNEY FRANKLIN 37 MORNING DANCE SPYRO GYRA (Infinity NF 9004) 37 54 (Columbia NJC 36122) 20 3 38 CHAIR IN THE SKY © OCEANLINER PASSPORT (Atlantic SD 19265) 24 2 MINGUS DYNASTY (Elektra 6E-248) 38 7 39 DON’T ASK 19 GENETIC WALK SONNY ROLLINS AHMAD JAMAL (20th CenturyFox/RCA T600) 16 10 (Milestone/Fantasy M-9090) 39 23 40 MORNING THUNDER 20 PRESSURE EDDIE DANIELS (LAX/MCA 3195) 19 17 (Columbia NJC 36290) 40 2 ON JAZZ THE FUNK, THE WHOLE FUNK, AND NOTHING BUT THE FUNK — Perhaps no figure has had as great an impact on American music (make that World Music) as the godfather of soul, James Brown. Brown's patented form of call-and-response, in which his litany of moans, screams, incantations and raps are answered in kind by a multiplicity of drum rhythms (played on percussion, horns, bass, guitars, and voices), is probably the most African music any American has yet produced, and the Godfather has had a reciprocal ef- fect on African popular musicians who venerate him as one of their own. If Brown's recent recorded output has been lacking in anything, well, it is probably conviction. Locked into monorhythmic vamps and quasi-disco arrangements, the angular tension and polyrhythmic celebration of his music has been de-emphasized in favor of a sweetened ‘ contemporary" sound. The same problem plagued his otherwise triumphant ap- pearance at New York’s Studio 54, now bereft of liquor license and beautiful people as Steve Rubell practices his tennis game in one of America's college dorm-styled prisons for white collar criminals. When Brown's Vegas-type band opened with ren- ditions of Herb Alpert and Chuck Mangione hits, it was one of the most pa- thetic moments I’ve ever experienced as a listener, and all of the godfather’s still remarkable energy couldn't rescue the first part of the show from this psychic letdown. The new material simply doesn't play to Brown’s strengths — his jubilant phrasing, incomparable rhythmic feeling and his knack of taking any trivial vocal spiel and turning it into ten minutes of melodic varia- tions. The second half of the show saw Brown trot out his A+ material, including “Try Me," so full of yearning and remorse you could feel the earth move, even if his band didn't. James Brown's faults are not in himself, but in the company he keeps; at 52, Brown shouldn't have to do all the splits and grandstanding stage moves that are his stock and trade, but rather needs to get a band of young, tough funkateers who can give it to him as good as he deals it, letting him rope-a- dope while they burn the arrangements up. Brown is a national resource, and he deserves better than he's getting from his current band and entourage . . . Perhaps he should check out what people like Blood Ulmer, Phillip Wilson, Ornette Coleman and Joseph Bowie are doing. Bowie and Defunkt played later in the week at the Squat Theatre, and while their conceptualizations leave something to be desired, the energy and good feeling of the band is infectious. Bowie was joined by brother Byron Bowie, a mean R&B tenor man of the first rank, and by the great vocalist Nona Hendryx, formerly of Labelle. Hendryx gave Defunkt a vocal dynamism and focus that they’ve really needed, recalling how Fontella Bass sounded with the Art Ensemble of Chicago. It’s a strong direction, and if they can tighten up the rhythm and get some more material (which Hendryx, as the main writer for Labelle, is certainly capable of), Defunkt is going to be leading the tactical forces of progressive funk (the old, mean, nasty, danceable funk) up from the beachead of the '80s. TROMBONING IN — George Lewis is probably the finest trombone player I've ever heard. This isn't meant to disregard the excellent work of people like Joseph Bowie, Albert Mangelsdorff, Roswell Rudd and J.J. Johnson; but, as one of my friends pointed out, "Every time I hear George play, he does at least five things I've never heard before." Com- bining this sense of surprise with a buttery tone, an extraordinary range of inflections and multi-phonics, and near-perfect technique and swing, Lewis is extending his instrument (continued on page 44) SANBORN VISITS SAN FRANCISCO — Jazz star David Sanborn was in San Fran- cisco recently to perform with the Eagles. The sax player did find some time, however, to stop by KTIM-FM for a chat with music director Michael Knight. Pictured from (l-r) are: Knight and Sanborn. PORTRAIT —* Charles Mingus — Prestige P-24092 — Producer: Charles Mingus — List: 9.98 The moody, often dramatic and atmospheric Mingus, with the help of stellar jazzmen Eric Dolphy, Jaki Byard and Dannie Richmond, to name a few, offer a microcosm of life on this double-set live LP recorded in 1964 and 1965. "So Long Eric" is a dual tempo piece, complete with atonal repartee that does not forsake the be-bop power of Mingus' base. "Praying With Eric (Meditations for a Pair of Wire Cutters)” is haunting and satirical, while “Cocktails for Two" caps the set with a humorous cacaphony of '20s and '30s ragtime pop extensions. XANADU AT MONTREUX, VOLUME 2 — Xanadu 163 — Producer: Don Schlitten — List: 7.98 Schlitten is a patron saint of the jazz mainstream, which is far from finished as this explosive set conclusively demonstrates. The visceral rhythmic attack of tenorist Billy Mitchell and the elliptical Lesterisms of Al Cohn pressure cook tunes like "All God's Chillun Got Rhythm” and "Cotton Tail” as Sam Jones and Frank Butler swing away mightily. But the real star of this set is the great pianist Barry Harris. MIDNIGHT SUN — Lou Donaldson — Blue Note Classic LT- 1028 — Producer: Michael Cuscuna — List: 8.98 Donaldson is to the survival of ensemble jazz what John Coltrane later became to jazz experimentation. While both came up during what was later called the "Parker era,” Donaldson is as unique in his stylings. The previously un- released material, recorded in 1960, includes “Candy,” which is powered by an unyielding rhythmic/percussive groove. Equally engaging is the boogie woogie spice added to “The Squirrel” and “Si Si Safronia.” The title track is no less infectious. JAZZ /1LBUM PICKS NUDE ANTS — Keith Jarrett — ECM ECM-21171 — Producer: Manfred Eicher — List: 8.98 Jarrett's more accessible pontifications on this live, double- record LP are played with a conceptual clarity often blurred by the pianist's superlative technique on previous efforts. Sax- ophonist Jan Garbarek’s lyrical conversations with piano are some of the brightest moments. “Chant of the Soil” stays in a low-down groove, while "New Dance" uses percussive and polyrhythmic textures as tools of celebration. "Sunshine Song” is the mellowest offering on this waxing. RELEASED — Patti Labelle — Epic JE36381 — Producer: Allen Toussaint — List: 7.98 The line between pop/jazz and pop/R&B is almost in- distinguishable, and this collaboration between groovemeister Toussaint and siren Labelle is right in the pocket. Together. Labelle and Toussaint take the sheen of Motown, the elegance of Philly and the rhythmic pulse of disco and transform it into an uplifting dance groove with New Orleans and Afro-Latin seasoning. With great tunes like "Give It Up” and "Find The Love,” and unusual production touches such as male background singers) this may be Labelle's strongest work. I’M COMING HOME AGAIN — Carmen McRae — Buddah B2D 6501 — Producer: Vic Chirumbolo — List: 7.98 McRae is one of the most unique song stylists in jazz, with a gruff yet satin voice, expressive phrasing and great story-telling depth. “I'm Coming Home Again" finds McRae in lush, sym- pathetic settings that recall the halycon days of Creed Taylor's CTI productions, several of these highly-arranged songs have great black contemporary and adult contemporary potential McRae gets great support from jazzmen like Cornell Dupree, Freddie Hubbard, Hubert Laws and Hank Crawford. Cash Box/April 12,1980 J

NEW DISPLAY ITEM — Capitol Records’ merchandising department has announced development of a new marketing item called the “Isosceles Wedge.” The wedge is a three- sided cardboard piece measuring 12" square x 12" square x (12" x 17") and can be assem- bled into different configurations that can be used as banners, mobiles, stand-ups or dis- plays on walls, in windows or on counters. The company reports that the wedge has been used with success in various album campaigns, including those for Dr. Hook, the Knack and Bob Seger. ' 'it ’ ;< C THE COUNTRY COLUMN (continued from page 27) Johnny Rodriguez was one of a panel of judges of the World Wide Talent competition of the Armed Forces, held at Travis Air Force Base, Calif, on April 1. Other judges included Lee Majors, Mac Davis and Jayne Kennedy. Stan Hitchcock recently completed taping the second series of his syndicated country music show. Narvel Felts has signed with the William Morris Agency. The Country Music Wagon Train will depart from Nashville April 1 1 for its 9,000 mile, three and a half year trek across the United States. Promoter Lee Hollingsworth and singer Polly Ann will be making the trip with three wagons, two of which will be outfitted with supplies and the third set up as a permanent stage, complete with generator. The purpose of all this is to “carry country music back to the people." Joe Sun will appear on PBS-TV’s “Austin City Limits” April 29. Sorry we missed the show, Ray. ..but to all the RCA folks who tried so hard, we had a good time anyway. TOGETHER AGAIN — Tompall, Chuck and Jim, collectively known as The Glaser Brothers, are back together after a seven year hiatus. Look for their debut single, “Weight Of My Chains,” on Elektra. jennifer bohler ?8 MLENT M otown Night MGM GRAND HOTEL, LAS VEGAS — Spotlighting the label’s 20th anniversary and highlighting the entertainment at the 22nd annual NARM convention here, Motown Night provided an awesome dis- play of the company’s musical achieve- ments throughout two decades. Starting with the presentation of the “Mr. #1" award to Motown chairman Berry Gordy, the proper atmosphere was set with a 15-20 minute video that followed, which highlighted the label’s musical history to the accompaniment of an orchestra and female trio. Among the acts spotlighted in the video were the Four Tops, the Supremes, Marvin Gaye, the late Tammy Terrell, Gladys Knight & The Pips, the Temptations, Smokey Robinson & The Miracles, Stevie Wonder, Diana Ross and the Commodores. Following the video, Smokey Robinson came on to solo. Singing tunes that span- ned his career, from such treasured oldies as “Shop Around,” "Going To a Go Go” and “Tracks Of My Tears” to his current "Cruisin’ ’’ and “Let Me Be The Clock," Robinson proved that he hasn’t lost any of his abundance of talent over the years. Soloing center stage, Robinson paced the show with an impressive professionalism, mixing jokes and touching anecdotes with his musical fare. Robinson showed that he is truly one of the brightest stars in the Motown galaxy. Following Robinson, the new Tempta- tions celebrated their return to the Motown label with a tight medley of many old favorites, including “Cloud Nine,” “My Girl” and “Papa Was A Rolling Stone." Highlight of the set, however, was the introduction of “Power," the group’s first single since its return to Motown. Following a brief intermission, the Com- modores came on to close the show with a powerful set that spotlighted Motown’s latest group to achieve superstar status. Showing that they truly belong in the Motown Hall of Fame along with such giants as Diana Ross, Stevie Wonder and Robin- son, the Commodores staged a spec- tacular show, evenly paced and highly ex- citing at the same time. Presenting such numbers as “Brick House,” “Three Times A Lady,” “Still" and “Sail On,” the Commodores soon had the audience in their grasp, alternately singing along and rocking to the music. On the eve of their special guest performance at the Tokyo Music Festival, half aworld and three days away, the group left the audience stunned with their showmanship. As the show ended, the 1 ,500 or so in at- tendance could only leave with the thought that if Motown’s next 20 years are as fruitful as the first, the music world is in for a big treat. richard imamura Mb he Bellamy Bros. THE PALOMINO, N. HOLLYWOOD — In concert, Dave and Howard Bellamy display an engaging performance style that breaks down the barriers between the country and rock idioms and continues to build in energy throughout their set. Which is no easy task, considering they open with perhaps their most popular number, the 1976 single "Let Your Love Flow.” But these guys are consummate professionals onstage, knowing innately how to bring an audience up, which they did over and over throughout the first show of a two-night engagement here recently. Lately, the duo has had most of its success in the country arena, with “If I Said You Had a Beautiful Body, Would You Hold It Against Me,” which was greeted with whoops and hollers from the Hollywood cowboys in at- tendance, and their most recent country chart topper, "Sugar Daddy,” from the "You Can Get Crazy” LP. Other tunes that the duo performed from their latest album included "Dancin’ Cow- boy," an uptempo selection that saw some peppy musical support from the Bellamys' support unit, the Diamond Backs. While the group can cook in a country rock style reminiscent of the New Riders and the Out- laws (without all the volume), they tend to rely more on melody, while Howard and Dave supply the sterling harmonies and acoustic guitar work. Carl Chambers was especially notable on some very tasty lead guitar work, while his brother Jesse Chambers held down one half of the solid rhythm section on bass while Rodney Price made up the other half on drums. With Danny Jones offering some crying pedal steel guitar work and Jon LaFrandre on keyboards, the Bellamys had a seamless musical unit. mike glynn ^I^TC/Wazmo Nariz THE WHISKY, L..A. — Mixing tense, taut rhythms with a lean, driving beat and in- sidiously catchy pop hooks, Virgin recording group XTC made their long- awaited debut here recently and offered the packed house intelligence, energy and a superb visual display that was as mechanically mesmerizing as their music. XTC leaders Andy Partridge and Colin Moulding led the vocal assault, as well as galvanizing the crowd with their deft fretwork on guitar and bass, respectively. Plunging headlong into an array of cuts from the “Drums And Wires” LP with un- flagging intensity, the quartet cracked through the lively “Life Begins At The Hop,” the dizzying, slightly off balance pop of the single “Ten Feet Tall,” and the tension rid- dled layers of “Complicated Game.” The obvious highlight of the set, though, was the underground hit"Making PlansFor Nigel.” The sharp, kinetic beat and ironic lyrics of the song whipped the crowd into a dancing frenzy. Clothed in simple black outfits, the group was also perfectly in- tegrated into the constant progression of oscillating black and white filmed patterns projected onto a screen at the rear of the stage, perfectly complementing the inten- sity of the music. Dave Gregory and Terry Chambers offered compact rhythmic sup- port, working in tandem to ground the ad- venturous melodies and keep the audience in step. Wazmo Nariz may hail from the Midwest but anyone who sports two neckties, as Nariz does, would hardly be expected to play corn-fed rock ’n’ roll. The pudgy-faced performer and his competent four-piece band meld Zappaesque lyrical influences with a sparse new wavish instrumental at- tack. Nariz' twisting, wrenching vibrato vocal and off-beat sense of humor shined on such tracks as “The Refrigerator Saga," “Lips,” "Stubbies,” and the Jonathan Richman-influenced encore “Checking Out the Checkout Girl.” Better pacing might help to improve Nariz’ set, but his spastic stage movements often brought a chuckle from the crowd. If Nariz didn’t exactly win over the audience during his first time out in L.A., his off-the-wall music did. mike glynn ON ST-dOF

Since developing a worldwide following with successful pop and R&B oriented material, the group has turned its attention to other music idioms to gain still wider audiences. The new LP contains two gospel- flavored songs written by lead vocalist/sax- ophonist Richie, who is responsible for many of the band’s hit songs, and by King, trumpeter and an original member of the band like McClary and Richie. The LP, which will be released in April, will include “Jesus Is Love" by Richie and King's “The Mighty Spirit.” King explained that the band is more es- tablished now and feels more freedom in selection of material for the band's albums. “Religious music can’t be used to es- tablish a group in the pop and R&B world," he said. Richie added, “When I start out writing a song, it’s not for one category. I think the new material will show people that the Commodores are a total music concept.” In addition to the gospel songs, the title track was described by McClary as an “acoustic, melodic tune with strong lyrical content.” "It reminds you a little of James Taylor,” he said, "but there are some other elements that aren't in James Taylor’s music.” ‘Back To Basics’ He said some of the material on the up- coming LP still embodies that celebrative, pulsating beat that distinguished the band during the “Machine Gun” days, but all the Commodores interviewed by Cash Box, predicted that music in the ’80s will go back to the basics, to more mid-tempo songs with solid lyrical content. “Groups like the Spinners, O'Jays and Dramatics will have a better opportunity in the '80s because their music has been con- sistent over the years," Richie said. McClary, agreeing, added, “History repeats itself, and I think groups like the Spinners and the Whispers, who have been refining their music over the years, are coming back.” All agreed that the key for black groups in the ’80s will be to develop strong material. “A song is a song no matter what in- fluence it may have in it,” Richie commen- ted. King added, “Black groups can’t sell on their name alone. Everybody should know you must have good material.” The other components for success in the ’80s, according to the Commodores, will The Commodores remain broad exposure through radio and touring. Regarding the Commodores’ own tour plans, the band is scheduled to undertake a world tour in late spring following release of the upcoming LP. This marks the first time the group has handled a major portion of its own promotion, according to McClary. The Commodores also expressed a desire to become involved in outside production, writing, arranging and con- ducting, but conceded that current produc- tion and tour schedules did not permittime- consuming commitments. Bassist Ron LaPread said that he has already worked with the group Seventh Wonder as producer, and is also slated to provide material for a new LP by Taste Of Honey, which he said he will produce. The group has been made several vary- ing propositions ranging from requests for production and writing collaboration to setting up and operating a record manufac- turn on the outside,” McClary quipped. “We sort of take turns working on outside projects. I think that Walter Orange (drum- mer) and Milan Williams are due for their turn on the outside,” McClary said. Richie said that because the group spends considerable time developing its own product, there has not been enough time to incorporate outside projects. However, in the interim, the Commodores have developed considerable clout to be in such demand. The band members said that continued prudence in business and in exploring out- side interests, coupled with ongoing mass acceptance of Commodores’ product will help them live up to the monicker ascribed to them by English critics that they are the “Black Beatles.” SOLAR STARS MIX IT UP — RCA Records last week threw a gala party at Les Mouches In New York to celebrate the concert appearances of Solar recording artists The Whispers. Lakeside, Dynasty, and Shalamar. Pictured at the reception are (l-r): Nidra Beard of Dynasty; producer Leon Sylvers; Robert Summer, president of RCA Records; and Jody Watley of Shalamar. )ash Box/April 12,1980 29

— INTERNATIONAL INTERNATIONAL DATELINE Argentina BUENOS AIRES — Jose Page, president of Velvet Records of Venezuela, and Stanley Steinhaus. manager of the U.S. subsidiary of the company, visited Buenos Aires to arrange the representation of the MCA Group in this market. Velvet has a global arrangement covering all Latin America, except Brazil and Mexico, where it is represented by Ariola. They signed a con- tract with Microfon Argentina, covering also Uruguay and Paraguay. Microfon is also launching the Arista catalog here, with strong promo backing. Sebastiao Bastos from APG of Brazil visited Argentina regarding tape duplica- tion, blank tape and other services to the in- dustry. He met executives from local com- panies and indie duplicators. Alberto Maravi, president of Peruvian diskery Infopesa, visited Argentina in rela- tion to the catalog of his company and searching for local product. He told Cash Box that he will start an affiliated company in Los Angeles, aiming at the U.S. Latin market. The LAMM (Latin American Managers Meeting) hosted by Phonogram and atten- ded not only by the managers of the Latin American affiliates of Polygram but also representatives from Spain, Portugal and the head offices in Baarn and Hamburg was a strong success, according to John Lear, managing director of the local company. Polygram will strongly promote some Latin American artists in Europe, one of them possibly being Brazilian lark Zizi Possi. Henk Hoksbergen vice president of Phonogram International and located in Baarn, reported that thegroup will continue its increasing participation in the U.S. market and will invest heavily in the development of talent. CBS managing director Hecio Cuomo awarded a golden record to the local Stan- dard Oil Company affiliate, Esso, for the sales of the volume 13 of the "Cordialidad Musical" series, started several years ago and selling exclusively at gas stations ow- ned or franchised by Esso. CBS' special products division has been doing very good business during the past month, including the pressing of 20,000 albums a week for a classical music series sold at newsstands by a book publishing outfit. American Recording SA will represent Dick James Music in Argentina, with a strong backing campaign on radio and TV planned. The company is headed by Miguel Angel Petinato and has the largest independent duplicating plant in this market, with intense involvement in the pop field planned for this year. TV Channel ATC has started its own records division, which will negotiate its distribution through one of the existing companies. Last December, Channel 13 signed a distribution contract with RCA for a label, with thefirstLP already prominently charted. German Klein is the manager of this ATC division. CBS managing director Cuomo also reports the signing of musician and ar- ranger Pablo Ramirez to an executive post at the A&R division of the company. Cuomo recently started a series of personal trips to different cities in the interior of the country to get acquainted with the reality of these local markets and to develop promotion and marketing strategies adapted to them. Sicamericana’s group Seru Giran, whose recent album appeared in the Cash Box charts during several weeks, will probably record for the U.S. market. Two proposals have been received for a production aimed at the States, with the group singing in English some of its hottest product. Seru Giran records for the Sazam label, devoted to contemporary rock by local artists. miguel smirnoff Canada TORONTO — Retailers were caught with their pants down recently, when some were accidentally or otherwise chiseling the con- sumer on the four-song, one-sided Joan Armatrading "How Cruel" release. Some retailers claim they weren’t told about the one-side distinction of the disc. A&M was forced to recall the albums and attach stickers denoting their special status. The label only recently issued the one-sider, af- ter releasing a live effort from Armatrading recorded here last year . . . Both Drastic Measures (distributed by CBS) and Martha and The Muffins (on Virgin), until recently snubbed by the local press, are garnering good reviews after big-league album releases. The recent lifting of a 10% surtax on ticket revenues for domestic artists perfor- ming in Ontario has been widely-hailed by industry sources, quite naturally. Until last spring, the tax exemption had helped secondary markets cope with spiralling talent costs. The provincial government reintroduced the tax as a means of creating more government revenue (already, foreign performers have a ten-cent-on-the- dollar tax added), but drew scorn from the industry, which was not consulted prior to the move. Indeed, the budgetary measure wasn't even discovered for a few days. Back to normal, at last The Canada Council for the arts has reallocated $500,000 this coming year for the recording of "un-commercial" artists domestically. The patron institution has been facing cutbacks, but managed to shift funds around . . A Montreal radio station reportedly picked up the first version of Warren Zevon's "Bill Lee” (then titled "Ballad Of The Spaceman"), and program- med it with a recent interview with the Mon- (continued on page 42) Domestic Canadian Acts Gear Up For Sales ’80 Comeback by Kirk LaPointe TORONTO — Based on qualitative artistic accomplishment and subsequent commer- cial successes, 1980 is shaping up to be a year for revitalization on the domestic recording activity front. Led by a new brigade of upstarts like The Powder Blues Band, Bryan Adams, Red Rider, Teenage Head and B.B. Gabor, and bolstered by rejuvenated efforts by veteran artists Dan Hill, Triumph, Rush, the Downchild Blues Band and CANO, this year's models are more than making up for a year of rather insignificant achievement for Canadian artists. Although 1978 had spawned successes like Nick Gilder, Trooper, Burton Cummings and others, 1979 had not followed up with much to match. Most artist and repertoire directors sur- veyed by Cash Box agree there was con- siderable scrutinization and reevaluation of Liberty-UA Bows Returns Ceiling, Revised Margin LONDON — As of April 1, all Liberty-United Artists and EMI America product will come within the scope of the 5% returns ceiling. With this action, all labels now controlled by Liberty-United carry a 5% returns ceiling. Liberty-United labels include Motown, Bronze, Rak, Ballistic, Fantasy, Stax, Source and Hurricane. In addition, a second change, applicable to Liberty-United Artists, EMI America and Ballistic product, comes into effect bringing a revised dealer margin for both record and tapes of 32%. This move brings Liberty- United into line with other major companies, including WEA and Virgin, that have revised dealer margins in an attempt to abolish rrp. Commenting on his company’s latest move, managing director of Liberty-United Cliff Busby said, “We have for some time felt it necessary to bring the tape and record margins into line and, although economic conditions have necessitated reducing the overall margin slightly, the tape margin has in fact been lifted to satisfy a long standing need." Bush Named Managing Director, EMI Records LONDON — Following the departure of Ramon Lopez as managing director of EMI Records, John Bush has been appointed successor, effective immediately. Bush has been with EMI for 25 years, previously working with EMI International heading companies in Norway, Mexico and Italy. INTERN/4TION/4L BESTSELLERS domestic talent rosters towards the end of last year, and all feel the changes in direc- tion are only now being felt. Jeff Burns, now CBS director of A&R af- ter a similar stint with the now-defunct GRT Canada, says, “I had to start with a clean slate, and so we cut much of the deadwood from the label. It became apparent that the company was not moving in the proper direction with its Canadian artists. There weren't many international deals struck up.” Burns, like all of his counterparts, stresses the crucial importance of inking American and international pacts for dis- tribution as a means of rationalizing and evincing profitability from well-produced projects. Although Capitol is the only major label with automatic below-the-border issuances for Canadian-signed artists, the strength of recent releases are leading to considerable international interest in domestic talent. Flurry Of Activity Rarely in recent memory has there been such a flurry of activity and positive reaction to the local scene, with significant charting and radio attention exceeding the standard tokenism bestowed on unproven domestic artists. Leading the way in weeks past has been the Powder Blues Band, whose “Uncut” release on RCA remains imbedded in the Top Ten nationally, having one time soared to the second spot behind Pink Floyd's "The Wall.” Most surprising is not that a domestic artist could capture such an audience, but that the blues-based genre has garnered the substantial following among record buyers in the country. The newest Rush album, “Permanent Waves,” has earned the band increased status as an airplay commodity, as has Triumph's “Progressions Of Power” disc. Those two hard-edged outfits, in particular, have until recently struggled to gain com- mercial radio acceptance of their work. The Attic Records-released Triumph (continued on page 42) Warwick Wins Grand Prize At Tokyo Fest TOKYO — Arista recording artist Dionne Warwick won the grand prize at the ninth annual Tokyo Music Festival, held March 30 at the Nippon Budokan Hall. Warwick won over an international field with her ren- dition of “Feeling Old Feelings.” Warwick, who earlier this year won a Grammy Award, received $12,000 for her efforts. Special guests at the festival were Motown recording group the Com- modores. Last year’s winner was Rita Coolidge of A&M Records. The local in- dependent, distributed nationally by CBS, has also scored in a big way with the Downchild Blues Band’s comeback album, “We Deliver,” and Teenage Head’s first for the firm, “Frantic City.” The Teenage Head album, much- anticipated after a cleverly-written but poorly-produced initial disc last year, is produced by ex-Bowie sideman Stacey Heydon and appearsto be the suitable vinyl accountrement to the band’s frenzied angst/energy onstage. Australia To Subsidize MUSEXPO Attendees NEW YORK — For thefifth straightyear, the Australian government will provide subsidy support to Australian companies that par- ticipate in MUSEXPO's sixth International Record and Music Industry Market, ac- cording to Roddy S. Brazilian Radio Show Debuts In Los Angeles LOS ANGELES — Loyola Marymount Un- iversity of Los Angeles has debuted the Brazilian Hour program on KXLU-LA, the campus radio station. Intended to bring Brazilian music to the Los Angeles area, the program airs on Sundays from 9-10 a.m. The program is produced by Sergio Mielniczenko and Floriano Regis, head of the Brazilian cultural department in Los Angeles. The program is the first of its kind in Los Anaeles. No replacement yet for the vacant Capitol Canada press/artist relations position, after Celeste Mulhern left last month . . . Recent reports that RCA will pick up Mushroom distribution are false, charges vice president and general manager Ed Preston. RPM Magazine com- mitted the gaffe recently by reporting off- the cuff remarks from a Mushroom exec. kirk lapointe Italy MILAN — Pirated pre-recorded tapes have been decreased to 35% of the market in the first three months of 1980, according to Guido Rignano, president of the AFI (Italian record manufacturers association). Follow- ing strong efforts by the AFI, in conjunction with the SIAE (Italian authors and publishers association), pirated tapes dropped from a 50% market share taken during 1979. Casablanca has renewed its licensing agreement with Durium for 1980. Donna Summer, on Casablanca, was the top female singer on the Italian charts last year. Currently on tour in Italy are many foreign groups, including Ginger Baker’s Energy and Wishbone Ash, and Italian “cantauri” (singer/songwriters) like Gianna Nannini and Fabio Concata. Private radio stations in Italy rose to 4,- 000 at the beginning of this year. At one of them. Radio Studio 105 in Milan, disc jockey Max Venegoni recently worked an uninterrupted 48-hour program, presenting a total of 660 new releases. SWITCHED-ON PLATINUM — CBS Masterworks artist Wendy Carlos was recently awar- ded a platinum record for "Switched-On Bach," the largest-selling classical album ever released. Carlos has just released "Switched-On-Brandenburgs . ” Pictured at the presen- tation are (l-r): Bob Campbell, director of marketing for CBS Masterworks; Rachel Elkind, producer and collaborator; Carlos; Dick Asher, deputy president and chief operating of- ficer for CBS Records Group; Peter Munves of CBS Masterworks; and Paul Myers, vice president of A&R planning and production for CBS Masterworks. ON JAZZ (continued from page 1 7) far beyond it’s supposed limitations. He’s also leading the way in the creation of new com- positional directions for modern improvisers — form and spontaneous invention become interchangeable. Perhaps it is best to label the work of Lewis and others like Anthony Davis, Leo Smith, Roscoe Mitchell, Anthony Braxton and Leroy Jenkins “the new struc- turalism,” because of their work is forging a vital link between jazz, Africa and the harmonic sensibility of 20th Century classicism; it is highly structured music that is searching for new directions other than those of pop jazz, punk jazz and freedom swing — directions that have nothing to do with the tyranny of the dance. In a recent Public Theatre performance with reedman Douglas Ewart, Lewis proved that it is possible to combine post-Schoenberg tonality with an African rhythmic feeling that avoids strict bar line demarcations, opting for a continuous flow of melodic counterpoints — a modern world ethnic music, a river of un- consciousness that can turn up in any number of continental tributaries. It is not atonal, but rather pantonal, meaning that you can choose to move in and out of tonality, finding unison or clash as each moment dictates. Their dialogs were marked by a high degree of textural sophistication (aided and abetted by Lewis's electronic computer tapes, which provide an unpredictable voice to play off of), great melodic diversity, extensive use of poetry and theatrical flourishes (“They came from the sun at the dawn of the earth . . . and they played music and the moon was driven back"), and an irascible sense of humor. George Lewis and Douglas Ewart created more contrasts and effects on acoustic instruments than most synthesizer players will ever get to. They are paving the way for a re-unification of all types of music in the '80s. VINYL PIPELINE — Earl Horowitz’s Pausa Records (9255 Sunset Blvd., Los Angeles) has a fine series of new releases highlighted by “Trilogue Live,” a colossal trio comprised of trombonist Albert Mangelsdorf, electric bassist Jaco Pastorius and drummer Alphonse Mouzon. Also included are pianist Tete Montoliu’s “Piano For Nuria,” "Singers Unlimited with Rob McConnell & Boss Brass," “Virtue" by Mouzon, and “A Day In Copenhagen” with tenorist Dexter Gordon and trombonist Slide Hampton . . . ECM has an impressive end-of- March release featuring “Playground," a collaboration between pianist Steve Kuhn and Vocalist Sheila Jordan, “Abercrombie Quartet” by guitarist John Abercrombie, “Swimming With A Hole In My Body” by guitarist Bill Conners. “Journal Violone II” by bassist Barre Phillips, and “Nude Ants” by Keith Jarrett with his Scandinavian rhythm sec- tion, recorded live at the Village Vanguard. Down the line in April will be an album from cellist David Darling and “Full Force," a follow-up to last year’s extremely successful debut by the Art Ensemble of Chicago (Roscoe Mitchell, Joseph Jarman, Lester Bowie, Malachi Favors and Don Moye) . . . Elektra has released a live set from the acoustic ensemble Oregon (Ralph Towner, Paul McCandless, Glenn Moore, and Collin Walcott) called “In Performance" and a debut from Side Effect, "After The Rain” ... In April, Arista will have a new recording by the Jeff Lorber Fusion called “Wizard Island" which features Chick Corea on two cuts, while May will see a new Brecker Brothers and a Tom Browne album on GRP . . . Two new re-issues from Milestone and Prestige. On Milestone is "A Blue Time" by the late trumpeter Blue Mitchell, featuring him in all-star settings from his Riverside period (1957-1962), and "Travellin' Light," which features some 1957 sessions by tenor great Ben Webster and an early '60s collaboration between the tenorist and young keyboardist Joe Zawinul, Webster’s roommate at the time, in his first album as a leader. From Prestige is "Portrait” by the late bassist Charles Mingus featuring such great stylists as reedman Eric Dolphy and pianist Jaki Byard (who also wrote the liner notes). Finally there is a re-issue of the work of pianist George Wallington called “Our Daylight." Wallington, a much overlooked player, was seminal accompanist in the teething stages of bebop; he’s joined here by — are you ready — Charles Mingus, Phil Woods, Donald Byrd and Max Roach. Studios Go Digital (continued from page 16) noise reduction capabilities and expanded dynamic range offered by digital tech- niques as indispensable for anyone “who is looking for a very clean sound.” Although digital recording has not made significant inroads in Nashville, the Sony PCM 1600 has been used during sessions in the country capital’s Columbia Studios, as well as at Woodland Sound. Jim Pugh, chief engineer at Woodland, where per- cussionist Farrell Morris recorded “Bits of Percussion and Jazz” for the Audio Direc- tions label, praised the sonic quality of the digital process, but said that his studio has made no definite commitment to buy or lease a digital system. “We’re looking into it,” said Pugh, citing the high costs and in- compatibility of digital systems as the key factors being considered by the studio. The overall outlook for the future of digital recording seems bright. Complaints about editing difficulties linked to numerically encoded sound signals promise to be resolved by a new genera- tion of digital editing machines being developed by the major manufacturers, such as the new 3M unit and the Sony prototype DEC-1000 editor. Digital technology is also being hailed by sound professionals as the key to new mix-down techniques that will be applied to analog recorded material as well as ditigal tapes. The enthusiasm of the digital proponents is best summed up by George Clabin, who said, “People must think ahead and realize that we are around the corner from a major new means of reproducing sound.” RIAA Supports Idea Of Television Special Saluting LP Industry NEW YORK — The RIAA board of directors has approved recommendations recently set forth by the organization’s public rela- tions committee for the publication of an in- dustry sourcebook and the production of a television special saiuting the record industry. The sourcebook committee, headed by Stu Segal, director of public relations for the Polygram Corporation and Stephen Traiman. executive director of the RIAA, will provide information on the RIAA and its various activities; an historical account of the growth of the industry; facts and figures on annual industry sales; a profile of the record-buying public; copyright and per- formance rights; a breakdown of manufac- turing facilities; challenges facing the in- dustry; lists of RIAA members and affiliated labels; and other statistical and general in- formation. The sourcebook will be released in sections so that new information can be inserted without reprinting the entire publication. The television project, which was proposed by Bruce Cohn Productions and presented by Dick Lippin of Stone Associates, evolves around the theme of popular artists "going back in time to per- form or interact with those who influenced their careers," according to an RIAA press release. Potential sponsors are currently being approached, according to Lippin. The RIAA television subcommittee in- cludes Mike Gormley of A&M Records; Herb Helman of RCA Records; Dennis Fine of Arista Records; Laurie Steinberg of CBS Records; Sherrie Levy of Phonogram/Mer- cury; and independent publicists Carol Ross and Morty Wax. CASH BOX NEW HOT GOLD — Chrysalis recording artist Pat Benatar's debut LP, "In the Heat of the Night, ” was recently certified gold by the RIAA. Pictured are (l-r): Sal Licata, president of Chrysalis; Neil Geraldo, of Benatar’s band; Benatar; and Scott Sheets, Myron Grombacher and Roger Capps of the band. RIAA Economic Study Documents How Record Industry Was Hurt In 1979 by Ken Terry FCC Approval Of AM Stereo Draws Mixed Radio Reaction NEW YORK — In order to document the record manufacturers' opposition to a change from flat to percentage mechanical royalty rates, the Recording Industry Assn, of America (RIAA) has furnished the Copyright Royalty Tribunal in Washington with an "Economic Study Of The Recording Industry.” Prepared by the Cambridge Research Institute (CRI), the study provides aggregate statistics for the years 1977-79 from 14 recording companies. Among them are Arista, Atlantic, Capitol, CBS, Elecktra/Asylum, Forte, Infinity, London. Publisher Groups Pushing For New Percentage Royalty by Joanne Ostrow WASHINGTON — A mountain of economic studies on the merits of the mechanical royalty rate, requested by the Copyright Royalty Tribunal to help in its determination of the need to adjust the current rate, was filed by interested parties last week. In addition to a study submitted by the RIAA (see separate story above), filings were also made by the American Guild of Authors and Composers (AGAC), the Nashville Songwriters Assn. International (NSAI) and the National Music Publishers Assn. (NMPA). Today’s rate of 2 34 cents per tune is dis- puted by authors, composers and publishers. But there is little agreement on how to refigure that rate. NMPA Study The NMPA's economic study, prepared by Robert R. Nathan Associates, supports the contention that the 2 3A-cent mechanical royalty “is wholly unreasonable as a ceiling rate.” Instead, NMPA maintains the royalty should be a percentage of the song's market value, meaning the retail list price. Its suggestion is 6%, a rate it said will remain reasonable until 1987 when the Tribunal is empowered to go through rate adjustment proceedings again. NMPA pointed out that aggregate mechanical royalties paid to songwriters and music publishers fell far behind record company income — to barely three percent of record sales. The publishers’ group report disputed the record companies' contention that in- creases in the number of records sold com- pensate for the ceiling rate. “Because the flat ceiling has not been reasonably ad- justed to reflect changes in current rates of (continued on page 36) Nashboro. Phonogram, Polydor, RCA, RSO and Warner Bros. All but one of these companies supplied statistics for 1979. By dividing the respondents' wholesale volume by the RIAA's estimate of the in- dustry’s total wholesale volume in 1979, the CRI researchers calculated that the respondents accounted for 70.9% of in- dustry sales last year. Noting a loss of 11.5% on the respon- dents' net sales, the study concluded, "One fact is strikingly evident from these exhibits: In terms of pre-tax profits (and losses), 1979 was the worst year for the recording industry in recent history." Excluding license income from masters licensed abroad, the responding com- panies lost $208.7 million on net sales of $1.8381 billion in 1979. compared to profits of $82.1 million on net sales of $2.0657 billion in 1978. The picture looks a little brighter, however, when last year's license income of $96.5 million (compared to $91 million in 1978) is added in. NEW YORK — According to reliable field sources, Cash Box has learned that CBS Records will raise the suggested list price of “The Wall” by Pink Floyd to $15.98 from $13.98, effective April 21. However, CBS declined to comment on the report. by Michael Martinez and Joanne Ostrow LOS ANGELES — Initial broadcaster reac- tion to the recent Federal Communications Commission (FCC) decision to permit stereo broadcasting by AM radio was mixed, due to the FCC's simultaneous adoption of the Magnavox AM stereo system. While some radio staffers maintained a wait-and-see attitude, others said that there were certain limitations inherent with the Magnavox AM stereo system. However, it was generally agreed that AM stereo would eventually mean clearer, better fidelity for music on AM radio. In the past, the better sound was only available on FM broadcasts. “I’m really thrilled that after all these years the FCC has decided to approve AM stereo," said Bob Kanner, chief engineer at RKO’s KHJ/Los Angeles, a station that tested AM stereo, “but as an engineer I'm a bit concerned about the commission’s adoption of the Magnavox system." Dave Forman, program director at KEZY/Anaheim, said, “AM stereo is AM radio's only salvation. This might spark the trend back to more music on AM radio.” Forman said that many AM stations that aspired to program AOR formats, such as KEZY, would surely benefit from “cleaner, fuller transmission.” The 4-2 FCC decision followed a lengthy, 18-month study by the government and ar- dent efforts by five companies with incom- patible and competing AM stereo systems NEW YORK — CBS is introducing a $5.98 list developing artist series with a dealer in- centive program that is considered excep- tionally generous by retailers around the country. All product in the new line, which will hit the stores April 14, will carry an “N" prefix. This was the prefix used on LPs in the for- mer CBS artist development program, which offered dealers a cost price scaled to $1 off list price. The "N”-prefixed albums will list at $5.98 until “it is deemed appropriate to charge the price customarily charged for new releases from established artists,” ac- cording to a CBS spokesperson. Producers, Artists Discuss Digital Recording Potential by Richard Gold This is the second article in a two-part series about the state of digital recording in the American music industry today. Part one (Cash Box, April 12) focused on the digital equipment that is available in major recording centers around the country and the viewpoints of studio representatives. Part two deals with the attitudes of producers and recording artists towards digital recording. NEW YORK — The newness, high expense, and incompatibility of digital recording techniques, coupled with the limited availability of computer-based sound replication equipment in recording studios around the country, are the key factors limiting the changeover of pop music producers and artists from the analog to the digital mode. Nevertheless, those producers and artists who have ex- perimented with the digital process — which measures the amplitude of an audio signal at ultra-high speed, then stores the measurements on magnetic tape in binary language — feel that it represents a Pressing Plants Increase Prices After PVC Hike by IVlarc Getner LOS ANGELES — In separate moves that could signal atrend among many of the ma- jor pressing plants in the country, the Precision/United Record Pressing plants in Nashville and Allied Record Company in Los Angeles have reacted to the April 1 PVC price hike by upping the prices they charge for pressing albums and singles. Two of the first pressers to announce a new price list are the Nashville-based Precision and United Pressing Plants. Up until April 9, both companies werecharging approximately 19-20 cents per single and 47-55 cents per album, with variable pric- ing. However, as of April 15, the two com- panies’ new price lists, which are also sub- ject to variable pricing, show an average in- crease of 2 cents on LPs and 1 cent on 45s. Allied Record Company of Los Angeles has also adjusted to the second PVC price hike since January by instituting new prices. The company, which presses LPs for Elektra and Disney and 7-inch records for RCA, has upped its LP prices (formerly listing for 50 cents) by almost 1 cent. The 45s were not subject to the price increase since they are pressed with styrene. While many of the nation's pressing plants plan on absorbing the 6% (2Vz cents per-pound of mix) price increase on polyvinyl chloride and others are still evaluating accounts, industry sources believe that many plants will elect to pass (continued on page 34) breakthrough which will have significant impact in the future. At present, the competing manufac- turers of first-generation digital recording systems are making concerted efforts to in- terest established producers and pop stars in using their equipment. According to Peter Asher, the producer of Linda Ronstadt’s current hit album, “Mad Love,” the St. Paul-based 3M Company was “very anxious” to have its 32-track Digital Master- ing System employed on the Ronstadt LP Asher said that he and the singer compared the 3M system with the Sony digital two- track and competitive analog machines at the Record One Studios in Los Angeles. “We found the 3M markedly better,” Asher said. Ahnough “Mad Love” was recorded in analog, it was mixed “entirely digitally,” Asher said. The producer was so im- pressed with the potential of digital recording, that he decided to make his next project, an LP by a new Los Angeles group called Ronin, a full digital production. “It made my life ten times easier,” Asher remarked. “When we mixed the Ronin album, we mixed on to two of the unused tracks on the 3M 32-track. The enormous advantage is that you can punch in and out of a mix at any time. This is something you could never do in a million years with analog.” Asher also said that he will “definitely" be using the 3M digital system when he produces James Taylor's next album sometime this summer. ‘Phenomenal Punch’ Mick Fleetwood, the founding member and producer of Fleetwood Mac, acted on NEW YORK — WEACorp.’sannouncement that it is raising the suggested list and wholesale prices on 113 multiple record and tape sets in its catalog has prompted many of the nation’s rack and retail ac- counts to adjust their prices accordingly, a Cash Box survey has revealed. The price changes instituted by WEA are Blanket Licenses Are Ruled Lawful NEW YORK — Circuit Judge Jon O. New- man of the United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit has ruled that the blanket licenses offered by ASCAP and BMI to television networks are entirely law- ful. The unanimous decision ruled that CBS, which had contested the policy, had failed to prove that blanket licensing restrains competition. The decision affir- med the initial ruling by District Judge Lasker in his 1975 dismissal of CBS’ com- plaint against ASCAP and BMI. Judge Newman’s decision marks the fourth round in the eleven-year-old litiga- tion, brought on Dec. 31, 1965 by CBS. The initial ruling by the District Court in 1975 was reversed in 1977 by the Second Circuit Court of Appeals, which ruled that blanket licensing was illegal as price fixing, but was reversed in 1979 by the United States Supreme Court, which sent the case back to the Court of Appeals with instructions to analyze blanket licensing. According to Edward Chapin, general counsel for BMI, blanket licenses do not restrict competiton because licensees always have the alternative of paying in- dividual publishers directly. Under the terms of blanket licensing, a licensee agrees to pay a fixed sum to a licensing agency, regardless of which material is used and the number oftimesitisused. Ac- cording to Chapin, “we now have to go back to a lower court and fix the rate that must retroactively be paid.” According to ASCAP president Stanley Adams, "this decision will surely be ap- plauded by the entire ASCAP membership. We hope very shortly to resume normal business relations with one of our most valued licensees, the CBS TV network." the first major suggested list and wholesale price shifts in 1980, and many accounts noted the irony of the move in view of the success CBS Records has had with its $5.98 catalog series. C4SHBOX MCA recording artist Rupert Holmes has long been recognized for his talent as a songwriter and producer, but it has only been within the last 1 2 months that his own six-year old recording career has finally come to fruition. His unique, musical short stories and penetrating modern obser- vances of the tangled web lovers weave has earned two Top 10 singles with the recent “Him” and the immensely popular “Escape (The Pina Colada Song)," which shot to #1 on the Cash Box Top 100 singles chart. Born in Cheshire, England, Holmes' family emigrated to the U.S. when he was quite young and the slight, bespectacled youth was raised in Nyack, N.Y. His budding talents as a songwriter flowered early, for while he was attending the Manhattan School of Music as a composi- tion major, he wrote a Top 10 hit for the little-known Buoys entitled “Timothy.” Next came tunes for the Partridge Family, in addition to compositions and arrangements for the Drifters, Platters and Gene Pitney, among others, and Holmes also arranged music for the Carol Burnett and Englebert Humperdinck TV shows. One artist who quickly became ena- mored with Holmes’ songwriting style was Barbra Streisand, who asked him to arrange and co-produce her “Lazy After- noon” LP. Four of histunes ended upon the album and Streisand ended up cutting more of his compositions, as did a host of others, including Barry Manilow, Mac Davis and the Manhattan Transfer. Holmes also produced records for such diverse talents as the Strawbs, Sparks and John Miles in London, building an international reputa- tion as a hitmaker. His own career, which started with the Epic LP “Widscreen" in 1974, was only moderately successful. After three albums — “Singles,” “Pursuit of Happiness,” and a self-titled effort — he finally found his groove, so to speak. Moving to the now- defunct Infinity label, he cut “Partners In Crime" and shot a bullseye right on the heart of American listeners. EXECUTIVES ON THE MOVE WEA Int’l, Warner Bros. Music Sales Figures Highlight WCI Annual Report according to the report. Despite the sub- stantial increase in returns, the study said that WEA was able to improve its cash collections last year by approximately eight percent over 1978's figure. The report discounted the theory that the increase in the suggested list price to $8.98 from $7.98 contributed to the industry's problems in 1979 by noting that only 40% of WEA’s unit sales of single disc albums and tapes listed for $8.98. According to the report, the record and music industry's problems last year must be seen in the perspective of the industry's 25 straight years of growth prior to 1979. From 1966 to 1969, industry revenues rose at a 16% compound rate. Growth dropped to a six percent rate from 1970 to 1973, but stabilized at nine percent in 1974 and 1975. From 1966 to 1975, therefore, industry growth was 10% compounded in dollars, roughly half from unit growth and half from price increases. However, from 1976 to 1978, industry growth exploded to 14% compounded in units and 19% in dollars. Several factors led the sharply ac- celerated rate of growth during this period, the report said. These included a “substan- tial” number of new entrants into the record-buying population; the proliferation of full-line record stores where both current and catalog product could be purchased; “sociological factors which caused the record buying habit to continue as con- sumers grew older”; the growth in demand for consumer audio equipment; and the emergence of pre-recorded tape, whose dollar sales doubled in the three years ending in 1978. The study said that while these trends diminished in 1979, they still remain essentially intact. Pointing to the emergence of numerous albums capable of selling millions of units per release during this period, the report said that the success of "Saturday Night Fever" and “Grease" "led to unrealistic ex- pectations by both manufacturers and retailers as to the industry's near-term potential." The albums accounted for ap- proximately nine percent of the industry's total domestic dollar volume in 1978, ac- cording to the report. Radio's "disproportionate" devotion to disco music in relation to its unit sales was also partly responsible for the downturn in the domestic wholesale record business last year, the report stated. As a result of broad disco airplay, said the report, there were less time available to promote records with wider sales potential. Concluding that the "factors responsible for the long-term growth of the recorded music business are fundamentally un- changed," the study reaffirmed detailed market research by WCI that “growth in consumer demand will continue.” U S. con- sumers have spent nearly $25 billion on audio equipment over the past decade, ac- cording to the report, and 83% of all U.S. households have audio playback equip- ment, with better than 50% having both record and tape players. NIELS HENNING ORSTED PEDERSON (LAX/MCA 3195) 20 18 (Pablo 2308 220) — 1 ON JAIL JAY BECKENSTEIN GROWS HIS OWN — Reedman-composer Jay Beckenstein is an American success story, with jazz roots that he traces to Charlie Parker, Coleman Hawkins, Lester Young, Cannonball Adderley and Stan Getz, and an R&B sensibility that encompasses the work of King Curtis and David “Fathead” Newman. Beckenstein and his band Spyro Gyra have established themselves as reigning heavyweights in the pop jazz/adult contemporary market with hits like "Morning Dance," "Shaker Song" and their newest effort “Catching The Sun" (on MCA). In only two weeks on the charts, "Catching The Sun" had risen to #54 with a bullet on last week's Cash Box top 100. It's a suede-glove sound, with airy, samba-inflected colors on top, a firm R&B pulse underneath, and Beckenstein’s pure, melodious saxophone improvisations floating through it all, a quiet fire that percolates without ever quite boil- ing over. “Catching The Sun" is a refine- ment of the directions Beckenstein has been working on since the astonishing success of his first album, a self-produced effort called "Spyro Gyra" which took off with sales of 225,000 in a matter of months without any promotion or touring outside of a several-hundred mile radius of Buffalo, New York. "That album was intended as a final statement, a gift, to the people who liked our music and supported it. I borrowed $30,000 to produce it, but I never expected it to go over as well as it did. Based on the success of that, we got an album on the late, great. Infinity Records called 'Morning Dance' which is still char- ted and has sold over 700,000 records in America and almost 1.000.000 world wide. The reason for our success is hard work. Since 'Spyro Gyra' came out we've been on the road for eight months a year, three years straight. The whole Spyro Gyra trip has been created by us and our fans, not by the record company. We've organized our own tour support and budgets, our own management. Our first album was strictly an independent deal until we got distribution with Amherst. Most im- portantly, we've gotten out into all of the towns jazz groups usually never played and built a following. A lot of people who envy our success never got out of New York City into places like Des Moines; they weren't willing to give up that studio money and make no money for a whole year. That's what we did, and we stuck with it. and that's why we got over." Do you see yourself as a jazz artist or a pop artist, I wondered? "Artistically speaking I consider myself nothing at all," said Beckenstein. "I don't label myself. So rather than call myself pop or jazz I prefer to think of it as contemporary. Economically speaking though I suppose I'm pop. But it’s funny with some critics. They'll call my music jazz, putting me in a category I wouldn't put myself in, and then they put me down for not being jazz. That’s contradictory to me, but I don't lose any sleep over it so long as the public accepts my music.” And what did Beckenstein see as future directions for the band? “Well, like you said, 'Catching The Sun' is a refinement of what we've been doing," he replied, "but for the next album — which we’ll be recording in June — the band and I feel we should become more experimental and take some more risks in instrumentation and variety of material — we don't want to simply become formulaic. I mean, the music we've been doing has been very satisfying, and we think it's helped a lot of jazz artists by opening up the doors to radio airplays. Right now there isn’t a lot of mainstream music played on radio, but a step has been made. Now at least it's not required to have a singer to get on the radio — you can get over with instrumental music, too.” (continued on page 48) SPIRALING UPWARD — MCA recording artists Spyro Gyra are currently soaring up the Cash Box jazz charts at #2 bullet with their LP "Catching the Sun." JAZZABUM PICKS ON THE ROAD — Count Basie and Orchestra — Pablo Today D2312112 — Producer: Norman Granz — List: 8.98 The prophet of Kansas City swing shows no signs of slowing down. "On The Road" is one of the most powerful big band recordings in recent memory, and the use of the Sony Systems Digital Recording equipment puts you in the front row of the audience.
