Gorrie) The Average White Band are still the most accom- plished blue-eyed soul unit going, and the first single from the band’s current “Shine" LP finds them in a polished, string-laden groove, with horn-brass-string trade-offs that should hit on pop, B/C. KENNY NOLAN (Casablanca NB 2269) Night Miracles (3:39) (Sound Of Nolan Music — BMI) (K. Nolan) Haunting swamps of synthesizer and cymbal touches unfold into a sinewy electric piano melody and Nolan’s rich, full-textured vocals on the title track from his current LP. Clicking percussives set the mid-tempo pace on this sexy A/C, pop tune. HUDSON (Elektra/Curb E-46648) Annie (4:03) (Lornhole Music — BMI) (B. Hudson. M. Hudson, B. Hudson, S. Rodney Franklin’s future as a pianist and a composer appears to be all in front of him. COMINGS AND GOINGS — There’s a new Eric Gale album coming through produc- tion at the moment that looks like a killer. Producer Allan Toussaint and executive producer Glenn Orsher have recorded half the album at Van Gelder studios in New Jer- sey, going for a real classic bar sound that still manages to be very contemporary in terms of modern jazz playlists. The players include, in addition to guitarist Gale, Arthur Blythe on alto, Harold Vick on tenor, Idriss Muhammed on drums and Charles Earland on organ (who was recently signed with Columbia) . . . The John Abercrombie Quartet, fresh off of a new album on ECM. turned in a strong opening set for The Jeff Lor- ber Fusion at New York’s Bottom Line. The guitarist’s fluidity and melodic acumen were in- comparable, and pianist Richie Beirach provided a sometimes stately, sometimes elfish comping that went way past accompaniment, establishing a shifting, intricate dialogue. His percussive wit and harmonic range were a pleasure. Also fine were bassist George Mraz and drummer Peter Donald, who tossed back a steady stream of rhythmic paraphrases and counter-melodies. John Abercrombie’s Quartet is creating a music that weds the spare chromaticism of Miles Davis to a pleasing assortment of rhythmic grooves, from backbeat to pure flotation and swing. The John Abercrombie Quartet is a good band reaching for maturity, and making it, too . . . POINTS WEST I Various Tour Plans, Strategies by Michael Martinez LOS ANGELES — Record companies regard international touring as an impor- tant marketing tool, whether the goal is to break an American artist initially overseas or to broaden the artist’s existing sales base. A Cash Box poll of 10 record com- panies revealed that each label considered international touring a viable marketing tool when coupled with other efforts such as TV, press and radio exposure. There are basically two types of tours — promotional tours, where artists meet with the press, appear on television and radio in various markets, and the actually perfor- mance tour. Record companies' expenditures to sup- port either a promotional or performance tour depends largely upon such factors as the availability of an artist's current product and how well it’s being received in a given market, the ability of the label to recover tour support investments and the artist’s previous track record in a particular market. In many cases, the labels surveyed create marketing and promotion cam- paigns in foreign markets that are designed to enhance both the artist’s sales base or to develop broader exposure. Evidence of the viability of international touring, both promotional or performance, was graphically offered through the success of A&M recording group Super- tramp, who toured internationally last year, selling approximately 10 million "Breakfast In America” LPs worldwide. "International touring is an extreme boost to record sales and an avenue to getting wider exposure and publicity,” commented Jack Losmann, vice president of A&M International, worldwide. Selection Of Venues Losmann further indicated that selection of venues is largely based on the artist’s in- tial acceptance in a given marketing. He said that prior to an artist’s tour, specific marketing plans are tailored to suit the act's degree of acceptance and exposure. Helmut Fest, vice president, inter- national, for the Capitol/EMI-A/UA Group, suggested that criteria for selection of venues depends basically upon the cost of transporting an act on an overseas tour, how the market will bear that cost and what type of venues are available. He added that if enough initial promotion by overseas af- filiate companies has not occurred, “a per- formance tour is a waste.” Fest suggested that promotional and performance touring should be scheduled in concert to enhance the effectiveness of advertisement, TV, press exposure and in- store product displays. He also maintained that in most Euro- pean markets, television was an essential outlet to breaking an artist, and that an ar- tist’s promotional tours were far more ef- fective than extensive use of film clips or video. Supporting Fest’s contention was Julian Shapiro, associate director of press for CBS International, who said, ‘‘TV is a very important component to breaking artists in Europe.” Further highlighting the importance of closely surveying the prime media outlets to promote an artist was Joe Cohen, inter- national product manager for RCA, who said, “In some territories extensive pre- release promotion must precede release of the artist’s product and a pending tour.” Pre-release Campaigns Citing Japan as an example, Cohen com- mented that some pre-release campaigns in Japan have lasted six months. He said that pre-release promotion of product in the U.K. might last only six to eight weeks. “It really depends on what avenues of ex- posure are most viable in a given market. Where the major avenue of exposure is print, such as in Japan, the promotion cam- paign mighttake longer. Where television is the primary medium, the promotion cam- paign is exposed more rapidly.” According to most of those surveyed by Cash Box, the most significant advantage scheduling a promotion tour prior to finan- cing full-scale performance venture is that a buzz can be created if key TV, press and radio outlets are used to expose a label's artists. The other major advantage cited of a promo tour was that the cost of transporting equipment, additional per- sonnel and travel expenses are eliminated. The bottom line on the viability of promoting and marketing international tours from the record companies’ standpoint, however, was best expressed by Phil Rose, executive vice president, WEA International, who said, "Unless we sell records, there's no way we can recoup tour support money.” Yearly Meetings Rose added that a combination of com- ponents — including pre-tour publicity, promotional tours, and, last but not least, a comprehensive marketing program — are discussed during seven meetings yearly among WEA companies and overseas af- filiates to decide the best plan for each ar- tist. He said that a list of artists are submitted to representatives in the international departments and foreign affiliates and then at the promotion-marketing conclaves, representatives from each region the artist is to tour recommend a marketing plan to fit each artist, based on acceptance of current product, initial promotional success and the prior record sales success an artist has gained in the given areas. Losmann of A&M explained that marketing support went beyond making sure the artist’s product was in stores where they'd be touring but that it also in- cluded in-store displays, merchandising aids and dealer tie-ins where such programs were effective. Dan Young, international product manager for Mercury, concurred with others on the importance of marketing when he suggested that because of the prohibitive cost of international touring, which has always been higher than its domestic counterpart, planning a tour in an area where an artist's product has not been enthusiastically received is "a waste.” The consensus, however, among all the labels was that international touring will remain an important component in each label’s overall marketing strategy. A&M’s tour schedule for 1980 includes the recent tour by the Police in India, Egypt and other areas of the far and middle east. Joan Armatrading is scheduled for a tour this summer in Europe and the U.K., while Peter Allen is slated for a tour of Australia. The group Styx, which recently completed a promo tour in Japan, is scheduled to begin a tour in the U.K. and Europe bet- ween June 5-28. The new marketing division recently for- med for Eurodisc Ltd. is now A&A Record Marketing, headed by managing director Andrew Pryor. Eurodisc Limited now um- brellas AIG Munich; its International divi- sion; Arista Records Ltd; Ariola Records (U.K.) Ltd; A&A Record Marketing; and the overall finance and administration division. NEW ROCK ON BANDSTAND — Dick Clark’s American Bandstand has been a pop in- stitution since theadventoftelevision, and although ithasgeared its shows toward mid- dle of the road acts for the past several years, the last few months have represented a time of strange and wonderful changes. Bands such as The Jam and ska funnyboys Madness have recently made appearances, but the strangest show yet was aired May 17. Rock anarchists Public Image Ltd. appeared on the program which has always ad- vocated songs that "have a good beat and are easy to dance to." Johnny Lydon (aka Rotten), who is the Dennis the Menace of the new rock, led the band through a two-song anti-set that probably aged the ageless Clark another 20 years. As the band wove its way into the haunting “Poptones,” Lydon nixed the famous lip-synch routine and star- ted pulling dancers onto the floor. Within seconds the scowling, prowling Lydon had cleared the bleachers and was pushing the startled disco crowd into one another. In the interim between the first song and “Careering,” Clark attempted to talk to Lydon, who had climbed the stairs to the raised platform and was smiling menacingly down on the bedlam below. However, the British hellion, clad in a baggy white suit, ignored the host completely. Before the confused cameramen cut away to a commercial, Lydon had overtaken the American Bandstand founder's famous podium and stood fast like a vic- torious Napoleon. Let’s hope the Plasmatics, which has added an exploding '55 T-Bird to its show, are on the summer schedule. McCARTNEY II — Paul McCartney, whose second LP should be arriving the stores this week, has shelved plans for making his "Band On The Run" film. Apparently Paul felt that the movie's theme had been used a little too often. Nevertheless, the ex-Beatle has nearly completed work on “Rockestra." a film for TV which is based around the super- session that Paul and wife Linda hosted two years ago and included members of The Who, Led Zeppelin, Pink Floyd and other famous British bands. The result of the rock ‘n’ roll summit meeting turned out to be the highlight of the “Back To The Egg" LP. McCartney has also reportedly prepared a script outline and composed 14 songs for a proposed full length animated feature based on children's story character Rupert Bear. McCartney's company, MPL, own the rights to the tale for tots. Another screen venture that McCartney recently finished was the promo video for his new single, “Coming Up." Those who braved Saturday Night Live two weeks ago got a chance to view the amusing clip in which McCartney plays 11 characters (including a mod-suited, mop topped Beatle) and Linda plays two. THE RHYTHM SECTION MICHAEL JACKSON IN A DUO — Michael Jackson joins Dave Mason in a duo single on Mason’s soon-to-be-released LP. The single, called “Save Me." is being released this week. Joe Wissert, who produced Boz Scagg's "Silk Degrees" LP. produced this Mason effort that is reportedly suitable for all formats. THE CREATION OF A BLACK MOR STATION — Keith Adams, operations manager/program director at KDIA in Oakland says. “KDIA will now become a station that programs soft easy listening music. We have deleted all funk, high energy and intense- sounding product. My primary records will be recurrents and oldies, and my secondary records will be familiar currents, which means the station will be extremely slow to add new music. We want records to be very familiar in the market before we play them. Our style will be very conversational, with lifestyle and human interest stories playing an important part in this new format. Though we have never heard of a black MOR format before, we are go- ing to try to create one." IN THE WORLD OF COVER RECORDS — The song "Gee Whiz," recorded by Carla Thomas several years ago, is bringing a great deal of attention and sparking several careers. Carla is enjoying renewed recognition as many radio personalities are playing her version of the song, back-to-back with the current Bernadette Peters version that is presently climbing the charts. A group called Interlude is also enjoying success with its rendition of this obviously versatile song. ONTHEROAD — The Commodores will start its largest tour ever in June, where the group will play 95 dates over a six month period. The tour will be in support of the group's tenth Motown album, “Heroes," which will be released this week. The tour will end in December with a date in Hawaii . . . Natalie Cole's album "Don't Look Back" is being released this week. In support of the album she will tour throughout the summer, starting next month. NAB HOLDS FIRST EEO COMPLIANCE SEMINAR — The National Association of Broad- casters (NAB) held its first meeting to help broadcasters understand the new processing standards of the FCC’s EEO policies. NAB attorney Enola Aird, who organized the seminar, mentioned that she is planning other seminars in other markets, with seven target cities be- ing discussed to give the maximum amount of coverage. A 51 -page booklet written by Aird called A Broadcasters Guide to Designing and Implementing an Effective EEO Program has also been made available to NAB members. The guide will be mailed to members in the May/June Info Pak. Additional copies are available to members at $3.00. for non- members, $9.00. The compliance seminar is scheduled to be held June 24 in Los Angeles at the Century Plaza Hotel. For attendance information call Ann Cotton at (202) 293-3560. MIAMI RADIO LENDS HELPING HAND — Commenting on Miami radio's reaction to riots that recently rocked the city, Jerry Rushian, vice president general manager at WEDR, said. "The station is located right in the heart of where rioting broke out. When we saw what was starting to happen, we began airing information about the rioting, but we tried to con- centrate on the more positive information rather than dwell on the killings and other negativities. The station had 200 to 300 people a day coming in and lending a hand to help people in the community who were burned out of their homes. We had volunteers on the phones in the station around the clock for a few days. We did not stay away from playing records as much as several of the other stations; we would simply interject information bet- ween music and it came in." Joe Fisher, operations manager at WRBD in Ft. Lauderdale, also mentioned that there was a great deal of rioting in his area. In anticipation of potential problems resulting from the strike, the station designed the Saturday before the rioting “Day of Pride Day." and started airing community spots about having pride in the com- munity. Telephone lines were opened to listeners who wanted to call and voice their opoi- nion. and several community leaders came to the station to discuss various community problems. A spokesperson at Rudy's Records and Tapes, which is located in the riot area* said," business is certainly off quite a bit, as there are now additional people out of jobs, so until money is put back in the area, records stores will suffer as people are trying to just sur- vive.” cookie amerson POP CROSSOVER POTENTIAL A Lover’s Holiday • Change • RFC/Warner Bros. INTERNATIONAL jCRIA Proposes Removal Of Tariffs On Studio Equipment INTERNATIONAL DATELINE (continued from page 37) TORONTO — The Canadian Recording In- dustry Assn. (CRIA) has submitted a brief to the Minister of Finance requesting the duty- free importation of studio equipment. The proposed amendment to the Customs .Tariff is necessary to allow Canadian studios to maintain competitive parity with their American counterparts, according to the CRIA. “The primary justification for the presence of a tariff duty in any industry is the protection of domestic industry,” said CRIA president Brian Robertson. “This justification is absent in the case of the ex- British, Japanese Companies Form Union-Sun Alliance TOKYO — Larry Page Ltd. of the U.K. and Discomate Records of Japan have announ- ced the formation of Union-Sun Alliance, a joint venture to market product in the respective countries. Under the terms of the agreement, artists on the Union-Sun Alliance will be produced or acquired by Larry Page for exclusive distribution in Japan by Discomate and by Penny Farthing Record Distributors in the U.K. Commenting on the deal, Takayasu Yoshioka, president of Discomate, said, “We view Union-Sun Alliance as both an opportunity to work closely with Larry Page, which we have been seeking for many years, and as the start of an enter- prise of international significance to the record industry.” While indicating that Union-Sun Alliance will have no official connection with his Rampage Records, Penny Farthing Records or the Full Page Of Hits publishing company, Page said, “Its sucess will be of paramount importance both to Discomate and myself in the months and years ahead.” Larry Page and Takayasu Yoshioki isting tariff on studio equipment. There are no Canadian manufactured substitutes for the equipment or parts needed for the building and maintaining of a world-class studio. Canadian studios are forced to look abroad for their equipment needs.” At the present time, according to CRIA, Canadian studios are comparable to top- flight studios elsewhere, but the present tariffs make the costs of setting up and/or maintaining this parity more difficult. In ad- dition, with the advent of new technologies, the CRIA expressed the fear that Canadian studios would begin to lag behind those in other countries. “The advent of digital recording equip- ment has now made the implementation of the proposal in this Brief more urgent,” Robertson added. “While American studios are already taking advantage of this great technological advance in recorded sound, the enormous cost to a Canadian studio or re-equipping with digital equipment when the studio must also pay sizable duties on this equipment, will seriously inhibit the spread of digital equipment into Canada. Relief from this duty will help Canada share in this new technology and will ensure Canadian studios a competitive place in the international studio marketplace." By-laws Amended The CRIA recently amended its by-laws to allow Canadian recording studios to become members. A special committee has been working on the import duty brief for the past year. “The exemption from tariff duty proposed in the brief is similar in many ways to the tariff exemption enjoyed by the Canadian film industry since 1937,” Robertson concluded. “The Canadian Recording Industry Association feels that it is somewhat anomalous that equipment entering the country for use in commercial motion picture production may enter Canada duty free, while equipment for use in sound recording studios is subject to a substantial tariff duty. There can be no justification for the fact that the same piece of equipment from the same manufacturer may enter Canada duty free if its destina- tion is a motion picture studio, but is subject to a tariff duty of at least 15% if the pur- chaser is a sound recording studio.” ‘Eurautomat’ Set For Sept. 23-25 In Brussels BRUSSELS — The Eurautomat trade ex- position has been scheduled for the Expo Rogier Center here, Sept. 23-25. The ex- position will feature numerous product and hardware exhibits, as well as sessions and workshops on various aspects of the industry. Italy MILAN — Minister Bernardo D’Arezzo has set up a committee, under the presidency of Riccardo Monaco, delegated to study a project of law against piracy in the record, tape and movie businesses. The committee offices are by the Show Business Juridical Institute, directed by Augusto Fragola. Records) switched to Ri- Fi, and has just finished recording an album, “Amore Amore,” including Italian and Neapolitan songs. Charly Music and many others. mario de luigi United Kingdom LONDON — The Virgin Films release of the long awaited Sex Pistols movie, The Great Rock'n'Roll Swindle, opened in London last week and garnered many rave reviews, as well as stoking up the youth/anarchy syn- drome yet again. Talking about the movie on London Weekend TV’s arts program. The South Bank Show, director Julian Temple said “The Pistols’ mission was to destroy rock'n'roll, and the film attempts to show this. It's also a blueprint for how to ap- proach the rock business.” Aside from the serious politico/socio cause and effect that motivated the Sex Pistols and the original English punk move- ment to gain public attention through the media, the film itself actually turns out to be a very witty comedy treated in a surprisingly traditional English manner. Coy titillation is used through segmented cartoon anima- tion to illustrate the seamy, sleazy side of the Pistols' off-stage antics; along with collaged stills of shock/horror press headlines and original film and video clips all strung together with a manager Malcolm McClaren's narrative explaining how to swindle as many record companies as possible in the shortest time available. Overall the movie contains masses of very English Benny Hill/Carry On Films-type smut-humour and reveals the successful, short, anti-heroes' cause of hyping rock- biz-hype and getting away with it with music as the last word. Virgin has backed up the Pistols’ move with an album release of The Great Rock'n'Roll Swindle soundtrack, the first 15,000 LPs of which contain a poster of the film. On June 6, the label is also releasing a single coupling “Stepping Stone," which is on the soundtrack LP, with “Pistols Propaganda,” a track that combines pieces of old songs with the voice of John Snagge, the person who once declared the end of World War II on BBC radio and who used to ghost some of Winston Churchill’s speeches. A&M Records has also moved into the movie soundtrack business for the first time by recently scooping worldwide rights to the likely blockbuster British rock musical Breaking Glass, starring Hazel O’Connor. O'Connor has written all the songs for the film, which will be released as a soundtrack LP in July, prior to the west- . end premier of the film scheduled for mid- August . . . A&M is also set to release a “six- pack” special collectors edition of all the Police hit singles, plus two previously un- issued recordings. The package will be released in a transparent wallet with five hit singles, plus a sixth singlethat is acoupling of a mono recorded version of “The Bed's Too Big Without You” and a live version, recorded in America, of “Truth Hits Everybody," a track from the platinum album “Outlandos D’Amour.” Yes members Chris Squire, Steve Howe and Alan White recently enlisted multi- keyboardist Geoff Downes and vocalist Treveor Horn to replace Jon Anderson and Rick Wakeman in the new 1980s Yes. Horn and Downes, who were better known as the chart hit group Buggies, recently won worldwide acclaim with their Island LP "Liv- ing In The Plastic Age.” Yes founding mem- ber Chris Squire said “We're a revitalized and regenerated band, working together once more as a strong, unified group. We are playing more positively and powerfully than ever, and we feel that now is the time we are going to re-invent the Yes idea." The group is currently recording in the studio I, and is scheduled to undertake a major North American and European tour at the end of the year. nick underwood For The Record In the May 24 issue of Cash Box. it was erroneously reported in the International Dateline column from Spain that CBS Records International artist Billy Joel had not received promotional support during his tour in that country. The report was based on erroneous information. COIN MACHINE CHICAGO CHATTER Coinbiz impresario Hank Heiser (otherwise known as branch manager at Empire Dist.- Detroit) has come up with a gem of an idea for generating some effective industry PR while at the same time benefiting a very worthy cause. Under auspices of the Detroit Chapter of Music Operators of Michigan and for the benefit of the Soupy Sales Telethon for Retarded Citizens. Empire is presenting "Follies 80. 1 a musical extravaganza, conceived, written and produced by Heiser. The program will take place at Empire’s Livonia premises on June 1, under sponsorship of various manufacturers represented by the distrib, including Allied Leisure, Atari, Bally, Cinematronics, Exidy, Gremlin/Sega, Midway, Rock-Ola, Stern and Tournament Soccer, who have made contributions to help defray the costs of the produc- tion. Recalling the spectacular Hank produced to launch the branch’s new quarters last year, you can bet the June 1 event will be a sensation. Empire staffers have constructed a 36 by 40 foot stage for the presentation and, along with local DJs, the Gaylord & Holiday vocal duo and guest performers, will participate — both on and off stage. An equipment display featuring a variety of amusement machines will also be a part of the program. Ad- mission charge is $25 per person and Hank told us that many ops have purchased ad- ditional tickets for various local political figures and civic leaders. The show is expected to get heavy mass media coverage . . . Another member of the talented Heiser family is Hank’s daughter, Joyce, who is making her acting debut in the upcoming movie “Hollywood Knights" and is currently in New York working on her follow-up film “They All Laughed,” which stars Ben Gazzara, Audrey Hepburn and John Ritter MOVING RIGHT ALONG — Channel 7 Eyewitness News (ABC-TV) spotlighted "Space Invaders" on the 6 o’clock telecast May 13. Reporter Frank Mathie and a camera crew had previously visited the Midway plant to film some assembly line footage and a brief interview with company president Dave Marofske, which was featured during the telecast. Mathie made some great comments about the game and also focused on "Galaxian” as well, term- ing it a worthy successor. EASTERN FLASHES Irving Kaye Co. recently appointed two new distributors in Oregon and Washington, respectively, to represent the factory's product line. As announced by company exec Bill Currier the firms are McKee Distg. of Portland and Northwest Sales of Seattle. “We are very enthusiastic about this new affiliation." commented Currier. “Both companies are aggressive and very much attuned to current merchandising trends, to give our products the proper exposure in that market." Incidentally. Bill put an abrupt halt to his most recent business trip, when he accidentally broke his foot. SORRYTOHEAR about the death of Mike Anderson, Jr., son of Mickey Anderson (Erie, Pa ). Mike's death, at age 41 . was a shock to everyone. He had been chief executive of the prominent distributorship. Our sincere condolences to the Anderson family. Rock-Ola Offers New Audiovisual Program CHICAGO — A completely new audio/visual service training program for Rock-Ola microprocessor operated phonographs, which is suitable for use by groups or individuals, is now available, ac- cording to the firm's senior vice president, Dr. David R Rockola. The new program consists of 127 full color 35mm slides coordinated with a taped audio discussion of each slide. A 132-page illustrated manual that duplicates the material covered by the slides and tape recording is provided to each student. As with previous Rock-Ola service train- ing programs, the new microcomputer ver- sion can be used to instruct a group or one individual. When utilized for group study, the instructor has the option of employing the taped audio portion or personally providing the explanation of each slide. The program can be stopped at any point, backed up to any previous slide, and then returned to the regular sequence. The flex- ibility of this program makes it ideal for use by individual service trainees since they can move along at their own pace and then revert back to previous slides if needed. All of the new Rock-Ola microprocessor controlled features including the Profit Set- ter. Hit Tracker. Opto-Sensor Record Selector and the new play stimulators, are fully discussed in the new service training program. Additionally, the standard mechanical and electrical components are also completely covered. Full details on the Rock-Ola Audio/Visual Service T raining Program are available from factory distributors. Atari Modifies ‘Asteroids’ Video SUNNYVALE — Atari, Inc. has developed a new modification kit designed to add more challenge to “Asteroids” and extra difficulty to the achievement of unusually high scores, according to Frank Ballouz. Atari’s director of marketing. As Ballouz explained, the modification accomplishes the following: The small fly- ing saucer fires immediately in the direction of the player as soon as it enters the screen. The missiles also have a “wrap-around” capability. Originally, the program was entered so that the saucers would fly one-sixth of the way across the screen before firing; and there was no wrap-around capability. Two revisions are currently in the field, namely, ROM REVISION 02, which has the flip-flop capability, and ROM REVISION 01 which does not. Kits are available immediately from Atari distributors. To determine which kit is re- quired the ROMs on the Asteroids PCB must be checked. If ROM code is "-01". or- der kit no 08-0303009. If ROM code is “- 02”, order kit no. 08-0303008. Ballouz also advised that Asteroids T- shirts are now available for purchase from Atari distributors. The shirts are a rich navy blue cotton/polyester blend for easy care and long-wearing durability, and are ador- ned with a bold graphic design showing a spacecraft blasting through a stream of asteroids, in full color. Grace Slick: Moving Through Time, Space And Rock ‘N’ Roll (continued from page 12) Korvettes Committed To LPs, Says President NEW YORK — Despite the naming of Joseph A. Ris as Korvettes’ new chairman and rumors of either a sale or motif change for its Fifth Avenue store, the retail chains’ commitment to its record division remains secure, according to Korvettes President Nick Palihnick. “There will be no change in the marketing or merchandising of records for the time being. We expect records to continue to be a dominant traffic producer at Korvette’s and we see it as a strong aid for both the present and the future,” he stated. It had been reported that the firm’s parent corporation, the Agache-Willot Corup of France, was considering chang- ing the motif of the Fifth Avenue store to that of the French Au Bon Marche chain although no commitment had been made at press time. WhileAu Bon Marche branches in France reportedly carry records as part of their inventory, they are regarded as more of a "high price, fashionable” store than Korvettes. At the same time, ex- ecutives of the firm denied rumors that the Fifth Avenue store might be sold to a group of diamond dealers as a diamond ex- change. Most recently, Joseph A. Ris became the third chairman and chief executive officer of Korvette's in thirteen months. He replaces Alain Mathieu, engendering the printed speculation that Ris would attempt to “re-establish Korvettes as New York’s chief discounter.” ASCAP Bows TV And Film Writing Seminar NEW YORK — ASCAP’s first TV and Film Writing Workshop will begin on June 10 at the Society’s New York City headquarters. Headed by TV and film composer Paul Chihara, the workshop will feature guest panelists from all phases of TV and film scoring, including composers, arrangers, producers and engineers. Writers interested in applying for par- ticipation are requested to submit a cassette tape containing two original com- positions and a resume to: ASCAP TV And Film Workshop, One Lincoln Plaza, New York, N.Y. 10023. Deadline for tape entries is June 6 The workshop, which will meet once a week for two months, is free of charge and open to everyone. with a variety of instruments, sound effects and dialogues, and brought about the ad- vent of the nine minute rock song. The album was also worthy of note because it employed the ideas of the Airplane family, an extended group that was composed of the band’s manager, friends, outside musi- cians and groupies. Slick, who was testing her limits as a songwriter at the time, penned “Rejoyce,” an ambitious interpretation of James Joyce’s Ulysses. Slick had approached Lewis Carroll’s Alice In Wonderland with a drug consciousness, in “White Rabbit,” but “Rejoyce" was an attempt at a new personal high. “I figured a lot of kids, who would not or- dinarily read would get interested if I wrote about the classics," said Slick. “Sometimes the business about good reading gets bor- ing. I was pretty much put off that stuff until I had read it under a different reality.” “The Crown Of Creation" album followed in '68, and it showed Kantner and Slick’s maturation as a songwriting duo. The LP also contains David Crosby’s “Triad,” which tells the story of menage a trois, and went right along with Slick’s concert ad- vocations of free love. Head On Clash 1968, the year after the counterculture clashed head on with authority at the Democratic convention, brought forth the Airplane's first live flight, “Bless Its Pointed Little Head,” a heavily political studio LP, “Volunteers," the jubilation of Woodstock, the nightmare of Altamont, the birth of Kantner and Slick's child China, and a series of ongoing drug and disturbing the peace related arrests for members of the band. "We used to love to play nasty little kids and irritate the cops,” said Slick. "We always knew someone would bail us out. When they’d tell us we were being taken down to the station, we’d say ‘Wow, big deal.' We loved pushing it in their face." In late 1969, Marty Balin, who fervently disagreed with the band’s musical direc- tion. exited to pursue a solo career, and Jack Cassady and Jorma Kaukonen left The Airplane to form Hot Tuna. Slick and Kantner were occupied in the studio with David Crosby, Graham Nash and Jerry Garcia and embarked on the first Jefferson Starship voyage, “Blows Against The Em- pire.” The Airplane, sans Balin, regrouped to form a new label in ’70 as well as to put out an album, “Bark.” The LP contained the hit "You're Only Pretty As You Feel,” and the label, an RCA affiliate, carried such acts as Hot Tuna, Papa John Creach and Kantner and Slick, who later released a duo album called “Sunfighter.” Slick was undergoing a series of delicate operations to remove nodes from her vocal cords in the '70s, which intensified the flar- ing emotions that surrounded the disap- pointing “Long John Silver" and the demise of The Airplane in 72. Cassady and Kaukonen were pursuing the Hot Tuna route and Slick, Kantner and studio musician David Freiberg worked on “Baron Von Tolbooth And The Chrome Nun” and the poorly crafted Slick solo LP, “Manhole” in 1973. The latter effort was positive proof of Slick’s retreat into alcohol. In 1974, Slick, Kantner, keyboard player Freiberg, and violinist Papa John Creach, drummer John Barbata, bass player Pete Sears and teenage guitarist Craig Cha- quico formed the second incarnation of the Jefferson Starship. The new band put out “Dragonfly,” which sold poorly, but via “Caroline," represented Kantner and Slick's reunion with Marty Balin. The new band went on to release three successful albums — “Red Octopus,” the band’s first #1 album) in 1975, “Spitfire” (which went platinum) in 1976 and the gold selling “Earth” in 1977. Friction With The Band Slick, whose marriage tolighting director Skip Johnson in 1976 had created friction with Kantner and the rest of the members of the band, decided to quit The Starship on the last leg of a German tour in 1978. “It all came down at once at The Lorelei festival in Germany,” recalled Slick. “I made the decision to leave when I was sick. The gig was cancelled, and the kids who had been left empty handed by the same promoter at the festival the year before bur- ned the stage down. We had one final gig in Hamburg and I decided to wear an 18th century milk maid’s dress on stage. When I came downstairs, someone remarked that I looked like a ’cute little Swiss miss,’ which really irked me. I went back upstairs, put on a Nazi uniform, got drunk and did a ‘get back at you for the Second World War routine’ for the show.” Slick, who has worn everything from a Hitler outfit to an LAPD uniform during her concert stage career and still has a bit of “Volunteer" in her, is currently concerned with family life. She claims she will be using "Dreams” producer Ron Frangipaneon the next LP with “just a basic rock'n’roll band." “ ‘Dreams' is a nice return for me," said Slick. “And I hope to tour after my second album comes out next fall. That is if the government hasn't fallen apart by then.” NARAS (Atlanta) To Sponsor Latin Confab LOS ANGELES — An international Latin music conference and exhibition will be sponsored by the Atlanta chapter of the National Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences (NARAS) from June 6-8 at the Columbus Hotel in Miami. The conference will feature discussions on the marketing and promotion of Latin product, recent developments in distribu- tion patterns and the proliferation of Latin music product in an international scope. For conference information, contact the Latin Music Conference, PO Box 557839, Miami, Fla. 33155. JEM, EG Combine For Experimental Label NEW YORK — JEM Records and EG Records have formed a new label, Editions EG, according to Marty Scott, president of Jem, and Mark Fenwick and Sam Alder, managing directors of EG. The new label will be exclusively manufactured and dis- tributed in the United States by JEM. Ed Strait, general manager of EG, said that Editions EG “will represent the more experimental, esoteric side of our artists’ talent, as well as select reissues from the j EG archives and new material we feel fits the format of the label." Editions EG will also release product from the Ambient and Obscure labels. The debut releases from the new label in- clude two Brian Eno collaborations, “The Plateaux Of Mirror” with Harold Budd and "Fourth World Volume 1 Possible Musics” with Jon Hassell. Future projects include a new Eno product from the “Music For” series and an Eno-produced LP by Laraaji. Spokespersons for Polydor Records and EG said that EG's new deal with JEM will not effect the label’s existing agreements with Polydor. Commenting on the pact, Scott said: “We look forward to this new and creative relationship with EG and its artists.” RCA Sets Campaign In Black Music Month NEW YORK — In support of Black Music Month, RCA Records will launch in June an extensive, nationwide marketing campaign on behalf of 17 albums by black artists, in- cluding Grey and Hanks, Odyssey, Machine, Chocolate Milk, Wax, Shalamar, the Whispers, Lakeside, Dynasty, Gene Chandler, Edwin Starr, Stephanie Mills, Leon Haywood, Skyy, Aurra, Count Basie and Ella Fitzgerald and Sarah Vaughn. One highlight of the support materials to be made available for the program is a dealer sales kit containing minis of all 17 LPs, logos of all associated labels involved, "Black Music Celebration” logos, and “Celebrate Black Music Month” headlines for in-store use across the country. Additional merchandising materials will include thousands of mounted and un- mounted 3' x 2VZ black and white posters showing all of the artists in the program: radio scripts for each of the artists to be used throughout Black Music Month: special Black Music Month orderformsand a 12" sampler disc containing current and upcoming singles from every album represented for in-store play. In addition, advertising support for the campaign has been set to run in trade, consumer and tip sheet publications throughout the month of June. B’nai B’rith Dinner Slated For June 7 NEW YORK — The 16th Annual Awards Dinner of the Music and Performing Arts Lodge of B’nai B'rith will be held at the Sheraton Centre Hotel on June 7. The din- ner will honor United Artists recording artist Kenny Rogers for creative achievement and RCA Records artist Roger Whittaker for humanitarianism. The master of ceremonies will be the noted country disc jockey Lee Arnold of WHN in New York. For tickets and more information contact Florence Lipper at (212) 937-7200. ; Audiophile Labels Unaffected V CBS’Entry IntoThe Market by sViichaeS Glynn LOS ANGELES — CBS Records’ entry into the audiophile record market via its new Mastersound series will have little impact on the distribution and marketing policies of existing audiophile labels, according to a Cash Box survey. The companies surveyed were confident that the present mix of distribution chan- nels — including factory direct, sub- distributors. hi-fi audio representatives and independent record distributors — is suf- ficient to meet the challenge posed by the CBS branch system. Tucker Perjury Count Hearing Is Postponed by Richard Gold NEW YORK — Federal District Court Judge Thomas C. Platt last week granted a delay to prepare evidence after hearing oral arguments to drop perjury proceedings against George T ucker, president of Super Dupers Inc. of Hasbrouch Heights, N.J. Defense attorney Richard Abrahamson argued that his client, who pleaded guilty in August to one count of wire fraud and one count of criminal copyright infringement (Cash Box, Feb. 16), had recanted the allegedly perjurous grand jury testimony in a timely manner in accordance with recan- tation provisions set out in Federal statutes. Tucker's attorney also argued that the same grand jury which had heard T ucker's testimony about his association with Norton Verner in counterfeit tape trafficking latei indicted him for perjury, in spite of a Federal grant of immunity. In addition, tht defense requested that John H. Jacobs, the government prosecutor, be disqualified from the case on the grounds that "the evidence here is presented in an affidavit filed by an attorney with personal knowledge of the case." Judge Platt expressed skepticism about the defense arguments. "A recantation is good, but not when everything is changed," Judge Platt remarked. “You can’t recant af- ter the prosecution discovers that the testimony was false.” The Judge also said that the immunity granted to T ucker had no bearing on the motion to drop the perjury proceedings. The defense request to disqualify Jacobs was called "pretty farfetched" by the Judge. “If you were to disqualify every lawyer who files an affidavit on the grounds that they have personal knowledge of a case you’d have no lawyers left at all,” Judge Platt commented. “Our business is not making a better phonograph record, it is making an audiophile record,” stated Herb Belkin, president of Mobile Fidelity Sound Lab, a leading supplier of half-speed mastered recordings. "Better phonograph records should be marketed through record retail- ing channels, but audiophile records are designed for demonstrating performance capabilities of high end hi-fi equipment and that’s the market we’re geared towards.” Joe Overholt, president of Direct Disk Lab of Nashville agreed, adding, “Ours is a specialty product and, as such, does not fit into the normal record manufacturers’ promotional and sales techniques. I don’t see us deviating from our normal course of business.” Three-Step Distribution Overholt explained that Direct Disk Lab operates with a three-step distribution process, which entails selling directly to audio reps, who, in turn, sell product to audio hardware stores, retail accounts and distributors, who also cover additional retailers and one-stops. “Our three-step system insures us the best deal possible for our product,” noted Overholt, who added that while Direct Disk product does not carry a suggested list price, retailers generally sell Direct Disk recordings (which include a growing num- ber of half-speed mastered pop and rock ti- tles) for $ 1 4-$ 1 7 . Overholt also indicated that “our wholesale price is contingent upon volume.” Baxter Boyington, marketing director for Nautilus Recordings, noted that while his (continued on page 19) Restrictions On Clear Channels Open 125 AMs LOS ANGELES — The FCC voted on May 29 to drop a special class of "clear channel” radio stations, which will make room for up to 1 25 new AM stations. Many of these new stations are expected to be owned by minority groups. Because of the FCC’s action, about 2,000 applications are expected to be filed for these new stations. It is also likely to spark last ditch legal action against the decision. Preference is expected to be given to ap- plicant organizations that are least 50% minority owned, as well as to those who will be providing the first full time radio service in their communities and to those who plan non-commercial operations. Presently, black, Spanish-speaking and other minorities combined own less than two percent of the nation’s 10,000 radio and television stations. A&M Set To Release 5” Disc By Squeeze NEW YORK — A&M Records will commer- cially release a 5" disc on June 25. The disc, "If I Didn’t Love You,” b/w "Another Nail In My Heart" by Squeeze, is packaged in a full color sleeve and has a list price of $1.99. The initial pressing, according to a label representative, was approximately 7,000. and will not exceed 15,000. The single will be subject to A&M's nor- mal return percentages, and. although the sleeve contains a disclaimer that “tiny records may not play on 'automatic' turntables,” a label spokesman noted that because of the record’s collectability, he foresaw almost no returns. The single is a “one-off” for which no merchandising aids have been provided. A&M has achieved notable success recently with unusual record configura- tions. Both a 10" Squeeze LP and a multi- single Joe Jackson box experienced sell- throughs. according to an A&M sales representative. Garland To Replace Greenberg At Atlantic? LOS ANGELES — Pending an official announcement this week, it appears that Les Garland, program director at radio station KFRC in San Francisco, will be named to replace Bob Green- berg as west coast general manager of Atlantic Records. When contacted by Cash Box last week, Garland would not confirm the appointment, but did say that he has resigned from KFRC. Greenberg and his brother Jerry, who was president of Atlantic, recently resigned to form a new Atlantic-distributed record company. C4SHBOX A&M recording artist Joan Ar- matrading's unique music collage, which incorporates jazz, blues, reggae, folk and rock influences, has continually evolved from album to album and has spawned a growing success. The music on the musician/singer/songwriter's current A&M release, "Me Myself I," which debuted this week #133 bullet on the Cash Box Pop Album Chart, is a more direct offering of her reggae and rock influence, and also an abstraction from the folk-rock sound that distinguished her first album, “Whatever's For Us." The black English woman by way of the West Indies first captured worldwide atten- tion on her second LP, "Back To The Night.” which featured the title track and gained enthusiatic kudos. Her follow up, the "Joan Armatrading" album, fueled even greater popular and industry accolades, with the single from the LP. "Love and Af- fection," fanning the fires of even greater enthusiasm. Armatrading's fourth LP, “Show Some Emotion," firmly established her as a talent to respect and to reckon with. But the hub-bub created by her burgeoning world-class success leaves the quiet artist unaffected, and. in her own terms, seeing herself as a songwriter originally, success for her “would be a lot of people recording the songs I've written." Born in the Caribbean, Armatrading, one of six children, moved with the family to Bir- mingham at age seven, where she shifted her career interests from law to music after exposure to artists like Marianne Faithful, Jim Reeves, Tommy Steele and Nat King Cole. She taught herself early to play both piano and guitar and spent a great deal of time composing songs. Following en- couragement of her brother, Armatrading began performing, which led to collabora- tions with poet/lyricist Pam Nestor. The Nestor/Armatrading writing duo lasted through the first two LPs before the music became more totally an Armatrading entity. On her current LP with producer Richard Gottehrer, the music continues to unveil the depth and clarity of her music perceptions. But always, the totally human quality ex- uding from her music attests to the power of music, in the right hands, as a translator of experiences-. Record Prossers, Jacket Manufacturers . ’ Yib' : 'rices During Summer (continued from page 7) “It’s difficult to predict what’s going to happen during the summer, because you never know when a raw material price hike will be announced, : said Precision presi- dent Joe Talbot. It’s all so closely tied to tne volatile mideast situation.” Reger Gouldstone, vice president of manufacturing for Pickwick International and general manager of manufacturing for Keel (Pickwick’s pressing plant), assessed ne current state of PVC from a different tac. ‘ PVC also has many other uses, es- pecially in the area of piping for houses,” 'said Gouldstone. ‘‘Because America’s economic situation is currently in a state of turmoil, housing is off, and there is a plen- tiful supply for the record industry. So, prices probably won't be increased.” Gouldstone went on to say that the rate of PVC escalation would probably slow down for the summer because of the current recession, and that there would probably be a stabilization of prices. Summer Stabilized Tom Arboit, the recently appointed plant manager for Capitol’s pressing plant, and Dwight Doerr, manufacturing manager for the Columbia Records pressing plant, agreed that because of the series of in- creases over the past four months, pressers would probably not see another PVC increase for the rest of the summer. They also concurred on the fact that the second quarter has pretty much always been soft business-wise. ‘‘There is usually a bit of slowdown in product after the first of the year,” said Ar- boit. "Business should probably level off, pick upin August and show a nice upturn by fall when the big releases come out." The raw materials situation has been met with a similar reaction by vinyl suppliers. One supplier that is approaching summer with a cautious optimism is Tenneco Inc. "Since business is slow, there is an abun- dance of raw materials. So, there probably won’t be an increase in prices on raw materials," explained Guy Disch, director of marketing/polymers for Tenneco Inc., one of the largest suppliers of vinyl com- pound. “However, there is always the possibility of an increase based on the oil situation. As long as there is no increase in the price of petrochemical feedstock, we won’t up our prices.” However, Howard Hill, president of the Keysor Corp., another vinyl compounds supplier, took a more matter-of-fact ap- proach to the raw material dilemma. “Just as all oil-based products are going up, ex- pect the prices of PVC to inflate.” Sluggish Season In direct relation to the slow summer business period for pressing plants, album jacket manufacturers have also entered into a sluggish season. To combat this slowdown, jacket manufacturers have diversified into other areas outside the record industry and considered making less expensive packaging configurations. "I think most record companies have come to grips with current conditions," said Floyd Glinert, executive vice president of Shorewood Packaging, one of the top four jacket manufacturers. “They’re not keeping the back jacket prints like they used to, and it's become pretty much of a hand-to- mouth situation between them and us. In addition, record companies have become more sophisticated in inventory manage- ment planning and are ordering quantities that are set for short term requirements." Glinert went on to say that one of the positive sides of the soft business picture was that it gave manufacturers, dis- tributors, suppliers, rack jobbers and retailers a chance to improve efficiency and operate their businesses more effectively. “Because of the downturn in business,” stated Glinert, "people have become more involved in professional management.” The escalation of pricing on paperboard has become of increasing concern to album jacket manufacturers of late. While manufacturers were subjected to a seven percent paperboard increase in March, they were also faced with another increase by a major supplier until recently. "A price increase of seven percent was to be effected by June 1,” explained Glinert. "However, we met with the company and told them it would be disastrous and coun- terproductive to our current economic situation They considered our complaints, as well as other jacket manufacturers, and they ended up rescinding their increase." On a more conservation-oriented note, Glinert maintained that Shorewood was considering, in the face of rising prices, manufacturing thinner and less expensive album jackets. BLOWIN’ IN THE WIND — A revival of Crosby, Stills and Nash and an appearance by three stray Eagles (Tim Schmit, Joe Walsh and Don Felder) highlighted Survival Sun- day III, held May 25 at the Hollywood Bowl. This year’s event served as a benefit for the anti-nuke organization Alliance For Survival, as well as a rallying point for those who wanted to stop the draft and a possible World War III. Social-political literature, outlin- ing the philosophies of seemingly every equal rights movement in creation, was passed out to concert attendees. And the '60s time warp factor was intensified even more by the presence of day-glow painted faces, peace flags and dove banners. At a backstage press conference folk great Peter Yarrow maintained that events such as this and similar upcoming rallies in California and Maine signaled a new political activism the likes of which he has not seen since the 1960s. “People have stopped being overwhelmed by the powers that be,” said Yarrow. “They are realizing that they do have some control over their own lives." Yarrow and bookend Mary Travers performed old classics (sans Paul Stookey) and were later joined by Graham Nash for a version of John Hall’s anti- nuke anthem, “Power." After numerous no nuke speakers, Nash played his own set and introduced David Crosby for two old favorites — “Carry Me” and "Lady Of The Island." The twosome was then joined by late addition Stephen Stills, and a spellbound crowd was treated to "Just A Song Before I Go,” “For What it's Worth” and "Teach Your Children.” “You approach political issues in a pretty sophomoric way when you in your 20s,” explained David Crosby in post-set interview. “But when you hit 30, you think a lot harder and you realize that you are responsible for the future, and that the issues at hand should be fought for within the system.” Speakers such as Bella Abzug, Dr. Helen Caldicott and physicist Michio Kaku, as well as commedienne Lily Tomlin, expounded on their philosophies in the interim between each musical act. New Orleans' own Dr. John, who was a member of Survival Sunday Ill’s house band along with guitarist David Bromberg and bassist Freebo, performed "Right Place” and other gumbo favorites, and Holly Near, Steve Goodman and Japanese folksinger Danny Ishio also performed during the day-long event However, the greatest musical surprise of the concert/con- clave was an appearance by Eagles Schmit, Walsh and Felder, who perfor- med “I Can’t Tell You Why” with the house band before they were joined by Stills for a hot jam that included the Beatles' "Get Back.” The 6 Vi hour con- cert, which mixed musical celebration with sobering political philosphy, culminated with a majority of the musical guests returning to center stage for the obligatory people's anthem, “Blowin' In The Wind.” . . . Political ac- tivism. which seems to be finding a musical resurgence of late, is approached more objectively on Peter Gabriel’s third self-titled LP, which ships this week on the Mercury label. Gabriel sings about the plight of student activist Stephen Biko in "Biko.” The six-minute ode uses African folk chants and synthesizer for a haunting musical backdrop to the anti-apartheid lyrical theme. Another song on side two of Gabriel's latest opus. “Not One Of Us.” discusses the mechanics of racial prejudice, and the single “Games Without Frontiers" questions the premise behind war. “Peter Gabriel" is the former-Genesis leader's most uncom- promising and musically austere work yet. And while there isn’t a song as commercial as “Soiisbury Hill" on the LP, it incorporates a plethora of exotic musical influences, and stands as one of the most artistically rewarding albums of the year. . . . Bass player Scott Roskin and his band Prairie Fire are pretty much taking the bull by the horns when it comes to the advancement of political ideas through music. When Roskin delivered the Bay Area-based band's single To Cash Box last week, he also dropped by the latest edition of the American Communist Party's newspaper. The Revolutionary Worker, the self-described rock-revolt band cops a “Mad as Hell and we're not going to take it anymore” attitude in its lyrics. And when performing live. Prarie Fire guitarist Greg Coon brandishes a guitar that is made in the shape of an M-16 rifle. BENEFITS — Genesis (and still there are three) brought its “Duke" tour to L.A. last week and capped its stay here by performing a surprise benefit concert at the Roxy on May 25. Michael Rutherford, Phill Collins and Tony Banks made the last minute date even more special by working the ticket booth at The Roxy on noon the day before the show. The show sold out in a matter of hours, and the three benevolent gentlemen pleased their fans by autographing LPs and pictures and rapping with the folks in line. Later, just before going onstage for its May 26 Greek Theatre performance, the art rock trio presented all the money it garnered from Roxy sales to the directors of Los Angeles-based St. Judes Hospital and Children's Hospital . . . Bonnie Raitt, Charlie Daniels, Mickey Gilley and Johnny Lee, four of the artists who have material on the soundtrack to the upcoming Urban Cowboy film, will appear at a special private party at Gilley's bar in Houston on June 5 as part of a world premieregala benefit. A mere$125 will procure a seat at the Galynn Theatre and round trip bus ride to the party, which gets underway at midnight. Proceeds will go to the Houston Child Guidance Center. BETTE FETE — Bette Midler appeared at Hunter’s Book Store in L A 's Westwood Village May 21 to sign copies of her new book. A View From A Broad The hardback is an account of The Divine Miss M s first world tour, and more than a thousand fans showed up to view the Diva of dish. Midler autographed several hundred copies of the book, which is currently on the nation's non-fiction best seller list. TIES THAT BIND — Tonight show band leader Doc Severinsen married TV writer/story editor Emily Marshall on May 17. The ceremony was held poolside at Severinsen’s home in Hollywood . Cash Box sends its best wishes to Mercury westcoast publicity head Eileen Schneider, who is recovering from the rheumatoid il- lness that sidelined her for several weeks. OPEN AIR JAZZ — The 1980 Berkeley Jazz Festival, which recently concluded in the California bay area village, hosted a full spectrum of jazz interpreters, ranging from the tasteful bebop of Art Blakey to the frantic funk-fusion musings of the ensemble of Herbie Hancock, Stanley Clarke, Carlos Santana, Jon Lucien and Alphonzo Mouzon. Though the Art Ensemble of Chicago was also scheduled to appear, delays while in transit from Europe prevented the avante garde outfit from showing. Saturday’s show was highlighted by the appearance of an all-star band composed of Freddie Hubbard, Hubert Laws, Ronnie Laws, Abraham Laboriel, Lee Ritenour, Harvey Mason, Ralph McDonald and Jorge Dalto. marc cetner 16 Cash Box/June 7. 1980

ON JAZZ COUNTRY KITCHEN — There’s jazz in them thar hills, too, if I may briefly pointyou in the direction of an impressive recent release by the folks at Arhoolie Records. The western swing movement swept the south during the 1930s and '40s, and people like Bob Wills were stars on a level that might make the Rolling Stones jealous. With a steady rolling 4/4 beat, chunka-chunka guitars, and the sweet rising sounds of violins (and mandolins, steel guitars, banjos, accordions, pianos, even horns), western swing combined the rhythmic syncopations of post-Louis Armstrong American music with rural strains of square dances, blues and the varied churches. Guitarist Eldon Shamblin, a white man, and guitarist Charlie Christian, a black man, grew up within 50 miles of each other in I Oklahoma, were unaware of each other, yet developed remarkably similar (and influen- . tial) electric guitar styles. You can hear strains of the olden days in the work of modern masters like Merle Haggard, JF Buddy Emmons and Norman Blake Volume 4 of "Western Swing" (Old Timey- i 119) features seminal bands from the 1930's like the Washboard Wonders; Modern Mountaineers and the Tune Wranglers, while Volume 5 (Old Timey-120) features the Light Crust Doughboys, Milton Brown, Ocie Stockard and the Universal Cowboys, among many others. “Adolph Hofner ‘South Texas Swing' ” (Arhoolie 5020) features the pivotal recordings of an early steel guitar master from the 1930's to the '50s; Dick Oxtot's Golden Age Jazz Band “Down In Honky Tonk Town" (Arhoolie 4010) features modernists dipp- ing into the old timey swing musics, led by ban joist Dick Oxtot and Terry Garthwaite (of the Joy of Cooking band), Pamela Poland, and Rita Black . . . Still interested? Well, CNP- Crescendo Records has got several vital releases by a man who, in a way, is a godfather of western swing — the great gypsy guitarist Django Reinhardt. With only two working fingers on his chording hand, Reinhardt created a virtuoso acoustic guitar style that has never been equalled. The bouncing 4/4 of the two rhythm guitars and string bass, and the ex- quisitely urbane improvisations of violinist Stephane Grapelli had an enormous influence on western swing and bluegrass, to which it bears more than a superficial resemblance. "Django 1935” (GNP 9023), featuring his first recordings, “The Legendary Django Reinhardt” (GNP 9039), “Django/The Quintet of the Hot Club of France" (GNP 9019) and “Django Reinhardt & Stephane Grappelli With The Quintet of the Hot Club Of France" (GNP 9019) are highly recommended . . .Not quite through yet. The people at Flying Fish records put out a lot of progressive country and bluegrass product, and my absolute favorite among the past year's releases is "Slumberin' on the Cumberland" (FF-095) by John Hartford (banjo), Pat Burton (acoustic guitar) and Benny Martin (ukulele and fiddle), with some of the best Buddy Emmons (pedal steel guitar) on record, as well as Sam Bush on mandolin and Larrie London on drums. It’s brisk, droll, atmospheric and very happy. Primo stuff . . . Oh, yes, one more rarity, if I may wax esoteric for a second — and why not? Hawaiian guitar shares a lot of the broad, slurring inflections of country music, and “Sol Hoopii/Master of the Hawaiian Guitar” (Rounder 1024) is a masterful portrait of one of the most sophisticated steel players in music from the '20s and '30s. VINYL PIPELINE — The big news this week is a fantastic new release from Columbia’s Contemporary Masters Series, Volume five of the Lester Young Story, "Evening of a Basie- ite” features rare material and unissued masters from 1940-41 with Count Basie and Billie Holiday & Her Orchestra, prime cuts from one of the most influential tenor saxophonists and improvisers in history. From the fountainhead of modern jazz comes Louis Armstrong Chicago Concert — 1956" with pianist Billy Kyle, bassist Dale Jones, drummer Barrett Deems, trombonist Trummy Young and clarinetist Edmond Hall. The album contains ex- cellent trumpet stylings from the man who practically invented the modern jazz solo. The legendary jazz singer, Betty Carter, is showcased in sessions from 1955-56 with pianist Ray Bryant, drummer Philly Joe Jones and a big band including Hank Jones on piano and Milt Hines on bass. It's called “Social Call" and is a valuable addition to a disgracefully small catalog. Drummer Max Roach is generally considered to be the greatest of all jazz percussionists, but he's also a provocative composer, as the re-release of “The Freedom Now Suite" demonstrates. Falling about halfway between post-bop and free music, this passionate record features vocalist Abbey Lincoln, tenor saxophone legend Coleman Hawkins, the late, great trumpeter Booker Little and Olaiunji, Ray Mantilla and Tomas du Vail on African percussion. “I Remember Bebop" consists of brand new recordings from the reigning masters of bop piano (Al Haig, Duke Jordan, John Lewis, Sadik Hakim, Walter Bishop Jr., Barry Harris, Tommy Flanagan and Jimmy Rowles), each man playing a program dedicated to the compositions of bop masters like Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie, John Lewis, Miles Davis, Thelonious Monk and Bud Powell. The series closes with a killer R&B album from the great singer Chuck Willis. "Chuck Willis — My Story,” which contains some essential big beat music from the early '50s . . . Also worth noting are three vintage releases from Arnold Caplin’s Biograph Records, featuring music from the Dawn catalog of the 1950’s. The African-inflected bebop of pianist Ahmed-Abdul Malik, trumpeter Ray Copeland and baritone saxophonist Cecil Payne. The spirit of Lester Young hovers approvingly over the tenor stylings of Paul Quinichette on “The Kid From Denver" (with Freddie Greene on guitar, Sonny Payne on drums, and Thad Jones and Jo Newman on trumpets) and Zoot Sims on “The Big Stampede" with Gus Johnson on drums . . . From Passport Records comes the newest and most accomplished album from the European progressive jazz-rock band, Brand X, entitled “Do They Hurt?" . . . Finally, from some independents, the excellent singer, Nanette Natal, checks in with “My Song Of Something" on Benyo Music. “Blues From Chicago" on Violet Records features some of the Windy City's best players, like Willie Anderson, Detroit Jr., Jimmy Lee Robinson, Ed- die Taylor and Odie Payne. And from Empire Productions comes “7 x” by altoist/com- poser Tim Berne, one of the most impressive new voices in jazz. Joining him are some ris- ing innovators, drummer Alex Cline, guitarist Nels Cline, baritone saxophonist Vinny Golia. bassist Roberto Miranda and trombonist John Rapson. Whew, that’s all for now. chip stern Cash Box/June 7, 1980 17

COUNTRY THE COUNTRY COLUMN CANADIAN SONGBIRD IN NASHVILLE — Following her concert at the Opry House May 21, Anne Murray participated in a ‘‘Meet the Press" type affair the next day in the local Capitol/EMI/UA building. Approximately 30 members of the local newspaper, trade and television press rapped with Murray for about half an hour. Among the many things dis- covered was Anne's secret ambition — to do films. She said she has looked at a few scripts, but nothing has yet to catch her fancy. Another interesting Murray quote. On the “Tomorrow Show," she revealed her main concern about opening nights and balancing show biz with motherhood to host Tom Snyder: “When I played the Riviera, my biggest opening night worry was . . . we had run out of diapers.” ONE LITTLE, TWO LITTLE, THREE LITTLE FOUR GUYS — When Gary Buck left the Four I Guys to pursue a solo career about a month ago, the group began I holding auditions to find a replacement. Well relax. They will not i have to change their name to the Three Guys. A replacement has been found in 28-year-old LaddieCain, who becamethefourth guy ! May 27. Cain was selected from more than 100 auditioners. : fl When Faron Young appeared at Jerry Lee Lewis' Printers Alley It 9m Club a few weeks ago, he was joined on stage by none other than SPr M the king of the road, Roger Miller and MCA artist Brenda Lee. .JWm m Several MCA execs were in the audience, including Young's ~ producer Ron Chancey. Mike Twitty, Conway's son, opened the Anne Murray show for Faron. Rounder Records artists Riders in the Sky will be the special guests of the Houston Pops Orchestra June 14 at the Kennedy Center in Washington, D.C. Their appearance is part of a special salute to T exas, and since the group is so akin to the native T exas cowboys, it is only fitting that they be included in the festivities. They are scheduled to perform four songs with the orchestra and two on their own. WHAT’S IN A NAME? Kenny Dale and Kenny O’Dell have been confusing people for years due to the similarity in their names. To further complicate the situation. Dale recently recor- ded one of O'Dell’s tunes, “Thank You Everlovin'" as his next Capitol single. The record was produced by Bob Montgomery. Another O'Dell, song, “Why Don't We Go Somewhere And Love,” was recorded by Bobby Vinton not long ago. The tune was previously a single by O’Dell and cut by Dottie West, Roy Clark, Bill Medley and Kenny Rogers. Vinton's project was produced by Larry Butler. WELCOME BACK — Attorney Sy Rosenberg, who for 16 years managed the career of Charlie Rich, has given up his law practice in Memphis to put down roots in Nashville. Rosenberg’s primary reason for returning to the music industry is to guide the career of singer/songwriter Gary Gentry, whom many have seen on the recent Hank Williams televi- sion tribute (Gentry was one of the Drifting Cowboys). Rosenberg's new address is 45 Music Square West. Urban Cowboy performers Bonnie Raitt, The Charlie Daniels Band, Mickey Gilley and Johnny Lee will appear at a private party at Gilley's as part of the film's world premiere benefit in Houston June 5. Guests will pay $ 125 for their seats at the Gay lynn Theatre, entitl- ing them to a round-trip bus ride to the party, which kicks off at midnight. All proceeds go to the Houston Child Guidance Center. Well here it is . . . the list of winners in the annual Music City In- vitational Tennis Tournament that took place a couple of weeks ago. The following is a list of categories and winners: Music Sharps — Allen Dick and James Dick: Music Flats — Phil Ehart and Clay Schell: High Notes— Mick Lloyd and Jerry Klein: Open Sharps — Dave Rowland and Gene Morris: Open Flats — David Skepner and Charlie Kates; Mixed Sharps — Margaret Ann Warner and Duard Sullivan; Mixed Flats — Julie Haley and Harold Bradley. One of the stars of the TV series “The Dukes of Hazzard," John Schneider, will be featured in his own CBS-TV special. “John Johnny Rodriguez Schneider Back Home." The special, which was shot on location in Atlanta, will air sometime in the Fall and will feature guest stars Barbara Mandrell, Ray Charles and Dom DeLuise. Al De Lory has been signed by Schneider to serve as musical director for his live concerts, as well as to work on the special. Johnny Rodriguez better put on his traveling boots — he's got a busy summer ahead of him. Ontario to tape “Nashville Swings,” and then stops in Little Rock, Ark.; Texarkana, Ark.; Independence, Ks.; Lake Charles, La.; Trinity, Tex. and Houston, Tex. jennifer bohler ATKINS HONORED WITH PORTRAIT — To thank him for his support of the cancer fund raising campaign, Chef Atkins was presented with a portrait of himself, which was painted by ARS Nova artist Helen Halter. GOSPEL NEWS The annual National Gospel Radio Seminar is set this year for July 18-20 in Dallas at the Dunfey Hotel. Registration will be on July 17 from 6-10 p.m. with some additional registra- tions on the following two mornings for late arrivals. The Gospel Radio Seminar is really a worthwhile organization, working to promote more music on gospel radio. Unlike the National Religious Broadcasters, which seeks to repre- sent the "preachers and teachers” and is fighting paying songwriters for use of music, the Gospel Radio Seminar seeks to encourage gospel radio stations to minister through music. The agenda for the event begins with a keynote address by Mike Sear^, president and general manager of WAEC in Atlanta. The first session is called Sales Motivation and will be headed by Karl Kettering, sales manager of WBYO radio in Boyertown, Penn. Kettering will lecture on Sales Skills later that day and the first day's sessions will conclude with a rap time where all the participants can air their likes and dislikes. The second day's sessions will be devoted to programming, with teaching sessions on the communication process, on-air promotion, format construction, Christian music programming and productions. The panel of speakers will include John Young, Bob Christie, Larry Alford, Gary McCartie, Craig Hodgson and David Benware. The luncheon speaker will be Rodney Snell of Sonshine Concerts. On Saturday night, the second day of the event, a banquet and new talent show will be presented as well as the Broadcaster of the Year award. On Sunday, the program will begin with a worship service, followed by sessions on Building an Image and one on the State of the Music Industry conducted by record company executives. The seminar comes the weekend before the Christian Booksellers Convention, also held in Dallas, to provide a convenient time and scheduling for those who would like to attend both events. Light Records has signed a new, long-term distribution agreement through Word's Un- ited Kingdom office with Ian and Bill Hamilton, according to Ralph Carmichael, president of the label. The agreement covers sales of Light Records and Lexicon Music product for England. West Germany, Switzerland and the Scandinavian countries. The Public Broadcasting System, which featured a gospel music special on one of its most successful shows ever, plans another special featuring Tennessee Ernie Ford, Aretha Franklin, Jessy Dixon, Barbara Mandreli, Andrae Grouch, Walter Hawkins, B.J. Thomas and Five Blind Boys From Alabama. It will be produced June 21 at Grandfather ML, N.C. Aga- janian, who has just been signed to the label, is involved in dirt bike racing as well as being billed as “the fastest flat-top guitar picker" around. The rumor that Light will release an album titled “How Do You Spell Relief" by Ugartechea-Agajanian-Kartsonakis is totally false. THE TV ALL-STARS — WDAS radio personaiitites competed against the Hollywood All Stars in a benefit basketball game to benefit the United Negro College Fund. Pictured are: Doug Henderson, WDAS air personality; Tim Van Patten, of The White Shadow TV series; David Simmons, Fantasy Records recording artist; Kevin Hooks, The White Shadow; Ernest Hardin Jr., The Jeffersons; and two patients at Childrens Hospital in Philadelphia where the players visited to sign autographs. THE RHYTHM SECTION THE TOTAL EXPERIENCE EXPERIENCE — Producer Lonnie Simmons who heads up Total Experience Productions with Don Alexander is expanding the company’s roster of new talent. Having coined the phrase, and, of course, produced the song “Oops Up Side Your Head” with The Gap Band, Simmons will soon be treating us to a male/female duo called Yarbrough and Peoples. The twosome are both keyboard players who have previously played with the Leon Russell Band and The Gap Band. The pair will have its first product released on Mercury Records in early July. The Gap Band will be back in the studio following completion of their tour. Stevie Wonder, who wanted the group to perform on his upcoming album, couldn’t wait until they completed their tour, and flew them in to go into the studio with him, but also just in time to attend his birthday party. THE ALL-STARS FOR UNCF — The Hollywood All-Stars recently played a basketball game against WDAS air personalities. The All-Stars consist of cast members from the television series, The White Shadow, Laverne & Shirley and The Jeffersons. Over 8,000 people were in attendance at the game, which raised over $18,000 for the United Negro College Fund (UNCF). Kevin Hooks and his wife Regina organized the Hollywood All-Stars, who were sponsored by Coca-Cola. The team is available to play radio personalities on a national basis for the benefit of the United Negro College Fund. For further information contact Joan Logue Henry at (212) 586-0610. THE MANY TALENTS OF MILLIE — Millie Jackson is scheduled to make her Broadway debut in mid-July with a show called “Black Tie and Champagne With Millie Jackson.” Jackson is scheduled for a two-week stint at the Princess Theater in New York, and the show may also feature The Fatback Band, which is presently on an east coast tour. The show is being produced by Spring Records. Be expecting Jackson’s upcoming release on that label called "For Men Only." It will be released in a few weeks. SUPRISES FROM THE SPINNERS — The Spinners’ new album, “Love Trippin,” was released this week with a few suprises on it. “Heavy On The Sunshine” is reportedly the next cut to be released as a single. The surprise is that lead vocals are being sung by John Edwards, Henry Fambrough and Ullanda McCullough. McCullough reportedly has an up- coming deal with Atlantic Records, which may garner her the production talents of Ashford & Simpson for her upcoming solo album, but that portion of the deal is still in the talking stages. On “I Just Want To Be With You,” Fambrough is doing lead vocal alone, and this is also a very pleasant surprise. CHICAGO PLANS SEMINAR/PARADE FOR BLACK MUSIC MONTH — Putting their heads together were Willie J. Barney, Barney's One-Stop in Chicago, Keith Jackson, RCA Records product manager, and Donald Clay, sales manager at Barney's, and they came up with The Illinois Black Music Committee’s music seminar and parade June 17-20. Clay is chairing the organization, which has received such overwhelming acceptance that Clay mentions that it will probably become an annual event for Black Music Month. The organization will hold a kick-off party June 3 at Roberts Motel to publicize the event to the public. “The object of the seminar is to make aware to the public that the music industry has not forgotten the Black contribution,” said Clay. The seminars will be held at Kennedy-King College in Chicago, where record labels will have representatives speak on specific sub- jects, ending with the parade on the 21st, where several local and national recording artists will participate. The seminars will cover subjects concerning jobs, the road a recording ar- tist must travel to stardom and other related topics. Clay also mentioned that “this is not a money making event, everything is free. There is the possibility that next year we may be able to initiate setting up a communications scholarship program for one of the colleges in the area.” ARTIST ACTIVITY — Phillippe Wynn recently signed a contract with Stroh’s Beer to write music for the company’s commercials . . . Betty Griffin, Mopres recording artist will show- case her talents in a special contest at Myron's in Los Angeles June 9. This appearance is a forerunner to her television debut as a featured vocalist with the Annette Thomas Singers on The Debbie Boone Special airing June 16 on NBC. cookie amerson POP CROSSOVER POTENTIAL CLOUDS — CHAKA KHAN — WARNER BROS.
