EAST COASTINGS THE YEAR IN REVIEW: WASHINGTON, D.C. Mechanical Royalty Review Dominates Washington News by Earl B. Abrams WASHINGTON - As 1980 drew to a close, the Copyright Royalty Tribunal's mechanical royalty rate setting proceedings continued to dominate Industry -related news out of the nation's capital. At presstime, the five CRT members were still reviewing responses from concerned par- ties to questions sent out by two Tribunal Commissioners (see separate story). In early December, the CRT wrapped up two royalty Issues. In both cases, it granted Increases in royalty fees - leading obser- vers to believe that the Tribunal will probably increase mechanical royalty rates too. In the first case, the Tribunal raised the annual jukebox fee from Its present $8 per box to $25 beginning Jan. 1, 1982, and to $50 effective Jan. 1, 1984. It also provided that adjustments for inflation shall be made the latter fee based on the Consumer Price Index between 1981 and 1986, effective Jan. 1, 1987. The Tribunal also ordered a 21% In- crease In the annual fee paid by cable television systems, effective Jan. 1, 1981. The current fee averages 1.1% on the gross revenues of cable TV systems. The new fee was set a 1.33% of gross, and is estimated that it will bring in about $24 million in 1981 - about $4 million more than the present rate. In both instances, parties have 30 days from publication of these orders in the Federal Register to appeal to a federal cir- cuit court. The CRT also took one other step in the cable TV field. It announced a formula for the distribution of the $14 million collected In 1978 by the Office of Copyright from cable TV operators. The Tribunal ordered that 4.5% of this sum be distributed to music license societies, with the bulk, 54%, going to ASCAP, 43% to BMI and 3% to SESAC. This decision has been appealed by the parties, principally the National Assn. of Broadcasters, the Sports Group, National Public Radio and the music societies. The year -long hearing before the CRT on mechanical royalties - 46 days, 32 wit- nesses, 7,000 pages of testimony - heard pleas for an upward increase In the fee by writers and publishers, which was opposed by the record Industry. Both the National Music Publishers Assn. and the American Guild of Authors and Composers asked that the new rate be based on a percentage of the suggested retail price of albums (continued on page 36) THE YEAR IN REVIEW: PUBLISHING Publishers Experience Banner Year With Crossover Success by Richard Gold NEW YORK - At United Artists Music, Harold Seider, president of the firm, called 1980 "The most profitable period In the company's history." The year saw UA develop a plan for "full -spectrum marketing of the copyright." This concept is meant to encourage wider use of copyrights held by UA through more ac- tively promoting ancillary outlets for them. These include commercials, theatrical and television properties, films and video in ad- dition to the publisher's traditional emphasis on recording of copyrights. Key 1980 executive appointments at UA Music included Brian C. Yell, general manager of United Artists Music Ltd. in London; Stephen L. Cotler, vice president and manager of Big 3 Music Corp.; Victor L. Guder, vice president, professional divi- sion, standard catalog; and Danny Strick, director of professional activities, West Coast. The Welk Music Group had three big charting hits with Linda Ronstadt's "Hurt So Bad," Eric Clapton's "Tulsa Time" and The Captain & Tennille's "Love On A Shoestr- ing." Welk scored high on the pop and country charts with "Could I Have This Dance," the Anne Murray single from the Urban Cowboy soundtrack. Willie Nelson also had a major country hit with "My Heroes Have Always Been Cowboys," from the Electric Horseman soundtrack. During Nashville's Country Music Week, The Welk Music Group garnered nine awards for the most performed songs in the ASCAP and BMI repertoires. During 1980, Welk Music opened offices in London and Munich. Broadway Hits MCA Music was a big hit on Broadway with the Evita score garnering seven Tony awards. MCA copyrights were heard in ma- jor motion pictures Ilke Urban Cowboy, Divine Madness and Smokey & The Bandit Il. MCA's country music writers Jerry Crutchfield, Jan Crutchfield and Dave Loggins were busy penning cuts for Crystal Gayle, Waylon Jennings, Kenny Rogers and other major country stars. A key MCA acquisition was the Infinity catalog, which includes works by writer/artists Orleans, and New England. MCA writers Robin Lane and Deborah Allen signed recording con- tracts with Warner Brothers Records and Capitol Records respectively. MCA writers Kerry Chater, Glen Ballard, Cana Merino and Mark Mueller landed covers by George Benson, The Carpenters, Barbara Mandrel) and others. Chappell Music Co. ended the year with 11% of the titles on the national pop singles charts representing a mix of product from Chappell, Intersong and Its administered companies, RSO Publishing Group and Virgin Records Publishing. Photo by Deborah Feingold Copyright Royalty Tribunal Approves Increase In Disc Mechanical Rate (continued from page 10) Coulter, sought comments two weeks ago from the parties on two possible plans - one, to adjust the current rate of 2.75 cents per song per album by a percentage of the amount record prices have Increased bet- ween 1975 and 1981, effective Jan. 1, 1982, plus several variations of this formula, and two, to raise the mechanical royalty rate to 3.25 cents per song per album, effective Jan. 1, 1982 with the fee changing to 4.5% of suggested retail price on Jan. 1, 1984. All the parties virtually unanimously opposed these suggestions. Music publishers, through the National Music Publishers Assn. (NMPA), asked the CRT to change the mechanical royalty fee to six percent of suggested retail price; songwriters, through the American Guild of Authors and Composers (AGAC), suggested an eight percent of list price fee. The record industry, through the Recording Industry Assn. of America (RIAA) opposed any change in the present 2.75 cents a song fee but late in the hearings suggested a for- mula for adjustments to take into account inflation. In the draft decision adopted Dec. 18, the CRT called for royalty payment of four cents per song per album, or 75 cents per minute of playing time or fraction thereof, whichever is larger, effective on records made and distributed after July 1, 1981. Other provisions included: On Dec. 1, 1981, CRT shall determine any changes in the royalty rate "directly proportionate to the change, if any, in average suggested list prices of albums subsequent to the first day of November 1980 to the last day of October 1981." Such action shall be taken each Dec. 1 thereafter. Average suggested list price shall be determined "from CRT -conducted surveys and/or studies ..." Affected parties may submit comments, surveys or studies to the Tribunal during the month of October each year. Voluntary agreements by the parties should be submitted to the Tribunal on or before Nov. 1 each year and will be given "due consideration." The adjusted rate, if any, becomes ef- fective Jan. 1 of the subsequent year. Where a manufacturer publishes no suggested retail price, CRT said it would use the average wholesale price of an album - meaning, it explained, the highest price at which the album normally is available for sale by the record manufac- turer to non-affiliated, regular customers. Wholesale price will be based on the average per -unit price on 100 or more albums shipped. Determination of the average wholesale price will be made by CRT. After the CRT Issues its final decision and it is published in the Federal Register, par- ties have 30 days to appeal 16 Cash Box/December 27, 1980 www.americanradiohistory.com

TALENT Stevie Wonder/ Gil Scott -Heron THE FORUM, L.A. - His benefit show at the Roxy for the children of LAPD victim Eula Love and his ongoing support to have Mar- tin Luther King, Jr.'s birthday proclaimed a national holiday sharply underscore Stevie Wonder's active presence in support of humanistic causes the past year. But such activities have anything but dulled his fans' appetite for one of his house party concert bashes. So, during the first of his two -night engagement here at the Forum, Wonder and his Wonderlove clan served up heap- ing, healthy and inspiring portions of good music and spirit. His two-hour set covered each evolutionary stage of the Wonder sound, from the "I Was Made To Love Her" days to the latest Tamla/Motown LP, "Hot- ter Than July," but it was more than a retrospective that could be packaged on a radio show. His personality and panache exhorted the audience to a feverish pitch even before he struck up the first notes to "For Once In My Life." But, as he launched his non-stop music attack, it was apparent his set would be tempered by his dedication of the per- formance to the late John Lennon. As Wonder wheeled through a collection of his songs including "My Cherie Amour," "Signed, Sealed, Delivered," "If You Really Love Me," "Superwoman," "Higher Ground," "Living For The City," "Boogie On Reggae Woman" and "Superstition," which have all achieved gold status, it became ap- parent why the artist's support has been consistent. His mixture of the party at- mosphere with thoughtful love ballads was expertly paced and swept the audience into its undulating patterns. Even through material from "Hotter Than July," such as "Rocket Love" and "Lately," fans received the music with the same anticipation. But the auditorium - fans and the 14 - member Wonderlove aggregation alike - came alive during the show stopper, the top charting "Master Blaster (Jammin')," when several guests, including the Com- modores, Syreeta, the Gap Band, Rick James and Gil Scott -Heron (who opened Wonder's show), joined him on stage for the finale. The audience joined the Wonder man in "jammin' " and didn't quit even as the artists danced from the stage. He was brought back on stage for an en- core of "Happy Birthday," the song from "Hotter Than July" that Wonder dedicated to Martin Luther King, Jr. As the audience finished the night in chorus from the corn- merative song, it was evident that there was no cause to worry that Steveland Morris had forsaken his music craft for the political arena, but had instead successfully joined them. It was apt that Scott -Heron opened his show. His always insightful music was evi- dent during his brief set, but the spirit of peace, which for him has blanketed his tablets, surely prevailed. michael martinez J:mmy Wynette FRONTIER HOTEL, LAS VEGAS - Epic Records recording artist Tammy Wynette is one of country music's leading songstresses, and at a recent engagement at the Frontier Hotel in Las Vegas, she delivered a delightful mixed bag of both old and new country favorites with the vitality that has earned her so many fans through the years. Although the show was quickly paced, Wynette's stage presence was com- manding, relaxed and warmly endearing. Her strongest assets, keenly developed through her own experiences, are the emo- tion and personal empathy with which she conveys the pains and pleasures of relationships in her songs. These feelings were clearly demonstrated on "'Til I Can Make It On My Own," which was a #1 record for her five years ago, her 1969 Grammy Award winner, "Stand By Your Man," and "Starting Over." Accompanied by an orchestra conduc- ted by her husband and a tight -knit band that includes six of her children, Wynette showed another side of her soulful balladeering and rendered two rousing medleys, including one with "Amazing Grace," "Will The Circle Be Unbroken" and "I Saw The Light." After allowing her three girls (who, collectively known as Sunshine, provide Wynette with strong background vocals) to perform their own song, "Blue Heartache," Wynette launched into the second medley. Comprised of her "favorite songs of late" and paying tribute to her fellow artists, she included very engaging covers of Anne Murray's "You Needed Me," Crystal Gayle's "Don't It Make My Brown Eyes Blue" and Dolly Parton's "Here You Come Again." mark albert arshall Tucker Band MUNICIPAL AUDITORIUM, NASHVILLE - In the words of Toy Caldwell, lead guitaris or the Marshall Tucker Band, "Tommy Caldwell wasn't a quitter, so we won't be either." That statement, made in the midst of a two-hour set in Nashville, says it all for the sextet, which hasn't given up on their roots since coming into prominence in the mid -'70s. Although displaying a somewhat harder edge on much of its material, the band still maintains the spacious country underpinn- ings and identifiable tonalities that, com- bined with a driving Southern backbeat, characterized the early MTB sound. The group's music is marked by a spirited blend of Southern traditional, subdued rock and provocative blues, exemplified best by such staples as "Can't You See" and "Run- nin' Like The Wind." Each of Tucker's six members is an in- tegral and inseparable component of the entire unit, yet three make a pronounced contribution to the band's overall identity. Jerry Eubanks, on woodwinds, adds a rich, reedy texture, especially when doubling Toy Caldwell's guitar lines on alto sax. Caldwell himself has an affinity for am- bitious, technical passages, and he plays them with such precision that, at times, the original framework is dwarfed in com- parison. The most outstanding musical quality of MTB, though, is the distinctive, nasal tenor of lead vocalist Doug Gray. He always delivers right on the money with a well -controlled wide vibrato kept on the pleasing side of a warble. The band featured some unpolished new material from its forthcoming LP. Recorded in Nashville, the album should be out in late January, and one tune, "Listen To The Wind Blow," is different enough from the group's usual fare that it should be of particular interest. Marshall Tucker was preceded by another act that will have new product released by February, .38 Special. The "Specials" have an interesting line-up: lead singer Johnny Van Zandt, three guitars and two drummers, plus a pair of female back- up vocalists. Van Zandt is a curious figure - honest and energetic, in love with his rebel homeland. He very much symbolizes the unpoetic and indiscreet working man, with a penchant for good times and good brew. Strutting across stage and twirling the microphone stand, he was somewhere bet- ween loveable and obnoxious, yet he and his bandmates coaxed a willing crowd into exuberant approval. The band's signature piece, "Rockin' Into The Night," received the largest response, but "Hold On Loosely," a cut from the soon - to -be -released album, deserved the most attention. A little like a Boston melody, "Hold On Loosely" is a rollicking, tuneful piece - the most commercially viable the band has to offer. If it received proper treat- ment in the studio, .38 Special could be holding tightly to something that really is special. tom roland Michael Urbaniak THE VILLAGE VANGUARD, NEW YORK - Primarily a fusion artist, Motown Records' Michael Urbaniak took fine advantage of a superb rhythm section to present another side of his musical personality during his recent run at the Village Vanguard. With a no-nonsense back-up provided by Roy Haynes, Buster Williams and Kenny Barron, the violinist was able to play straight ahead and place his imprint on traditional and standard vehicles with a refinement and grace sometimes lost in his electric onslaughts. A wistful "Sometimes I Feel Like A Motherless Child" tapped much of the spiritual and church core of popular music, and a smooth, even -keeled "Maiden Voyage" showcased the violinist's jazz chops. Urbaniak proved himself no stranger to the language of tradition dis- playing a comfort and ambience rarely documented on his records. Drummer Haynes was, as always, a powerhouse. Not surprisingly, the veteran Haynes set the tone and intensity - pushing, prodding and pacing the unit - while bassist Williams and pianist Barron embellished the melodic and rhythmic in- ventions suggested by Urbaniak. Although sometimes slipping into lackluster cliches and routine devices, the band frequently managed to bring something interesting and unique to tried and true vehicles. For Urbaniak, the willingness to work with an unfamiliar and highly accomplished group of sidemen indicates a very laudible desire to present himself as a more com- plete and interesting musician. It is also an indication that his taste and growth are not confined to one particular style. One might expect a musician with a reputation built solely on an electric or fu- sion style to have trouble fitting into a traditional situation. Michael Urbaniak remained always in the front, pursuing his ideas with clarity, warmth, cohesion and conviction. fred goodman Mickey Gilley and Friends COPACABANA, NYC - If John Travolta was present Saturday night at the debut of Sid Bernstein's country music series at the Copa, he wasn't visible. There was only a medium of yee-haw fever at the first of four performances given by Mickey Gilley, Pasadena, Texas' honky tonk proprietor, pianist and balladeer and his former warm- up, vocalist, Johnny Lee, with the "Urban Cowboy Band," The Copa has a seating capacity of 518 if you don't mind sitting on the amps. There are no serious dead spots in the room, but feedback and decibel level proved a hin- drance to the musicians and an annoyance to the customers, who had dropped $15 a head plus a two -drink minimum for the oc- casion. Since Gilley's last metropolitan -area ap- pearance (Belmont Park), The Urban Cow- boy Band has undergone some changes. Bass guitarist and occasional arranger Sid- ney Pomonis, longtime Gilley drummer and back-up vocalist Mike Shillaci, and fleet - f ingered lead guitarist Rocky Stone remain from the Red Rose Express/Urban Cowboy Band. Steel guitarist Eli Stone, keyboardist Ed Hill, and fiddler Johnny Hofmann are new players; Hofmann had been with the band for exactly one week. Following a two -song intro by the band, Johnny Lee romped through a well paced 75 minutes, wooing the audience with energy boosters like Marshall Chapman's "Rode Hard and Put Up Well" and easing them down with contemporary love songs like "Aoni," the latter from his new LP. Gilley launched his segment with rippling piano riffs while singing "Closing Time," an odd choice for an opener. He zipped through his numbers, slowing the pace for his ballads, which emphasize his warmth of tone. One or two flash country rockers were included, but he had to cajole a slightly res- tless audience into singing the familiar chorus on the George Jones chestnut, "Window Up Above." Just when things were becoming predic- table, Johnny Lee returned to help pick up the tempo with the biggies from "Urban Cowboy", with Lee on rhythm guitar and Gilley on piano. Alluding to his Louisiana roots, Gilley (with Lee) concluded the show with a perculating version of the Cajon fid- dler, Doug Kershaw's "Diggey Diggey In." When Gilley gets it on, the audience always gets off. linda solomon ary Myrick and the Figures r THE WHISKY, L.A. - Epic recording group Gary Myrick and the Figures have developed a substantial local following of loyal fans in the 16 months or so they have been gigging here as a band. With the release of their self -titled debut LP a couple months back, that same core of fans has not only grown slightly in number, but ap- parently become more devoted to Myrick and his simple yet energetic brand of pop/rock. Judging from the throng of teenagers tightly wedged together in front of the stage, mouthing the lyrics to each and every number, Myrick's music has an ap- peal to some that goes beyond mere atten- tiveness. Indeed, the Dallas born singer/guitarist can be effective delivering a line in his slightly nasal voice with a par- ticularly venomous edge. But it's the songs' hooks which draw the listener in and never let go. Such songs as "She Talks In Stereo," "Living Disaster," "Model" and "The Party" are perfect cases in point. The Figures' rhythm section has the ability to jump In right on cue around a hook and add the type of instrumental muscle that can push Myrick's sometimes raging vocals to the limit. At those times, the sheer power behind the vocal makes one believe that this is a band to keep one's eye on. michael glynn www.americanradiohistory.com

Veteran Acts, Soundtracks Reign Over The Charts In 1980 Rogers, Ross, Jackson, Pink Floyd, And Queen Take Top Poll Prizes "While perennial chart toppers such as Billy Joel re-emerged with hit product, Urban Cowboy and Xanadu had a profound impact on the charts." In a year of rapidly shifting musical tastes and trends - from the quiet but wide rang- ing impact of country and adult contem- porary to the much ballyhooed yet more sporadic successes of new wave - ul- timately it was the established recording acts that reigned over the Cash Box charts in 1980. Such perennial chart -toppers as Billy Joel, Bob Seger, Michael Jackson, Queen and Pink Floyd all re-emerged this year with best-selling albums and singles. In fact, on the Cash Box Year End Award Polls, Queen won the Pop Singles Award as Top Group with two #1 singles, "Another One Bites The Dust" and "Crazy Little Thing Called Love," while Pink Floyd took top Vocal and AOR Group honors in the Album category with its first LP in almost three years, "The Wall." Billy Joel scored heavily with his "Glass Houses" LP, which yielded two Top 10 singles, "You May Be Right" and the #1 "It's Still Rock And Roll To Me," as did Bob Seger with two singles from the "Against The Wind" LP, the title track and "Fire Lake." Both artists also had two additional top 25 singles. Michael Jackson was, once again, the most popular black contemporary crossover artist of the year, winning the Top Black Contemporary Male Crossover award in both the singles and albums categories for his "Off The Wall" LP (on the Pop LP chart 52 consecutive weeks) and 45s "Rock With You," "She's Out Of My Life" and the title track. He also racked up the Black Contemporary Male Vocalist awards in both singles and albums and finished second and third in the Pop Albums and Singles awards, respectively. Linda Ronstadt, another well established name in pop music, replaced Rickie Lee Jones as Top AOR Female Vocalist in Pop Singles, while the Rossington Collins Band, which includes former members of the veteran southern rock outfit Lynyrd Skynyrd, took Top New Vocal Group kudos in Pop Albums. Heart, yet another veteran hit band, was Top Mixed Group. No one, however, symbolized the in- tegration of country into the pop mainstream in 1980 better than Kenny Rogers. Rogers dethroned Billy Joel as Top Male Vocalist for Pop Albums with an astounding four charting LPs: the recent #1 "Greatest Hits" set (which includes the #1 single, "Lady"), "The Gambler," "Gi- deon" and "Ten Years Of Gold." His achievements are also recognized by his winning five other Cash Box Year End awards, including the Top Male Country Crossover crown. In addition to two #1 singles this year - "Coward Of The County" and "Lady" - Rogers had a top five duet with Kim Carnes, "Don't Fall In Love With A Dreamer," and another top 20 track, "Love The World Away." While tightened radio station playlists and reticence on the part of programmers to play many new artists cleared the way for the success of established acts, a few new acts did score rather dramatically. A pop- ular soft rock sound and help from ubi- quitous Doobie Brother Michael McDonald enabled newcomer Christopher Cross to unseat vet Rod Stewart as Top Male Vocalist for Pop Singles in 1980 on the strength of the #1 "Sailing" and top 5 "Ride Like The Wind." Indirectly, the Doobies influence also helped Robbie Dupree garner the Most Promising Male Vocalist awards in the Pop Singles and Albums categories with the easy pop/rock sound of the top 5 "Steal Away" from his self -titled debut album. Another track from the LP, "Hot Rod Hearts," cracked the top 20. The record buying public's recep- tiveness to adult contemporary or MOR music this year was responsible, to a large degree, for the success of new Australian group Air Supply. An indication of the radical turn in popular tastes from 1979 to 1980 is perhaps best exemplified in Air Supply's capturing of the Top New Group award in Pop Singles, won last year by pop - /rockers The Knack. It was no surprise, however, that the new unit also took Top A/C Group honors in the same category. Although 1980 was the year that disco was to have died, as many even refused to acknowledge the term and switched to thé euphemism "dance music" instead, the charts told a different story. Two largely dance oriented numbers by rock bands, Queen's "Another One Bites The Dust" and Blondie's "Call Me," were the one and two top singles of the year, respectively. Another track in the year's top 5, "Upside Down," helped Diana Ross to make a big comeback this year and allowed the former leader of the Supremes to take the Top Female Vocalist awards in the Pop Singles, Albums and Black Contemporary Albums categories away from Donna Summer. Moreover, it was the masterful dance production team of Bernard Edwards and Nile Rodgers, the leaders of last year's Top Group in Pop Singles, Chic, who aided the veteran Motown star in winning her titles. Yet another dance cut, "Funkytown" by Lipps, Inc., held the top spot on the Cash Box Pop Singles chart for five weeks in May and June, enabling Lipps to emerge as Top Duo and Top New Duo in Pop Singles and Top Duo in Pop Albums, replacing Peaches & Herb and the Blues Brothers. Rookie group S.O.S. Band also turned a dance floor smash into a #1 pop single in 1980 and won the Most Promising Group awards in Pop Singles and Black Contemporary Albums and Singles, as well as Top New Group in both the former and latter categories. Veteran vocal group The Spinners was another act making a reappearance on the B/C and pop charts this year with back to back dance cover hits of "Working My Way Back To You" and "Cupid." The Four Seasons and Sam Cooke remakes earned a revamped Spinners the Top Black Con- temporary Crossover Group title in Pop Singles. Other veteran R&B vocal acts to re- emerge this year with hit crossover product were Ray, Goodman & Brown (formerly known as The Moments) and Smokey Robinson. Other Black Contemporary artists who parlayed dance oriented tunes into awards included Stephanie Mills, who copped the Top Female Vocalist, B/C Singles prize from Donna Summer and prevented Ross from making a clean sweep in all four Female Vocalist categories. Newcomer Irene Cara nabbed the Top New Female Vocalist award for her rendition of the title track from the motion picture soundtrack to Fame as well as the ballad "Out Here On My Own." The award was won last year by Anita Ward for yet another dance tune, "Ring My Bell." Soloist Prince notched up three titles, Top New Male Vocalist, B/C Singles and Albums, in addition to Most Promising Male Vocalist, B/C Albums, for his self -titled LP and the dance single "I Wanna Be Your Lover." If the presence of dance music on the charts in 1980 was as strong as ever, the previously mentioned impact of A/C has never been greater. Kenny Rogers was far ahead of the field in garnering the Top A/C Male Vocalist award in Pop Albums, repeating last year's effort, and Singles, dethroning Barry Manilow; while Olivia Newton -John and Anne Murray won the Top A/C Female Vocalist awards in Pop Singles and Albums, respectively, knock- ing out Barbra Streisand in both categories. Like Rogers, Anne Murray was once again able to capitalize on a very strong country base in 1980 to effectively cross her over into pop. The result was a repeat per- formance as Top Female Country Crossover artist in both Pop Albums and Singles. Another act with strong pop, not to mention rock, ties, The Dirt Band, won the Top Country Crossover Group in Pop Singles with the hits "An American Dream" and "Make A Little Magic." Perhaps the most significant indication of country's infiltration of pop playlists in 1980 can be seen in the fact that several ar- tists more closely associated with "pure country" had crossover hits this year. The Oak Ridge Boys became the Top Country Crossover Group, Pop Albums, while Waylon Jennings slipped in as Top Male Country Crossover artist in the same category. The two acts replaced the Charlie Daniels Band and Kenny Rogers, in their respective categories. However, Charlie Daniels was not without a pop hit in 1980, as the patriotic "In America" single sailed to #10. Don Williams, a top selling country ar- tist internationally, made his first heavy in- roads into the pop singles chart with "I Believe In You," currently at #25. "While 'dance music' prospered in 1980, new wave pop and rock didn't fare as well as industry experts had anticipated." Although new wave rock and pop in general didn't fare as well commercially as industry experts anticipated in 1980, several groups with established cult follow- ings did break through the pop barrier this year with hit singles, as well as a few new acts. Britisher Gary Numan had the highest charting single in the genre with his top 5 "Cars," while Devo received the first gold LP of its career due to the top 15 success of the dance oriented rocker "Whip It." While The Clash became the first band from the early U.K. punk movement to achieve a top 25 single here, as it did with "Stand By Me (Train In Vain)," new group The Pretenders was the biggest hit of the lot, as its gold self - titled LP debut spent nine weeks in the top 20, spurred on by the top 15 single "Brass In Pocket." Other new rockers who received ap- preciable pop airplay during the year after breaking out of dance -oriented rock clubs were The Vapors and The B -52's. L.A.'s The Motels won a hard fought battle with Boston's Robin Lane & The Chartbusters for the Most Promising Mixed Group, Pop Albums, award. Most Promising Female Vocalist in Pop Albums, Carolyn Mas, also took her music in more of a new rock direc- tion in 1980. Most Promising Vocal group The Kings seemed to blend a new wavish approach with pop/rock hooks. The new wave rock cum reggae of The Police caught on around the world and pushed the band to Top International Group, Pop Singles, award. Although the soundtrack to the motion picture Urban Cowboy won out over rather stiff competition as Top Soundtrack, Pop Albums, that hardly tells the whole story of the effect soundtracks had on radio and retail this year. Not since the heyday of Saturday Night Fever and Grease in 1977 and 1978 have soundtracks had such a profound impact on the charts. While Urban Cowboy spawned at least four top 25 singles and led the country/pop craze with Johnny Lee's #1 "Looking For Love," Joe Walsh's "All Night Long," Boz Scaggs' "Look What You've Done To Me" and Mickey Gilley's "Stand By Me," the soundtrack from Roadie delivered Eddie Rabbitt his first top 5 pop hit, "Drivin' My Life Away." Nearly neck and neck with Urban Cowboy was the Xanadu soundtrack, and while both hit the #1 spot on the album chart, Xanadu had the edge in charting singles. Four singles from Olivia Newton - John and Electric Light Orchestra climbed into the top 15 and "Magic" struck #1, while a fifth, the Cliff Richard -Olivia Newton -John duet "Suddenly," is already bulleting in the top 20. Two other soundtracks delivered #1 singles during the year: American Gigolo, which included Blondié s "Call Me" and The Rose, which earned Bette Midler her first chart topping record with the title ballad. Fame, of course, drew two top 40 tracks, including the top 5 title cut, for Irene Cara, while a cover of the Spencer Davis Group's classic "Gimme Some Lovin' " was a top 20 hit for The Blues Brothers from the soundtrack to the duo's self -titled movie. The soundtrack from the movie Honeysuckle Rose, which featured country star Willie Nelson, gave the veteran perfor- mer a top 25 pop single, "On The Road Again." In Jazz, Bob James garnered two awards, in both the Top Soloist and Top Duo (with Earl Klugh) categories, while the Crusaders won as Top Group and George Benson took Top Vocalist honors. The Crusaders and Benson additionally cop- ped Top Jazz Crossover Group and Top Jazz Soloist awards in Pop Albums for the year, while Spyro Gyra was named Top In- strumental Group. Fusionists Hiroshima was the Top New Artist in Jazz. Quincy Jones was named Top Producer. In the miscellaneous categories, Rodney Dangerfield's Casablanca album took the Top Comedy award, while the Chipmunks' Excelsior LP, "Chipmunk Punk," was the Top Novelty record. The Top Compilation LP was the "Winners" collection from l&M Teleproducts, distributed by RCA. Michael Glynn Cash Box/December 27, 1980 P-1 www.americanradiohistory.com

JAZZ ON JAZZ MERRY CHRISTMAS FOR MILES - With a 12 -record, $125 Miles Davis box set already in the stores from Prestige, Columbia Records ships its own six record collection of the trumpeter's work this week. Carrying a list price of $29.98, Columbia hopes that its set will be in the stores long enough to garner some sales from Christmas shoppers. Like the Prestige set, the Columbia box contains nothing that hasn't previously been released. In this instance, the set consists of the five most popular Davis LPs on Columbia: "Sketches of Spain;" "Miles Ahead;" "Porgy and Bess;" "Kind Of Blue" and "Bitches Brew." But don't think that's the end of the Miles box mania, CBS' vice president of jazz and progressive marketing, Vernon Slaughter, reports that the label "plans to do a more definitive box on Miles for next year, perhaps a 10 -record set. If we could do a concise broad, cross section, I think it would have particular merit." Was Columbia using the boxes to take advan- tage of interest in Davis that it cannot fill with new recordings, Slaughter replied: "We're trying to get Miles to finish his new project, and I have no idea when it will be done. But we're trying to be careful. If we wanted to flood the market, we could come out with a Miles Davis album every other week" ... Inner City Records has also been pursuing an active reissue policy with its Jazz Legacy series, and this week has ad- ded six more LPs to that catalog, including albums by Clifford Brown, Don Byes, Roy Eldrige, Bobby Jasper, Lucky Thompson and Buck Clayton. The series will add releases by Gerry Mulligan, Al Cohn, J.J. Johnson, Willie "The Lion" Smith, Jimmy Witherspoon, James Moody and Jonah Jones in January ... Among the small labels, Bent Records has "Odo Op 8 Fx" by guitarist Baird Hersey, and Jazz ala Carte Records has released "Farrell's Inferno" by saxophonist Joe Farrell with John Guerin, Bob Magnussen, and Victor Felman. From overseas comes a new release: "Rockin' in Rhythm" is a collection of Ellingtonia by The Widespread Depression Orchestra with clarinetist Bob Wilber on the Swedish Phonetastic label. BETTY CARTER'S SOCIAL CALL - In a recent interview with Cash Box, the superb vocalist Betty Carter discussed her reasons for starting Bet -Car, the record company she has been marketing out of her home in Brooklyn since the first half of the '70s. "It was a tug of war for me with the big labels, because I'm afraid they really didn't know what to do with me. They got excited when I did the album in '61 with Ray Charles. They figured 'Oh boy! She's gonna go big!' But you're never big when you do it with somebody, it's never like do- ing it yourself. In those days, commercial radio stations were only playing records that were three minutes long, and every tune on the Ray Charles Lp was five, six, eight minutes long. So you knew it was never gonna get any commercial airplay except on late night FM jazz programs. I knew I wasn't ready for what they wanted. I can't be commercial, because con- servative is just not my shtick and I've gotta be me. I'd have to search for something, patch something, really think commercial, which would change my whole lifestyle. I understand the record companies, that it's all about money. And I understand that I'm really not that commercial person who's gonna make them a whole bunch of money. But in the '50s we did have record companies that would record artists because they were potentially good. And some artists grew up on record labels. Art Blakey, Horace Silver, Miles Davis, those kids grew up on Prestige and Blue Note." As an owner of a small independent label, does Carter feel any increased interest from the major labels for acts that can be inexpensively produced and return a small but consistent profit? "They're realizing that only now," opines the singer, "because they're in such dire straits." fred goodman MUCH ADO ABOUT MILES - Jazz trum- pet trend-setter Miles Davis, who currently has a 12 album set out on Prestige Records featuring his previous work, will soon have a six -album package out on Columbia Records, with promises of more on the way. THE PARIS COLLECTION, VOL. 2 - Clifford Brown - Inner City 3011 - Producer: Vogue Productions, Paris - List: 7.98 A mature, front-line trumpet stylist, who, along with drummer Max Roach, made some of the finest hard -bop recordings of the '50s, "Brownie" continues to be enjoyed, studied and adored nearly 25 years after his death. If this 1953 session is not up to par with Brown's collaborations with Roach, it has little effect on his solo prowess. He is relaxed and in control. ( :4 4 MIDNIGHT SUN - John Stubblefield - Sutra SUS 1004 - Producer: Allen Rosenblatt - List: 7.98 Saxophonist Stubblefield is well known to patrons of New York jazz clubs as an inventive and reliable improvisor, but his talents are only sparsely documented on disc. EXECUTIVES ON THE MOVE CBS Promotes Three In Major A&R Executive Restructuring NEW YORK - CBS Records announced last week a major restructuring of its A&R executive staff. Effective immediately, Len- nie Petze has been named vice president and general manager of the newly formed Epic/Portrait label. Petze will report directly to Don Dempsey, senior vice president and general manager of Epic/Portrait/CBS Associated labels. Mickey Eichner has been appointed vice president of national A&R for Columbia Records. Eichner will report directly to Bruce Lundvall, president of the CBS Records Division. Greg Geller has been appointed vice president of national A&R for Epic Records. Geller will report to Dempsey. According to CBS, the creation of Epic/Portrait under Petze's direction marks a new approach by the company to A&R and talent development. Petze will have complete A&R control over the Epic/Portrait label, whose artists will be Petze EI drawn from all areas of music, including rock, pop, R&B and country. Petze will devote the majority of his time to seeking out and developing the creative talents of artists, many of whom he will produce. Combined Logo All product released by Epic/Portrait will be marketed and merchandised by the E/P/A marketing team. The label will be identified by the combined Epic and Por- trait logos. The first artist signed to Epic/Portrait by Petze is Barry Goudreau, guitarist with the Epic recording group Boston. In addition, the Portrait roster currently includes Ringo Starr, Frannie Golde, 20/20 and Gene Man- son. Commenting on Petze's appointment, Lundvall said, "I have full confidence that Lennie will take the Epic/Portrait label into the creative vanguard of the industry." Petze has been vice president of national A&R for Epic Records since 1977. He joined the label in 1970 as local promotion manager for Epic/Associated labels in Boston. He was subsequently promoted to northeast regional promotion marketing manager, and in 1975 moved to New York as director of east coast A&R for Epic. Mickey Eichner, in his new post, will have overall responsibility for the supervision and development of Columbia Records' east and west coast A&R staffs and the label's entire artist roster. He will maintain an ongoing review of the Columbia roster, seek out and sign new artists, and liaison with the label's merchandising, promotion, artist development and publicity depart- ments in scheduling th release of Colum- bia albums and sing) s. Eichner will also work closely with the &R departments of CBS Records Internat onal's subsidiaries, joint ventures and lice sees. Prior to his promotion, Eichner had been vice president of east coast A&R for Colum- chner Geller bia Records since 1974. He joined the label in 1972 as director of independent produc- tions. Gregg Geller, in his new capacity, will be responsible for the overall development and direction of Epic Records' east and west coast A&R staffs and artist roster. In addition to acquiring new talent for the label, Geller will work closely with the Epic promotion, merchandising, artist develop- ment and publicity departments in planning the release of Epic albums and singles. His responsibilities will also include liaison with A&R departments of CBS Records Inter- national's subsidiaries, joint ventures and licensees. Geller returns to Epic after three years with Columbia A&R. Since 1979 he has ser- ved as vice president of contemporary music east coast A&R for Columbia Records. Previously, he was director of east coast A&R for Columbia. Independent Record Labels Announce Four New Distribution Agreements NEW YORK - Four independent record companies - Reflection Records, First American Records, Adelphi Records and Ambition Records - recently announced new distribution arrangements. Jack Levy, president of Reflection, an- nounced an extensive nationwide network of independent distributors for his label. Reflection's distributors and their respec- tive territories are, in the East: Malverne Distributors (New York City); Progress Records (Ohio, Illinois, Michigan, Indiana, Missouri, and Buffalo, N.Y.); and Schwartz Brothers (Washington, D.C. and Philadelphia). Western distributors and their headquarters are: Associated (Phoenix); Big State (Dallas); California Record Distributors (Glendale, Calif.); and Pacific Record Distributors (San Fran- cisco). Reflection's Southern distributors and their headquarters are: Bib (Charlotte. N.C.); Stan's (Shreveport, La.); Tara (Atlanta); and Tone Distributors (Hialeah, Fla.). Jerry Dennon, chairman of the Seattle - based First American label, said that his company's product in the Philadelphia territory will now be handled by Chips Distributing. According to Gene Rosenthal, president of Adelphi, his label had revamped its U.S. and Canadian distribution system, adding Tone (Florida); MS (Illinois); Action (Ohio); Associated (Arizona); Hot Line (Ten- nessee); Stan's (Louisiana); and Phonodisk (Canada) to its network. Steve Leeds and Bruce Rosenstein of Ambition, announced thatJem Records will handle national distribution for the label's first release, "Declaration of Indepen- dents." Rounder Records will distribute the record in the northeastern United States. In Canada, the record will be released by Attic Records via its subsidiary, Basement Records. POINTS WEST Video Suppliers, Duplicators Adopt Anti -Piracy Systems by Michael Glynn LOS ANGELES - Legitimate home video suppliers and duplicators are continuing to move swiftly in the development and im- plementation of videocassette anti -piracy systems, as evidenced by Warner Home Video's (formerly WCI Home Video) recent adoption of the Serial Number Identifica- tion (SNID) encoding system developed by S/T Videocassette Duplicating Corp. While S/T's SNID system is the latest in the line of video anti -piracy systems and devices which have been created and tested during the past five years, technology and manufacturer support in this area has progressed to the extent that, as one trade group official noted, "we could see a workable industry -wide solution within the next year." According to Bill Follette, vice president and general manager of S/T, the SNID system will become available to all of the duplicator's customers "for a small sur- charge," with price "dependent on the volume of the particular order." The firm, which developed the Stop Copy anti - counterfeiting system for'/4-inch U Matic in 1972 and 1973 and later '/2 -inch VHS and Beta formats, has also experimented with anti -piracy devices on package labels, as well as yet another coding system to protect advance review copies of video programs. Summer Signs Worldwide Pact With Geffen Label LOS ANGELES - Nesuhi Ertegun, presi- dent of WEA International and Ed Rosen- blatt, president of Geffen Records, recently announced the signing of Donna Summer to an exclusive, worldwide contract. The announcement comes amidst litiga- tion between Summer and Casablanca, Neil Bogart, Joyce Bogart and Rick's Music. A hearing in the case has been set for Sept. 8 in Los Angeles Superior Court. Summer has charged that the defen- dants have breached their contract and that the contract was made on fraudulent grounds. The defendants, particularly Casablanca, have sought an injunction to block Summer from performing her ser- vices for another label. Commenting on the new Summer con- tract, Ertegun said, "She (Summer) is an in- ternational talent of tremendous magnitude and a woman who has truly achieved worldwide status." Summer began to attract attention while living and singing in Germany. The only drawback to the device, which the firm considers a "minor" one, is that it is not yet compatible with high-speed duplicating processes. "We're a large volume duplicator, not a high-speed duplicator," S/T's Follette pointed out. "Under the present SNID system, each cassette is given a separate 'fingerprint' and no cassettes have the same duplication number." However, Richard Bloeser, director of the Motion Picture Association of America's Film Security office, which engages in film related legal and copyright research as well as coordinating film/video anti -piracy efforts with various law enforce- ment agencies, indicated that "the question of a workable (anti -piracy) prototype device that can be used with high-speed duplicating systems" is still central to reaching an industry -wide solution. "We ourselves have been doing research on film print and video anti -piracy ... and we're hoping that more of the companies will adopt some sort of anti -piracy system," said Bloeser. "We've seen a tremendous in- crease in video piracy. In the past 11 months, the FBI has seized more than 15,- 000 (illicit) video tape copies, with their arrests resulting in 46 convictions and some 70 (defendants) still awaiting trial in the U.S. alone. The manufacturers and sup- pliers ultimately make the decisions on the system, though, and we work with them and urge their cooperation." Most video software suppliers share Bloeser's concern and have already im- plemented or utilized some sort of anti - piracy system. According to Time -Life Video marketing vice president Jon Peisinger, "On our one release to date (The Kink's 'One For The Road'), we utilize the Stop Copy system and we will be im- plementing further anti -piracy devices on our product in the future. We've been quite active in our dealings with the MPAA and the RIAA (Recording Industry Association), as well as the ITA (International Tape Association) and we support the efforts of these organizations in any way we possibly can." Peisinger also noted that the future adoption of the SNID system was "a con - (continued on page 18) Kaye Leaves A&M Posts LOS ANGELES - Lance Freed has been named president of Almo/Irving publishing and Bob Grace president of Rondor Inter- national, both publishing arms for A&M Records following Chuck Kaye's resigna- tion from both posts in August. Kaye has formed a publishing outfit with David Gef- fen, who recently bowed his label. MUSIC NOW FOR THE FUTURE - One of the most recognizable victims of the in- dustry wide recession, that has at last begun to lift, is the new act. That's the band over in the corner with miniscule sales figures, the contract that is running out or hasn't been renewed and its arms thrown up in the air in frustration. And while labels still wait for that ever elusive Boston/Foreigner/Journey clone - the high -voiced, hard rock band that has the hooks and melodies to draw in the pop audience and the volume and drive to hit the AOR fans - many of the most talented acts are being overlooked. A case in point is Group 87. The San Francisco -based band's debut LP was put out by Columbia some four months ago, in one of those major manufacturer's releases that Robinson Crusoe and Friday would have had trouble wading through during their island stay and hasn't been heard from since. The band had two strikes against it from the start: (1) it was an instrumental group, and (2) its future -oriented style was caught in the netherworld between jazz and rock. "We signed our deal with Columbia during the fat Saturday Night Fever era, but the crunch hit when we started to record," said Group 87's Peter Maunu. And alas, 87 was on its way to becoming yet another recession casualty. "It was a tough work item," said Columbia A&R man Terry Powell in reference to the band's failure to connect. "There was a lot happening at the time AOR-wise, and we had our priorities. There are just not a lot of stations that will go on that jazz fusion sound." Picking up on Powell's thought was 87 member Peter Maunu. "We had no hit or AM cut. and you can't really dance to the music, so naturally we didn't do that well." Powell went on to say that the highly sophisticated threesome was not afusion band and asked what kind of vehicle they could pursue to get their music heard. Aye, there's the rub. The tight playlists, narrow formats and cloned rock of this era of $8.98 list in a five dollar world does not breed musical adventure. And yet there is hope. The notoriety of such avant gardists as Robert Fripp and Brian Eno is greater than ever before. And Group 87, who based their name on a post - World War II German literary commune. might finally find an audience in the '80s The band, composed of noted session horn player and synthesist Mark Isham. former Frank Zappa band bassist Patrick O'Hearn and Maunu, who has played guitar for Jean-Luc Ponty and the L.A. Express, might just become progressive music's flagship in- strumental band for the 1980s. Maunu describes the band's sound, one in which Godfathers Fripp and Eno would smile proudly upon, as "a tapestry of sound built off of a visual image." The in- terested can catch the recession -torn band that is making "mood" music for the future and finding itself out of a con- tract at the Savoy Tivoli in San Francisco on Sept. 4. A WONDER -FULL NIGHT - When Stevie Wonder plays a West Hollywood nightclub for more than three hours on a Sunday night and debuts six new songs, you know it's a gala event. And everyone from Berry Gordy, Jr. to Jack Nicholson turned out at the Roxy Aug. 24 for the Wonder man's $100 a ticket benefit for the daughters of Eulla Love. the Compton woman who was allegedly murdered by L.A. police in a gas bill dispute. Wonder's set was intermittently broken up by guest appearances by Betty Wright, who sang "Clean Up Woman," Jermalne Jackson, who offered "Let's Get Serious," Teena Marie, who rendered "Deja Vu," and Buddy Miles, who blasted out "Them Changes.' But the night clearly belonged to Lil' Stevie and Wonderlove. While Mr. Fingertips trot- ted out all of his hits for the occasion, he bowed some great new material from his up- coming "Hotter Than July" LP. Two songs, "Ribbon In The Sky" and "Lately," are string - filled ballads in the classic Wonder tradition. Motown's main maestro also unveiled the first single from the LP that should be out in three weeks. The cut is entitled "Master Blaster Jammin'," a hot reggae/rock cut that tips a hat to Bob Marley. If the new songs are afiy indication, the new disc will not only mark the first time in four years that Stevie hasn't sung about plants, but a return to the commercial pop direction he was travelling on "Songs In The Key Of Life." THE SOUTH'S DOIN' IT AGAIN - Ever get that feeling you're having deja vu. Just as television seems to be reverting back to its early days with such shows as Real People. That's Incredible and Speak Up America, rock 'n' roll is seeing a trend back to the days of the early '70s and Southern Rock. The success of such bands as Molly Hatchet, Henry Paul Band, the Johnny Van Zant Band, the Rossington Collins Band and Blackfoot are evidence that the sound of the loud and proud is flourishing. On a recent swing through L.A., Blackfoot leader Ricky Medlocke took time out from his tour with Point Blank and Foghat (two other bands that seem to tour 366 days of the year) to ex- plain his viewpoints on the phenomenon, "The beer drinkers and hell raisers are back," said Medlocke. "I think I've seen more cowboy hats on this tour than ever before." Medlocke explained that the success of the music is part of the outgrowth of unity in America. "People are showing their pride again like they did when The Alimans and Marshall Tucker happened in the early '70s," offered Medlocke. "There's a little red- neck in everybody. It's just showing itself a little more these days." DOO-WOP ON THE COAST - Those young East Coast harmony sensations, Fourteen Karat Soul, have been making a bit of noise out here on the coast playing to SRO audiences recently at the Magic Theatre in San Francisco, and now, at the Odyssey Theatre in L.A. in what group manager Stan Krause describes as an "a cappella doo wop opera," entitled "Sister Suzie Cinema." The half hour program, a love tone poem to Hollywood stars and starlets, is part of the Mabou Mines' and playwright/director Lee Breuer's experimental theatre production (along with Breuer's A Prelude To A Death In Venice) and is not to be missed. For further info, call 396-6111 or the Odyssey. ANKA'S ARMY - Paul Anka, who is celebrating his 25th year in the music business this summer, is still one of the top crooners in his genre. While most of Las Vegas strip is reporting a dramatic loss in business, Anka's nightly performances at Caesars Palace have been sell outs. On his recent tour of the East Coast and Midwest, the man who began his career at age 15 by penning the hit song "Diana" and has gone on to write such classics as "My Way," played before 76,110 people and brought in an astronomical $858,681.95! And last month, the youthful looking 40 -year -old broke a record at New York's Belmont Park by playing before a crowd of 42,000. JOHN, ALBERT CHAT AT BASH - An Aug. 25 bash at the Palomino in L.A. to commemorate the 10th anniversary of MCA artist Elton John's U.S. premiere drew top label execs, who awarded John a five- foot plaque displaying the artist's 12 gold singles. Shown chatting at the soiree are John (I) and George Albert, Cash Box president and publisher. marc cetner 14 Cash Box/September 6. 1980 www.americanradiohistory.com

OLD HABITS - HANK WILLIAMS JR. - ELEKTRA - 11 REPORTS Westwood One Begins 'Live From Gilley's' Specials NASHVILLE - Westwood One, in associa- tion with Gilley's Communications, Inc. is set to begin producing a series of hour-long radio specials which will emanate from Gilley's Club in Pasadena, Tex. The specials are tentatively set for an air date in October, according to Norm Pattiz, presi- dent of Westwood One. A performance by Loretta Lynn will kick off the first "Live From Gilley's" and each subsequent show will feature a variety of ar- tists who play Gilley's. Jim Duncan will host the weekly show while David and Sanford Brokaw are set to produce. "Gilley's" marks Westwood One's first foray into the country area of radio syndica- tion. Other of the company's syndicated programs include "Doctor Demento," "Off the Record With Mary Turner," "Spaces and Places," "Shootin' the Breeze," "The Great American Radio Show," "Ace and Friends," "Star Trak," "Special Edition with Sid McCoy" and "The Rock Years." West Virginia Troupe Performs Wheeler Play NASHVILLE - Singer/songwriter Billy Edd Wheeler has written a play which will be performed by the Theatre Arts of West Virginia troupe. Titled Mossie and the Strippers, the play will go into production in the Fall, and will be performed at Cliffside Amphitheatre near Beckley, W.Va. The play is set in the coal fields of Ap- palachia and concerns Mossie, the wife of a retired miner, and her fight against coal operators who try to strip mine her land. According tu producer Ewel Cornett, 31 performances have been booked for the play's six -week tour of the East. Kelly Opens Promo Firm NASHVILLE - Barbara Kelly has formed Barbara Kelly Promotions, an independent record promotion company located at 1217 16th Ave. South, Nashville. Kelly began her career in record promo- tion in 1973 working Randy Barlow product as an independent. She then became head of promotion for Gazelle Records in 1975 and in 1978 moved onto Republic Records. where she assumed a similar position. CONWAY AND BIG AL MEET WITH WAXX - Following a concert in Eau Claire, Wisc., MCA artist Conway Twitty and Warner Bros. artist Big Al Downing took a few moments to meet the staff at that city's country radio station, WAXX. Pictured are (l -r): Jim Adams, DJ; Ray Sherwood, MD; Rex Lane, DJ; Twitty; Downing; Bob Holtan, station manager; Jan Hoffman, DJ; and Tim Wilson, PD. THE COUNTRY MIKE TM PROGRAMMING - Three new major market stations have relinquished their autonomous programming and converted to the "TM Country" format in the past 90 days. In an effort to bolster Arb ratings, WSKW/Cleveland, WNOE/New Orleans and KYGO/Denver, have joined hands with TM Programming, a subsidiary of The TM Com- panies of Dallas, Tex. The company now boasts a country roster of more than 60 markets, and, according to vice president and general manager Lee Bayley, every station is enjoy- ing a substantial increase in the ratings. "There's no doubt that our 'TM Country' format is the best in the business," Bayley contends. "It's being recognized as such and widely ac- cepted all over the country as the industry notices its impact on ARB ratings in all markets." PERSONALITY PROFILE - Bob Jones is currently program and music director at KIKX/ Tucson. A native of that area, Jones attended Pima College in Tucson while working as the district manager for Majestic Paint Corp. In 1974 Jones began part-time work in radio at KCUB/ Tucson until he took another part-time position with KHOS/Tucson in February 1975. Then after another stint with KCUB, and again KHOS, Jones was transfered by Majestic Paint to Killeen, Tex. where he again went to work part-time at KIXS, a local top 40 station. Then after another part-time adventure at KDAV/ Lubbock, Jones quit his position with Majestic Paint and ill moved back to Tucson to pursue a radio career on a full-time basis. Bob Jones In 1977 Jones began at KIKX handling the 7:00 p.m. to midnight shift. On Aug. 26 Jones was appointed to program director in addition to his music director duties. Country radio is finally taking to the air ... literally. On Aug. 23 WKMF/ Flint, Mich. hosted the sixth annual Capton Phogg Balloon Classic featuring the world altitude record holder Chauncey Dunn. After winning the morning balloon race, Dunn was on hand as program director Lee Phillips did an afternoon long live broadcast from up in the clouds ... And at WHK/ Cleveland morning man Gary Dee was the guest of the Blue Angels in a media ride to kick-off the Cleveland National Air Show at Burke Lakefront Airport over the Labor Day weekend. Country music artists Zella Lehr, Jimmy Dean, Roy Clark, The Four Guys and Larry Gatlin recently played a benefit concert at John Ascuagas' The Nuggett in Reno. KBET/ Reno aired a live remote broadcast from the Nuggett to raise money for 12 year old Rick McKinley, a leukemia victim from the Reno area. The California State Fair was carried live from Sacramento over the Labor Day weekend by KRAK. The live broadcast featured many events including performance by Lynn Ander- son, Joe Stampley, Mickey Gilley, Eddie Rabbitt, Kenny Rogers, and Dottie West. Program and music director Scott Seiden of WQQT/Savannah, Ga. has announced his resignation from those posts. Seiden cited the lack of "proper tools" to effectively compete in that market. He can be reached at (912) 232-4182. Dan Dixon has been appointed music director at WCXI/ Detroit. Dixon will take over the duties from Bill Ford who had handled both the music director and program director posi- tions. In celebration of its 11th anniversary, KRAM/Las Vegas sponsored acarnival at Jaycees park on Aug. 21. Entertainment was provided by three local bands, and proceeds from the festivities will go to Cerebral Palsy of South Nevada. RCA Records in conjunction with WEEP/Pittsburgh held an Elvis Presley Film Festival on Aug. 23. Many prizes were given away including the newly released eight record set, "Elvis Aron Presley." Floyd. THE RHYTHM SECTION SIDEMAN OUT OF THE BOX - AVI recording artist David Benoit has been enjoyed by many listeners without them ever knowing who he was, or what he did. Benoit, who recently released his second album for AVI titled "Can You Imagine?" has played piano with a variety of artists including Gloria Lynne, Larry Carlton and Lanie Kazan. With Lynne he toured while she played several clubs including the Lighthouse in Hermosa Beach, Calif. With Carlton the young pianist played on the guitarist's gig in Montreux. With Kazan, Benoit served as music director and conducted her band for two years. But his covert penetration into the music market does not stop there. Benoit played keyboards on the soundtrack to the hit film Nashville, and had a hand in the ABC-TV documentary Attica. He also performs on the soundtracks to other movies such as Borderline and the low -budget horror film Blood Beach. Most recently, Benoit played on Jermaine Jackson's LP "Let's Get Serious." But with the release of his latest album, much of his prior achievements may become passe. While the music has a decidedly jazz bend, Benoit spices his sound with a dab of Latin and domestic funk. "I don't see my music in terms of jazz," Benoit told Cash Box. Though in- fluenced by keyboardists like Herbie Hancock, Oscar Peterson and Bill Evans , Benoit said that he composes and thinks of music in terms of a symphony. "But the way I play is very jazz oriented," he said. While his first AVI LP, "Heavier Than Yesterday," did not attract much attention, his current album has been steadily gaining airplay on jazz and progresive black contemporary stations, particularly in the northeast and on the west coast. EXECUTIVE SHUFFLE ON THE LEVEL - The recent executive realignment instituted at Black Music Assn. (BMA) by newly -elected president LeBaron Taylor has resurrected questions regarding the financial solvency of the BMA. However, Jules Malamud, vice president and chief operating officer of the association since its inception two years ago, refuted contentions that the BMA was losing money. Malamud, who vacated the post, but will continue to serve the organization as consultant to president Taylor, said that "like other industry associations and businesses we are suffering the same problems. But we're a strong organization." Part of Taylor's realignment of the BMA structure was admittedly aimed at controlling staff expenses, but no BMA members flatly confirmed that the changes were due to serious economic deficiencies. Malamud also denied that his new role with the organization came about in any other way than amicably. Malamud, who opened up a consultant firm called Jules Malamud Associates, will act as the BMA's liason between other trade groups, trade publications, the association's chief officers and record companies. Malamud also told Cash Box that he will also serve as consultant to other organizations, but that his involvement will not interfere with his BMA role. He plans to join the association's top brass during meetings in Chicago, which will be aimed at plotting BMA activity for the upcoming year. CALLING WRVR - United Artists recording artist Noel Pointer recently dropped in et WRVR/New York to thank the staff for supporting his latest LP, "Calling." Pictured standing are (l -r): Bat Johnson, DJ; Milton Allen, local promotion manager, New York, EMIA/UA; and Bob brio, programming assistant, WRVR. Pictured seated are (l -r): Pointer; and Patricia Prescott, music director. ON JAZZ HAPPY BIRD -DAY! - We celebrated Charlie Parker's 60th Birthday on Aug. 29. He died 25 years ago this past March at the age of 35. Why all this hullaballoo about the anniversary of a jazzman's birth? The answer is threefold. First, we all tend to be taken with round num- bers, so 60 seems as round a set of digits as any. Second, that fact that this year corres- ponds to the quarter -century mark of his death seems more than coincidental. Third, Charlie Christopher Parker did what no one else has ever done for jazz: he changed it forever. You first read about "The Year of the Bird" in these pages last winter when writer David Hammelstein approached some of us with the idea. Chicago clubowner Joe Segal took the initiative and had buttons made up proclaiming it, and George Wein and Ira Gltler produced a concert for the Newport Jazz Festival. With all the attendant publicity, we were off ... or so it seemed. On the surface, Parker's high living, heavy drinking, drug abuse and womaniz- ing hardly makes him a candidate for canonization. Yet, his contribution was so immense that we tend to overlook his faults. Those who rose with him remain living bebop legends: Dizzy Gillespie, Thelonious Monk, Kenny Clarke and the rest. As Bob Krasnow of Warner Brothers put it, Parker simply "opened up a new door." TEE, GIBB & GADD - In between A couple of vignettes about Parker are in recording sessions for the forthcoming LP order. Recently, tenor saxophonist Dexter by Columbia recording artist Barbara Strei- Gordon was playing a set at New York's sand. album producer Barry Gibb of RSO's Bottom Line when he felt his trousers leav- Bee Gees relaxes with keyboardist Richard ing his hips. Slipping backstage for a mo- Tee and drummer Steve Gadd, who often ment, Dex requested support in the form of team up in the Warner Bros. group Stuff. a safety pin. His manager, Maxine Gregg, Pictured are (l -r): Tee, Gibb and Gadd. proffered a "Year of the Bird" button and af- fixed it to the drooping area. Dex looked over his shoulder, smiled and quipped, "Just one more thing I owe to Bird." Krasnow has mentioned to friends that Parker's contribution to the alto sax parallels Jim' Hendrix's pioneering work on the guitar, Mlles Davis' performance on the trumpet, and Lennie Bruce's gift to comedy. "Guts for innovation," Krasnow called it. Ok, America, the acid test. What did you do to celebrate Parker's birthday? The Chicago Jazz Festival presented three groups in an all night bash for Bird, including Dizzy Gillespie, James Moody, Al Haig, Max Roach and Ray Brown; Ira Sullivan, Red Rodney, Chris An- derson, Bill Lee and Wilbur Campbell; and Jay McShann, Bud Johnson, Claude Williams, Gene Ramey and Gus Johnson. National Public Radio broadcast the entire Festival. In other developments, WKCR-FM in New York featured Parker's music for 24 hours. WRVR here also featured Bird on its "Jazz Masters" hour for two consecutive Mondays and aired actualities and Bird tracks on the 29th. Art D'Lugoff had planned a spectacular all-night celebration at the Village Gate, but had to cancel when his stars headed for the Chicago Fest. Jazzmobile parked at its "home" at Grant's Tomb in the Apple, where Barry Harris, Bill Hardman and Junior Cook played some of Bird's work. For those who want the most complete recorded output of Parker, consult the following LPs: Warner Brothers' six -record boxed limited edition set (6BS 3159); "The Complete Studio Sessions" on Savoy (S5J 5500); "The Verve Years" on Polydor (1948-50, VE -2-2501; 1950-51, VE -2-2512; 1952-54, VE -2-2523), in addition to "Bird and Pres" (VE -2-2518 and "Norman Granz Jam Session" (VE -2-2408); "One Night At Birdland" (JG 34808) on Columbia's Contemporary Masters Series; "Summit Meeting at Birdland" (JG 34831) which also includes "Bird With Strings" (JG 34832). Columbia has hinted that it will release more of Parker's work in the near future. Somehow, the celebration has faded. When we arrived at Charlie Parker's big day, we seemed burned out. Did we over BIRDon you America? In any case, Happy Bird -day to all. arnold jay smith TOP 40A LBUMS Weeks On 8/30 Chart 1 GIVE ME THE NIGHT GEORGE BENSON (Owest/Warner Bros. BMI In Copyright Suits Vs. Two Clubs NEW YORK - Broadcast Music, Inc. (BMI), the music licensing organization, has in- stituted copyright infringement actions in United States District Court against two Manhattan night clubs, City Limits and High Rollers. The suits allege that copyrighted songs were performed at the clubs without authorization and in violation of the U.S. Copyright Act. The songs involved in the action against City Limits are: "I Hear You Knocking," by Dave Bartholomew and Pearl King, published by Unart Music Corp.; "The Bot- tle Let Me Down," by Merle Haggard, published by Blue Book Music; "Dead Flowers," by Mick Jagger and Keith Richard, published by Abkco Music, Inc.: "She's No Angel," by Wanda Ballman and J.W. Arnold, published by Acuff -Rose Publications, Inc.; "My Gal Is Red Hot," by Ron Hawkins and Jacqueline Magill, published by Big Seven Music Corp.; "Panama Red," by Peter Rowan, published by Rowan Music; "Oh Pretty Woman," by Roy Orbison and Bill Dees, published by Acuff -Rose Publications, Inc.; and "Return of The Grievous Angel," by Gram Parsons and Beau Brown, published by Wait and See Music. The songs involved in the action against High Rollers are: "Relight My Fire," by Daniel E. Hartman, published by Silver Steed Music Inc.; "Rockin' Robin," by Jim- mie Thomas, published by Recordo Music Publishers; "We Got The Funk," by Brenda L. Reynolds, Nate Edmonds and Albert Williams, published by Sugar Hill Music; "Contact" by Edwin Starr, Robert Dicker- son, and Arthur E. Pullman III, published by ATV Music Corp. and Zonal Music Inc.; and "Rapper's Reprise," by Sylvia Robinson, published by Sugar Hill Music. In the complaints, BMI seeks statutory damages together with attorney's fees and court costs. Black Retailers Bite Into New Queen Single (continued from page 8) Fields and Stein explained that while the company is happy with the radio success of the single and its sales figures, the next step is to boost album sales. Retail Push Fields explained that field merchan- disers for black music have begun to set up displays in black retail outlets, or pop stores that do considerable black music business, to increase Queen's visibility in such markets. He further said that sales personnel were making efforts to place the album in both pop and black music bins for maximum exposure for both kinds of con- sumers. To encourage retailers to continue restocking the product in large quantities, a one-shot 10% discount was offered to retailers shortly after the record was released. In another move to boost album sales, Fields explained that an intensive cam- paign to gain in-store airplay was being launched, with an emphasis on other cuts from the LP getting attention in the black market. Both Stein and Fields admitted that the staff at Elektra/Asylum headquarters in Los Angeles had not envisioned "Another One Bites The Dust" as a single, but the label's brass did react in time to take advantage of a market opening for the first time to Queen. 'Shogun' Soundtrack RSO will have an opportunity to enhance its reputation as the pioneer in soundtrack marketing this Fall when it releases the score to Shogun, the television miniseries based on James Clavell's best selling novel. The music for the 12 -hour NBC spec- tacular was written by Oscar -winning com- poser Maurice Jarre whose credits include Lawrence of Arabia and Doctor Zhivago. Coury, who estimates that somewhere in the neighborhood of 120 to 150 million viewers will tune into Shogun when it airs the week of Sept. 15, believes the project has two important factors going for it. "First of all, the book itself is a classic, one of the all time best selling adventure novels," he says. "Secondly, due to the ac- tors strike, a lot of the competitive networks are not going to have their new Fall shows on the air. So in a sense, NBC will almost have a monopoly on new major network programming." Despite the huge built-in audience of potential record buyers, Coury points out that Shogun presents some unique marketing challenges. "Even though a hun- dred million people or more may see it, they're all going to see it in one week, which is different from a movie that can run for months and months and months while con- tinuing to sell albums. "From our point of view, then, this is an experimental project in the sense that we are using different avenues to exploit it from a merchandising and marketing standpoint. For example, the album will be distributed through book stores. This is a natural since the book sold more than 6 million copies. "We're also looking at a tie-in with the Safeway supermarket chain, which will be selling both the softback and hardcover editions of the book in its 2,400 stores. We probably won't be in all 2,400 stores, but we are going to try to be in as many of them as we can with the album placed as close to the book as possible." Chester Upped At Famous Music LOS ANGELES - Julie Chester has been promoted to the position of vice president for Famous Music, a division of Paramount Pictures Corp. Prior to acquiring his new post, Chester has been west coast professional manager for Famous. WB Realigns Progressive Music Wing; Lourie, Gooding Named To New Posts LOS ANGELES - In a reshuffling of the Warner Bros. progressive music depart- ment, due to the departure of Ron Goldstein who became vice president and general manager of Island Records, Charlie Lourie has been named as the label's director of progressive music, while Bob Gooding assumes the post of manager, east coast marketing and promo- tion of progressive music. In his new position, Lourie will be respon- sible for all aspects of the label's progressive music activities. Gooding will oversee marketing and promotional ac- tivities for the department on the east coast. operating out of Warner Bros.' New York of- fice. Lourie will be based at the label's headquarters in Burbank. Lourie, prior to his recent appointment, was a Warner Bros. product manager for the past three years. Before joining Warner Bros., Lourie was general manager of Douglas Records, as well as director of marketing for Blue Note Records and director of merchandising at Epic Records. RSO HOLDS ATLANTA MEET FOR 'TIMES SQUARE' RSO recently held an Atlanta meeting to discuss sales, promotion, merchandising and advertising strategies for the forthcoming mo- tion picture Times Square and accompanying RSO soundtrack. Representatives of PDI, AFD (the film's U.S. distributor) and EMI (the film's international distributor) were also on hand. Pictured are (l -r): John Frisoli, Polygram Distribution, Inc. (PDI) president; Prior to joining Warner Bros., Gooding served as national promotion director, jazz/progressive music, for Arista Records. He was previously programming executive at radio station WCOL in Columbus, Ohio and has published a midwestern jazz magazine, "Jazzper." He has also worked with PBS and National Public Radio. The appointments were made by Tommy LiPuma, vice president of progressive music for Warner Bros. Records. Z-brah Records Bows Label In Los Angeles LOS ANGELES - Z-brah Records, a newly formed Los Angeles -based record label, has just released the debut album by its first signing, Cricket. To support the com- pany's product, Z-brah president Hal Kern has named Bret Kennedy O'Hara to direct national marketing and artist development for the label. Z-brah headquarters is located at 155 North La Peer Drive, Los Angeles, Calif.
